2 A.1705

[a] By the QUEEN:

A Proclamation, for dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the speedy calling another.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS we have thought fit, by and with the Advice of our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Tuesday, the 1st Day of May next; we do, for that End, publish this our royal Proclamation, and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly; and the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of the said Parliament, are discharged from their meeting on Tuesday, the said 1st Day of May next.

And we being resolved to meet our People, and have their Advice in Parliament, do hereby make known to all our loving Subjects, that we will speedily call a new Parliament.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the 5th Day of April, 1705, in the fourth Year of our Reign.

God save the QUEEN.

By the QUEEN:

A Proclamation, for calling a new Parliament.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS by our royal Proclamation, bearing date the 5th Day of this Month of April, we did dissolve the last Parliament, and declared our Intentions of speedily calling a new one; we do accordingly hereby further declare, that, with the Advice of our Privy Council, we have this Day given Order to our Keeper of our Great Seal of England, to issue out Writs, in due Form, for the calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Teste the 2d Day of May next ensuing the Date hereof, and to be returnable on Thursday, the 14th Day of June next following.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the 23d Day of April 1705, in the fourth Year of our Reign.

God save the QUEEN.

[a]By the QUEEN:

A Proclamation.

A NN ER.

WHEREAS we have caused our Writs to be issued for the calling of a Parliament, to meet, and be holden, at Westminster, on the 14th Day

of June next; we, by the Advice of our Privy Council,

do hereby publish and declare, that the said Parliament shall be prorogued, of the said 1.4th Day of June, to Thursday, the 6th day of September next ensuing; and we have given Order to our Keeper of our Great Seal of "England, to prepare a Writ patent, under our Great Seal, for proroguing the same accordingly. And we do hereby further declare, that convenient Notice shall be given, by Proclamation, of the Time when the said Parliament shall be holden, and fit, for the dispatch of Business; to the end that the Members of both Houses may order their Affairs accordingly.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the one-and-thirtieth Day of May, 1705, in the fourth Year of our Reign.

God save the QUEEN.

By the QUEEN:

A Proclamation.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament, which by our Writs, for that Purpose issued, was called to meet at Westminster, on Thursday, the 14th Day of June last, was, by virtue of our Writ patent, under our Great Seal of England, on that Day prorogued to the 6th Day of September next; we, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby ,pul?lish and declare, that, the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said 6th Day of September, to Thursday, the 25th Day of'Qflo-hernext; and we have given Order to Our Keeper of our Great Seal of England, to prepare a Writ patent, under our Great Seal, for proroguing the same accordingly. And we do hereby further declare our Pleasure, that the said Parliament shall, on the said 2 cth Day of October next,'be held, and fit, for the dispatch 6f divers weighty and important Affairs; and the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly at Westminster, on the said 25th Day of October next.

"Given at our Court at the 13th Day

of Augitjl 170.5, in the fourth Year of our Reign.

ON which Day, being the first Day of the Meeting of this Parliament) pursuant to the Proclamation hereunto annexed, and the Writs, which had before issued for that Purpose, and the several Writs of Prorogation before mentioned; and his Grace the Duke of Devonshie, Lord Steward of Her Majesty's Houshold, having made the second before annexed Commission, or Deputation, under his Hand and Seal, bearing date thfe 15th Day of October instant, to the Right honourable Francis Earl of Bradford, the Earl of Radnor, Lord Dartmouth, and

several Members of the House of Commons therein named, impowering them to administerthe Oaths to such Members as were returned; the Earl of Bradford, as also several Members of the House of Commons, named in the said Commission, together with the Clerk, and Clerk Assistant, and other Clerks, attending in the Place before-mentioned, they administered the Oaths accordingly to such Members as appeared: Which being done, the Members all repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons.

After which, a Message was delivered from the Queen by Mr. Aston, Deputy Gentleman-usher of the Black Rod:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her immediately in the House of Peers.

And accordingly the House went up to attend her Majesty; who was pleased, by the Right honourable the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal of England, to command the Commons to return to their House, and chuse their Speaker, and present him to her Majesty on Saturday Morning next.

And the House being returned; the Lord Marquis of Granby acquainted the House, that their first Business was, to chuse their Speaker.

And thereupon he moved, that John Smith, Esquire, being an honourable Person, that had fat a considerable Time in Parliament, and thereby acquainted with their Orders and Methods, and one, that was known to be zealous for the Succession, as established by Law, and well qualified for so great aTruft, might take the Chair, as Speaker: Which Motion was seconded by Sir John Holland.

Then the Earl of Dyfert recommended to the House William Bromley, Esquire, who had also been long in Parliament, and was very well versed in the Methods and Proceedings of the House; who had, through Times of much Difficulty, served his Country with a constant Application to the Business of it, and steady adherence toil's Interests; had faithfully, and with great Ability, discharged several publick Trusts reposed in him by Act of Parliament, and in the last Parliament had very worthily supplied the Chair of the Committee of Elections: And therefore he moved, that he might take the Chair of the House, as being very well qualified for the fame; wherein he was seconded by Sir Thomas Hanmer.

Whereupon, and after several other Members had spoke, feme for Mr. Smith, and some for Mr. Bromley;

The Clerk (according to the Duty of his Place) put the Question upon Mr. Smith, as it was first moved, and seconded; viz.

That John Smith, Esquire, do take the Chair, as Speaker.

Novembris. 1750.

provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall come in question, touching the Return, Election, or matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in debate; and that all Members, returned upon double Returns, do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That no Peer of this Usual Orders. Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election for any Member, to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, as a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear any Person hath been tampering with any Witnesses, in respect of their Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemea-nor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, That if it shall appear any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members, to serve for the Commons in Parliament, the same is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of England.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall lee, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Mr. Speaker reported, that her Majesty was pleased, The, Queen'* upon Saturday last, to make a most gracious Speech to sported, both Houses of Parliament; and that he had obtained a Copy thereof; which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I HAVE been verydefirous to meet you as early, as I thought you might be called together, without Inconvenience to yourselves.

And it is with much Satisfaction I observe so full an Appearance at the Opening of the Parliament; because it is a Ground for me to conclude, you are all convinced of the Necessity of profejeuting the just War, in which 1 we

4 An n. i ° Novembris.

7

we are engaged, and therefore are truly sensible, that 'tis of the greatest Importance to us to be timely in our Preparations.

Nothing can be more evident, than that, if the French King continues Master of the Spanijk Monarchy, the Balance of Power in Europe is utterly destroyed; and he will be able in a short Time to engross the Trade, and the Wealth, of the World.

No good Englishmen could at any Time be content to lit Hill, and acquiesce in such a Prospect; and at this Time we have great Grounds to hope, that by the Blessing of God upon our Arms, and those of our Allies, a good Foundation is laid for restoring the Monarchy of Spain to the House of j the Confe-

quences of which will not only be safe and advantageous, but glorious, for England.

I may add, we have learnt by our own Experience, that no Peace with France will last longer than the first Opportunity of their dividing the Allies, and of attacking some of them with Advantage.

All our Allies must needs be so sensible, this is the true State of the Cafe, that I make no doubt, but Measures will soon be so concerted, as that, if we be not wanting to ourselves, we shall fee the next Campaign begin offen-fively on all Sides against our Enemies, in a most vigorous Manner.

I must therefore desire you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, to grant me the Supplies, which will be requisite for carrying on the next Year's service, both by Sea and Land; and at the same Time to consider, that the giving all possible Dispatch will make the Supply itself much more effectual.

The Firmness, and Conduit, which the Duke of Savoy has shewn amidst extreme Difficulties, is beyond Example.

1 have not been wanting to do all that was possible for me, in order to his being supported.

I ought to take notice to you, that the King of s

Troops have been very useful to this End. Your Approbation of that Treaty last Sessions, and the Encouragement you gave upon it, leave me no doubt of being able to renew it for another Year.

I take this Occasion to assure you, that not only whatever shall be granted by Parliament, for bearing the Charge of the War, shall be laid out forthat Purpose, with the greatest Faithfulness and Management, but that I will continue to add, out of my own Revenue, all I can reasonably spare beyond the necessary Expences for the Honour of the Government.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

By an Alt of Parliament, passed the last Winter, I was enabled to appoint Commissioners for this Kingdom, to treat with Commissioners, to be impowered by Authority of Parliament in Scotland, concerning a nearer and more compleat Union between the two Kingdoms, as soon as an Alt should be made there for that Purpose: I think it proper for me to acquaint you, that such an Alt is lately passed there; and I intend, in a short Time, to cause Commissions to be made out, in order to put the Treaty on foot; which I heartily desire may prove fuc-cefsful} because I am persuaded, that an Union of the two Kingdoms will not only prevent many Inconveniencies, which may otherwise happen, but must conduce to the Peace and Happiness of both Nations; and therefore I hope, 1 shall have your Assistance in bringing this great Work to a good Condufion.

There is another Union I think myself obliged to recommend to you in the most earned and affectionate Manner, I mean an Union of Minds and Affeltions amongst ourselves: It is that, which would, above all Things, disappoint and defeat the Hopes and Designs of our Enemies.

I cannot but with Grief observe, there are some amongst us, who endeavour to foment Animofiiies; but I persuade myself, they will be found to be very few, when you appear to assist me in discountenancing and defeating such Practices.

Vol. 15.

I mention this with a little more Warmth, because there have not been wanting some, so very malicious, as even in Print to fugged, the Church of , as

by Law established, to be in danger at this Time.

I am willing to hope, not one of my Subjects can really entertain a Doubt of my Affeltion to the Church, or so much as suspect, that it will not be my chief Care to support it, and leave it secure after me; and therefore we may be certain, that they, who go about to insinuate Things of this Nature, must be mine and the Kingdom's Enemies, and can only mean to cover Designs, \^hich they dare not publickly own, by endeavouring to distralt us with unreasonable and groundless Distrusts and Jealousies.

I must be so plain, as to tell you, the bed Proofs we can all give, at present, of our Zeal for the Preservation of the Church, will be, to join heartily in prosecuting the War against an Enemy, who is certainly engaged to extirpate our Religion, as well as to reduce this Kingdom to Slavery.

I am fully resolved, by God's Assistance, to do my Part.

I will always affectionately support and countenance the Church of England, as by Law established.

I will inviolably maintain the Toleration.

I will do all I can to prevail with my Subjects to lay aside their Divisions; and will study to make them all safe, and easy.

I will endeavour to promote Religion and Virtue amongst them, and to encourage Trade, and every thing else, that may make them a flourishing and happy People.

And they, who shall concur zealously with me in carrying on these good Designs, shall be sure to find my Kindness and Favour.

Resolved, Nemine conlradicente, That an humble Ad- Address dress be presented to her Majesty, returning the Thanks the Queen'* of this House for her most gracious Speech to both Houses Speech of Parliament: To congratulate the glorious Success of her Majesty's Arms, and those of her Allies; and to allure her Majesty that this House will effectually enable her to prosecute the War with Vigour, to support her Allies, and to restore the Balance of Power in Europe: And likewise to express the deep Sense we have of the Blessings we enjoy under her Majesty's most happy Government; and gratefully to acknowledge her Majesty's most affectionate Care to, support the Church of England, as by Law established, her Resolution to maintain the Toleration, and to encourage the Trade, Union, and Welfare, of her People; and further to assure her Majesty, that we will assist her in the defeating all such Practices as tend to foment Animosities, and distralt her Majesty's Subjects with unreasonable and groundless Distrusts and Jealousies.

Ordered \That a Committee be appointed, to draw up an Address, upon the said Resolution, and upon the Debate of the House:

And it is referred to the Lord Marquis of Hartington, the Earl of Dy/ert, Mr. Walpole, Mr. Solicitor-general,

Churchill, Esquire, John Gape, Esquire, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates; and the Petitioner was duly chosen by a Majority of legal Voters, and ought to have been returned a Burgess, to serve for the said Borough; but William Stone, the Mayor, hath returned Mr. Gape, in wrong to the Petitioner; and used several illegal Practices for Mr. Gape, polling several unqualified Persons for him, and refusing several to poll for the Petitioner, that were qualified; and Mr. Gape, and Mr. Ayleward (the Town-Clerk) and other Agents

of Mr. Gape's,did, by Bribes, Threats, and other un-

lawful Means, procure many Votes, to the Prejudice of the Petitioner and the Rights of the said Borough; And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of Edmund Webb and John Webb, Esquires, Ludgerihall was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that Election, at the Election of Members, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Ludgershall, in Wiltshire, the Petitioners, and Walter Kent and Thomas of

That Noyes privately prepared a List of such Persons, as he thought fit to allow to vote, and, without following the usual Order at former Elections, polled only the Persons named in his Lift, among whom were several unqualified Persons; and, as soon as he had gone through his Lift, he proceeded to declare the Election, without polling a great Number of qualified Persons who offered to poll for the Petitioners: and the said Bailiff hath returned the said Mr. Kent, and Mr. Powell, although the Petitioners were fairly elected by a Majority of good Votes: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

Northmore-, and they told him that the Election would be disputed in Parliament, but if he would put his Mark (being an illiterate Man) to an instrument then produced (which was not read to him) it would save him the Trouble of being sent for up to London; upon which the Petitioner did put his Mark thereto; and being soon after informed that it was a Return of Mr. Northmore and Sir Simon Leach, he immediately, with Mr. Fortescue and Christopher Yendall, went to the High Sheriff, and told him, that he had been unknowingly imposed upon to sign the last Return, and advised the Sheriff', to return none but the first; yet the Petitioner is informed he hath returned both: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

The Lord Marquis of Hartington reported from the Address on Committee, appointed to draw up an Address, to be the Queen'* presented to her Majesty, upon the Resolution of Thurs- sPeech-day last, and upon the Debate of the House, that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was twice read, and is, as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled, are met together, with minds fully disposed to assist your Majesty in compassing the great and glorious Designs, mentioned in your most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament; for which we beg Leave to return our most hearty Thanks, and at the same time to congratulate the glorious Success of your Majesty's Arms, and those of your Allies.

We are fully convinced, that the Balance of Power in Europe can never be restored, till the Monarchy of is in the possession of the House of Austria, and that no Peace with France can be secure and lading, whilst the French King shall be in a Condition to break it; and therefore your faithful Commons are fully retolved, effectually to enable your Majesty to carry on the War with Vigour, to support your Allies, and make good such Treaties, as your Majesty shall judge necessary, to reduce the exorbitant Power of France.

D It

The Queen's Speech to be confide red.

The Queen appoints to be attended

Hertford

Borough

Election.

14 30 — 6° Novembris. 1705.

It is no small Encouragement to your Commons chearfully to grant the Supplies necessary for those great Ends, to find a frugal Management, and a just and prudent Application, of the public Money.

We cannot omit, upon this Occasion, most thankfully to acknowledge your Majesty's Goodness, in continuing to contribute out of your own Revenue to the Expences of the War.

We want Words to express the deep Sense we have of the many Blessings we enjoy under your Majesty's most happy Government: We are thoroughly fenlible of your affectionate Care to support and countenance the Church of England, as by Law established, your Resolution to maintain the Toleration, and to encourage the Trade, Union, and Welfare, of your People.

This being the happy Condition of all your Subjects, it is the greatest Concern imaginable to us, to find, your Majesty has so just Reason to resent the Ingratitude of some, who endeavour to foment Animosities and Divisions amongst us; and we cannot without Indignation reflect, that there should be any so malicious, as to insinuate, that the Church of England, as by Law established, is, or ever can be, in danger, for want of your Majesty's Care and Zeal to support and maintain it. Your Majesty's exemplary Piety, your steady Adherence to the Church of England, leave no room to doubt, but that thele Suggestions proceed from your Majesty's and the Kingdom's Enemies, who, to cover their own Dif-affection to the present Establishment and Administration, endeavour to distract your Subjects with unreasonable and groundless Distrusts and Jealousies.

Your Majesty may be assured, that your Commons will zealously concur in every thing, that may tend to discourage and punish such Incendiaries, and to disappoint your Enemies both at home and abroad.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That this House doth agree to the said Address.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know her Majesty's Pleasure, when Ihe will be attended by this House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, take into Consideration her Majesty's most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament.

And then the House adjourned till Tuesday Morning next, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of Henry Ireton, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that at the last Election of Members, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, the Candidates were Allen Bathurst, Charles Cox, Tho. Onslow, Esquires, and the Petitioner: That several corrupt Practices were used for obtaining Votes for Mr. Bathurst and Mr. Cox, the Steward and Bailiff of the said Borough behaving themselves very partially at the Time of taking the Poll, and yet the Petitioner had a great Majority of legal Votes above any of the other Candidates; notwithstanding which, the said Steward, and Bailiff, has, by one Indenture, returned Mr. Bathurst and the Petitioner; and, by another Indenture, Mr. Bathurst and Mr. Cox, in prejudice to the Petitioner, although the Steward and Bailiff were well informed, that Mr. Bathurst was a Minor: And praying the Justice of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they d6 examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Mr. Speaker reported, that he, with the House, did Yesterday present their, humble Address to her Majesty; and that her Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I take very kindly the Confidence you express in my Care of the Publick, and your Concern for the Occasion 1 have had to complain.

I return you my hearty Thanks for the Assurances of your Support and Assistance, which, by God's Blessing, I shall always endeavour to improve for the Advantage and Happiness of my People.

Ordered, That the House be called over upon this Day Fortnight.

Ordered, That all such Members, as shall not then attend, be sent for in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take into Consideration her Majesty's most gracious Speech.

And the same was again read by Mr. Speaker.

And a Motion being made, for a Supply to be granted to her Majesty:

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of that Motion.

A Petition of John Wynn and William Nicholls. Esquires, Montgomery Bailiffs of the Town and Borough of Poole, John Price and Griffith Buckley, Esquires, Bailiffs of the Town and e ion' Borough of Llanvilling, and Jenkin Lloyd, Gentleman,

Mayor of the Borough of Lanidloes, in the County of Montgomery, as well on the behalf of themselves, as of the rest of the Burgelfesof the said several Boroughs, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, who have an undoubted Right to elect a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Montgomery, intended to have chosen John Vaughan, Esquire, to have been their Representative in this present Parliament; but they were deprived of their Votes, for want of due Notice of the last Election; That the Bailiffs of Montgomery, particularly George Beddoes, Tanner (one of them) combining with Shoemakers, and other mean Tradesmen and Rabble of the Town, to bring in Mr.

Charles Majon (whom the Petitioners would not have entrusted) did, by Surprize, unduly and illegally elect, and return, Mr. Mason, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Ordered, That an Account of the publick Money, for Publick the Year 1705, and what hath arisen in that Year, and Money, been applied to the former Years, be laid before this House by Mr. Lowndes, Secretary of the Treasury.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of John Hungerford, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that on the 14th of May last the Election of Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for Scarborough, came on, the Candidates being Robert Squirt, William Thompson, and the Petitioner: That the Bailiffs of Scarborough returned the said Mr. Squire and Mr. Thompson, as duly elected, although the Petitioner ought to have been returned with Mr. Squire, the Petitioner having more qualified Votes, than Mr. Thompson: And praying Relief in the Premises.

A Petition of Ann Corbett, the Widow and Relict of Erasmus Corbett, late of Henllys, in the County of Pembroke, Esquire, deceased, Charles Owen, of Nash, in the said County, Esquire, and Dorothy his Wife, and Joan Corbett, Spinster, being of the Age of Nineteen Years (which said Dorothy and Joan are the Daughters and Coheirs of the said Erasmus Corbett, who was the eldest Son and Heir of Thomas , late of Nash

aforesaid, Esquire, and Dorothy his Wife, both now deceased) was presented to the House and read; setting forth, that the said Dorothy, the Wife of the said Thomas Corbett, being seised in Fee-simple of the Capital Messuage, called Nash, and other Lands in the said County, of about £. 90. per , did, in 1655, convey those Premises to Trustees, to the Use of the said Tho. and Dorothy, for their Lives, and then to the Use of their first and every other Son in general Tail, then to their Issue Female, then to the Heirs of the Body of the Heirs of their Body, and the Reversion in Fee remained, undisposed of, in the said Dorothy, by the said Settlement: That the said Thomas, Dorothy, and Erasmus, being dead, the said Coheirs became entitled to the Premises: That, upon the Treaty of Marriage between the Petitioners Charles and Dorothy, it was agreed by Thomas and Ann Corbett, the Grandfather and Grandmother of Dorothy and Joan (being both Infants) in regard no Partition could be made of the Premises, without great Expence, that the Premises should be settled upon the Petitioners Charles and his Wife, and their Issue j in Consideration whereof, the said Joan was to have £. 1,000. paid her by Charles, for her Share, which is more than *tis worth: That Dorothy is now of Age, but Joan wants about two Years of hers; fb that (he cannot yet make good the said Agreement: And praying, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for confirming the said Agreement, it being for the Advantage of the said Infant Joan.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Vaughan, Mr. Manley, and Mr. Latigharn, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A PETITION of Charles Esquire, was pre-

fented to the House, and read; setting forth, that at the lall Election of Members, to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Bishops Castle, in the County of Salop, Henry Brett, Charles Mason, Richard Harnage, Esquires, and the Petitioner, flood Candidates; and the Petitioner and Mr. Harnage were duly elected by a great Majority of legal Voters of the said Borough, and ought to have been returned; but Morris Pugh, Bailiff of the said Borough, refused to take the Votes of many, who would have voted for the Petitioner and Mr. Harnage, and admitted others, in the same Capacity, to vote for the other Candidates; whereby, and by Bribery, and other undue Practices of the said Mr. Mason, he and Mr. Brett were returned, in wrong to the Petitioner: And praying, that the House will appoint a Time for the Petitioner to make Proof of the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Complaint being made to the House, that Sir Hopton Williams (a Member of this House) hath been served with a Process out of the Ecclesiastical Court, upon a Libel exhibited against him there by Dame Frances Williams (in which Prosecution one Edward Cooke is Proctor, William Taverner, Solicitor, and Thomas Be.fier, Apparitor) in Breach of the Privilege of this House;

Ordered, That it be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections, to examine the Matter of the said Complaint; and that they do report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Complaint being made to the House, that one William Lowin hath assaulted Sir John Hawles (a Member of this House) and his Servant, in Breach of the Privilege of this House;

Resolved, That the said William Lowin, for assaulting the said Sir John Hawles, and his Servant, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said William Lowin be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

A Petition of several Freemen of the City of Coventry, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that before and at the last Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the said City, many illegal Practices were urcd on the behalf of Sir Christopher[laics and Mr. Gery; and that by

Riots and Tumults, and Partiality of the Sheriffs of the said City, many were deterred from giving their Votes, according to their Intentions; by which undue Practices, the Petitioners conceive, they are deprived of their legal Representatives: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take her Majesty's most gracious Speech into further Consideration.

And the same was again read by Mr. Speaker.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, to return the Thanks of this House, for her tender Regard to the Good and Welfare of both her Kingdoms of England and Scotland-, for her great Care, and Endeavou -, to settle the Succession of the Kingdom of Scotland in the House of; for preserving the

Peace, and promoting the Union, of the two Kingdoms: And to allure her Majesty, that this House will, to the utmost of their Power, assist her Majesty to bring this great Work to a happy Conclusion; and likewise, that the will be graciously pleased to direct, that the whole Proceedings of the last Session of Parliament in Scotland, relating to the Union of the two Kingdoms, and the Settlement of the Succession of Scotland in the House of Hanover, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House, as are of her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

And then the House adjourned till To morrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Memorandum :In the Computation for Recruit Horses, there is reckoned only for such, as are certified upon Oath to have been Lit within the aforesaid Time; since which, there are more Horses dead, and continue to die daily; so that the Sum is daily increasing, of which a further Account is expected over.

Answer to Mr. Secretary Harley acquainted the House, that their Addrefe. Address, with relation to the Proceedings of the last Union with Session of Parliament in touching the Union

Scotland. of the Kingdoms of England and Scotland, and the Succession of Scotland, having been presented to her Majesty, her Majesty was pleased to give an Answer in these Words:

I take very kindly the Sense you express of my Endeavours to promote the Protestant Succession, and the Treaty of Union in Scotland.

I have given Directions for complying with your Address; and you shall have the State of that Matter, as soon as it can conveniently be sent you.

A Petition of Daniel Sadler, Agent for Tran (port Ser- Transeort vice in Holland, in the late War, was presented to the Service. House, and read; setting forth, that in 1698 and 1699 the Petitioner did draw from Rotterdam three Bills of Exchange, for £. 5,000 upon the then Commissioners of Transports for his late Majesty, for which the Petitioner gave the King Credit, which Account was adjusted by the Commissioners of Accounts for the Army and Transport Service; and though the Transport Commissioners accepted the said Bills, there yet remains unpaid £. 2,000 Principal, besides Interest, and Charges, which, they alleged, they could not pay, for want of Money; upon which, the Possessors of the Bills have since imprisoned the Petitioner: And praying, that the House will make the Possessbrs of the said Bills Satisfaction, as the House shall think meet, and thereby prevent the Ruin of the Petitioner, and his Family.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table.

Queen's Letter to the Parliament, 18th June, 1705. ANNE R.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

IT has been our great Care and Concern, ever since our Accession to the Crown, to preserve the Peace, and promote the true Interest and Advantage, of that our ancient Kingdom, and, above all, to have your present Establilliment so secured, that both you, and after Ages, may reap the Benefit thereof.

You are now again met in Parliament, and, no Doubt, with a full View of all your present Circumstances; which we heartily wifti may be seconded with such Endeavours on your Part, as what may bell accomplish what we so really design.

In your last Meeting we recommended to you, with the greatest Earnestness, the settling of the Succession of that our ancient Kingdom in the Protestant Line; and several Things having since happened, which shews the great Inconveniency of these Matters continuing in Suf-per.ce, we cannot but at present moll seriously renew the Recommendation of this Settlement, as being convinced of the growing Necessity thereof, both for the Preservation of the Protestant Religion, and the Peace and Safety of all our Dominions, and for defeating the Designs and Attempts of all our Enemies, and to prevent any Objection to the said Settlement, that can be suggested from the Views, or Fears, of future Inconveniencies, that may happen to that our Kingdom from thence. We shall be ready to give the Royal Assent to such Provisions, and Restrictions, as shall be found necessary, and reasonable, in such a Cafe; and therefore we mull still leave it upon you, as most necessary for all the Ends abovementioned, that you go to the Settlement of the Succession, before all other Business.

We are fully satisfied (and doubt not, but you are) that great Benefit would arise to all our Subjects, by an Union of Scotland and Enand that nothing will contribute more to the composing of Differences, and extinguishing the Heats, that are unhappily raised and fomented by the Enemies of both Nations, than the promoting of every thing, that tends to the procuring the fame: Therefore we earnestly recommend to you, to pass an Act, for a Commission to set a Treaty on foot between the Kingdoms (as our Parliament of England has done) Vol. 15.

for effectuating what is so desirable, and for such other Matters and Things, as may be judged proper for our Honour, and the Good and Advantage of both Kingdoms for ever; in which we shall most heartily give our best Assistance.

The Supplies, granted by the-Parliament, for maintaining the Forces, with the Forts, Garrisons, and Frigates, are now at an end; and these being still necessary to be maintained, as likewise, that the Magazines of Arms and Ammunition be duly fumished, for the Peace and Security of the Kingdom, specially nowin time of War, we doubt not, but you will provide the Supplies needful, in such Manner, as may be most ealy, and effectual.

We have named the Duke of Argyle to be our Commissioner, to represent our Person in this Session of Parliament, as one, of whose Capacity, and Zeal for our Service, and the Kingdom's Good and Advantage, we are fufEciently allured, and no less hopeful, that he will be to you acceptable.

We have fully impowered him to declare our firm Resolutions, to maintain the Government both in Church and State, as by Law established; and likewise to consent to such further Laws, as shall be thought needful for that End.

We have allb impowered him to give the Royal Afi-sent to such good Laws, as shall be concluded, for the advancement of Piety, and discouragement of Immorality, for the better encouraging and improving of Trade and Manufacture, the further securing of private Rights and Conveyances, and for promoting the more easy and speedy Administration of Justice, and, generally, for what may be found, for the Good and Advantage of the Kingdom; in all which, and whatever else may contribute to the Happiness and Satisfaction of our People, you shall have our ready and chearful Concurrence. And so we bid *you heartily farewell. Given at our Court at Windsor Castle, the 18 th of June, 1705, and of our Reign the 4th Year.

By her Majesty's Command,

Sic subscribitur.

DAVID NAIRN.

II. Resolve of Parliament, 17th July, 1705.

Resolved, That this Parliament will not proceed to the Nomination of a Successor, till we have had a previous Treaty with England, in relation to a Commerce, and other Concerns, with that Nation: And further it is resolved, that this Parliament will proceed to make such Limitations and Conditions of Government, for the Reftification of our Constitution, as may secure the Liberty, Religion, and Independency, of this Kingdom, before they proceed to the said Nomination.

Act for a Treaty with England.

The Estates of Parliament considering, with what Earnestness the Queen's Majesty has recommended to them the settling of the Succession to the Imperial Crown of this her ancient Kingdom in the Protestant Line, failizing Airs of her own Body, and also to enter into a Treaty with her Kingdom of England, as the-most effectual Way for extinguishing the Heats and Differences, that are unhappily raised betwixt the two Nations, and 19 prosecution of her Majesty's royal and just Purpose of having a Treaty set on foot betwixt her two Independent Kingdoms of Scotland and England, without which, these Things, of great Consequence betwixt them, cannot be accommodated; therefore her Majesty, with Advice and Consent of the Estates in Parliament, do enact, statute, and ordain, that such Persons, and Quorum thereof, as shall be nominated and appointed by her Majesty, under the Great Seal of this Kingdom, shall have full Power and Commission, like as her Majesty, with Advice and Consent aforesaid, doth hereby give and grant full Power, Commission, and Authority, to the said s Persons, and their Quorum, to convene and meet at such Time and Times, and in such Place and Places, as her Majesty shall please to appoint, to treat and consult with such Commissioners, as shall be authorized by Authority

And the said s Commissioners for both the said s Kingdoms shall, according to the Tenor of their respective Commissions, set down and reduce their Proceedings in the said Matter into three several Writings and Instruments, each of them to be subscribed, and sealed, by the said s Commissioners, and their Quorum; to the end that one of these Writings, or Instruments, may in all Humility be presented to the Queen's Majesty, and another of the said s Writings, or Instruments, to be offered to the Parliament of and the

Address of the Parliament of Scotland to the Queen, 4th September, 1705.

May it please your Majesty:

We, your Majesty's most loyal and dutiful Subjects, the Noblemen, Barons, and Burgesses, assembled in Parliament, do in all Humility represent to your Majesty, that, in Compliance with the Desire of your Majesty's royal Letter, whereby you earnestly recommend to us to pass an Act, for a Commission to set a Treaty on foot betwixt the Kingdoms of Scotland and England, and for a nearer and more compleat Union between them, and for such other Matters and Things, as may be judged proper for your Majesty's Honour, and the Good and Advantage of both Kingdoms for ever, we have, by our Vote, agreed to the passing of the said Act, in the most fair and equal Terms, that could be ex-pcdled, leaving to your Majesty the Nomination of the Commissioners for this Kingdom, and the Time and Place of their Meeting with the Commissioners of England.

But tho' we have in that Act forborn to take any Notice of a Clause in a late Act of the Parliament of England, intituled, "An Act for the effectual securing " the Kingdom of England from the apparent Dangers, " that may arise from several Acts, lately passed in the 4C Parliament of Scotland," by which Clause the Natives of this your ancient Kingdom of Scotland are, after the 25th Day of December next, to be adjudged and taken as Aliens, born out of the Allegiance of the Queen of England; yet we cannot but with all Submission signify to your Majesty, as Sovereign of beth Kingdoms, that tye, and the whole Nation, whom we represent, are. most

A. 1705.

sensible of the great Injuries done us by that Clause; whereby were are denied the Right and Privilege in England, which the Natives of England do enjoy in Scotland, and which we have constantly enjoyed in England, as a legal and necessary Consequence of our being natural-born Subjects of the same Sovereign, and hath always been sustained, as a mutual Privilege, in the Courts and Judicatures of both Nations.

For which Reason we have found it absolutely necessary, for maintaining the Honour of this Nation, to agree and order unanimously, that the Commissioners, to be nominated by your Majesty for this Kingdom, shall not commence any Treaty with England, until first the said Clause in the English Act be repealed.

We must therefore in all Humility entreat, and hope, from your Majesty's Goodness and Justice, that in your royal Wisdom you will take such Course, as the said Clause in the Act of the English Parliament may be repealed, to the Effect the aforesaid Treaty of Union, so much desired, may commence, and proceed with the wish'd for Success.

Subscribed, in Presence, by Warrant, and in Name of the Estates of Parliament, by,

May it please your Majesty,

Your Majesty's most humble,

most obedient, and most faithful,

Subject and Servant, SEAFIELD, Chancellor,

Sic subscribitur. I. N. D. P.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take into Consideration the Accounts of the Publick Revenues, and Debts, ever since her Majesty's happy Accession to the Crown.

And the Accounts of the respective Grants in Parliament, for the Publick Service of the Year 1705, what Monies have arisen by those Grants till the 8th Day of November, 1705, to what Services the same have been applied, and what other Monies have been applied to those Services, was read.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the Accounts of the Publick Revenues, and Debts, ever since her Majesty's happy Accession to the Crown, be adjourned until this Day Seven-night.

Ordered, That a Monthly Account of the effective Men on board the several Men of War, for the Years 1702, 1703, and 1704, be laid before this House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of Colonel John Rice was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioner having petitioned this House, the last Session of Parliament, for Debentures to be given him for the Arrears of Pay, and other Demands, for a Regiment of Horl'e, by him brought over into their late Majesties Service, upon the Capitulation of Limerick, the 3d of October, 1691, upon the Publick Faith, then given by their said Majesties General in Ireland, the House referred the said Petition to a Committee, to examine, and state, the Matters of Fact; who thereupon reported, that the Petitioner had fully proved the Allegations of his Petition; and that therewasdue to him, for Arrears of Pay, £.8,110. 17*. 6 besides the Value of the Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, of the said Regiment, taken from them, amounting to £.3,310, which the Petitioner was forced to pay the Captains, pursuant to an Agreement made upon bringing them over, Jfc appears by a Copy of the said Report, taken out of the Journal of this House, and annexed to the Petition: That, upon this Report, the House ordered a Clause to be added to the Bill, for punishing Mutineers and Deserters, fsfr. for Debentures to be made out, and delivered to the Petitioner for his said Arrears; and palfed the said Bill, with the Clause, and sent it up to the House of Lords, for their Concurrence; but the House of . . upon passing the said Bill, left out the said Clause, with other Clauses of like kind, not upon the Merits of the said Clauses, but for other Reasons (as informed) and this happening at the end of the Session, the Petitioner had not Time for any other Relief: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for Debentures to be given him for his just Demands, and great Services, aforesaid, that thereby the Ruin of the Petitioner, and his Family, may be prevented.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same to the House.

Ordered, That it be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of Colonel Samuel Vernier was referred.

St. Albans Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Elediou. Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Henry Killigrew, Esquire, complaining of an undue Elc&ion and Return of John Gape, Esquire, to serve for the Borough of St. Albans:

That, upon the Poll, there were,

For the Petitioner - - - 233.

For the fitting Member - 234.

That the Right of Election, in general, was agreed to be in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Freemen, of the said Borough, and in the Housholders there, paying Scotland Lot:

But whether any Person had a Right to demand his Freedom, and whether all Persons, admitted to their Freedom, had a Right to vote in the Election of Members, to serve in Parliament, were the Points in Question with respect to the Right of Election.

The Petitioner's Counsel infilled, that all such, as had served Seven Years Apprenticeship to any Freeman within the Borough, and the eldest Sons of Freemen, born after their Fathers were made free, had a Right to demand their Freedoms; and that Freemen, made upon such Right, or such, as were made free by Redemption, viz. paying £. 5 according to the Constitution, only had a Right to vote in such Election.

That the fitting Member's Counsel infilled, that no Person had a Right to demand their Freedom; but all Persons were made free at the Discretion of the Corporation; and every Person, so made free, had a Right to vote.

In order to make out the Right of the eldest Sons of

Freemen, and of such, as had served Apprenticeships, the

Counsel for the Petitioner infilled, that St. Albans was

a Corporation by Prescription; and as to the Usage in

that respect, they called several Witnesses;

Who said, it was always reputed in that place, that such, as had served Seven Years Apprenticeship to a Freeman in the Place, and such, as were the eldest Sons of Freemen, born after their Fathers were made free, had a Right to their Freedom.

That they never knew honorary Freemen made, till King James Charter; but, if any Tradesman had a mind to settle in the Town, and the Mayor and Aldermen judged such Tradesmen necessary, or convenient, for the Town, it was usual to admit such Person paying £. 5 to the Use of the Corporation: And, to that purpose, they produced the Constitution, or By-laws, of the Corporation; which was read.

That, in answer to this, the fitting Member's Counsel infilled, that St. Albans was a Borough by Prescription, but had ivs fi:ft Incorporation in the Time of Edward VI. That the fitting Member's Counsel offered also to produce the Charter of King Charles II. as a Charter of Confirmation; and the Petitioner's Counsel admitted it: And from both Charters the fitting Member's Counsel inferred, that the Right of Freedom must be by Charter: That the first Charter being within the time of Memory, there could be no Prescription to any Right of Freedom; but that the Mayor and Burgesses might admit, or refuse to make, any Person free, at their Discretion.

Mr. Richards, who had been Town-clerk nine Years since, said, that honorary Freemen had been made before King James Charter; particularly, Dr. Harris was an honorary Freeman, and voted at an Election in King Charles the Second's Time; but it was admitted, he had served in Parliament for that Borough.

That, upon this Evidence, the Committee came to this Resolution:

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford, is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and such Freemen only, as have a Right to Freedom by Birth or Service, or have it by Redemption, and in the Housholders, paying Scotland Lot.

That, the Right being thus settled, the Petitioner's Counsel infilled, that the Petitioner was entitled to a Majority of qualified Votes; and also, that they should

Krove some ill Practices, at this Election, by the fitting lember's Agents.

That Evidence was given as to three, who offered to poll for the Petitioner, and were Housholders, paying Scotland Lot; but were denied, as not paying Scotland Lot.

As to the Point of honorary Freemen, and Freemen made by King James's Charter, it appeared by the Evidence, that near an equal Number had been polled on both Sides; but that, which was infilled on by the Petitioner's Counsel, as moll material to the determining, whether the Petitioner, or fitting Member, was duly elected, was, whether a Number of 34, who at this Election offered their Votes for the Petitioner, had made a good Demand of their Freedom; for the fitting Mem-V ber's Counsel admitted their Qualifications, and that they had offered their Poll for the Petitioner.

And as to this, several Witnesses were examined on both Sides.

That the fad, that was admitted on both Sides, was, that about three Years and a half ago, and before the Election preceding this last, on a Court Day, when the Mayor and all the Aldermen were assembled, these 34 met together at the Court-house, in order to be made free: That the Door of the Council Chamber, where the Mayor and Aldermen were, was kept (hut: That the Mayor going to the Door (but not out of the Room) to speak to his Son, the Aldermen cried, " Adjourn, " Adjourn;" and accordingly the Serjeant, attending, adjourned the Court, without calling in any of these 34 to be made free.

Charles Turner said, he was sent for by the Duchess of Marlborough; and he went to her, and she desired his Vote for both Admirals: That he answered, he was engaged for Mr. Gape-, to which the Duchess replied, she had no Prejudice to Mr. Gape-, but it was the Queen's Desire that no such Men should be chose, for such Men would unhinge the Government; and the Papists Horses flood saddled Day and Night, whipping and spurring.

John Miller said, that he was asked by one to go to my Lady Marlborough's; and, when he came, the Duchess asked him, who he was for; and he answered, for Colonel Churchill, and Mr. Gape: Thereupon the Duchess asked him, if he would be for such Men, as were against the Queen's Interest, and the Good of the Nation? That she asked him to oblige her with one Vote; and he laid, he thought- he did, by giving her Brother one.

The Translation of the King of Spain's Letter to her Majesty, 22 OS 1705.

Madam, my Sifter,

I had not delayed to remind your Majesty of my sincere Respects, had I not waited for a good Occasion of doing it; which 1 have now met with, in having the Honour *0 let you know, that the Town of Barcelona has surrendered to me, by Capitulation. I make no doubt, but you will receive this great News with an entire Satisfaction, as well because this happy Success is but an Effect of your ever glorious Arms, as by reason of those kind and tender Sentiments of a Parent, with which you consider me, and all, that may contribute to the Advancement of my Interest.

I inuft do this Justice to all your Officers, and private Soldiers, and in particular to my Lord Peterborough, that he has shewn, throughout this Expedition, a Constancy, Valour, and Conduct, worthy tire Choice which your Majesty has made of him; and that he could not give me greater Satisfaction, than he has done, of the great Zeal and Application, which he has equally shewed for my Interest and Service. I owe the feme Justice to your Brigadier-general Stanhope, upon Account of his great Zeal, Attention, and most prudent Conduct, of which he has given me Proofs in all manner of Occasions; as also to all your Officers of the Fleet, and principally to your worthy Admiral Shovel!, alluring your Majesty, that he has seconded me in this Expedition with an inconceivable Readiness and Application, and that no Admiral can ever make me more content than he has done. During the Siege of Barcelona some of your Majesty's Ships, together with the Troops of the Country, have reduced the Town of Tarragona, and the Officers remained Pri-loners of War; other Troops of the Country at the same Time made themselves Masters of the Town of Girona by a Stratagem; the Town of Lerida has submitted to me, as has also the Town of Tortofa, on the River Ebro; so that all the Places in Catalonia are taken, except the Town of Ro/es. Some Places in Arragon, not far from Saragojfa, have declared for me; and the Castle of Denia, in Valentia, still holds out, and has repulsed the Enemy:

Four hundred of their Horse have entered into my Service, and a great Number of their Foot have deserted. This Madam, is the Condition, in which your Arms, and the Inclination of the People, have placed my Affairs.

1 need not tell you, what puts a Stop to the Course of these Conquests: It is neither the Season, nor the Enemy: Thole are noObftaclcs to your Troops, wrho desire nothing more, than to be in Action, under the Conduct they now are. The taking of Barcelona with so small a Number of Troops is remarkable enough; but few Examples will be found of what has^happened in this Siege: Seven or Vol. 15.

Eight thousand Men of your Troops, and Two thousand Papers re-Miquelets, have surrounded and inverted a Place, which fading 30,000 French were not able to do. rffainni.

After a March of thirteen Hours they climbed up Rocks and Precipices, to attack a Fortification, stronger than the Town, of which the Earl of Pelerborow fends you a Plan; and two Generals entered with the Grenadiers, on this Attack, with Sword in Hand; where the Prince of HeJJe met with a glorious Death, after so many noble Actions; and I hope, that his Brother, and his Family, will always have your Majesty's Protection. With 800 Men they forced the covered Way, and all the Intrenchments, and Works, one after another, to the last Retreat, against 500 Men of the Troops, that guarded the Place, besides the Reinforcement they had received; and in three Days after they were Masters of the Place.

The Town was attacked under the Castle, and the Cannon and Artillery were again landed with inconceivable Pains and Labour. Two Camps were maintained, and a Communication preserved between them, though near three Leagues distant from each other, against a Garrison almost as numerous as our Army, and who in Horse were twice as strong as ourselves. The first Camp was so well intrenched, that it was defended with 2,000 Men, besides the Dragoons, while the Attack was carried on with the rest; and as soon as a Breach was made, the Disposition was formed, for giving the Assault with the whole Army.

These, Madam, are Circumstances, that perhaps distinguish this Action from any other.

There happened another Accident, which was never known before. The Cruelties of the pretended Viceroy, and the Report, that he intended to carry away several Prisoners, contrary to the Capitulation, had stirred up the Burghers, and some of the Country, to take Arms.

The Garrison being employed in loading their Baggage, in order to march out the next Day, found themselves in very great Confusion, and all Things tending to a Slaughter, when your Majesty's Troops entered the Town, with the Earl of Peterborow; and, instead of busying themselves with plundering, as is usual in lixch Occasions, they appeased the Disorder, and saved the Town, and even the Lives of their Enemies, with a Discipline, and Generosity, without Example.

Nothing remains, but that I return you my moil respectful Thanks, for having sent me so great a Fleer, and so good and valiant Troops, to assist me. After such happy Beginnings, I thought it proper, according to the Opinion of your Generals and Admirals, to maintain in Person the Conquests we have made, and to shew my Subjects, who are lb affectionate to my Person, that I cannot abandon them.

I receive so great an Assistance from your Majesty,

[and your generous Nation, *] that I am overcome with your Goodness, and in the greatest Confusion, that I should be the Occasion of so great an Expence for the supporting of my Interest. But, Madam, I give up my own Person, and my Subjects in , who expose

their Lives and Fortunes, upon the Assurances they have of your generous Protection. Your Majesty, and your Council, know better than we, what is necessary for our Preservation. We shall wait for your Majesty's Succours, with an entire Confidence in your Goodness and Wisdom. It may be seen, what Forces are necessary:

It may also be seen, how great a Diversion we shall give to France. It cannot be doubted, but they will make their utmost Efforts against me, as soon as possible; and 1 doubt not, but the feme Efforts will be used by my Allies, to defend me.

What can be said to you, Madam ? Your Goodness gives you the Inclination, and your Power furnishes you with the Means, to support those, whom the Tyranny of France would oppress. All I can suggest to your Wisdom, and that of your Allies, is, that the Forces, employed in this Country, will not remain useless to the

The Translation of a Letter to the Queen from the Junta of the Military Arm of Catalonia, 23 1705.

Sacred royal Majesty,

The Principality of Catalonia being free from the heavy Yoke, suffered by the violent Oppression of France, and restored to the Center of its Felicity, under the easy and desired Dominion of our adored Monarch Charles the 3d (whom God protect) whereunto your Majesty has been pleased to contribute so powerfully, by the Forces of your Crown, is indispenl'ably obliged, prostrate at the royal Feet of your Majesty, to an eternal Acknowledgment of lo sovereign a Favour, with repeated Thanks to your Majesty for the Quality, Number, and Goodness, of the Troops, which have acted with singular Regularity, punctual Obedience, and inimitable Valour j as also for the Choice of the General, my Lord the Earl of Peterborovu, who commands them; since

there is none, that can exceed him in Valour, and few, who can equal him in understanding the Art of War. His Discretion, Affability, and Gentleness, are the attractive Loadstone of the Hearts of the Catalonians; who love and value him, as the Instrument of their Felicity, respect him for his Person, and for his Character of ^'‘jneral of your Majesty; and hope, from your Matty's Goodness, and the generous Strength of the English Nation, a Continuation, with the greatest Efficacy, of effectual Succours, for maintaining the Principality under the gentle Dominion of our King and Lord, and for promoting the great Work of restoring him to the Throne of his Ancestors. Thus all our Felicity, and the Quiet of Europe, will be owing to the glorious Conduct, and sovereign Direction, of your Majesty. God protect the lacred royal Person of your Majesty, as we desire, and is necessary for us.

From the Camp of Sarria, near Barcelona, 23d October, 1705.

The Junta, named by the King our Lord, of the Military Arm of Catalonia.

The Translation of a Letter from the City of in Catalonia, to her Majesty, 15 ,- 1705.

Madam,

We should be wanting to the Law of good Vassals of our King and natural Lord, Don Carlos the Third (whom God protect), if we did not return your royal Majesty the Thanks due to you, as we do hereby give the fame, for having favoured him, in the Conquest of this Principality, with the powerful Fleet, governed by the most excellent the Earl of General

by Sea and Lind; who, by his great Zeal, Direction, Constancy, and Valour, mattering all Difficulties, and overcoming Impossibilities, which presented themselves in the Enterprize, has obtained a glorious Triumph over the Cattle and Fort of Monjuich, and over the City of Barcelona, and, with it, over the rest of the Principality. We do therefore repeat to your Majesty our just Acknowledgments; assuring your Majesty, that, as this good Fortune fills us with Joy and Acclamation, so it does however much afflict us, that the Distance between your Court and this City deprives us of the Accomplishment of our Desires, which is personally to throw ourselves at the royal Feet of your Majesty, as we do by this Letter execute it with cordial Affection, there being none so much concerned in this singular Enterprize, as the City, and ourselves. May your Majesty enjoy repeated Congratulations, since it has been your Arms that have placed our Catholick Monarch on the Throne of this Principality; and we hope, that in what ' he has further to do, for conquering the Monarchy, your Majesty's royal Protection will not be wanting to him, whereon we rely for Succels.

We beseech God to prated your Majesty's Person, as is necessary. Vici, October 15, 1705.

Madam,

Your royal Majesty's

most obliged humble Servants,

The Counsellers of the City of rich.

The Ext rad of a Letter from the Earl of Peterborough

to her Majesty, 13 October, 1705.

The King of Spain has very obligingly eased me of the Necessity of giving your Majesty an Account of Particulars. ' Upon the whole, I believe, your Majesty's great Goodness will make you graciously accept of my Endeavours. I shall only say, Madam, my Thoughts and Actions shall never have any other View but your Majesty's Glory, and the Good of my Country'.

1 would say more to your Majesty of your Officers, and Troops; of the great Assistance from the English Fleet; of the Courage, Cheerfulness, and exact Obedience, of your Soldiers; if 1 did not think their Actions did sufficiently recommend them to your Majesty's good Opinion, and to the World; but I must not omit to let your Majesty know, how happy we have been in a perfect Agreement with the Officers of the States General, of Sea and Land. Nothing has been desired from the Dutch Admirals, or offered to the Dutch Generals, which has not been complied, even beyond what could be hoped, or reasonably desired.

I do not solicit your Majesty for the necessary Supports of all Kinds, for this happy Beginning. Your Majesty, your Allies, and your Parliament, can never abandon a King, beginning his Reign with an Action of such Resolution and Courage, nor a whole Province, and your own Troops, entirely depending upon your Wisdom and Goodnels.

We all rest assured of the Care and Protection of the best of Princes, and have nothing to desire so earnestly of Heaven, as the Preservation of your sacred Person, and the long Continuance of a Life of such Consequence to the whole World.

Mr. Strode reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir Stephen Evans, and Henry Cornish, and Company, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, upon the said Petition, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the said Petition, it appeared, that the Petitioners clothed the Marine Regiment under the Command of Admiral Killigrew, in the Years 1691 and 1692; which

amounted to the Sum of £.4,103 nr. of which

they received only £. 2,620. 19J. l'o there remains due to the Petitioners the Sum of £. 1,482. lis.

That- the Petitioners produced to the Committee two Letters of Attorney, under the Hand and Seal of Admiral Killigrew, one dated the xoth of April, 1691, for the Sum of £.1,730. 141. id. the other dated the 5th of April 1692, for the Sum of £. 2,37a. 17 whereby the Petitioners were empowered to receive the said several Sums of the then Treasurer of the Navy, for clothing the said Regiment; all which was testified by the said Admiral KWigrew, who was present at the Committee, and owned the said Debt.

That it appeared also to the Committee, that the Petitioners did make Application to the late Commissioners, appointed by Act of Parliament for stating the Accounts of the Army, in order to have Debentures made out for the said Sum of£. 1,482. 12 id. but the said Commissioners were of opinion, that the Marines not being on the Land Establishment, they were not empowered to Rate the Accounts for Arrears due to them, nor make odt Debentures for the fame.

And that, upon the whole Matter, it appeared to the Committee, that the Petitioners have fully and clearly made out all the Allegations set forth and contained in their Petition; and that there is justly due to them the Sum of £. 1,482. ta s.id.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Strode and Mr. Harvey do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Assistants, Etldiftone of the Corporation of Trimty-house of Deptford Strond, Light-house. was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there being a dangerous Rock, called the Eddi-fione, lying off Plymouth, upon which divers Ships had formerly been call away, in 1696 a Light-house was begun to be erected thereon by the Petitioners Direction, and in five Years was finished, with great Expence and Hazard, to the good liking of as well the Commanders of the royal Navy, as all Persons trading in Shipping; it not only being for their Safety, for avoiding the said Rock, but also a Direction to all Ships patting through the Channel: That the said Light-house was preserved until the late dreadful Storm in N, 1703, when it was blown down, and fix People, who lived therein, to attend the Light, periftied: That the speedy rebuilding of the said Light-house may be a Means to preserve, not only her Majesty's Ships, but her Subjects; but, for that the Duties, received for the said Light-house, ceased, after the same was destroyed, and did not defray the Charge of erecting and maintaining the fame, by several Thousand Pounds, and the substantial rebuilding thereof will take up a much greater Sum; the Petitioners pray, that Encouragement may be given towards the rebuilding the said Light-house, and maintaining the fame, by enlarging the said Duties, before granted for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee; aDd that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same to the House.

Mr. Secretary Harley acquainted the House, that her WhitCmd Majesty, in pursuance of the Address of the House the

last Session, had cauled a Survey to be taken of Whit- ar ur* sand Bay, and Por-de-nac Point, with respect to the Use and Conveniency of a Harbour, and Light-house, pro-poled to be made, and erected there, and an Estimate of the Charge thereof; and that her Majesty had directed the Papers relating the reunto, to be laid before this House: And lie presented the same to the House accordingly.

And the Titles thereof were read.

And the said Papers are as follow viz.

In obedience to his Royal Highness Commands, signified to the Matter, Wardens, and Assistants, of

Trinity-houfo, by Letter from Mr. Burchett, of the 25 th of September last, we have, according to the Appointment that had been made of us, taken a strict and careful Survey of Whitfand Bay, and Por-de-tiac Point, with respect

to

4 Ann.

29° Novembris.

to the Use and Conveniency of an Harbour, and Light-house, proposed to be made, and erected, there; and do, from the bed of our Judgments and Observation, humbly report our Opinion thereon as follows:

IV kit far'd Bay, in its present Condition, is no way secure, cither against an Enemy, or the Weather: The Depth of Water within Cowloe Rock (the Place proposed

for an Harbour) is from four to two Fathom, shoaling gradually, and so narrow, as not to admit a Ship to wind in without touching the Ground; which is foul with Rocks, both within and without, till you come into the open Part of the Bay, in Thirteen Fathom Water, where it is sandy; for which Reasons, we cannot judge it capable of being made an Harbour for Ship?, drawing above eight or ten Foot Water; and such must be unavoidably in danger, whenever the Wind is from the North-weft to the West South-weft, by reason of the very great Seas, that will then fall into the said Bay, notwithstanding the Mole proposed should be built: Besides, a Westerly Wind, which is fair to carry Ships up either the North or South Channels, will confine them in the said Bay.

The Charge of building the Mole, necessary for making the said Harbour, will, according to the best Calculation we were capable of making with the Assistance of a proper Surveyor, amount to no less than 170,023. s. 8 d. as may appear by an Estimate thereof, which, with that of the Light-houses also, is hereunto annexed.

As to the Light-houses (for there ought to be Two, if any, to distinguish them from that of that are

likewise proposed to be built on Por-de-nac Point, the Charge thereof is computed at£. 1,211. 5 We cannot conceive the Navigation to be in any need thereof, or that they can be of any Use, unless to Coasters, bound about the Land's End to or from the North or South Channels; but rather, that they may prove dangerous to Ships homeward bound from the Westward, or Southward, by drawing them too near the Shore.

So that, from the Consideration of all that has been before observed, it is our Opinion, that the making an Harbour, and Light-houses, in Bay, and on

Por-de-nac Point, can be of no such Advantage to the Navigation of this Kingdom, with respect either to the Safety, or Conveniency, of her Majesty's or Merchants Ships, as may answer, in any Proportion, to the Charge of doing thereof. Which is, with all humble Submission, laid before his Royal Highness.

Henry

November 17th, 1705. Henry Collins,

Ben.

the Petition of Colonel John Rice was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, upon the said Petition; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is, as followeth; viz.

That, upon the Surrender of Limerick, the 3d Day of October, 1691, upon the publick Faith, and Assurances then given the said Colonel, by the General of their late Majesties Army in Ireland, of being received, entertained, and continued, in their said late Majesties Service, and paid according to the English Establishment, lo long as their Majesties kept any Regiments in their Service, he did thereupon reject the great Offers, that were made hirh by the French Generals, for carrying the then Regiment of Horse under his Command into France, and joined their said late Majesties Army with the fame; and was accordingly received, and mustered, and had Winter Quarters, Money, Provision, and Forage, given them, as to oth er English Regiments; and continued in their late

Majesties Service with his said Regiment, from the said Surrender of Limerick, the 3d Day of October, 1691, to the last Day of January following, the Day they were broke by Brigadier Villiers, by Orders of the then Lords Justices of Ireland, and their Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, taken from them for the publick Use, to make up, and recruit, other English Regiments.

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, that the said Colonel Rice finding his Captains very apprehensive,

by General Sarsfeld (otherwise called Earl of Lucan) and the French Generals, to carry the said Troops into France, whither they were resolved to go, unless the said Colonel would give them his own Security for the Performance <of the said publick Faith; he thereupon, in Confidence of the said publick Faith, and Assurances given him, as aforesaid, and to prevent the Enemy's Designs in carrying the said Troops into France, found it absolutely necessary to agree to his said Captains Demands; and did therefore give and perfect a Bond of Ten thousand Pounds Sterling to his said Captains, to perform the said publick Faith to them; that is to say, to pay them, and their Subaltern Officers, and Soldiers, their full Pay, according to the Eng/ish Establishment; and also to pay them the

full Value of their Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, if taken from them; and further to pay for, and answer, all other Damages, that they might or should sustain by the Breach and Non-performance of the said publick Faith: In pursuance of which Agreement, and in discharge of the said Bond, the said Colonel Rice did pay them theirfullPay, according to Establishment,

and did likewise pay them for their several Troops, Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, which by a Reference, and the Mediation of Friends, he compounded with them for /.450 aTroop, for each of the fivcCaptainsTroops of the said Regiment, being about half the Value, that each of the said Captains Troops were appraised at, the Horles, Arms, and Accoutrements, of the said Colonel's own Troop being valued by the said Brigadier Villiers at One thousand and Sixty Pounds; which added to the forementioned Value of the said Captains five Troops, makes, in all, £. 3,310. Which said Sum of^.450 aTroop, and their full Pay, as aforesaid, the said Captains did, under their Hands and Seals, own the Receipt of, and released the fnne to the said Colonel, gave up, and cancelled, the said Bond of^. 10,000 as aforesaid; and gave a Letter of Attorney, arid full Power to the said Colonel , to put in for, recover, and receive, from their late Majesties, or the Parliament of England, the said Sums of Money, due to them for their laid Pay, and Value of their Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, so by the said Colonel paid, as afore saidI; with full Power to release, acquit, and discharge, the; lame, as he should think fit.'

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, by the Account of the said Regiment, Rated, by Order of the Lords Justices of Ireland, by the Commissioners of Accounts, appointed by his late Majesty, for Rating the Accounts of the Army in that Kingdom, that there was due to the said Regiment for Arrears of Pay, to balance the said Account, the Sum of£.8,no. 17J. 6d. besides the Value of their Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, as afore let 1 thj which said Account, signed by the said Commissioners of Accounts, was proved before the Committee, together with a Duplicate thereof, signed by the Auditor-general of Ireland, and remaining in his Office.

So that, upon the whole Matter, it appears to the Committee, that the said Colonel hath done eminent Service to the Publick, in bringing over his laid Regiment into their Majesties Service, and hindering it, and other Regiments, going into France; and that he hath fully and clearly proved, and made out, all the Allegations, and Matters of Fact, set forth and contained in his Petition; and that there isjuftly due to the said Colonel Rice, for Arrears of Pay by him advanced, as aforesaid. the Sum of Eight thousand One hundred and Ten Pounds, Seventeen Shillings, and Six Pence, together with Three thousand- Three hundred and Ten Pounds, being the Value of his own and the five Captains of the iaid Regiment's Troop Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, being all his own proper Debt, and Money laid out by him for the publick Service; and that he is a great Sufferer, by being so long out of his Money, for a great Part of which he pays Ten per Cent. Irish Interest, besides other Losses and Disappointments he met with, by the Loss of his Command; for which, and the good Services he rendered the Publick, it doth not appear to the Committee, that he had any Compenfuion.
