Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Agmondesham, in the County of Bucks, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir Baronet,

complaining of an undue Election and Return of William Lord Cheyne, and Sir Samuel Baronet, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Agmondisham, in the County of Bucks:

That the Petitioner's Counsel in the beginning declared, they should not bring in question my Lord Cheyney' % Election.

That the first Point, that came in question before the Committee, was, of the Right of Election.

That the Petitioner's Counsel infilling, that the Right was in all such Housholders, as did not receive Alms; whereof a Poll was taken, and the Numbers were thus: For the Lord Cheyne - - - 90.

For Sir Sam, Garrard - - - 84.

For Sir Tho. IVebJler - - - 91.

But the fitting Member's Counsel infilled, that the Right of Election was only in the Housholders, paying Scotland Lot; and that the Poll being call up under such Qualifications, the Numbers were.

For the Lord Cheine - - - 58.

For Sir Sam. Garrard - - - 54.

For Sir Tho. Webster - - - 41.

That the Petitioner's Counsel infilled, that the Inhabitants, not paying Scotland Lot, if they did not receive Alms, as well as those paying Scotland Lot, had been used to be polled in this Borough; and that the first Set of Men had commonly come under the Denomination of the [long Poll, the other under the Denomination of the*] short Poll.

That the Evidence, that was offered, to prove the Right of Election, was, as follows:

First, they produced the Report 16 Januarii, 10

between Sir Roger Hill and Sir John Garrard; when it was agreed by the Counsel, that the Right was in the Inhabitants of the Borough, being Housekeepers, not receiving Alms.

In the next Place they called several Witnesses.

Dudley Penner said, he had been acquainted with the Borough ever since the Year 1674. He said, he paid Scotland Lot, and had been Constable; and particularly remembered the Election in 1680; and all Hous-holders voted then, except such, as received Alms.

These Words are supplied from the original Report.

That the fitting Member's Counsel also called Matthew Evans;who said, that since the Year 1680, no

Persons thought themselves safe, without a Majority of Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot; but before that Time, they did look upon it, that the Inhabitants at large, who did not receive Collection, had a Right; and ever since they have given the long Poll the Liberty of voting. He said, he remembered no contested Election before the Year 1680; and that it was the Consideration of their Poverty, that excused them from paying Scotland Lot. He said, there was a Work-house set up at about two Years ago, or longer, by Sir Webster, and some said, they must give their Vote for Sir Tho, Webster, or they should get no Work.

And that, upon this Evidence, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Agm, in the County of Bucks, is in the Inhabitants, paying Scotland Lot only.

That thereupon the Petitioner's Counsel at first offered, what by qualifying some, who were refused their Votes for the Petitioner, and by disqualifying others, that voted for Sir Samuel Garrard, to make a Majority for the Petitioner; but that Part was afterwards given up.

As to ill Practices, the Petitioner's Counsel examined one William Barnes; who said Mr. Leper, Madam Drake's Steward, told Wm. Johnson, that, rather than he should be for Sir Thomas Webster, he was ordered to give him 40 s. And he actually'fee him give him Money; but what the Sum was, he could not tell.

He also said, that, being under the Window of a Room, where the said Mr. Leper and one Henry Bishop were locked up, he heard M r. Leper tell , rather than he should be for Sir Thomas, he had Orders to give him £. 3. 10s. He said, the Window was shut; but he heard this through the Window.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Hertford, in the County of Hertford, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House j which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Thomas Clark Esquire, and also upon the Petition of the Inhabitants, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Richard ston, Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Hertford:

That the Numbers of the Poll, as it was taken, were. For Mr. Cefar ----- 348.

For Mr. Goulston- - - - 319.

For Mr. Clark, the Petitioner 256.

That the Right of Election was the first Point controverted.

That the Petitioner's Counsel infilled, that Hertford was a Borough by Prescription; and that the Right of Election was anciently in the Inhabitants, being Hous-holders, not receiving Alms; but if any Right of voting was acquired by Charter, it was only to such Freemen, who were made free pursuant to their Charter; who ought to be, at the time of their being made free, Inhabitants within the Borough, or the Parishes thereof, the number of Freemen in the Out-parishes not exceeding Three Persons at any one Time.

That the fitting Member's Counsel infilled, that the Right of Election was in the Mayor, Aldermen, and in all the Burgesses, or Freemen, and in the Inhabitants, being Housholders, not receiving Alms.

That the Petitioner's Counsel, to prove Hertford a Borough by Prescription, and to make out the Right of Election, produced a Return of 26 Edw. I. by which it appears, that Hertford then sent Burgesses to Parliament; and 'tis said, they were elected per tem burgenjium.

That they also produced a Charter, primo;

which Charter is expressed to be ad humHem petitionem inhabitantium burgi et villa de Hertford: And Queen Mary does thereby grant to the Inhabitant?, in thele Words, quod de catero fit et erit incorporatum de uno Ballivo et burgenjibus; ac burgum ilium corpus corporation et politiam, in re, fablo, et nomine, de fe, im-perpetuum facimus, ordinamus, et in plenum erigimus et ereamus, per prafentes. And that Charter further grants

to the Bailiff and Burgesses, Power of chusing into the Office of Burgess omnes et singulos nentes et inhabitantes infra diflum burgum, qua gubernationi illius forent necess'arios.

That they also produced a Charter of King James the First; reciting, that the Borough of Hertford is an ancient Borough, and used, by several Names, divers ancient Rights, Liberties, and Franchises, tom per verfas litter as patentes diversorum progenitorum et -tecejforum nojlrorum, nuper Regum et Reginarum Anglia,

quam ratione diversarum prascriptionum et confuetudimm, in eodem burgo ufitat. et habit. By which the Mayor and capital Burgesses have Power to make as many of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, or the Parishes of the Borough, Burgesses, as they shall judge necessary for the profit of the Borough; dummodo burgesses, inhabitantes extra burgum pradiftum, non excedant aliquo uno tempore numerum trium personarum.

That they also produced Ibme Returns; 15 Car. I.

16 Car. I. 13 Car. idi; in which 'tis said, that the Persons therein named, cum omnibus cateris inhabitan-tibus burgi pradiEli, defied the Burgesses thereby returned.

That the Petitioner's Counsel produced also several Copies of Freedoms; some, in King Charles the First's Time, which run in this Form; That the Mayor and capital Burgesses, ratione libert' granted to them by King James, made free:

Other Copies of Freedoms in King Charles Second's Time, which run in this Form; That the Mayor, Aldermen, virtutelibertat' et privileg granted to them by King Charles the Second, made free:

OtherCopics in King William the Third's Time, which run in this Form; That the Mayor and Aldermen, virtute libertat' et privileg' by divers Kings to them granted, made free:

Other Copies in the Year 1699, and 1700, generally admitting to Freedoms, without naming any Authority.

That the fitting Member's Counsel, to prove, that Persons, living out of the Borough, had anciently, and from time to time, been made free of the Borough, produced several Books of the Corporation {Lib. A, B, C, and D) by which it appeared, that several Persons, to about the Number of Twelve, from the Year 1592 to 1668, living out of the Borough, had been made free of the Borough, to carry on particular Trades there; and other Persons had been made free by Redemption.

That the fitting Member's Counsel then produced a Return of the Year 1678, and offered to prove, that the Indenture of Return had been subscribed by several Freemen, who were Foreigners; but the Petitioner's Counsel admitted it, and that other Returns, from that Time, had been signed by Freemen, living out of the Borough:

And at last produced the Resolution of the House, upon an Election, controverted between Mr. Monson and Mr. Goulfton, 13 Willielmi III. " That the Right

" of electing Members, to serve in Parliament for the " Borough of Hertford, is in all the Freemen, and " also in the Inhabitants, being Housholders, and not " receiving Alms."

That, upon this Evidence, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hertford, is in the Inhabitants, not receiving Alms, and in such Freemen only, as, at the Time of their being made free, were Inhabitants of the said Borough, or the Parishes thereof, the Number of the Freemen, living out of the Borough, not exceeding Three Persons.

That the Right being thus determined by the Committee, the Petitioner's Counsel infilled, that, by adding several to their Poll, and disqualifying many others, who voted for the fitting Member, they should make a Majority for the Petitioner.

And the Petitioner's Counsel excepted, and gave Evidence by several Witnesses (viz. Kenton, James Smith, John Archer, Jer. Swtfe, B. Cooler) to Four . Persons, as Inmates; and to 162 Persons, as not inhabiting in the Borough at the time of their being 23 made

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the said Committee, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the said Return, and Election, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, that both Indentures were between the same Parties, and that the Sheriffs Hands and Seals were to each Indenture.

And the Merits of the Election depended on the Qualification of the elected, the Majority on the Poll being admitted to be for Mr. Bacon and Mr. Chambers.

That the Counsel for Mr. Blofield and Mr. Palgrave infilled, that no Person, who was not free of the City of Norwich, was capable of being elected, to serve in Parliament for the said City.

That the other Candidates were not free at the time of their Election, was admitted.

That, to prove, that none but Freemen were capable to be elected, Mr. Blofield and Mr. s Counsel

first infilled, on the Usage, and called Mr. William Ellwys , who was very near 40 Years of Age, and said. that he had known Norwich ever since 1677; and that all, who have been chose to serve, in his Time, for the City of Norwich, were free, except Mr. Bacon and Mr. Chambers, and Sir Nevill Cateline, who was made free soon after he was chose, and before he was returned.

The next thing Mr. Blofield and Mr. s

Counsel infilled on, was, a By-law, made at an A flem-bly, held in Norwich 28th October 1640; by which it is enacted, that any one, that shall give his Voice for any Man, not free, to be chosen Citizen for the Parliament,

That, for Mr. Bacon and Mr. Chambers, the Counsel infilled, that Norwich was a County, as well as a City; and the Freeholders had a Vote, as well as the Freemen.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported the Conference; and that it was managed by the Earl of Stamford; who acquainted them, that the Conference was desired by the Lords, to communicate to this House an Address, grounded upon the Resolution of their Lordships, of the 6th of December instant, to which this House had agreed; to which Address they desire the Concurrence of this House.

Which Address he read, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table.

The said Report being read at the Table, the Address is, as followeth; viz.

Die Jovts, 13* Decern. 1705.

Resolution — WE your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Sobjects, Church not the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and in Danger. jn Parliament assembled, having taken into Consideration your Majesty's most gracious Speech at the opening of this Parliament, have, upon mature Deliberation, come to the following Resolution:

Resolved by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in Parliament assembled, That the Church of England, as by Law established, which was refeued from the extremest Danger by King William the 3d (of glorious Memory) is now, by God's Blessing, under the happy Reign of her Majesty, in a most safe and flourishing Condition; and that whoever goes about to suggest,

Vo l. 15.

and insinuate, that the Church is in danger under her Majesty's Administration, is an Enemy to the Queen, the Church, and the Kingdom:

Which, we humbly beg Leave to lay before your Majesty: And as your Majesty has been pleased to express a just Indignation against all such wicked Persons; ft> we assure your Majesty, that we shall be always ready, to the utmost of our Power, to assist your Majesty in discountenancing, and defeating their Practices. And we humbly beseech your Majesty, to take effectual Measures for the making the said Resolution publick, and also for punishing the Authors and Spreaders of these seditious and scandalous Reports, to the end that all others may, for the future, be deterred from endeavouring to distract the Kingdom with such unreasonable and groundless Di ft rafts and Je&loufies.

Act, made in the nth and 12th Years of the late King William, for the better governing the Watermen on the River of Thames, the Governors of the Watermen's Company have Power to appoint 40 Watermen, to ply on every Lord's Day, for the carrying Passengers cross the River, at a Penny a-piece, and, after Charges deducted, to apply the Overplus to poor decayed Watermen, and their Widows: That in the said Parish there arc above 280 Families of Watermen, who have above 640 Children, besides Servants, whole Services will, in Time, make them Inhabitants, most of whose Masters are in her Majesty's Service; by whose loss at Sea whole Families become chargeable to the said Parish, the poor Watermen thereof receiving little or nothing from the said Governors: That the Money earned by the Watermen of St. Margaret's, Westminster, is applied to the Support of the poor Watermen of that Parish; and there being ar Bill depending in the House, for the better ordering and governing the Watermen and Lightermen, upon the River of Thames, the Petitioners pray, that a Clause may

be added thereto, that the Money, arising by the Ferries within Lambeth Parish, on the Lord's Day, may be applied to the Support of such decayed Watermen, and Lightermen, and their Widows, and Orphans, as are within the said Parish.

And that afterwards her Majesty had been pleased to Queen'* make a mqft: gracious Speech to both Houses which he Speech, had obtained a Copy of: Which he read to the House, and is, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

THE Unanimity of your Proceedings in this Parliament has already had so good an Effect all over Europe, that I cannot but take notice of it to you with great Satisfaction.

The good Disposition you have shewn, in doing your Part so fully towards an Union with Scotland, is also very acceptable to me j and I hope, it will prove for the Advantage and Quiet of both Kingdoms.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I mud not omit to take this Occasion of returning you my hearty Thanks for the great Pifpatch of this seasonable Supply, which you have given me. I look upon it as a lure Pledge, that the same Zeal and Affection for my Service, and the Good of the Kingdom, will carry you through -all the necessary Parts of the publick Business in this Session.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In case you now think of some Recess, as is usual a this Sealbn, I make no doubt, you will afterwards return with the same good Disposition to give all possible Dif-;

patch to the publick Affairs still depending, and bring jhis. Session of parliament to a happy Conclusion.

Mr. Walpole reported, that the Committee, appointed to give his Grace the Duke of Marlborough the Thanks of this House, for his great Services performed to her Majesty, and the Nation, in the last Campaign, and for his prudent Negotiations with her Majesty's Allies, had given his Grace the Thanks of this House accordingly; and that his Grace thereupon laid,

I am so sensible of the great Honour, that is done me by this Message, that I cannot have the least Concern at the Reflections of any private Malice, while I have the Satisfaction of finding my faithful Endeavours to serve the Queen, and the Kingdom, so favourably accepted by the House of Commons.

Mr. Conyers reported from the Committee of the whole

House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, a Tax be laid upon all Grants o5f Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, and Pensions, made since the sixth Day of February, One thousand Six hundred Eighty-four.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Tax be a fifth Part of the Value of the Graot at the time of the Grant made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, granted by an Act of the first Year of her Majesty's Reign, and continued by several subsequent Acts, till the 24th of June, \ 706, be further continued, from the 23d Day of June, 1706, until the 24th of June, 1707.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a further Duty be laid upon all Low Wines, or Spirits of the first Extraction, made or drawn from any foreign Materials, or any Mixture with foreign Materials.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in, upon the said Resolutions; and that Mr. Solicitor-general, Mr. Conyers, and Mr. Lowndes, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Sir Robert Doversreported from the Committee, t& Edition#

whom the Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Affittaftts, kight-hou e* of the Corporation of Trtnity-koujt of Deptford St fond, relating to the Edifione Rock, was referred; that, the Allegations of the Petition being fully proved, the Committee had come to several Resoluticms, Which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place* and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Light-house on the Edystone Rock, mentioned in the Petition, was, during the Handing thereof, of publick Use and Benefit to this Kingdom, a Means to preserve her Majesty's Ships of War, and the Shipping,

Live*, and Estates, of her Subjects, and for the Good of Navigation in general.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, since the said Light-house was destroyed, her Majesty's Ships of War, and also those of her Subjects, passing by the said Rock, have been, and still are, exposed to great Dangers and Hazards, and several of them, not yet heard of, have, in all probability, been loft thereon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the speedy rebuilding the said Light-house is absolutely necessary, for avoiding the Dangers attending the Navigation and Trade of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee',

That the House be moved, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

A Petition of the Mercers, Silkmen, Lacemen, Milliners, and other Traders, of the City of , was pre-

fented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners labour under insupportable Misfortunes by the long and frequent publick Mournings for foreign Princes, not being able to fell their Goods, nor employ the many Thousands of Poor, who have always had their -Dependence on them: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises, and Relief therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the said Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Levant Trade has been of great Advantage to this Nation: That in the Act of Navigation, made 1 a Car. there is a Clause, which permits the Importation of any Commodity from the Straits, or Levant Seas, to be laden from the usual Ports of lading the re, though the Commodities be not of the Growth of those Places; by virtue of which Clause, Leghorn is now become a Mart for Turky Goods, and our Tu Goods, taken as Prize by the French, and those of French Importation from 4fta, are fold there, and fraudulently brought into England by Jews, and others, not only for their own, but

(as is conceived) for French Account likewise, to the great Encouragement of their Woollen Manufactures, y felling the Proceed thereof, when good Markets offer here, and consequeotly to the Discouragement ofour own, and, if not timely prevented, to the Ruin of the Levant Trade: And praying such Relief therein, as the House shall think proper.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Saturday come-seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Increase, and better Preservation, of Salmon, and other Fish, in the Rivers of this Kingdom; and that the Lord William Powlett, Mr. Durnmer, Mr. Morgan, and Sir William Bowes, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

That the main Points in difference were,

First, As to the Persons, who had a Right to their Freedom:

And, in the next Place, the Power of the Corporation to make Persons, living out of the Borough, free, by Redemption.

That, as to the First, the Petitioners Counsel infilled, that all Persons, having served Seven Years Apprenticeship within the Borough, and the Elder Sons or Freemen, had a Right to their Freedom.

The Sitting Members Counsel infilled, that all, as well the younger, as the elder. Sons of Freemen had a Right to their Freedom.

That, as to the latter, the Petitioners Counsel infilled, that the Corporation had a Power to make any Perfoti free, whether they inhabited within the Borough, or out of the Borough.

The Sitting Members Counsel infilled, that such Persons, as had no Right to their Freedom, could not be made free, except they were Inhabitants within the Borough.

Worcester A Petition of several Inhabitants of the Borough of Roads. Eroitwich, in the County of , and of several

other Persons, that live between the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, and the City of

cester, on the behalf of themselves, and many other Persons, who are concerned in Carriage of Salt, Iron, Coals, and other Wares and Commodities, between the City of Worcester, and Birmingham aforesaid, and other Places, with Waggons, Carts, Packs, and other Carriages, was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, that the Highway between Worcester, and Bir-

mingham, leading through the Parishes of Claynes, Mar-tyne, Nufftngtree, Salzvarpe, and St. Mary Wilton, are so very much destroyed by the great Carriage of the aforesaid Commodities, that they are almost impassable, several Carts and Waggons having been there broke, the Goods spoiled, and many Horses loft; and the Inhabitants are incapable of repairing the same by the Laws now in force, to the great Prejudice of Trade in that Part of the Country: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for charging a Toll upon all Horses, Carts, Coaches, Waggons, and Droves of Cattle, that shall pass and repass through the said Way, for a Term of Years, for Repair of the said Highways.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Cox, Mr. Foley, and Mr. Wylde, do prepare, and . , bring in, the Bill.

Mr. Farrer reported from the Committee, to whom inthArrears. the Petition of Colonel Fenner was referred, the Matter, upon the Petition of John Fara and George Ford, Serjeants, and the non-commissioned Officers, and Soldiers, late under the Command of the Earl of Drogheda; and also upon the Petition of Richard Tinker, Samuel Bel-ward, John Ckifwell, and Samuel Lewis, on behalf of themselves, and several others, non-commissioned Officers, and private Soldiers, of the Lord (late Colonel

Coot's) Regiment of Foot; as it appeared to the Committee, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read; and are, as follow; viz.

Upon the said Petition of John Fara, and others.

That the Committee having examined the Allegations of the said Petion, it appeared by an Account, examined, stated, and certified, under she Hands of the late Commissioners, appointed by Act of Parliament to state the Accounts of the Army, that there is due to the Petitioners, for their Services in Ireland, the Sum of,£.1,392.

17 s. o That it also appeared to the Committee, that the Pe-tioners did make Application to the late Paymaster-general of her Majesty's Forces, in order to have Debentures made out for the said Debt; but could not obtain the fame, for want of a Letter of Attorney, signed by the Colonel, and a Majority of the Captains, to impower some particular Person, pursuant to the said Act, to take out Debentures, the said Act of Parliament requiring Seven Captains to sign such Power.

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, that several of the Captains of the said Regiment are dead, and others in foreign Parts; so that Debentures cannot be taken out, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee find, that the Petitioners have fully and clearly made out all the Allegationscontained in their said Petition; and that there isjuftly due to them the Sum of £.1,392. 17 o\d.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Mr. Farrer and Sir Thomas Littleton do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, by the Testimony of Captain Rutter, that there are but Seven Captains living; whereas the Act of Parliament required a Majority of Thirteen Captains, to impower a Person to take out Debentures, and state their Accounts; and Two of them refused to sign any Power for the Petitioners getting their said Debt, so certified by the said Commissioners to be due to them.

And that upon the whole Matter, the Committee find, that the Petitioners have fully and clearly made out all the Allegations contained in their said Petition; and that there is justly due to them the Sum of,£. 1,233. 19*.

1 £d.but for want of the Majority of Captains to impower a Person to take out their Debentures, the same remains still in the Hands of the late Paymaster-general of her Majesty's Forces.

A Petition of Pdul Chamberlain, Doctor of Physick,

was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Petitioner having observed the Burthen of annual Interest, at 5, 6, 7, and 8 /. per Cent, paid for some Millions of Money out of the Exchequer, on several Funds, he has thought on certain Means to pay off the said Debt, as also to prevent the falling under the like unhappy Circumstances for the future:' And praying, that he may be heard, when, and in what Manner, the House shall appoint.

Mr. Conyers (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Cldrk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties of Excise on Beer, Ale, Cyder, and other Liquors, granted by an Act of Parliament, in the fifth Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, for the Term of Sixteen Years, to commence from the 17th Day of May, 1697, and are charged with such Lottery Annuities, as are therein mentioned, for a Term of Years, which will expire at Michaelmas, 1710, be continued, from the Expiration of the said Term granted of the said Duties by the said former Act, for a Term of 95 Years from thence next ensuing.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Sum of Two Millions Five hundred Seventy-five thousand Seven hundred Sixty-one Pounds, Sixteen Shillings, and Two Pence, be raised by the Sale of Annuities, for the Term of Ninety-nine Years, to commence from Lady-day now next ensuing.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the additional Subsidy of Tonnage and Poundage, the Duties on Coals, Culm, and Cinders, and the said Duties of Excise on Beer, Ale, Cyder, and other Liquors, granted, or continued, in this Session of Parliament, as those Branches respectively shall commence, and take Place, be charged with the Annuities to be sold, as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties of Excise, granted by the said Act of the fifth Year of their late Majesties Reign, after the Lottery *5

Annuities, therein mentioned, shall be paid off, or sufficient Money shall be reserved for paying off the fame, shall be applied towards the Payment of the Annuities now to be purchased.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That lb much Money, as, over and above the Produce of the said additional Subsidy of Tonnage and Poundage, shall be necessary to discharge the Annuities to be purchased, as aforesaid, for the first Two Years of the said Term, be raised, and kept in the Receipt of the Exchequer, and issued from time to time, for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the like Duties upon low Wines, or Spirits of the first Extraction, as, by an Act of the third Year of her Majesty's Reign, are continued from the 24th Day of March 1706, be made payable from the 24th Day of March, 1705, until the Commencement of the said former Act, for the Uses and Purposes in that Act expressed.

The laid llesolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill, or Bills, be brought in, upon the said Resolutions; and that Mr. Solicitor-General, Mr. Conyers, and Mr. Lowndes, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no more Petitions this Session of Parliament, for private Bills, after Fhurfday next.

A Petition of the Portreeve, Mailers, Clothiers, and Newfound-Inhabitants of the ancient Clothing Town of Lnd Trade,

in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Trade to Newfoundland was of greatest Advantage to England, whilst we were in the Possession thereof, many Hundreds of Ships being therein employed, and Thousands of Sailors yearly bred thereby, and the Royal Navy then manned with less Difficulty, than of late Years: That, during the Prolperity of that Trade, great Quantities of our Woollen Manufactures were exported thither yearly, the Returns whereof was chiefly Money, and Bullion: That of late Years the French have possessed the greatest Part of the said Island, and the bell fishing Ground, where the Fish comes sooner, than where the English fish; whereby, in Time of Peace, they forestall the Markets; and by this Means they have increased their Navigation to that Degree, as to enable the French to man out such Fleets, as none of their Predecessors ever did, having above 700 Ships yearly employed in that Fishery, to the almost utter Lois of our Trade there: And praying, that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, that such Provision may be made, as may oppress the French in this advantageous Trade, and restore the English to the Advantages they once reaped thereby.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Answer of the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, relating to the Newfoundland Trade, shall be taken into Consideration.

Upon the several Petitions of John Pedley, Esquire, and of the Mayor, and divers Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Huntington, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of Sir Baronet, to serve for the said Borough; and also upon the Petition of John Negus, late Mayor, and several other Burgesses, complaining of an undue Election," and Return, of Edi Hartley, Esquire, to serve for the said Borough:

That the Petitioner's Counsel alleged, that the Right of Election was in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses; and the same was admitted by the other Side.

That, upon the Poll, the Numbers were.

For Sir John Cotton - - - 73.

For Mr. Wortley - - - - 73.

For the Petitioner - - - - 64.

That the Points, the Petitioner's Counsel went upon, were two; viz. Bribery, and Treating; and by the first, they alleged, they should disqualify so many of Sir John

Cotton's Voters, as would leave the Petitioner, Mr. Pedley, a great Majority.

That, as to the Bribery, the Petitioner's Counsel called several Witnesses:

Geo. Sexton laid, that at the latter End of April, or the Beginning of May, he was present, when Mr. Christopher Bray came into Mr. Wheat ly's Wine-cellar, and told Mr. Wheatly, that he, and the rest of the Burgesses, that should vote for Sir John Cotton, should have a Guinea a-piece: And further, that he was present, when Sir John Cotton defiied Thomas HodcPs Vote; and Hodd telling Sir John Colton, he could not vote for him, Sir John Cotton gave Hodd a Guinea, and then Hodd promised Sir John Cotton his Vote.

Geo. Sexton, Wm. Beard, and James Taylor, gave Evidence, that 26 Persons, who had given single Votes for Sir John Cotton, had acknowleged themselves to have received a Guinea a-piece: And Wm. Beard and James Taylor, amongst the rest, said, that they had themselves received a Guinea each of the said Mr. Bray, to drink Sir John Cotton's Health: And Taylor said, he

believed.

Joel Taylor, Husband of Do, being called, denied,

that he had received more than a Guinea; but said, Mr. Bray promised him fix Guineas, ,if he would give his last Vote for Sir John Cottonand that it was about three Weeks before the Election.

And Vincent said, that the Burgesses were treated with Drink, and Tobacco, on the Election Day.

In Answer to which Evidence, Sir John Cotton's Counsel insisted, that Sir John was a Person of a considerable Family and Estate in the County, and had an Invitation from many of the Burgesses to stand. They acknowleged the Distribution of several Guineas to everal of the Burgesses; but said, it was only an Act of Sir John's Charity and Generosity, of which some poor Women, as well as Men, that had no Votes, and others, that voted against Sir John, as well as those, that voted for him, did participate.

That, as to Sir John's being invited, they called

Then some Witnesses were called, to prove Bribery and Corruption by Mr. Wortley, and Mr.

She said, her Husband was a Labourer, and played on the Fiddle, and had been absent from her several Weeks, part of which Time he was at Kimbleton; and that she was threatened by Mr. Dowfe, the Receiver, if she gave Evidence against Mr. Wortley and Mr. Pedley.

Edward Nicholls said, that John Corbett, three Days after Sir John Cotton had declared he would stand, was (landing at his Door; and Sir John asking him, who he would be for, Corbett answered, he could not tell, for there was a Debt of £. 10 or 15 due from Mr. Wortley, for Drink at a former Election: That afterwards Corbett told Nicholls, Mr. Turk had promised him, he should be paid > and that Corbet voted for Mr. Wortley and Mr. Pedley.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petitions, relating to Parton Harbour, were referred.

And the Report was read, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which are, as follow j viz.

First, upon the Petition of Mr. , and others:

Mr. Atkinson said, that he has known Parton Harbour

Seven-and-twenty Years; and that the same is not sufficient for carrying on the Coal Trade thereabouts, by reason there is not sufficient Depth of Water, to carry out and in the larger Ships, and by reason of a Lodge of Rocks, going in; but that the same may be enlarged, and made a better Harbour than Whitehaven, from whence the larger Ships cannot load Coals above four Times in a Year, and is not a sufficient Harbour to receive and dispatch the Shipping, employed in the Coal Trade in those Parts; and that he has gone to to

load Coals, rather than lie at Whitehaven for his Turn, because it would not answer the Charge of lying by so long; and also several of the smaller Vessels, for the same Reasons, have gone from Whitehaven to load at Parton.

That, if Parton Harbour were enlarged, and improved, as he conceives it might, it would much add to the Con-fumption of Coals in those Parts, and be no Prejudice to those exported from Whitehaven, because there is a Vent for as many, as both Places can supply.

That, if Parton were so improved, it would be a Safety for Ships coming from the Westward, the Wind being at South South-east; whereas now they cannot, if the Wind takes them short, reach , but mult

make for Scotland.

That he has loaded from the Rocks at Parton; and that Mr. Fletcher is the reputed Owner of the Salt Works and Rocks there; and never heard, that Sir John Lowther claimed them: And said, there is a small Duty paid to Sir John Lowther for Anchorage at , but none

for Coals, that he knows of.

Mr. Cragg, of Whitehaven, said, that he well knows Parton and Whitehaven: That Parton is a computed Mile from Whitehaven; and that Parton Harbour will hold but Nine or Ten small Ships at a time, of which but Four or Five can load at once, and only at Spring Tides: That he thinks Parton may be so enlarged, as to hold more Ships than Whiteh; and 'tis the general Opinion of the Owners and Mailers of Ships at Whitehaven, that Parton Harbour may be made to carry two Foot deeper Water than Whitehaven; and that it would be a Security to their Shipping in stormy Weather, and an Increase to the Coal Trade.

That there is above 5,000 Chaldrons of Coals now lying at Parton, for want of Shipping to carry them away: That, if Parton Harbour were improved, it would help to supply Ireland with Coals, Whitehaven not being sufficient for that Purpose: but the Scotch do it; for that he has seen 20 or 30 of their Ships employed in the Coal Trade at a time at and that Parton

Coals are 2 s.a Ton better than Scotch Coals, and are also better than Whitehaven Coals; and yet the Exportations from thence are not lessened, since Parton has been a Harbour: And believes, there may be Trade enough for both Places, without a Prejudice to either, but for the Good of the Country.

That there may be 80 or 100 Sail of Ships, that use the Coal Trade at Whitehaven and Workington; and but only the Key Tire can load at a time at Whitehaven, and usually keep their Turns; so that a Ship may lie three or four Months, before {he can load; and, if Parton were enlarged. Ships might make four or five Turns for one, and larger Ships lie there, than at Whitehaven.

That Mr. Fletcher is Lord of the Manor of and, as such, has claimed the Stones, and Salt Pans, between high and low Water Mark at; and Sir

John Lowther never made any Pretence to them; and

Vo 1. 15.

113

that he bought a Steer, to lay his Coals on, of one Tyson, who first bought the same of Mr. Fletcher.

Mr. Millner said, that Parton Harbour lies more safe from the Sea, than Whitehaven; and believes it capable of great Improvements, so as to hold larger Ships, than Whitehaven; and that, if it were so, there might be as many more Coals vended, as are now from

Mr. Airy, Mariner, said, that he has known Parton Harbour near 40 Years; and that the same is not sufficient to receive the Shipping, that might be employed in the Coal Trade there: That the same may be enlarged; and it will much increase the Coal Trade to Ireland, and elsewhere, who are supplied from Scotland.

That Parton Coals are better than Scotch Coals; and therefore the Irish would not buy them, if they could have Parton Coals.

That the Coals, gotten either at Parton, or,

must be shipped, where gotten, because the nearer the Shipping, the less will be the Charge of Carriage.

That Parton is rocky and sandy, and so 'tis at haven; and thinks, the improving Parton Harbour will be of Security for Whitehaven Shipping; for that, on a Southerly Wind, they may reach , when they cannot Whitehaven, but mull run to Scotland.

That Mr. Fletcher is Lord of the Manor of ',

and Owner of the Salt Pans, and Stones, between high and low Water Mark; and that he loaded Stones there near 40 Years ago, and never heard, that Sir John Lowther had any Right to them; but has seen Sir John's, Servants cut the Coal Bags, when they have been set down at low Water: That Sir John has Coals near Parton, from whence he, as well as others, ship them off.

Mr. Brookes said, that, if Parton Harbour should be enlarged, he conceives, it cannot prejudice the Revenue; for, though more Officers be employed, the Duties on Coals will answer the Charge, with advantage to the Publick, an Officer being now there.

Mr. Carnes, Mr. Milner, and Mr. Craggs, laid, the Persons, who have signed the Petition, all live at Whitehaven, and are considerable Merchants, and Owners and Mailers of Ships; and that they have often heard them say, they lay under great Inconveniencies for want of a Harbour at Parton.

And it appeared by a Certificate, signed by many of the Merchants, Mailers and Owners of Ships, at Whitehaven, that 'tis their Requell, that Parton Harbour be enlarged; which, they conceive, will much contribute to the Increase of Navigation, the Benefit of the adjacent Country, and a means of saving many Ships, when lie exposed at Whitehaven to many Dangers.

That, upon the Petition of Sir John Lowther, the Evidence produced, was

Mr. Edward Hall; who said, he had been a Servant to Sir John Lowther 23 Years, and had known Whitehaven Harbour 20 Years; which had been very much enlarged by Sir John Lowther, and the Coal Trade there much increased by his Means: That there is good coming in for Shipping, and safe lying the re, and no Duty paid for Coals, except a small Matter of a Farthing a Ton, for Anchorage, which Sir John offered to take off, if they would pay a Pier Keeper.

That, in time of Peace, there was always more Coal* at Whitehaven, than Dublin, or other Places, would take off; and has known Sir John Lowther take off his Workmen, because he could not fell his Coals fast enough; and believes, there might be feme Hop to the Coal Trade, upon Sir John's railing the Price of them.

That the Shipping don't lie by at Whitehaven for want of Coals, or Conveniency of lading, but for want of a Market for them; for that they may load in four or five Tides, and never knew them to lie by two or three Months at a time.

That the Charge of carrying Coals to the Shipping at Whitehaven is 144/. per Ton, at Parton 12 and that Ships may always go into- Whitehaven Harbour, but into Parton only in fair Weather, and small Shipping; and believes, there is no Anchorage at Parton, because 'tis

Harbour!

rocky, and but Ten Foot Water there at high Water and 14 Foot at Whitehaven: And that Parton is not capable of being made a good Harbour.

John Thompson, Sailor, laid, that he knows both -ton and Whitehaven Harbours; and believes, Parton cannot be made so good a Harbour, as Whitehaven; for that 'tis all rocky, and the Ground foul, and no Anchorage, and dangerous going in; whereas Whitehaven is a loft sandy Beach, and may safely run a Ship on Ihore there, and go in at any time; but, if it blows a Storm, there is no coming near Parton; yet, he believes, it may be enlarged.

That he has loaded Coals several times at and never staid above six Weeks for his Turn, though he has known fbme flay two Months in War time; and that Shipping may be loaded fad enough at Whitehaven, for that five Tire of Ships may lie there at a time, of iz in a Tire; and he has loaded in the third Tire; and that Whitehaven may be made a very good Harbour, but Parton cannot.

William Soleby, formerly Sir John Lowther' % Groom, — that he knows Whitehaven and Parton Harbours, and thinks Whitehaven a better and larger Harbour, than Parton can be made, which lies more open to the Sea; and knows, that Sir John has put off his Workmen, for want of Sale for his Coals.

Mr. Main and Mr. Waller said, that in 1704 the Commissioners of the Customs sent them, as Surveyors-General into the Country; and they were at Whitehaven, where they observed, the People were clothed with Irish Manufacture; and that they imported there Butter, and other Commodities, contrary to Law: They were also at Parton, and found there a fraudulent Practice of trading with Ireland; and, if it should be made a Harbour, the Queen must be at more Charge for Officers to look after the Customs; and it may open a large back Door, for a Trade there from Ireland; and know not, whether it will be any Advantage to Trade; but the said Commissioners think, there are too many Places for landing of Goods, which gives the greater Opportunity of running the m.

That they have heard, and believe Whitehaven to be a better and more convenient Harbour than , which is rocky, and Whitehaven sandy j but are no Judges, whether Parton be capable of Improvement, or not.

David Hartley, Boatswain of the that he

was born at Whitehaven, and has known the Harbour there 30 Years, and was two Years' Matter of a Ship; and very well knows Parton, which is 14 Foot deep at a top Spring Tide, and Whitehaven 18 Foot: That Parton Harbour is all rocky, and there is no anchoring the re, so must put by it; and many Ships have been spoilt at the Pier; and thinks, it cannot be made a good Harbour.

That Whitehaven is a sandy Harbour; and he has known so much Dispatch in lading the Ships there, that the Pursers have staid behind at Dublin, to fell the Coals; and that Sir John Lowther has sent Coals to the West of Ireland, to be sold, for want of a Market.

That Whitehaven may be made Six Foot deeper than now it is, and may be enlarged, so as to hold 200 Sail of Ships safe, and the bed ary Harbour in as

he believes; and that he never saw any want of Coals there, but might ship more off, if they had a Market for them.

That he never knew Ships lie two or three Months at Whitehaven for Lading, but they generally load in the Niep, to be ready against the Spring Tides, and can load three Ships in two Days at a time; and there are about 50 Sail of Ships employed in the Coal Trade, which usually take their Turns, and cannot well fail without Convoy, which often flays for the Parton Ships, and which, though they are but small, yet cannot get out in many Springs, for want of a sufficient Draught of Water, which cannot be had at; and if Parton were made a Harbour, yet could they not make four or five Voyages to one from Wiutehaven now.

Henry Dixon, a Sailor these 1 a Years, — that he has been a Sailor at Whitehaven and Parton Six or Seven Years; and that Whitehaven is a pretty Place, and a sandy Harbour, and Parton is all rocky, and cannot be made so good a Harbour as Whitehaven, where there is 18 Foot at high Water, and may be deepened Six or Seven Foot; and there is at Parton but 14 Foot, and it cannot be deepened above a Foot more.

That Whitehaven may hold 200 Sail of Ships, and he has loaded there at Six Ships in a Tire at a time; but 10 or 12 may load, if there be Coals and Hands enough.

John Bray, Sailor, laid, that he served his Apprenticeship at Whitehaven, and has been a Sailor 14 Years: That 'tis a sandy Harbour, and Parton rocky, as far as Low-water Mark, and no Anchorage; and he loft a Ship there, and has known Ships overset at Whitehaven; but does not know, whether Parton is capable of being made a Harbour, or not: It may be made deeper about a Foot and half, and Whitehaven five Foot; and that in Stress of Weather he would rather make for Whitehaven, than Parton, the same Wind serving for both Harbours, except it takes them short from the North, and then they cannot fetch Whitehaven.

Roger Brijco said, he knows Whitehaven, and has been

there several times, as a Supercargo from th;

and that the Harbour there may be improved and enlarged.

Mr. Lowther laid, that he has viewed, and taken Draughts of, both the said Harbours; and that Whitehaven is sandy, and Parton rocky, and dangerous to get in, especially at South-weflerly Winds, it lying open; but Whitehaven is safe, and sheltered by a high Hill from those Winds; and 'tis a general Complaint, that Ships suffer thereby at Parton.

That Whitehaven Harbour is large enough for all the Ships employed in the Coal Trade in those Parts, and may be enlarged, to hold 300 Sail, for the doing whereof Sir John Lowther is willing to contribute; but opposes the making a Harbour at Parton (though he has more Coals there, and nearer to the Harbour, than any body else, and can load them id.a Ton cheaper than at Whitehaven) because he thinks, the more Coals are shipped there, the fewer will be at Whitehaven; and that will be a Prejudice to the Town of Whitehaven, and himself also, he claiming the Ground, where the Harbour is intended to be made, by Grant from the Crown.

That, if there were a greater Demand for Coals at Dublin, or elsewhere, Sir John Lowther could supply it; and wrote to Sir Robert Southwto use his Interest to help him off with the Sale of them at Cork, Kinfale, and Plymouth; and Sir John will now engage to furnish Dublin at the same Rate he now fells his Coals.

That Mr. Lowther produced a Certificate, signed by many of the Justices of the Peace, and other Gentlemen, of the County of Cumberland, Merchants, Tradesmen, Matters and Owners of Ships, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Whitehaven, setting forth their Reasons against making a Harbour at Parton:

And also another Certificate, signed by the High Sheriff, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen of the Grand Jury, and other Gentlemen and Freeholders, of the County of Cumberland, at their Quarter Sessions, held at Carlisle the 18th of December last, to the like Purpose.

Mr. Lowther also produced a Copy of a Grant from King Charles the 2d, dated the 4th Day of March, in the 30th Year of his Reign, made to Sir John Lowther, and his Heirs, of all that Soil, or Ground, containing about 150 Acres, lying between the high and low Water Marks of the Sc* near Whitehaven, with the Rocks thereupon, which extends from East to West zoo Yards or thereabouts, and from North to South two Miles, or thereabouts; the Bounder thereof Southwards being Brainjby Beck, adjoining to Lands of the said Sir John Lowther, and the Bounder North being Morejby Beck, adjoining to a Parcel of Land there, called Lewca, paying 20 s.per Annum into the Exchequer for the fame. A Petition of several Merchants of the Town and Newfound-County of Poole, trading to the Parts of Newfoundland, land Trad*, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, since the Petitioners Remembrance, the land Fishery, brought vast Treasure to this Nation, and employed above 30,000 Men per Annum, whereof 8,000 never were at Sea before; but now the French have in a manner ingrafted that Trade, by possessing themselves of near Six-sevenths of the fishing Ground; so that, by fishing few Ships in a Place, they are always sure to make good Voyages, and the Fish comes with them about six Weeks tooner, than to the Places we yet enjoy, whereby they arrive at Market Six Weeks sooner than us, to their great Advantage, and our Loss; and now they employ 30,000 Men in this Fishery, that they have taken from us, and within few Months, with Fire and Sword, over-run all our Settlements there, and so disturb our Fishing, that, unless a sufficient Force be sent thither, to reduce them, we shall utterly be forced to abandon that Country, and Trade: That not only the French but the Americans, much conduce to the Ruin of the said Fishery, by bringing Rum, Sugar, Molofles, and Tobacco, which is lo coveted by the Men employed in the Fishery, and lb closely followed, that they neglect their Business; the Americans allb furnish them with Provisions. Shoes, Hose, Soap, Nets, Lines, (Ac. at an under Rate, than the English, who used to supply them therewith, can do, to their great Prejudice, and, at the End of the Fishing Sealbn, carry away many Fishermen, who would otherwise go for England, and consequently help to man1 the Fleet: That the commanding Officer, presuming to trade, often inflicts military Punishment on the Inhabitants, the easier to engross the Trade; which may prove fatal; and the Convoys being appointed so late, the Season is so far advanced, 'ere they fail, that the bell Fishing Sealbn is over, before they arrive: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Matters aforesaid, so as that this advantageous Trade may be restored and preserved to England, as formerly.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to th# Committee, to whom the Matter of the Trade to Newfoundland is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Clifton Dartmouth Har-dress, on behalf of themselves, and many others of the adjacent Places, trading to Newfoundland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Newfoundland Trade hath been found very beneficial, not only on account of Merchandizing, but a great Nursery for Seamen; but is at present liable to the Insults of the French, and the late going out of the Convoys bath been the Ruin of the Merchants Fishing Voyages: And praying the House to lay the Matter before her Majesty, that the Petitioners may have such Assistance of Men of War, as may seem meet.

Ordered, That the ConGderation of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom it was referred to consider of the Trade to Newfoundland.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration and examined into the Allegations of the said Petition,

It appeared to them, that in the Year 1689 the said Regiment was commanded into Ireland, and in their Paf-lage at Sea they loft in a Storm 124 Horses.

To prove which, several Witnesses were examined; viz.

Colonel Carpenter said, that there was loft 47 Horses

aboard the Ship where he was.

Fran. Turner said, there was loft 40 aboard his Ship.

Henry Vandaivsaid, there was loft 24.

That it appeared to the Committee, by the Testimony of several Officers of the said Regiment, that a Party of this Regiment, being sent to conduct the Cannon to Limerick, wasfurprized by Sarsfield near that Place, and ' great Part of them were killed, and their Horles and Accoutrements taken by the Enemy.

That a great Part of their Clothing, and Accoutrements, were loft near Belfafi.

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, by the Testimony of Colonel Carpenter, Mr. and

Mr. Robert Banks, and several others, belonging to the said Regiment, that Brigadier by reason of the

' aforesaid Losses, was forced to cloarh the said Regiment three Years successively; but neglected to make application for Money by contingent Warrants, to make good those Losses, as is usual in such Cases, but applied only for Money upon Account, in order to complete and fit the Regiment for Service, which, when the Accounts came to be Hated, was found to be charged to the Pay of the said. Regiment.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee do find, that the Petitioners have fully proved all the Allegations contained in their said Petition; and that, by reason of the aforesaid Losses, and the Omission of the said Brigadier VII/iers, in not applying for contingent Warrants, for Money, to make good those Losses, there is aDeficicney, of^.3,875. iSr. i of to answer the several and respective Balances of the Officers and Soldiers of that Regiment.

The Commons have agreed to the Amendments, made by your Lordships to Clause A.

The Commons do likewise agree to the first Amendment, made by your Lordships to Clause B, Pr. 1. L. 8.

The Commons disagree to the 2d and 3d Amendments, made by your Lordships, L. 13, 14, and 15, for these Reasons:

lft, Because they cannot consent to repeal a Clause, which was made to redress a Grievance, so frequently complained of in Parliament; and your Lordships, by your Amendment, though it excludes only Persons from fitting in the House of Commons, that shall have new Offices, or Places of Profit, under the Crown, hereafter to be created, and the Commissioners, Sub-commissioners, and Receivers, of the Prizes, do admit some Provision of that Nature to be reasonable.

adly, Because a total repeal of the said Clause would admit such an unlimited Number of Officers to be Members of the House of Commons, as may destroy the free 15 and

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that he had received a Letter, signed by James Dillon and William Staunton, relating to the Bill for the Relief of Colonel John Rice.

And the said Letter was read, and is, as followeth; viz.

Mri Speaker,

WE have addressed ourselves to Sir D. Colt, to Mr. Solicitor-General, and then to my Lord Trea-fiirer, about a Bill, that is to be passed for £. 12,000, in behalf of an Irish Papifh Colonel, called John Rice.

We sent the Lord Treasurer a Copy of the Matter, that we will prove, as clear as the Sun, against Rice; which Matter will lave the Queen £. 12,000. We are now informed, that Rice, knowing this Matter, does give out, that it is to be proved by one Patr. Hurley, a Person guilty of Perjury in Ireland: But, Sir, we hope, you'll not suffer the Nation to be fooled out of so much Money by such an Imposition; for tho' it is true, that Hurly drew some Papers for us, yet he never was, nor shall be, concerned in the Proof. Sir, we were never tainted, nor never was yet sworn in any Case, being bred Soldiers. Send to my Lord Treasurer for the Copies of our Affidavits; and, since the Queen's Service requires it, we will now appear, to prove them, without any Concern with Hurly. If we save the Queen so much Money fairly, it is a Service worth looking after; and we desire you. Sir, to put a Hop to the Bill, till we are heard to the Matter we writ to my Lord Treasurer. If what we have to offer, be not fair, it can be no Hindrance to Rice, for we may be heard in an Hour, as well as in an Hundred; but no Well-wisher to the Government can be for him, when they hear, our Allegations are proved, and that we prove ourselves to be never otherwise reputed, than honest Men, and good Subjects,

Your humble Servants,

Friday, 8th James Dillon,

February, 170$. Wm. Stanton.

Sir Richard Onslow reported, that the Managers appointed had met the Lords at the Conference; and that it was managed, on the Part of the Lords, by the Duke of Somerset; who said, the Lords had defined this Conference, to preserve a good Correspondence between the two Houses: And said, that their Lordships do insist upon their Amendments to Clause B, by this House added to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better Security of her Majesty's Person and Government, and of the Succession to the Crown of England in the Protestant Line, for the Reasons following; viz.

The Lords insist upoa the second and third Amendments, made by them to the Clause, marked B, Press 1. L. 13, and 14, which relate to the repealing the Clause in the Act, intituled, An Act for the further Limita- tion of the Crown, and the better preferring the Rights " and Liberties of the Subject," whereby Persons, having Offices or Places of Profit, or Pensions from the Crown, are made incapable of serving as Members of the House of Commons;

First, Because they conceive, that the said general disabling Clause ought to be repealed, as inconsistent with the Nature and Constitution of the English Government. For to enact, that all Persons, employed and trusted by the Crown, shall, for that Reason alone, become uncapable of being trusted by the People, is in effect to declare, that the Interests of the Crown, and of the People, must be always contrary to each other; which is a Notion, no good Englishmen ought to entertain.

Secondly, They think, such a Clause is manifestly injurious to the People of England, who are the proper Judges of what Persons are fit to represent them in the House of Commons; and therefore a Clause, which, in so great a measure, deprives the Electors of their Freedom in chusing, seems to be built upon a Supposition, that the People are become either so corrupt, or so ia-sensible, that they ought no longer to be trusted, in the same Manner, they have always hitherto been, with the Choice of their own Representatives, and may often deprive them of the Service and Assistance of the most valuable Men in the Kingdom; for that will always be the Cafe, when the Crown makes a right Choice, in filling Offices with Gentlemen of Interest, Probity, and Understanding.

Thirdly, The Lords apprehend, that the excluding Officers from fitting in the House of Commons may tend to increase the Number of Pensions there; which, they think, would be infinitely of‘more dangerous Consequence.

Fourthly, The Act made in the last Reign, for the frequent Meeting and Calling, of Parliaments, was intended, and seems to be, an effectual Security against any real Prejudice to the People, by introducing an excessive Number of Officers into the House of Commons: For the Nation, having such frequent Opportunities of new Elections, may help themselves at pleasure, by lessening the Number of Officers, or totally forbearing to chuse any of them; and this they certainly will not fail to do, as soon as they find them to be a Grievance.

Fifthly, The Government has subsisted happily, for many hundred Years, without any disabling Law of this Nature; and the Lords have observed, that the clamorous Discourses, spread about, in relation to the great Number of Officers fitting in Parliament, have been chiefly since the late happy Resolution; and yet within the Compass of that Time more excellent Laws have been made, for declaring, and securing, the Rights and Liberties of the People, and the Freedom of Parliaments, than in the Course of some Ages before; which does ' demonstrate, that there has been hitherto no Mischief from Persons in Office; and gives the Lords Cause to think, that such Clamours, though they may have created some Prejudice in the Minds of well-intentioned Persons, yet took their true Rife from ill-designing Men, who observed, with Regret, theaftive Zeal, with which those, who were in Employments under the Crown, 23 supported

Pensions may be so precarious, that this Consideration alone may be allowed to affect Mens Votes, at least as much as an Office.

Sixthly, The Form and Method of the Amendment, made by the House of Commons, in naming such Officers, as they are willing should lit among them, and letting the general disablingClause remain as to all others, can never be reduced to such a Certainty, as may rea-l'onably be agreed to If the Lords had agreed to the Amendment, as it was sent up by the House of Commons, great Numbers would have been made uncapable of fit ting in Parliament, whom the Commons never intended to exclude. The Lords could still enumerate many other Officers, to whose Continuance in the House, they believe, the Commons could have no Manner of Objection, or, at least, for whose Exclusion no good Reason can be alleged; and many more may be involved in the same Misfortune, who may not now be called to mind. There needs no greater Demonstration, that this may be, than that, after the House of Commons had sent up the Clause B, in which they enumerated all the Officers, they then thought fit to allow to fit, and which they continue to say, in the Reasons delivered at the last Conference, was a competent Number, they have nevertheless, by an Amendment, made to their own Amendment, allowed many hundreds of other Officers to be capable of fitting, who flood absolutely excluded by their Amendment, as it was first sent up to the House of Lords.

Lastly, The Lords can never agree to this new Amendment, made by the House of Commons to their Clause B, as it was delivered at the last Conference, because that would be to admit, that the House of Commons cart amend an Amendment, made by themselves; than which nothing is more plainly against the Custom of Parliament, and the known Course of Proceedings between the two Houses, which, the Lords think, ought to be ever kept sacred. This Course of Proceedings is founded upon undeniable Reason: For if either House might be admitted to amend their own Amendments, it would directly tend to make Proceedings between the two Houses endless, and introduce all Sort of Confusion and Disorder in passing of Bills.

The Lords infill upon their 6th Amendment, Line 38;

Because the same is adapted to their former Amendment.

The Lords do also insist upon their 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, itth, and 12th, Amendments;

Because these depend upon the other Amendments, on which the Lords have infilled: For they cannot think it reasonable, that any Disabilities, or Incapacities, should take place in respect to a Parliament, before that Time duly thofen, and which had fat; much less in respect to a Parliament, continued only for six Months, to obviate Difficulties, which may occur to the Successor, and to preserve the publick Peace at so critical a J undure, as that of her Majesty's D'emife without Issue: And, on the other hand, the Lords think it reasonable, that such new Incapacities, as are thought necessary to be ordained, ought to take plaice as soon as may properly be, to the end it may the sooner appear, whether such Alterations will be justified by Experience.

And the said Reply, and Minutes, are, as follow; viz. Vo 1.51.

The same of the Wine Merchants, humbly laid before the Right honourable Sidney Lord Lord High Treasurer of England, together with a Reply to the late Report of the Commissioners of her Majesty's Customs.

YOUR Lordship t#ing pleased to signify, by Mr.-Lowndes, to the Commissioners of her Majesty's Customs, that you referred to them the Allegations of our last Petition, and ordered them to lay before your Lordship a true State of the Matter of Fadl, together with their Opinion, what was fit to be done therein; we humbly crave Leave to reply to the Mistakes they have made.

Be pleased to allow us to intermingle those Hardships, wherewith we have struggled.

By reason of the Credit, that was formerly given at the Custom-house to the Wine Merchants, they were, upon Presumption of having the same Credit continued, encouraged to enlarge their Importations.

These larger Importations proved to the great, and foie, Advantage of the Crown; and, to carry them on, the Merchants did export great Quantities of Corn, and Woollen Manufactures, to Spain and Portugal, the Produce of which could not be brought home in several Years.

But after they had thus dispersed great Part of their EffeCls abroad, and lodged great Part of the rest in the Hands of the Vintners at home (from either of which they could not raise Money) they, though they could not recall this their expanded Trade, were surprized by an Order of the Lords of the Treasury, which required speedier Payment, than had been usual.

However, they did to their utmost comply therewith, and paid in their Money as fast as they could raise it; but, that they might hasten their Payments, they were forced to press the Vintners to that Degree (who used to have longer Credit) and thereby broke many, who would have flood; and the Merchants thus, not only ruined many Vintners, but also lost their own, otherwise, good Debts; and by this Means several of the Merchants were likewise broke.

The Merchants loft besides by the Wines they had by them; for few Persons in the Wine Trade buying with ready Money, and Wine being no staple Commodity, they, to comply with that Order, were forced to fell their Wines at publick Sales, and fold them (though they were found, and such, as had paid the full Duty) for less than the Customs they had paid for them. This they did by Wines, which, in their ordinary Course of Trade, they should have got Profit by.

Soon after the War broke out; and then great Part of their Estates were seized in Spain, as well as their Ships were taken by the Enemy, and destroyed by the many violent Storms.

They have greatly suffered by the late additional Duty, which has been. paid wholly by the Importers, the Merchants being not able to get one Peny the more for their Wines.

They have suffered for want of a regular Convoy from Portugal; because, on that Account, their Ships, which lhpuld have been here in December, or January at far-theft, have not come, these last three Years, till , and September; and thereby their Wines have been lo decayed, that great Part of them would not pay the Custom.

They have likewise suffered by having great Quantities of Port and Viana White Wines on their Hands; these bearing a very'low Price, now there are so many French Prize White Wines to be had, great Quantities of which have been fold for less Money, than the Custom of a Tun of Portugal Wine amounts to.

They have further suffered by the Sale of all Prize Wines in general; because the Vintners, and Coopers, have bought those Wines with the Money, with which they should have paid the Merchants.

It is impossible to carry on the Wine Trade, without giving treble the Credit, that is given to the Merchants

by

Bonds given for Duties,

144 r 20Februarii. . 1705.

by the Crown; and so the Merchants arc obliged to trust Vintners, not only with the first Cost, £ of their Wines, but allb with what they have paid at the Custom-house; and yet the Merchants receive no ready Money, but generally trust the Vintners 18 Months, or more, though responsible Men; and this they do, without receiving any Interest.

There are but few Merchants, can make any considerable Importations on their own Stocks; and yet, if they could, that Stock, though very large, would thus in one Year's Importation be, for the moll part, in the Vintners Hands, and there being no dependence on their Payments, to carry on the ensuing Year's Importation} so that, if the Wine Merchants are hardly used, and have not Credit given them at the Custom-house, they cannot make any considerable Importations, and by consequence the Revenue will fink.

Added to their other Hardships, their Credit (which is of the last and greatest Importance to Merchants) hath been unnecessarily exposed, the Commissioners of the' Customs having tent their Officers, to post on the Pillars of the Exchange an Order, therein certifying, That, if the Wine Merchants did not immediately pay off their Bonds at the Custom-house, Prosecutions would come out against-them; and this at a Juncture, that struck at the Root of their Credit: Many of them, before that Time, had Credit, to draw Bills for what their Occasions required; but after this, no Wine Merchants Bills (for a Considerable time) would (whether they had Bonds unpaid, or not) be taken; and, for this Reason, they could not value themselves on their Effects abroad.

The said Commissioners also sent to the Office of the Custom-house, where they pais their Entries, a List of the Wine Merchants Names, who were in Bonds at the Custom-house, and ordered (contrary to Law) the Entries of such Merchants should be stopt. This (their Ships being the n, in the River) put them to the last Extremities; for others, who seldom paid (one with another) £. 100 per Annum, could pass their Entries, whilst those, that paid from to £. 6,000 per , were exposed. These two last mentioned Hardships were the Foundation of almost all our Misfortunes.

That the Commissioners do not allow, that the same of Smalley comes up to the Point, the Merchants cannot but wonder; for, whereas they are pleased to report to your Lord ship, that he broke, and therefore they were obliged to abate him a great Part of the Principal, they affirm, he paid his whole Principal, and had his Bonds delivered up, without paying Interest; nor did he abscond, till the Commissioners ordered the Extent: And the said Smalley was more capable of paying Interest, than many of your present Petitioners; for though his Effects were at that Time abroad, and he could not then, without felling Part of his Estate, pay his Bonds, yet, when his Bonds were delivered up, without paying Interest, he had still an Estate left in England, besides his Effects abroad.

And here we humbly refer to the publick Books, which will demonstrate, how great a Disadvantage it will be to the Revenue, to discourage the Wine Merchants from giving Bonds. Without giving Bonds, Importations will be (for the above Reasons) almost destroyed; and yet the Crown hazards little by Bonds, the Extent (though other Creditors lose all theirs) securing^generally die whole Debt of the Crown; and the bad Debts, the Crown makes, are inconsiderable, in proportion to what every Man makes in his private Trade.

Permit us to set down, that in the Years 1700 and 1701 (which was the Time the Wine Merchants were made easy, and allowed Time for the Payment of their Bonds) the Customs amount to X. 888,073. 14;. 3 d. but since that Time they have funk almost half in half; the two last Years (notwithstanding the late additional Duty) amount to but £. 529,323. 3*. 4 whereas, had the Merchants had their usual Credit continued to them, they would have very much increased their Importations

from Portugal and Italy, and to have paid almost as much Custom, as in time of Peace.

As to the Interest, which the Commissioners report to have been paid by some Merchants of , it is

humbly hoped, that That will be no Precedent; by reason that those, who did comply, were not general Traders, and the Sums, they paid, were small, the whole not amounting to the Interest of s Bonds.

As to the Merchants of the Out-ports, they paying £. 4. ioj. per Tun less Duty, than the Merchants in London, can better afford it j and besides, they have many other Advantages in Trade, which the Merchants in London are deprived of.

Little Wine being exported, and consequently little Drawback thereon, it is humbly hoped, will make the Wine Merchants appear, as they are, the better Tenants to the Crown.

But the Wine Merchants have Debentures for many other Commodities, which they export, and also Certificates for Allowances on damaged Wines, which they have paid into the Treasury at the Custom-house, on account of their Bonds, now standing out against them; for these they have not had any Interest, though many of them were of as old a Date, as their Bonds.

It is a farther Hardship on the Wine Merchants, that, they have not the same Advantage, that the Importers of other Commodities have: For when their Commodities come to a bad Market in England, they can export them, and are allowed their Drawback, which is near the full Custom; but the Wine Merchants, who import found Wine, which, after they have paid the full Duty, decay on their Hands, cannot, by exporting those Wines, obtain the same Advantage; which if they could, the Drawback would be more than the Value of such decayed Wines.

What Encouragement there may be, when there is an open Trade, they -cannot pretend to prophesy; but humbly presume, that during this War, there is most occasion for Money, and therefore the greater Reason to encourage the present Importers.

The greater Encouragement is given them, the greater will be their Importation; which will make Wine cheaper, less encourage Retailers to sophisticate, and consequently consume more neat Wine, and thereby, of Course, increase the Revenue.

If the Discouragement, and Lodes, the Wine Merchants have met with (which have funk their Estates} are not considered, and relieved. Men, who are new Undertakers, and not acquainted with the Wine Trade, will (carce expect to succeed; for the many careful Merchants, who have gained Experience both at home and abroad, will be miserable Examples, how unlikely it is for them to thrive by trading in Wine.

As to what the Commissioners are pleased to report, concerning Wine Merchants having received Interest from the Crown, when they were, by Bonds, indebted to the fame; they own, the Charge very heavy, but at the same time solemnly declare, that they never received any such Interest.

As for the solemn Settlement the Commissioners are pleased to report, that the Wine Merchants agreed to; they know nothing of any such, nor did they ever (well knowing the Wine Trade could not bear it) sign any such Petition, wherein they agreed to pay Interest: They did indeed promise more pundual Payment of their Bonds for the future, and they have done their utmost to comply therewith; but, if the many unforeseen recited Accidents, and Hardships, have disabled them, they hope, your Lordship (since Care and Industry hath not been wanting on their Part) will, from your own innate Justice and Compassion, excuse them.

As to those, which trade with ready Money; they not only trade £.8 per Cent, cheaper than those, which

trade upon Credit, but they also chuse their Customers; and upon both these Accounts are greater Gainers than Traders upon Credit: And we dare appeal to the

Custom-

Custom-house Books for Profit of, that the Traders upon Credit have moil advanced the Revenue.

Before we conclude, we cannot but with great Grief, acquaint your Lord ship, that near one fourth Part of the Wine-merchants, who in 1700 made their Application to the Treasury, have since failed, and ten times the Number of Vintners (who might in all Probability, for the most part have continued their Trade, and paid all their Debts, had not their Credit been so exposed, and torn in Pieces, by the aforementioned Hardships) have also broke.

We beg Leave further to acquaint your Lordship, that many of your present Petitioners, who have struggled with all these Inconveniencies, and with the greatest Difficulties, and paid their Principal, will inevitably be reduced to the Condition of the aforesaid afflicted
