The preceding Minute is read to them: They earnestly press that instead of 25th March next, it may be the First Day of next Trinity Term; and promise to make no Application for further Favour, if they do not comply by that Time. Mr. Clayton (according to Order) reported from the Committee, to whom the Petitions, relating to the Trade to Newfoundland, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are, as follow; viz.

That the said Committee, having taken into their Consideration the Answer from the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations to an Order of this House, as also several Petitions, to them referred, ordered several Papers to be laid before them, in relation to the said Trade, and examined several Witnesses to the Occasions of the Loss, that England now sustains in the said Trade, and received their Opinions, how the same may be retrieved, and improved; viz.

Mr. Roope; who said, that he has been an Inhabitant of St. John's Harbour, in , for many

Years, the Trade whereof is now almost overrun by the french; for that they having a strong Fort and Garison at Placentia, to secure their Shipping, and proteCl their Trade, the French fend their Convoys, and fishing Ships, early in the Year to Newfoundland; whereby they are able to compleat their Fishing, and return home, and to the foreign Markets, a Month or two sooner than the English j and by their Strength have driven the English from, and possessed themselves of, the best Bays and fishing Banks, in that Bland; and more particularly, that Captain Lloyd, then (and now again) Commander

of Fort William at St. John's, and the Forces there, having used the Soldiers in that Garison very barbarously, near thirty of the Soldiers at times, deserted and went to the French at Placentia; and in January last the French by them knowing the Circumstances of the English at St. John's surprized the Harbour by Night, murdered several Inhabitants, and plundered the rest, carrying away from thence, and other Harbours, to the Value ofj£. 100,000. and laid Siege for five Weeks to the Fort; but by the Courage and Conduct of Captain Moody, the then Commander, the Fort was preserved, and the French retired.

That he, the said Roope, was, amongst some other of the said Inhabitants, carried Prisoner to Placentia; where

25

he got Intelligence, that the French King had resolved a total Reduction of the English trading in that Island.

Captain Moody gave the Committee an Account of his Garison, and the Siege he sustained five Weeks, with 50 Men, against 600 French Canadians and Indians, loling but two Men in the Siege (excepting twelve, thatperished with the cold, in doing their Duty) killing (according to the best Account he could have) about 200 of the Enemy, when they retired, committing many Barbarities upon the English Planters, in their Return: And laid before the Committee his Journal marked A, of his whole Proceedings, whilst he was Commander of the said Fort, which was about fifteen Months, he succeeding Captain Lloyd; and was brought home, to make room for the said Lloyd again, but never knew, or saw, any Order for the lame. And the said Captain Moody laid before the Committee two Certificates, marked B, from the Inhabitants, and Commanders of Ships, of his Behaviour during his Command in Newfoundland.

Several of the Soldiers of the said Garison laid a Representation in Writing before the Committee, marked C; whereby, among other Grievances, they complain, that, when Captain Lloyd came to the Command of the said Fort, there was eight Months Subflstence due to the Garison, which he had received; but, denying the fame, prevailed with them to allow him one half, to pay them the other; which he did, but it was in Goods, at extravagant Rates; whereby they were deprived of near |ths of their said Subflstence:

And that it was customary for him to let the Soldiers to hire, in the Fishing Season, at £. 16 per Head, taking the Money to himself, and pretending to allow them the Valueofj£. 6 in Goods, and Cloaths, as aforesaid, which were not worth 50 s.as by the said Representation, marked C, more fully appears.

Doctor Jackson, Minister of the said Island, laid

before the Committee a Representation, marked D, of the Fort and Trade of the said Island, with Complaints against the said Uoyd, and his Garison.

Mr. Campbell said, that the French have settled 250 Indians upon our Parts, about Trinity Bay, and annoy the English in Summer as well as Winter, and have murdered many of the Inhabitants; and referred the Committee to the Representations of the Merchants, laid before the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, marked E.

Mr. Comins, Merchant, also laid a Representation of the Newfoundland Trade before the Committee; and the same was read, marked F.

Mr. Roope likewise laid before the Committee a Representation of a Constitution from Newfoundland in the Winter Season, marked G.

Commodore Bridge said, that when he was at Newfoundland in September, 1704, upon the Complaint of the Garison, of the intolerable Hardships they had suffered under Captain Lloyd (their then Commander) and that if the Commodore would not remove him, they would unanimously desert to the Fr; to prevent which, he commanded Captain Lloyd on board him, and left Lieutenant Moody Commander of the Place in his Room; who had a very good Character, not only from the Garison, but the Inhabitants also.

That he brought the said Lloyd from Newfoundland into England; who, upon his arrival here, made an Interest to reinstate himself again in his Roft at Newfoundland; whither he was sent in November last; and there told the said Bridge, that he had been at a great Expence in making such his Interest in England, but that he was resolved, the Inhabitants of Newfoundland should pay the same, and also what Losses he had sustained thereby; and that he had made such an Interest in England, that he would keep his Government there three Years.

That he has often went into, and come out of, the Fort, and has not sten any one Centinel upon Duty, under Lloyd's Command.

4 Ann. 12° Februarii. 147

That, notwithstanding this Testimony against Captain Lloyd, itappeared byAtteftations of the laid Commodore Bridge, which he himself gave in writing to the Commissioners for Trade, upon Lloyd‘s being brought into England (marked H) bearing date the 12th September, the 13th October, and the 6th December, 1704; viz.

That Captain Lloyd has at all Times acted like a Man of Honour, and good Governor, and given good Encouragement to the Industry of the People, and Fishery; and that by his prudent Management the Desertion of many of the Garison in Newfoundland was prevented; and that they desire, for the Good of that Country, that the said Captain Lloyd may be continued amongst them; but that he should repair to England, to represent the Uneasiness of the Garison in Newfoundland, because not relieved; which was-the foie, and no other, Reason, for his being ordered for England.

That, as to the improving, and securing, the said Trade, by what fell from the Opinions of divers Merchants, and others, attending the Committee, it appeared to be necessary, that fishing Ships to Newfoundland should not be liable to Embargoes, and the Men therein to be free from pressing, upon the outward-bound Voyages.

And, for the security of the said Trade, some were of opinion, that there ought to be four Forts, besides St. John's, in Newfoundland, viz. one at Ferryland, another upon Carbonier Island, another at Trinity Bay, and another at Bonnavice', for the Inhabitants to retire to

in the Winter, with their Effects, from their various Coves, and fishing Places, which are at remote Distances upon the said Island.

But Colonel Richards, an Engineer, and who was several Years Commander of St. John's, was of Opinion, that, as Forts would be very chargeable to the Government, he thought them useless; for that in Winter, when they should be useful, they can be but a flender Security; because, as all Ditches about such Forts must be filled with Snow, it would be easy for a Body of Men to enter the Forts; and that he could think of no better Way, than to repel Force by Force, by equalling at least, if not outhumbering, the Enemy.

And that, upon the Consideration of the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Conservation, and Encouragement, of the Fishery and Trade to Newfoundland, is of the greatest Importance and Advantage to this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the French have encroached upon us in Newfoundland, and possessed themselves fix Parts in seven of that beneficial Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the uncertain, and unseasonable, failing of the Convoys to and from Newfoundland, has been a great Dif-couragement ^nd Disadvantage to that Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That theimprelfing of Sailors, and Fishermen, employed in that Fishery, has been very prejudicial to that Trade, and ought to be prevented.

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That our present Scarcity of Seamen, and the increase of the French Seamen, antes chiefly from the visible Decay of our Newfoundland Fishery, and the Growth of theirs.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the better carrying on, and securing, the said Trade, there be fix Convoys, of fourth Rate Ships of War, yearly appointed: one to go with the Ships for Salt, to Portugal, by the 10th of February, and two to go with the fishing Ships by the 10th of March, from the Southern Channel, and one from Milford Haven, for the North fishing Ships (those Convoys to cruize, when at Newfoundland) and two other Convoys more, to go with the Sack Ships by the aoth of May, that the billing Ships may return by the 20th of September yearly.

Mr. Clayton reported from the Committee, to whom Newfound-, it was referred to draw up an humble Address, to be land Tradtf presented to her Majesty, in relation to the Newfoundland Trade; that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the feme was twice read, and is, as followeth; v

May it please your most Excellent Majesty:

WE, your Majesty's most loyal and dutiful Subjects, the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled, humbly take Leave to represent to your Majesty, that the Conservation, and Encouragement, of the Fisherjj and Trade of Newfoundland, is of the greatest Importance and Advantage to this Kingdom.

That the Encroachments of the French, the Accidents of the War, and the Uncertainty of Convoys, have very much impaired this Fishery; for the restoring whereof to its former Condition, nothing can more contribute, as we humbly conceive, than a certain and fealbnable Departure of the Convoys to and from Newfoundland, with Protections for the Seamen, and Fishermen, employed in that Trade; which is the best Nursery of Seamen for this Kingdom, and is so likewise to the French, whose Naval Force is much increased thereby.

We do therefore most humbly recommend to your Majesty this so beneficial Trade; and pray, that, for the better carrying on, and Security, thereof, your Majesty would be graciously pleased to give the necessary Orders, that timely Convoys, of good Strength, be appointed yearly for this Trade, as well for the Merchant Ships, going to Portugal for Salt, as for the Fifiling Ships, failing from the South and North Chanel, as likewise for the Sack Ships; which Convoys, when arrived

4 Ann.

i6° Februarit.

I5S

rived at Newfoundland, may cfuize upon that Coast, and protest the several Harbours from the Enemy, and return, as early as may be, with the Fithing Ships from thence; and that your Majesty would give such further Directions, for the Preserva'tion of this Fishery, as to your Majesty, in your great Wisdom, and provident Care . of your good Subjects, trading to shall

seem meet.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Address.

'Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

Army Mr. Bacon reported from the Committee, to whom Arrears! the Report of the Petition of the Commission and Non-commission Officers, and Soldiers, now or late belonging to the Regiment, commanded by the honourable Brigadier Villiers, afterwards by Major-general Leveson, and now by Major-General Harvey, on behalf of themselves, and of the rest, now in Service in Portugal, was committed, the Matter, as it appeared to them, which they had directed him to report to the House j which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is, as followeth; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, by the Accounts x>f the Lord Coningsby, and Mr. Fox, late Paymasters of the Forces in Ireland, that the Money, paid for cloathing the said Regiment, by Assignments, and otherwise, from the First of September, 1689, to the First of April, 1692, amounts to more than the Off-reckonings for that Time, by jC-3*555- oj* 3^- an<i that the 259 Horses, proved to be loft by two Misfortunes, mentioned in the said Petition, remain charged to the Regiment, for £.2,590, both amounting to£.6,145. os. but by the Book of the late Commissioners, appointed by Act of Parliament to state the Accounts of the Army, there appears only £.3,875. i8j. icf d. to be proportioned, and charged an Article of Deficiency in the Account of each Officer, and of each Troop j which is the exact Sum petitioned for.

That it likewise appeared, that the said late Commissioners did, pursuant to the Authority given them by the said Act, give Certificates for Debentures to the said Regiment, to the full of what was due to them upon the Establishment; but they had no Power to give Certificates for Debentures for Losses, which happened to that Regiment, which have been usually paid by contingent Warrants.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I CANNOT but take this Occasion to return you my hearty Thanks for the great Care and Concern you have shewn, to promote every thing in this Session, that may tend to the publick Good.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I inult thank you, in particular, for your having (o fully complied with your Assurances to me at the opening of this Parliament, that you would give all possible Dispatch to the publick Supplies. There is scarce any ' Instan'ce to be given, where so great, and I hope, effectual. Supplies have been perfected in so short a Time.

I look upon this to proceed, not only from your great Zeal for the publick Service, but from a just Imprelnon upon your own Minds, that there is a Necessity of making

Sir William Strickland reported from the Committee, importing appoined to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Lords certain at a Conference, for disagreeing to the Amendments, made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to *. impower 'Thomas Cary and George Hatley, of London, Mer- Lords chants, to import the Remainder of a Quantity of French Amend-Wine from Copenhagen, contrafted for before the first menU* Day of January, 1704; that they had drawn up the same accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

The Commons disagree to your Lordships Clause, marked A.

ift, Because the Trade to Portugal is now the most advantageous to England, by our exporting vast Quantities of Woollen Manufactures, Corn, Tin, Lead,

Leather, from hence, and Fish from Newfoundland, and importing chiefly Wine, and Oil, and other useful Commodities; notwithstanding which, the Balance of Trade rests so much on our Side, that we have always Effects there ready to supply our Army, and that of our Allies, with a large Overplus.

idly, Because the Traders to Portugal, relying upon the Act prohibiting the Importation of French Wines, have sent, and are now fending out English Manufactures, to a very considerable Value, in return for which they have ordered Wines of the Growth of Portugal, and freighted Ships for that Use; so that, if your Lordships Clause should pass, it will be of fatal Consequence to those concerned in that Trade.

3dly, Because the said Merchants, and others, are now settling a Trade and Correspondence with Catalonia, and other Parts of Spain, which have declared for King Charles the Third, and are now fending several Ships, laden with our Manufacture, to return with Wine and Fruit from thence; which the Liberty, granted by your Lordships Clause, will put a flop to, and thereby wholly destroy the Prospect of that beneficial Trade.

4thly, Because it will not only encourage our Enemies, and discourage our Allies in Portugal and Spain, but will create greater Difficulties to the Nation, in paying the Armies abroad, and remitting the Subsidies to our Allies.

5thly, Because your Lordships Clause repeals several Acts of Parliament, which are found to be very beneficial to the Trade of this Kingdom.

The Commons disagree to your Lordships Amendment in the Title,

Because it relates to, and depends upon, Clause A.

[Riots in the Mint.]

Sir Gilbert Heathcot, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of William Hucks, Esquire, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the late riotous Proceedings in the Mint in Southwark, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was read, and is, as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, having taken the said Petition into their Consideration, took the Examination of the several Persons following; viz.

Mr. Edward Rooke, Constable, said, that he was present, when a Warrant, signed by the Commissioners of Bankrupt, issued against Thomas Jones, was carried to the Mint, supported by two Warrants under the Hands of four Justices of the Peace, with 20 Constables more, in order to regain a Parcel of Beer, that the said Jones had procured Credit for from the Petitioner, and carried into the Mint; and when he, with the rest of the said Constables, came to the Mint Gate, they were met by a great Number of Minters, in a riotous Manner, armed with Clubs and Staves, and told them, that they should go no further, till they told them their Business; which they did do, and shewed them the said Warrants; but, notwithstanding, they opposed the said Constables, and knock'd down one of the Messengers, to whom the Commissioners of Bankrupts Warrant was directed.

That, when they came to one Baylye's House, where they suspected some of the Beer to be, he, looking out of the Window, told them with many Oaths and Imprecations, that, if any Person laid his Hand upon his Door, of Window, he would fire upon them; and accordingly did so, and shot one of the Company in the Eye, through a low Window, and fired at them again in the Cellar.

That afterwards they went to one Mason's House, where they found some of the Petitioner’s Beer; but one Pledwell, a Minter, dared any Person to touch the same, at their Peril: And the Rioters threatened, that, if the Constables offered to take any one out of the Mint they would knock all the Constables Brains out; and that the said Justices might be damn’d: Upon which Threats, they thought it Prudence to retire.

Mr. John Barnes said, that he being with some Company at the Vine Tavern in the Borough, two or three Days after the said Riot, a Body of the Minters, with one Bayly, with a drawn Sword, at the Head of them, forced into the Room, where he was, and swore, they were the Villain Hucks’ Friends, and, if they would not deliver him up to them, to be pumped, and undergo the Law of the Mint, they would serve them, as they would him, when they caught him; but Mr. Keeling, the Master of the Tavern, with great Intreaties persuaded them to retire; which, after some Time they did; but, in their Way went to the said Mr. Barnes’ House and Brewhouse in the Mint, and forced the same, to search for the said Hucks, and voted him out their pretended Society; and such of them, as were his Debtors (he being a common Brewer there) bound themselves under an Oath, that they would never pay him one Farthing of their Debts; which will prove his Rub, if he cannot be remedied therein.

170 23° Februarii. A. 1705.

[Riots in the Mint.]

That the said Minters have several Clubs, and a Chairman presiding amongst them, being attended by Beadles and Constables of their own making, by whom they send for the Offenders of their Laws; as one of which was he, the said Barnes, so sent for, when voted out of their said Society, as aforesaid.

---

Mr. Gwynne said, that Bayly, Jones and Shrimpton, were the three Ringleaders of the Minters, when they came a second Time to search for Mr. Hucks, who narrowly escaped them.

Mr. Ladd, and several other Justices of the Peace, being acquainted with the said Riot, told the Committee, that they sent out their Warrants, with about Twenty Constables, with a Precept to inquire into the said Riot.

Mr. John Darby, one of the said Constables, said, that he went with his Fellow-constables to take up the Persons of the Rioters named therein; but they were opposed by above 100 of the Minters, with one Jones, Powell, and Shrimpton, at the Head of them, all armed with Clubs and Staves, and the very Persons, named in the Warrants, amongst them.

That they having seized the said Shrimpton, the said Minters rescued him again, and cried out that they would one and all stand by him, although the said Shrimpton has had two Warrants issued out against him for high Treason.

Mr. Clifford, the Beadle, said, that he, knowing the said Minters, mentioned in the Warrants, told their Companions who they were, and advised them to deliver them up to Justice; but they, with horrid Curses, refused so to do, saying, they would first sacrifice their Lives, by endeavouring to destroy all the said Constables, before any one of their Members should be carried out of the Mint.

Mr. Yewen, an Officer of the Marshalsea, said, that he some Time since arrested a Gentleman in the Mint, got him out from thence, and hurried him to the Waterside, into a Boat, was pursued by the Minters, who lined the Shore, and endeavoured to intercept him; whereupon he ordered the Boat to land him, and his Prisoner, at Trigg's Stairs, and there got him into a Coach, in order to secure him in the City; but the Minters overtaking them, knock’d down one of the Coach-horses, and carried off the Prisoner. The same Night, the said Yewen going to bed about Ten a Clock, a Number of the Minters came, and surrounded his House, and threatened to murder him; to avoid which, he got out at the Top of the House; and they then, in revenge, threatened to pull down his House, got into his Cellar, and what Drink and Brandy they could not devour, they let run about, the Cellar (he keeping a publick House) to his great Loss.

Mr. King, another Constable, said, that one of the said Minters having made an Assault upon two Men, and one of them being thought to be murdered, the said Minter was committed for Murder to the County Goal; whither he, with eight more of his Assistants, endeavouring to carry him, a Mob of the said Minters, and Queen's Benchers, rescued him, and carried him into their Gaol, to secure him; where, though he produced his Warrant, and demanded him, yet they refused to deliver him, and gave him an Opportunity of escaping in the Night.

Mr. Francis Smith, an Officer belonging to the Borough Court, said, that he went to summon a Jury to attend the Coroner in the Mint, where a Child was found murdered; and, when the Jury were sitting, a Body of the Minters, hearing of the Verdict of Murder, broke open the Door, where they were, and seized the said Smith, and pumped him at ten Pumps, and at six of them twice, and then threw him five Times into the black Ditch, being composed of human Filth; and when a Constable helped him out with his Staff, they threatened to serve him so, for his Compassion: And after the said Smith was out of the said Ditch (almost smothered) they made him lay his Hand upon a Brick, covered with Sir Reverence, and upon his Knees made him swear in these Words: "I Francis Smith am a Rogue in grain:

"And God damn my Body and Soul, if ever I come into the Mint again:" And then made him kiss the Brick, and drove him out of the Mint in a miserable Condition, with Scorn and Derision.

Mr. Robert Cook, Cornchandler, said, that he having some Houses in Westminster, one of his Tenants run in Arrear of Rent to £150 (having a Lease of his House) and then went into the Mint; where he going to him, to desire only his Delivery of the Key of the House, in order to let the same, his said Tenant gave out to the Minters, that he was a Bailiff; and, though be offered to prove himself otherwise, by Gentlemen they knew in the Borough, yet he was seized by eight Men, disguised in Canvas, and Masks upon their Faces, and by them pumped at ten or twelve several Places, and necked at every Pump; and after that crowned him with a Chamber Pot, full of Excrements, and then threw him into the said black Ditch, over Head and Ears; and after he had crawled out from thence, they made him roll himself in a great Heap of the same Filth, taken out of the said Ditch; by which Cruelty his Head was bruised and broken in several Places, his Ears filled with the said Filth, he almost lost both Sense of Sight, and Hearing, and with great Difficulty got to his own House; where he was constrained to keep his Bed many Days, the Physicians despairing of his Life, it being in November last.

Mr. Toegood said, that in January was twelve-months, he, going into the Mint, to demand Monies due to him, was given out to be a Bailiff, and seized by about twenty of the Minters, in Disguise; who cut his Cloathes off his Back, picked his pocket of Fifty Shillings, and then threw him three Times into the said black Ditch; where standing up to the Arms-pits, they made him dive three Times, once for the Queen, and twice for their honourable Society.

Mr. Ashe said, that last Week, having Business in Southwark, he saw a great Crowd of the Minters, who taxed him with being one of Mr. Hucks' Friends, and threatened to serve him, as they would have done Mr. Hucks; but he having the good Fortune to be protected by the Inhabitants of the Borough, who reproving them for such their barbarous Practices, and Threatenings, they insolently replied, that if the Lord Chief Justice Holt himself were there, they would pump him likewise, and give him the Law of the black Ditch.

The several Justices of the Peace, residing in the said Borough, acquainted the Committee, that, as the Law now stands, they have not sufficient Power to suppress these Riots and Disorders in or near the Mint.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolution following:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there ought to be some immediate Remedy found, to redress these extraordinary Riots and Disorders for the future.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that Traitors, Murderers, Felons, and other Criminals, as likewise several Persons sheltering themselves from their Creditors, within the Limits of the Mint in the Borough of Southwark, have assembled themselves in great Numbers, and are harboured and protected there with a strong Hand against Justice, in a riotous and tumultuous Manner, to the Obstruction, and in Defiance, of Justice; which Practices, if not timely prevented, may be of dangerous Consequence.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, humbly desiring her Majesty, graciously to give such Directions for prosecuting the Offenders in the Mint, in Southwark, according to the utmost Rigour of the Law.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

[Answer to address.]

Mr. Secretary Hedges acquainted the House, that their Address, in relation to the late riotous Proceedings in the Mint, in Southwark, having been presented to her Majesty; her Majesty was pleased thereupon to say, That she will forthwith give Directions for prosecuting the Offenders in the Mint, as is desired.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Newcastle under Line, in the County of Stafford, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as followeth j viz.

Upon the Petition of Crew Esquire, and John Lawton, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of Sir 'Thomas Bellott, Baronet, and Rowland Cotton, Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Newcastle under Line:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, or Freemen refient.

That, upon the Poll, the Numbers were.

For Sir Thomas Bellott — — 182.

For Mr. Cotton — — — 173.

For Mr. Offley — — — 168.

For Mr. Lawton — — — 138.

But the Petitioners Counsel infilled, that they should disqualify so many of the Sitting Members Voters, on account of Treating, and corrupt Practices, as would make the Petitioners have a great Majority: And to this they examined several Witnesses.

John Clowes laid, that one Robert Rhodes came to him, to the Swan, and pulled out nine Guineas and an half, and said, if he would vote for Sir Thomas Belloit and Mr. Cotton, they were at his Service; but he refused to take them: That afterwards he received two half Crowns of Richard Welsh, to drink the Sitting Members Healths: That Bourne afterwards met him, and offered him £. 5, for 2lb. of Fish, worth but two Groats, on account of his Vote for the Sitting Members; and that Mr. Burslem, the Receiver General of the County, offered him £. 10, for his Vote for them, to be paid him after the Election; but he laid, he would not trull: And that, about Six or Seven a Clock next Day, Mr. Welsh brought him £, 3, in Part of the 10, which he received; and the said Clows not being satisfied, that be bad not brought all the £. 10, told him, he

hoped, Mr, Burslem was sufficient to answer the Remainder: That he himself, and several others of the Sitting Members Voters, were treated at and

other Places, at several Times; and the said Treating was carried on till within three Days of the Election: And he gave an Account of about Thirty Persons, that had been treated; and he law Richard Wiljb, an Agent of the Sitting Member, pay a Reckoning. Clows voted for Sir Thomas Bellott, and Mr. Offley.

Thomas Eccles said, his Brother William gave him £. 5 to vote for Mr. Cotton, and Wm. Mac hell offered him 40 s.to be for Sir Thomas Bellott-, but he did not receive the 40 s.

Tho. Clows said, that at the latter End of April last; he was in Company with Thomas Bagnall and John Biddle, and also with one Joseph Lilly, who was an Agent of the Sitting Members: That the said Mr. desired of Bagnall and Biddle to give the Sitting Members their Votes; and they saying, they were engaged, Mr. Lilly offered, and paid, them £. 3 a-piece, to vote for the Sitting Members, and desired Clows to take notice of the Consideration, that, if they did not vote so, he might have the Money again; and that the said Lilly acknowleged, that he had received, fix- Guineas

of Sir Tho. Bellott:Bagnall and Biddle voted for the Sitting Members: That Lilly likewise threatened several Persons, that owed him Money, to fend them to Gaol, if they did not vote for the Sitting Members.

John Brougham said, that Richard Welsh had often solicited him to vote for the Sitting Members, and, about a Month before May Day, gave him 50 s. of Mr. Cotton's Money, to put out a Boy, on Condition he should vote for the Sitting Members, otherwise he would have voted for the Petitioners. He said, he bought a Cow with the 50 s.

Ralph Barker said, he was solicited several Times by Mr. Burslem to vote for the Sitting Members, and on that account, received 22 s. at twice, from John Holland, by the Direction of Mr. Burslem; but he voted for the Petitioners. He gave Evidence also of about Thirty Burgesses, and some of their Wives, who were treated at several Places within a Week of the Election, and some but three Days before the Election.

Tho. Dudley laid, he solicited Votes for the Sitting Members: That a Week before the Election he met with Sir Thomas Bellott, who asked him, if he had not an Interest in one Hall; and that he telling Sir Tho. Bellott, that Hall wanted Money, he had £. 10 brought him the next Day by John Richards, and Robert Rhodes, who bid him give it to Hall, or do what he would with it; lb he engaged his Vote for the Sitting Members: That he offered to lend the said Money to on the Condition of his voting, and to take Hall's Bond for the Re-payment of the same quarterly; and that Hall refilling to receive the Money upon those Terms, he afterwards met Sir Thomas Bellott, and acquainted him with it} and Sir Tho. Bellott bid him keep to the Text, and keep the Money himself: He voted for Sir Tho. Bellott and Mr. Offley; and said, since Michaelmas he had been sued for the Money.

That the Witnesses, examined by the Sitting Members Counsel, were, first, to invalidate the Petitioners Evidence. And to this Point they called

Ben. Owlton; who said, he had been with Thomas Dudley (examined on behalf of the Petitioners) in October last; and that Dudley told him, that Mr. Offley wanted Witnesses; and that he believed, he knew something of the Matter; and, if he would give Evidence for the Petitioners, he should have £. 100 or £. 50, for Seven Years, without Interest; and on that pulled a Letter from Mr. Offley out of his Pocket: And that he was also with Mr. Dudley, the Monday before he came from Neivcajllei and Dudley pulled out some Farthings and Halfpence, and said, he was to have so many Guineas for coming up to be a Witness.

Dudley was called, to confront him; and he, in a fblcmn Manner, denied what Owlton had charged him with: He owned, he had several Letters from Mr. Offley, but never any to that Effect,

Mr. Ra. Wood said, he was employed by John Richards to sue Dudley, for the ^.10 received of him; and that being arrested for it, he bad put in Bail; and having had some Discourse with Dudley about it, hedid not pretend, it was given him, but laid, he had Squandered it away, and he would take care to satisfy Richards.

' Richard Michell said, that Tho. Clows was a Person of

no Reputation, being a Labourer; and that he had taken some of Michell's. Goods, and fold them.

It appeared, that the late Duke of Sc bomberg, by a Warrant under his Hand, dated the 29th Day of July, 1689, directed to the Mayor and Sheriffs of the City of Chester, did require the said Mayor and Sheriffs to appoint a convenient Place for the Reception of the sick and wounded Soldiers, brought over from the Camp in Ireland.

Pursuant to which said Warrant, the said Mayor and Sheriffs, by the Advice of the Doctors and Surgeons, did appoint and take a large House belonging to the Petitioner, called the Grey , situate in the City of Chester, for the Use of the Soldiers; and that the said House and Ground thereto belonging, was made use of for the publick Service, as an Hospital for the said sick Soldiers, for several Years, as appeared by a Certificate under the Vo L. 15.

Hands of the said Mayor and Sheriffs, dated 21st January, 1691.

Sir Henry Dutton Colt reported from the Committee, Irish to whom the Petition of Captain Baird and William Arrtar‘* Hamill, Trustees for the Officers and Soldiers, who served in Londonderry, during the Siege there, in the Year 1689, and of such, during the late War in Ireland, as supernumerary Officers, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, having examined into the Allegations of the said Petition, do find, that the Services of the said Officers and Soldiers, in the Time of the Siege, was in a great measure the Occasion of reducing the whole Kingdom of Ireland to his late Majesty's Obedience.

That it appeared also to the Committee, by the Testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Stewart, Captain Edmunds, and several other Officers, who were in that City, during the Siege, that their Sufferings were very great, for several Persons, that were in the City during the Siege, to the Number of about 12,000, perished by Sword and Famine: That eight Regiments were in the City, some of which were Horse, especially Part of Colonel Baker's Regiment, but were at last reduced to Foot; such' being their Extremity, that they were forced to kill their Horles, and eat them: Afterwards they lived upon Tallow, Hides, and Starch, till such time as they were relieved by Major General Kirke.

That his late Majesty King William was so well latis-fied with their Services, that he promised them Compensation; and his Letter to Doctor Walker and Colonel Michelburne, dated the 16th of Auguj 1689, his Majesty was pleased to Use the Words following;

"We will therefore, that you rely on our royal " Favour towards you; and also, that in our Name you " assure the Officers, and Soldiers, and Inhabitants, of " that our City, that we will take fitting Occasions to " recompence their Services and Sufferings in ourCause,

" so that neither they, nor any other of our loving Subjeefts, shall ever have reason to repent them of a faithful Discharge of their Dut,-."

That it appeared, the Petitioners Father, Edmund Blancheville, was seised of a considerable Estate in Ireland, of the yearly Value of 700, which Estate was granted by his late Majesty (of glorious Mertiory) to the now Earl of Albemarle.

That by the Articles cf Limerick, all Persons, therein comprehended, were to enjoy their Estates, and to have their Outlawries and Attainders reversed.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that the said Edmund Blanchroil'e did claim the Benefit of the said

Articles; and on the 10th Day of July, 1694, he was heard on his said Claim, and was adjudged within the same; but the Commissioners for the Forfeitures alleging, he had taken Protection, Time was given till after Michaelmas then following, for the King's Counsel to be heard.

That accordingly, on the 26th of November, 1694, the Matter was again heard in Council; and, upon Debate, it was adjudged, by a Majority of fix against three, that the said Edmund Blancheville was within the Articles.

That on the 13th of Sep:ember, 1699, the Matter was again heard before the Council; who did again adjudge the said Edmund Blancheville to be within the Articles of Limerick, in the Words following; viz.

" This Day the Cause being again moved, and no " Cause being shewn by the King's Counsel, whereby " to alter us in our Opinion, we think fit to declare, " that nothing hath been made appear to us, or offered " by his Majesty's Counsel, or any other, whereby to " induce us to believe, that the said Edmund -

" ville did either take, or receive, Protection, or that he " ought, on that Account, to be excluded from the " Benefit of his Adjudication of being within the " Articles of Limerick."

That it appeared to the Committee, that, notwithstanding the aforesaid Adjudication, the late Trustees, for Sale of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, have seised, and fold the said Estate, which they valued at £. 643 per Annum.

That it appeared to the Committee, that, by the Marriage Settlement of Edmund Blancheville, the Sum ofj£. 1,400 was securedon the said Estate, for Portions for the Petitioners; but being advised, that the Estate was not forfeited, they omitted claiming the same j so that now the Petitioners are reduced to the utmost Extremity of Want and Misery.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution} viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition; and that they are real Objects of Companion, and justly deserve the Favour of the House.

Ordered, That the Report do lie upon the Table.'

Mr. Ducket reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of 'Thomas Fitz Richard AJUon (complaining of divers ill Practices in the Fleet Prison) was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, having examined Part of the Matters complained of, find the feme as follo.weth: a»

That, after several Orders of the Committee, served upon Anthony Grindall, Warden of the said Prison,

Robert Saunders, Register of the Marriages there, and other Officers, to produce their Accounts, Books, and Registers, of Marriages, Licences, and Certificates of Marriages, in the said Prison, and the Profits arising the reby, they at several Times produced several Books of Registers, as the true Books thereof, which, by the Face of the Books, and by Examination of Witnesses thereupon, appeared to the Committee to be sham Books, and not the true and secret Register kept there.

That many Marriages were omitted therein; many therein, without the Parson's Name, by whom married; many others, without the Degree, Quality, or Place of Abode, of the Parties married, as by the Act of the 6th Year of King William the Third, touching Marriages, they ought to be.

That it also appeared by the said Books, and Witnesses, that it is usual to have betwixt 20 and 30 Marriages there on a Day; and that, from the 19th Day of October,

1704, to the iath of February, 1705, 2,954 of such Marriages (besides those omitted) were there celebrated, at between 12 s.and aor. or more, per Couple.

That the said Officers have produced no Licences* Certificates of Banns, Certificates of Marriages, or Accounts thereof.

That there have been many Abuses therein, relating to the Subject; to wit, concealing, by private Marks in the said Books, the Marriages of such, as will pay for it; and giving Certificates of Marriage to such, as were never married.

That the said Warden, Register, and other Officers* have been privy to the said Marriages; and that they have received great Shares out of the Profits thereof.

That the said Paribas, Register, and forne other of the said Officers, concerned therein, are Prisoners to the said Warden; and that it was in the Power of the said.

Warden to have prevented the said Marriages.

That there are great Penalties, by several Acts of Parliament, on the Parsons, Register, Clerks, and Parties, fb marrying, or married; to wit, 100 on the Parson,

£. 100 on the Register, and Clerk; and 20 on the Husband married.

That by several Acts of Parliament there is due to the Queen, for every Licence of Marriage 5 r. for every Certificate of Marriage 5J. for the Marriage of every Person whatsoever, 2 s. 6 d.and, over and above, for the Marriage of every Person, worth £. 50 per Annum, or £. 600, aor. and for the Son of every such Person 10 x. and greater Duties on higher Degrees or Qualities.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolution following;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That the Queen has been defrauded of all, or the greatest Part of, t he Duties, due by the several Acts, on Marriages, Births, and Burials, by the unlawful Marriages-in the Fleet Prison, without Licence, or Certificates of the Banns of Marriage, which ought to have been paid ‘ for the said Marriages.

Ordered, That the Report do lie upon the Table.

Amendment of the Law.

Lords upon the Amendments, made by this House to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Amendment of the Law, and the better Advancement of Justice;

Ordered, That Mr. Compton, Sir , Lord

Comtingsby, Sir Tho. Littleton, Mr. , Sir Richard Onslow, Mr. Paget, Sir Thomas Powys, Mr Sir

Gtlbert Dolben, Sir John Haw/es, Mr. Mr. Brom-

ley, Mr, Winnington, Mr. Lowndes, Colonel Byerley, Mr. Coke, Lord Windsor, Mr. Scobell, do manage the said Conference.

And the Managers went to the Conference:

And being returned;

Sir Gilbert Dolben reported the Conference; and that it was managed by the Duke of; who acquainted

them, that the Lords have agreed to several of the Amendments, made by this House to the said Bill, and disagreed to others of them; for which they gave their Reasons: Which Reasons Sir Gilbert Dolben read in his Place, and delivered the Bill, and Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table; and the Reasons are as follow:

The Lords do not agree to the first Amendment, made by the Commons, Pr. id, Line 27, which is to leave out the Clause, requiring Attorneys to file their Warrants, as is thereby directed;

ift, Because Warrants of Attorney ought, by Law, to be filed upon Record.

2dly, This Law is founded upon good Reason: For Filing the Warrant is the proper Way of making it appear to the Court, who is the Attorney, that he may be liable to answer for Irregularities, and ill Practice; and also, that he has a sufficient Authority to act for the Party in the Suit.

3dly, The Suitor always pays for the Charges of filing the Warrant, and therefore the Attorney ought to be obliged to file it in due Time.

4thly, In most of the Statutes, made for Reformation of Jeofails, particular Care has been taken, to make Provision for the punishing the Neglect of filing Warrants of Attorney: And the Lords thought themselves the more obliged in the particular to follow the Example of former Parliaments, and to require the Warrant to be filed the same Term, the Attorney takes upon him to act by virtue of such Warrant;

1 ft, Because, among the many Cafes, to which Relief is given by this Bill, there is no Help, where a Warrant of Attorney is not duly filed:

idly, Because, although there are many Laws in this behalf, yet there has been of late a total Neglect of putting any of them in Execution.

The Lords agree to the 2d, 3d, 4th and 5th, Amendments, made by the Commons.

The sixth Amendment, made by the Commons whereby the Clause, impowering Courts of Law, after I flue joined, to examine such Witnesses, as cannot be present at the Trial, the Lords do not agree;

I ft, Because they take such a Power to be necessary, for the Advancement of Justice, and preventing Delays, which, in many Cafes, may be the Occasion of the intire Loss of the Party's Right, and are often of very ill Consequence, especially among Persons concerned in Trade, as well Plaintiffs, as Defendants: For the same Proof, which by this Clause is required, to enable the Courts of Law to take the Depositions of Witnesses, who cannot be present at the Trial, will be sufficient, as the Law now stands, to oblige the same Court to put off the Trial, till the Witnesses can return into England, or be restored to their Health, so as that they may be present at the Trial: The Inconvenience therefore of the Want of such a Power is manifest.

2dly, This Clause does make at least as full a Provision for a just Indifference in point of Examination of such Witnesses, as the Law has provided for all Examination of Witnesses, in Courts of Equity.

3dly, This Clause may prevent many tedious Suits in Courts of Equity: For when Persons cannot try their causesin due Time, by reason the Witnesses cannot be

present, they will be trying all Experiments, rather than lose the Testimony of their Witnesses.

4thly, This Clause is drawn with such Caution, that no Examinations can be taken in the Courts at Law, till after I flue be joined: and the Depositions can only be made use of upon the Trial of that Issue; nor even in that Cafe, if it falls out, that the Witnesses, who have been examined, can afterwards be personally present at the Trial, either by Recovery of their Health, or by the unexpected Delay of their Voyages.

The Lords have agreed to the several Amendments, made by the House of Commons, Pr. 4. Line 15th, L.

21, and Line the last; and also Pr. 6. Line 7 th, Line 8th, Line 20, Line 25, and Line 3 5.

The Lords have also agreed to the Amendment, Pr. 7th, Lihc 6; and to the Amendment Pr. 8th, Line 38.

As to the Amendment Pr. toth, whereby the Commons leave out from the Word " Heir" Line 8th, to the Word " and, " Line the last of that Press (which is the Clause relating to the Courts of Equity) the Lords do not agree, for the following Reasons:

That Clause consists of Three Parts:

As to the first; Part of that Clause, which requires the Bill to be filed with the proper Officer, before any Process be issued thereupon against any Defendant; the Lords conceive this Provision to be agreeable to Reason and Justice, and ancient Course in all Courts of Equ ty: For at the Conclusion of every Bill the Plaintiff prays the Court, that Process of Subpirna nuy issue, requiring the Defendants to appear; which demonstrates, that the Process ought to follow the Bill, and not go before it; and that the contrary Practice is a manifest Abuse, only tending to encourage Suits.

2dly, The restoring the Law in this particular will prevent many vexatious Delays, and great Expences, to the Parties, by taking away all Occasions of Disputes about the Regularity of filing of Bills, and about obtaining Costs, and other Questions relating to that Matter, which frequently happen.

3dly, The Lords believe, that this Method will prevent many causeless Suits, by obliging the Plaintiffs to advise with Counsel, in drawing and settling their Bills, before they begin to sue; for by this Means they will have Time to consider, and be well adviled, of the ilea-fonableness of their Pretences; whereas now they begin Suits, sometimes only with a Prospect of terrifying innocent Men to a Compliance, from a Dread of the Process, and at other Times they are drawn in to fend for Subpoena's by ignorant and vexatious Persons, who are to gain thereby: and so they seldom consider of the Cause of the Suit, till after it is begun.

4thly, The Lords hope, that no Regard to any Profits or Advantages, which may arise from the Increafeof the Number of Subpoena's, can have such Weight with the House of Commons, as to hinder them from giving Relief to the People of England, in lessening the Number of vexatious Suits.

As to the second Part of the Clause, which obliges the Plaintiff, in Courts of Equity, to serve the Defendant with a Copy of the Bill, at the same Time the Subpoena is served upon him; the Lords do not agree to leave it out of the Bill, because they conceive it to be reasonable, and to carry great Advantages along with it.

ift, It seems very convenient, that Defendants, at the same Time they are served with Process, should be made acquainted with the Matter, for which they are sued.

2dly, If the Plaintiff be obliged to give the Copy of the Bill, at his own Expence, to the Defendant, it is likely to be the most effectual Way to prevent the Tedi-oufness and Impertinence of Bills, which (as generally drawn) are a great Reproach to the Court, as well as an intolerable Vexation to the Suitor.

3dly, This would contribute to the Cure of another very general and great Abuse, in making many Persons Defendants, unnecessarily, and for Vexation only.

4thly,

5 Ann,

4thly, This Teems to be the more reasonable, because it puts Plaintiffs and Defendants upon a more equal Foot in Courts of Equity. This Part of the Clause provides expressly that the Plaintiff shall be reimbursed the Charges he was at for the Copy of the Bill, in case he prevails in the Suit; and, if he does not; he has no Reason to pretend to it; whereas, without this Clause, Defendants in Courts of Equity arc in a very unhappy Condition: The Plaintiff is at Liberty to make as many Persons Defendants, as he pleases, all of them are obliged to take Copies of the Bill, which the Plaintiff may make as long, as he thinks fit, and every Defendant must put in his Answer; and when they have been at all this Charge, which generally amounts to a considerable Sum, the Plaintiff can, of Course, dismiss his own Bill against all or any of them, for twenty Shillings Costs a-piece.

It has been objected, that, in some Cafes, this may occasion great Expence to the Plaintiff: and, as the Course now is, several Defendants may appear by one Clerk, and then they may all make use of the same Copy of the Bill.

The Lords think, that, though it be true, that several Defendants may appear by the same Clerk, who may make use of one Copy only, yet, if the Matter were thoroughly examined into, it would be found, that very few of those Defendants have escaped paying for distinct Copies of the Bill.

If the Commons are of opinion, that some Causes may be of such a Nature, that the giving Copies of the Bill to all the Defendants may be too expensive, andun-necessary, they may, if they please, make an Exception of those Causes, as the Lords have already excepted Suits in the Exchequer, for Recovery of Tythes; or they may oblige the Plaintiff only to serve the Defendants with true Copies of the Bills, without requiring, that such Copies be signed by the Officer of the Court; which will take off all Pretence of the Greatness of the Expence, and will discover, that the Ease of the Plaintiffs is not the true Ground of opposing this Part of the Clause.

As to the third Part of the Clause, which takes away the ingrossed Copy, Abstract, or Tenor, of the Bill, usually sent with the Commission to take the Defendants Answer; the Lords do not agree to the leaving it out of this Bill;

Because such Tenor, though it was really a true Copy of the whole Bill, can never be of any Use to the Defendant; and yet all the Subjects of England, who have the Misfortune to be sued in Chancery, must pay for this a considerable Sum, more or less, according to the Length of the Bill, although they can have no Advantage by it: But that, which makes the Abuse upon the Subject more notorious, is, that this ingrossed Abstract, or Tenor, is never any true Copy, or sensible Abstract, of the Bill, but for the most Part, an impertinent Scrible, and often a Piece of waste Parchment, without any thing contained in it, relating to the Matter of the Suit.

The Lords think, wheh Clerks and Officers in Courts of Justice perform Matters, which require Skill, or are obliged to undergo Trouble, they ought to have just Fees and Encouragements; but they hope, when so gross an Abuse and Imposition is discovered, and laid open to the House of Commons, they will not endure, that it should be continued, nor suffer the private Advantage of Clerks to stand in Competition with the general Ease of the Subject.

As to the Clauses A and B, the Lords have agreed.

Resolved, That this House will take the said Report into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

The Commons cannot agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships to a Bill, intituled, An Act for raising the Militia for the Year 1706, notwithstanding the Month's Pay, formerly advanced, be not repaid; and for an Account to be made of Trophy Monies: by inserting in the ad Press, L. 33, after " Year," " since " the 25th Day of June, which was in the Year of our " Lord 1696;" for some Reasons, for which the Commons can never depart, as well as for the Reasons following:

1. The adding those Words being an implied Acknowlegment, that your Lordships think, it is just, an Account be given of the Trophy Money, collected since that Year, before any new Charge of the same Kind be laid upon the Subject, the Commons conceive, it is altogether as just and reasonable, that an Account should be likewise given of all such Monies, as have been col-lcfted before the Year 1696, and which remain unaccounted for; in regard the Subject has as much Right to be satisfied in the one Cafe, as in the other, whether the Sums, they have paid for Trophies, have been duly applied to that Ule; and there being no means so effectual, of obtaining that Satisfaction, as by the Proviso in the Bill.

2. Care being taken in the Bill, that it shall not extend to Places, where by reason of any Treasurers absconding, failing, or being dead, an Account cannot be passed, the Commons conceive, that the requiring an Account to be given of the Trophy Money, collected as well before, as since, the Year 1696, under such Restriction, cannot occasion any Hardship or Inconvenience.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in order to the speedy and more complete manning of her Majesty's Navy, for the Year 1766, the Justices of Peace, and other Civil Magistrates, throughout the several Counties, Ridings, Cities, Towns, and Places, within the Kingdom of En, Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick upon be impowered, and

directed, forthwith to make, or cause to be made, ftri<ft and diligent Search for all such Seamen, or Seafaring Men, as lie hid, and are not in her Majesty's said Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Justices, and other the said Civil Magistrates, do take up, fend, conduct, and convey, or cause to be taken up, sent, conduced, and conveyed, all such Seamen, or Seafaring Men, to be delivered on board some of her Majesty's Ships or Vessels in Sea Pay, or to such Persons, as shall be appointed to receive the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Penalty be inflicted upon every Person, who shall presume to harbour or conceal such Seamen, or Seafaring Men.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Reward be given to every Person, who shall discover, and take up, such Seaman, or Seafaring Man, as aforesaid, the same to be distfibuted and paid to every such Discoverer, or Person so taking up such Seaman, or Seafaring Man, respectively, out of the Money given for the Service of the Navy. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Conduit-money be allowed, for conveying and fub-sifting such Seamen, or Seafaring Men, according to the present Usage of the Navy.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Encouragement of the said Service, cveiy Seaman, who shall be turned over from one Ship to another, shall be paid his precedent Wages, which shall appear to be due to him, before such Ship, to which he shall be turned over, do go to Sea, either in Money, or by a Ticket, which shall entitle him to an immediate Payment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all such able-bodied Landsmen, who are liable to be raised for the recruiting her Majesty's Land Forces, and Marines, be raised for the said Sea Service, in the like Manner, and delivered on board some of her Majesty's Ships or Vessels in Sea Pay, or to such Persons, who shall be appointed to receive the same.

Amendment of the Law, — Reasons to be offered at Conference.

198 ip° Martiu' ^.1705.

Martis, 19° die Martii;

Anno 5* Ann* Regin*, 1705.

Prayers.

MR. Pultney reported from the Committee, appointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Lords at a Conference upon the Amendments, made by this House to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Amendment of the Law, and the better Advancement of Justice; that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to* report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were r«ad, and are as follow; viz.

The Commons do not infill upon their Amendment to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Amendment of the Law, and better Advancement of Justice, Pr. 2. L. 27, to leave out the Clause, requiring Attorneys to file their Warrants.

But the Commons do insist upon their Amendment, Pr. 3. L. 27, to leave out the Clause, impowering the Courts of Law, after Ilfue joined, to examine such Witnesses, as cannot be present at the Trial, for the Reasons following; viz.

1 ft, For that, when a Witness is examined in open Court, upon any Trial at common Law, Questions may be asked him, upon a Cross-examination, by the Court, the Jury (who should not be deprived of any lawful Means, whereby they may bell be informed of the Fast, whereof they are the foie Judges) or by the Counsel at the Bar, to lift out the Truth of this Evidence, nay, very often, the disordered Look of an Evidence, a faultering in his Speech, or such like Circumstance, may be a Guide to the Jury, as to the Credibility of the Evidence; of which many Instances might be given, were it not a Matter already so well known.

2dly, A Witness, when (worn and examined, in the Face of the Court and Country, will be under a greater Awe of Truth, and more cautious of not forswearing himself, for fear of being detested, and immediately committed by the Court for Perjury } in which same the Court does at the same Time usually direct a Prosecution; whereas Depositions (taken in the Mannerproposed by the Clause) may be made by a profligate Person, who (intending soon after to go beyond the Seas, and to continue out of the Kingdom, or pretend Sickness, or Disability to attend, till after such Depositions shall have been made use of upon the Trial) may more easily be wrought upon to perjure himself, when he thinks he is without the reach of Punishment.

3dly, The Commons do admit to your Lordships, that Depositions are allowed as Evidence in Trials at common Law, where such Witnesses are out of the Kingdom, or under a Disability to attend, though the Witnesses be then living; yet they cannot but be of opinion, that the Use of such Evidence, upon Trials at common Law, ought, for the Reasons abovementioned, to be as little encouraged as may be; to the contrary whereof (as the Commons do conceive) the Method, laid down by your Lord ships in this Clause, will, in Time, turn all viva voce Evidence into Paper Proof, upon all Trials at common Law.

4thly, It may happen very often, that the Manner of wording such Depositions (either through the Ignorance, Mistake, or Cunning, of the Clerk) may give a Turn to the Fast, very different from what the Witnesses meant, or from what might have appeared upon his Examination viva voce in open Court.

5thly, Upon Depositions, taken in Courts of Equity, if the Witnesses differ as to Matters of Fast, or the Credit of the Witnesses is suspected, the Courts of Equity are so far from relying on such Depositions, that they direct Ifluesto be tried at Law, in order that the Witnesses may be there examined in open Court, where the Credit of the Witnesses will be con side red i but (as it

«7

seems to be intended) by this Clause Depositions, taken at Law in all Courts, ttiuft be allowed as Evidences.

And lastly, The Commons are so sensible, that the Examination of Witnesses viva , upon Trials at common Law, is (by the Experience of many Ages) found so be grounded upon so goocf Reason, and of such Security to the Property of the Subject, that they cannot content to so great, and (as they conceive) dangerous, an Alteration in so fundamental a Part of the Law, as will be made by this Clause: Nay, though the Commons should admit, that, in the particular Cafes instanced by your Lordships, there may be an Inconvenience, as the Law in this Point now (lands, yet, they apprehend, such an Alteration would produce a much greater Inconvenience; and which of the two is most to be avoided, 'tis no hard Matter to determine.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time* were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Mr. Pultney do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

Mr. Pultney reported, that they had given to the Lords the Reasons for infilling upon one of the Amendments, made by this House to the said Bill; and acquainted them, that this House doth not infill upon one of their Amendments, and had made several Amendments to another of them, to which they had before disagreed; and had left the Bill, and the Amendments, with their Lordships.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir John Francklyn and Sir Richard Halford:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement and Increase of Seamen, and for the better and speedier manning her Majesty's Fleet, without any Amendments.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir John Francklyn and Sir Richard Ho ford:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Amendments, infilled on by this House, and also to the other Amendments, Vol. 10.

A PROCLAMATION.

ANNE, R.

WHEREAS our Parliament (lands prorogued to the Two-and-twentieth Day of this instant October, we, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publishand declare, that the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Two-and-twentieth Day of October, to Thursday, the Twenty-first Day of November next ensuing; and we have given Order to our Keeper of our great Seal of England, to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly. And we do hereby further declare our Pleasure, that the said Parliament shall, on the said Twenty-first Day of November be held, and (it, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs; and the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly at ,on the

laid Twenty-first Day of November next ensuing.

Given at our Court at K, the Twenty-first: Day of October 1706, in the Fifth Year of our Reign.

God save the Queen.

Mr. Speaker,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her immediately in the House of Peers.

A Bill for the better regulating the nightly Watch, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, that her Majesty had been pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament; but the Noise being great, he had desired, and obtained, a Copy thereof, to prevent any Mistakes therein: Which he read, and is as followed); viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I HOPE we are all met together at this Time with Hearts truly thankful to Almighty God for the glorious Successes, with which he has blessed our Arms, and those

[a] At tke beginning of this Journal Is inferud the fallowing -printed Proclamation.

of our Allies, through the whole course of this Year j and with serious and steady Resolutions to prosecute the Advantages we have gained, till we reap the desired Fruit of them, in an honourable and durable Peace.

The Good uefs of God has brought this happy Prolpect so much nearer to us, that, if we be not wanting to our-ftlves, we may, upon good Grounds, hope to fee such a Balance of Power established in , that it shall

no longer be at the Pleasure of one Prince to disturb the Repose, and endanger the Liberties, of this Part of the World.

A just Consideration of the present Posture of Affairs, of the Circumstances of our Enemies, and the good Dif-position of our Allies, must needs excite an uncommon -Zeal, and animate us to exert our utmost Endeavours, at this critical Conjuncture.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

As I am fully persuaded, you are all of this Mind, so I must earnestly desire you to grant me Supplies, sufficient for carrying on the War next Year in so effectual a Manner, that we may be able to improve every where the Advantages of this successful Campaign; and, I allure you, I shall make it my Business to lee all you give, applied to those Ends, with the greatest Care and Management.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

In pursuance of the Powers, veiled in me by Act of Parliament, both in England and Scotland, I have appointed Commissioners to treat of an Union between the two Kingdoms; and though this be a Work of such a Nature, as could not but be attended with great Difficulties, yet such has been the Application of the Commissioners, that they have concluded a Treaty, which is at this Time before the Parliament of; and I

hope, the mutual Advantages of an intire Union of the two Kingdoms will be found so apparent, that it will not be long, before I shall have an Opportunity of acquainting you with the Success, which it has met with there.

Your meeting at this Time being later than usual, I cannot conclude, without earnestly recommending to you to give as much Dispatch to the publick Affairs, as the Nature of them will admit* it being of the greatest Consequence, that both our Friends, and our Enemies,

should be fully convinced of your Firmness, and the Vigour of your Proceedings.

The Lord Marquis of Hartington reported from the Committee, appointed to draw up an humble Address (upon the Refutation Yesterday) to be presented to her Majesty; that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was twice read, and is, as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humble Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

And, with all Thankfulness to Almighty God, we congratulate your Majesty upon the signal Victory, obtained by your Arms, and those of your Allies, under the Command of the Duke of Marlborough, at Ramillies; a Victory, so glorious and great in its Consequences, and

attended with such continued Successes, through the whole Course of this Year, that no Age can equal.

And as your Majesty's Allies have the wed their Firm-ness, and good Disposition, to carry on the War with Vigour, so the Commons of England are determined, that no speciousPretences of Peace shall divert' them from their steady Resolutions of enabling your Majesty to improve, in all Places, the Advantages of this successful Campaign.

The Experience, your Commons have had, of the prudent Administration, and the great Care and Management, in the Application of the publick Aids, encourage us to allure your Majesty, that we will chearfully give such speedy and effectual Supplies, as, by the Continuance of God's Blessing upon your Majesty's Arms, may establish the Balance of Power in Europe, by a iafe, honourable, and lading Peace.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Lid Address, by adding, at the End thereof, these Words:

" We beg Leave likewise to return your Majesty our " hearty Thanks, for your promoting the Union betwixt " England and Scotland; whereby your Majesty (hews " your great Concern and Tenderness, not only for the " present, but the future, Happiness of both Kingdoms."

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolveed, That this House do agree with the Committee, in the said Adcirels, so amended:

And the same is as followeth;

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humble Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

And, with all Thankfulness to Almighty God, we congratulate your Majesty upon the signal Victory, obtained by your Arms, and those of your Allies, under the Command of the Duke of Marlborough, at Ramillies; a Victory, so glorious and great in its Consequences, and attended with such continued Successes, through the whole Course of this Year, that no Age can equal.

And as your Majesty's Allies have shewed their Firm-nef's and good Disposition, to carry on the War with Vigour, so the Commons of England are determined, that nofpeciousPretences of Peace shall divert them from their steady Resolutions of enabling your Majesty to improve, in all Places, the Advantages of this successful Campaign.

The Experience, your Commons have had, of the prudent Administration, and the great Care and Management in the Application of the publick Aids, encourage us to assure your Majesty, that we will chearfully give such speedy and effectual Supplies, as by the Continuance of God's Blessing upon your Majesty's Arms, may establish the Balance of Power in Europe, by a l'afe, honourable, and lading Peace.

MR. Speaker reported, that the House did Yesterday attend her Majesty with their humble Address; and that her Majesty was pleased thereupon to give this gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I THANK you heartily for this Address, and the Assurances of giving me effectual Supplies, to carry on the War, and to obtain a safe and honourable Peace.

I am glad to find you are lb well satisfied with the Application of the publick Money.

As to the Matter of the Union with Scotland, so in all other things, I shall Hill be delirous to promote the present and future Happiness of my People.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Forty thousand Men be employed in the Sea Service, for the Year 1707, including 8,000 Marines.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding four Pounds a Manner fern, be allowed, for maintaining the said 40,000 Men for 13 Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and twenty thousand Pounds, be allowed, for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Service of the Year 1707.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, ThataSum, not exceedingThreehundred and Fifty-seven thousand Pounds, be granted to her Majesty, for the maintaining of Guards and Garilons, and for Payment of Invalids, for the Service of the Year 1707, including Five thousand Men, to serve on board the Fleet.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Forty thousand Men, which were raised, to act in Conjunction with the Forces of her Majesty's Allies, be continued for the Year 1707.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight hundred Ninety-three thousand Seven hundred and Six Pounds, Eight Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to her Majesty, for

Vol. 15.

maintaining the said 46,000 Men for the Service of the Year 1707.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the additional Forces, of 10,000 Men, be continued for the Year 1707.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Eleven thousand Seven hundred Sixty-two Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Ten Pence, be granted to her Majesty, for maintaining the said Ten thousand Men for the Service of the Year 1707.

Mr. Secretary Harley acquainted the House, that he was commanded by her Majesty to acquaint this House; that her Majesty had appointed Tuesday, the 31st Day of December inllant, as a Day of general Thanksgiving to Almighty God, for the great and wonderful Succefies, God hath blessed the Arms of her Majesty, and her Allies, in this Year; and for imploring the Continuance of his Blessings, and for the restoring, and perpetuating. Peace, Safety, and Prosperity, to her Majesty, and her Kingdoms, and the Nations and States in Alliance with her; and, for the greater Solemnity of that Day, her Majesty will go to St. Paul's Church: And that her Majesty hath been pleased to give necessary Orders, for providing convenient Places in the said Cathedral for the Members of this House.

Resolved, That the humble Thanks of this House be returned to her Majesty, for her gracious Favour, in communicating to this House her Intention of going to St. Paul's Church upon the Day of Thanksgiving for the Succefies of her Majesty's Arms, and those of her Allies.

Ordered, That the said Thanks be presented to hef Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

Resolved, That this House will attend her Majesty, as a House, to St. Paul's Church, upon the Day appointed for a publick Thanksgiving.

A Petition of the Proprietors of the Army and Transport Debentures, on behalf of themselves, and others, was offered to the House.

And the Question being put. That the Petition be brought up;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

The Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, that the said Debentures were issued for Services, performed about 13 Years since, but have carried Interest, at £. 5 per Cent, only from 1701: That no

Principal has been paid, but such, as has been funk by forfeited Estates in Ireland j and all those being fold, there remains unsatisfied Debentures to the amount of about £. 960,000. That by an Act, i° Anna Regina (for preserving the publick Credit) whatsoever of the said Debentures should remain unpaid by the said Forfeitures, should be made good in the next Session of Parliament, with Interest at £. 5 per Cent, after the 34th June, 1703; and Provision has been made for three Years Interest only; which causes a Discount of £. 30 per Cent, upon the said Debentures, to the great Dishonourof the publick Credit: And praying, that Provision may be made, for paying off the said unsatisfied Debentures.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Officers in her Majesty's Army, under the Command of his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, in Flanders, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they have a long time been possessed of Debentures, for their Service in the late War, whereof they have received but two Years Interest, as yet: That the Petitioners intirely depend upon the Promise of an Act of Parliament (to make good Deficiences) that such Debentures, as should remain unsatisfied by the Produce of Irish Forfeitures, should be made good the next Session of Parliament; which being not yet done, the Petitioners pray, that Provision may be made, for paying the Principal and Interest, remaining due on the said Debentures.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, and Grand York Jury, at the General Quarter Sessions of Peace, held ^eSlltry* at Bradford, in and for the West Riding of the County of York, the 10th Day of October, 1706, and after, by Adjournment, at Shejfeild, the 15th Day of October aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by Act of Parliament, made the 27th Hen.
