else within the County, where the Premisses lie, before the Custos Rotulorum, and two Justices and Clerk of the Peace, or two of them at the least, whereof the Clerk of the Peace to be one: That the Petitioners are of opinion, that Act hath not had its intended Effect, because the Clerks of the Peace are not obliged to give Security for the lafe keeping of the said Inrolments, and that there is no convenient Place appointed in each County* for keeping the same in: That the Petitioners conceive, the same might be remedied within the said West Hiding, and much to their Advantage, if all Bargains and Sales of any Manors, Lands, or Tenements, within the said West Riding, were to be inrolled before the Register, or his Deputyr, appointed by a late Act, made in the ad Year of her Majesty's Reign, for the publick registering of all Deeds, Conveyance', and Wills, within the said West Riding; there being good Security given by the said Register, for the safe keeping of all Deeds, committed to his Custody, and a convenient Building, for that Purpose, erected at Wakefeild: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for inrolling of Bargains and Sales of any Manors, Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, within the said West Riding, with the Register, lately appointed by Act of Parliament* instead of their being inrolled before the Custos Rotulorum,

Justices of the Peace, and Oierk of the Peace, of the same Riding.

From the House of Commons, December, 1706.

Sir,

THE House of Commons having taken Notice of the Absence of several of their Members, I am commanded to acquaint you with it, that you may give -

immediate Summons to all the Members of tins House,

Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, within your County, to attend their Service in Parliament on Tuesday, the Fourteenth of January next; the House of Commons intending to proceed further, with all Severity, against all such of their Members, as shall then neglect their Attendance: And you are to give an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done hereupon, unto.

Sir,

Your humble Servant.

My Lords and Gentlemen,.

I AM glad of this Occasion to repeat to you my great Satisfaction in your several Adidrelfes, presented to me in the Beginning of this Session.

The Zeal and Affection, which you expressed in them for my Service, and the common Caule of , cannot fail of being a great Encouragement to all our Allies.

The particular Notice which you have taken of the Eminent Services of the Duke of , is also very

agreeable to me; and I make noQuestion, but it will be so to the whole Kingdom.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I am to thank you, in a very particular Manner, for the more than usual Dispatch of the Bills of Supply, with which you have now presented me.

This Will enable me to put all our necessary Preparations for next Year into a great Forwardness, and must needs have a very good Effect, for improving the Advantages of the last Campaign.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I suppose you will think it convenient to make fomt short Recess, during the Holy-days.

The Zeal and Unanimity, you have already shewn, are a sufficient A durance to me, that you will all return in the same good Temper and Disposition, to dispatch what remains of the publick Business.

And then the House adjourned till the

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled, taking into our Consideration the many eminent Services t>f John Duke of Marlborough, whereby the Glory of your Majesty's Governrtient, the Honour and Safety of your Kingdoms, and the Interest of the common Cause, have been so highly advanced, do, with all Submission, address ourselves to your Majesty's most sacred Person, humbly to desire, that, as your Majesty is, at your Expence, grac'tously pleased to erect the House of Bleinheim, as a Monument of his glorious Actions, and the House of Peers, by your Majesty's Permission, have given rife to a Law, for continuing his Honours to his Posterity, we, your Majesty's obedient Commons, may be permitted to express our Sense of so distinguishing a Merit, and our ready Disposition to enable your Majesty to make some Provision for the more honourable Support of his Dignity in his Posterity, in such manner, as shall be most agreeable to your Majesty.

Thus the Gratitude of the whole Kingdom will remain upon Record to after Ages, and encourage others to follow his great Example.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know her Majesty's Pleasure, when she will be attended by this House.

.And then the House adjourned till To-morrovr Morning, Nine a Clock.

Conyers (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in ht the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow: viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-nine thousand Pound,

be granted to her Majesty, for the Payment of another Year's Interest of the unsatisfied Debentures, charged upon the Irish Forfeitures.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the further Sum of Ten thousand Pounds be allowed to the Office of Ordnance, towards making a Wharf and Storehouse at Portsmouth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Twenty thousand Pound, be granted to her- Majesty, for the Land Service to be performed by the Office of Ordnance for the Year 1707.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Forty-four thousand Pound, be granted to her Majesty, towards defraying the Charge of transporting Land Forces.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Five hundred Pound*, be granted to her Majesty, for the Charge of circulating Exchequer Bills for another Year.

Mr. Secretary Harley acquainted the House, that he bad a Message, signed by her Majesty, m answer to their Address Yesterday, relating to the Duke of Marlborough.

And he delivered the same to Mr. Speaker; who read the same to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

ANNE, R.

HER Majesty, in ednsideration of the great and eminent Services performed by the Lord in the first Year of her Reign, as well by his prudent Negotiations, as her Plenipotentiary at the Hague, as by his Valour and good Conduct in the Command of the Confederate Armies abroad, thought fit to grant to him, and the Heirs Male of his Body, the Title of a Duke of this Realm, and, as a farther Mark of her Favour, and Satisfaction with his Services, and for the better Support of his Dignity, her Majesty granted to the said Duke, and the Heirs Male of his Body, during her Life, a Pension, of £.5,000 per Amum, out of the Revenue of the Poll Office; and an Act having passed this Sessions, for settling the Honours and Dignities of the Duke of Marlborough upon his Posterity, and annexing the Honour and Manor oiWoodflock, and House of , to go along

with the said Honours, it would be very agreeable to her Majesty, if the Pension of £.5,000per Annum be continued, and limited, by Act of Parliament, to his Posterity, for the more honourable Support of their Dignities, in like manner, as his Honours, and the Honour and Manor of Woodstock, and House of Blenh, are already limited* and settled.

Kensington, "January the 9th, 170 $-.

Resolved, That a Bill be brought in, for continuing and settling upon John Duke of and his

Posterity, the Pension of Five thousand Pounds Annum, already granted by her Majesty, for the more honourable Support of their Dignities, in like manner, as his Honours and Dignities, and the Honour and Manor of Woodfiock, and House of Blenheim, are already limited, and settled; and that Mr. Secretary Hurley, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Lord Granby, Mr. Solicitor General, Colonel Strangewayes, Mr. Mr.

Portman, and Mr. Lowndes, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing a Burgess to lerve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Newport) in the Counter of Cornwall, in the room of John Spark, Esquire, deceased.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Saturday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill for the further and better Relief Employment, and Maintenance, of the Poor.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

for the Prussian Troops.

IT having been proposed to his Majesty the King of Prussia, on the behalf of her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, by his Highness my Lord Prince and Duke of Marlborough, as also on the be half of the High

and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces, that his Body of Troops, confiding of 21 Squadrons, and Nine Battalions, which served the last Campaign in Brabant, be quartered, during this Winter, between the Maefe and the Rhine, according to the Repartition of Quarters, made on that behalf by H. High Mightinesse, a Copy whereof is hereunto annexed; his Majesty the King of Prussia, to give a fresh Proof of 'his Affection and Zeal for the Interest of the common "Cause, has been pleased to consent to the Quarters, so appointed; and it is agreed, on the behalf, as well of her Majesty the Queen, as of their High Mightinesse, with the Plenipotentiary of his Majesty the King of , the Baron de Schmettau, on the Conditions following:

Ift.

That her Majesty the Queen shall, with the Concurrence of their High Mightinesse, during the Time of Winter Quarters, to commence from the Day, the Troops of Prussia shall pass the Maeje, and to end, when they

shall repass the said River, the year ensuing, consent to pay unto his Majesty the King of: ift, The Agio,

or the Difference, between Bank Money, and the current Coin of Germany, according as the same was regulated, during the Campaign; and that for Eleven Squadrons, and Two Battalions, quartered, according to the said Repartition, in Countries and Places, where Bank Money is current, and also for the General Officers; which Agio amounts to 9,845 FI. 10 Sols, Dutch Money, fer Month. 2. One Moiety, for the Bread of the said Body, shall be paid to the King of Prussia which Moiety, after the rate of 10,207 Rations, at Two Livres a Ration, comes to 12, 758 tl. 3 Sols, per Month. ,3. As to the Forage, after the rate of 5,594 Rations a Day, at Three Crowns a Ration, there shall be paid 4 1,95$FI. Dutch Money, per Month; which Money, for Forage, shall be directly paid by England and the States to the Bailiwicks and Districts, where the Troops shall be quartered, upon the Account of Forage, which such Bailiwicks and Districts are to deliver to the Troops of Prussia; the Remainder to be paid by his Majesty the Kingo i Prussia:But as for the Country of Cleves, and the District in the Upper Part of in the Pof-

fession of his Majesty the King of Prussia, Payment shall be made to Commiflfaries, named by his Majesty. The said Bailiwicks and Districts are, upon that Foot, to discount every Month with the Officers of the Troops, and to pay them, in ready Money, the three Crowns per Ration, received by them, in Consideration of what Horses shall be short, and for which Forage has not been delivered; but when the Troops shall repass the Maeje, as well during the Winter Quarters, as after, and at the opening of the Campaign, they shall be on the Foot of the 7th Article of the Treaty of 1701, as well in respect of the Agio, as of Bread, and Forage.

II.

Payment of the said Money shall be exactly made every Month, on the Part of her Majesty the Queen, as also of their High Mightinesse.

HI.

Notice shall be given jointly, on the Part of her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, and of his Majesty the King of Prussia, and also of the high and mighty Lords the States General, unto the Ministers of the Potentates, in whole Countries the Troops shall be in Quarters.

IV.

Provided the Conditions above specified be duly performed, the Troops of his Majesty the King of Prussia shall remain in the Quarters above-mentioned, between the Maeje zn&tht Rhine, during this Winter; and they shall be under the Command of his Highness my Lord Duke of Marlborough, or of the first General, who, in the Absence of his Highness, shall command in Chief the Armies of her Majesty and the States; which first General shall correspond, upon all Occasions, with the Count de I.ottum, General of Foot to the King of Prussia, or with such other General, as, in his Absence, shall command in Chief the said Body of Troops of his Prussian Majesty: And, in case the Enemy should, during the Winter, assemble any considerable Force, to undertake any Enterprise of Consequence, which may oblige his Highness my Lord Duke, or such General, as, in Vol, 15.

his Absence, shall command in Chief, to bring Troops into the Field, to oppose the Attempts of the Enemy, then all the said Troops of Prussia, or any part of them, shall

likewise be assembled, as the Commander in Chief shall judge necessary: In the same above-mentioned they shall likewise pass the Maeje, and receive the same Treatment, in regard of the Agio, Bread, and Forage, as they had last Campaign; but with this Difference, that, as for the Forage, it shall then be delivered in intire Rations out of the Magazines of the States.

His Prussian Majesty does further engage himself to cause the said Body of Troops to make the next Campaign in a complete State j and, to that Intent, they shall pass the Maeje, and join the Armies of her Majesty the Queen, and of the States, under the Orders of his Highness my Lord Duke of Marlborough, or of such General, as, in the Absence of his Highness, shall command in Chief the said Armies, as soon as the Troops of her Majesty and the States shall go out of Quarters, to form an Army, unless it be otherwise agreed on between his Majesty the King of Prussia, and her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, and their High Mightinesse.

In Testimony whereof, the present Convention has been ligned, on the Part of her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, by his Highness the Prince and Duke of Marlborough, and, on the Part of his Majesty the King of Prussia, by his Plenipotentiary the Sieur Baron Schmittau; their High Mightinesse having consented, by their Resolution of the Seventeenth of this present Month of November, to the same Conditions for the Moiety, which regard the said Payment of the States of the United Provinces. Done and ligned at the Hague, this Twenty-fourth of November, 1706.

The Prince and Duke of Marlborough. (L. S.)

Translation of the Treaty with the Landgrave of Hesse Cajjell, concluded at Cajjell, May the 20th, 1706.

A Convention between her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain and their High Mightinesse the States General of the United Provinces, on the one Part, and his moll Serene Highness the Landgrave of Hejje Cassel on the other, concerning the March of his moll Serene Highness's Troops to Italy, and the augmenting them with Two Regiments of Horse, which make 720 Horse.

III.

FIRST, His Moll Serene Highness promises, that his Body of Troops shall march to Italy, immediately after that this Convention shall be approved by her Britannic Majesty, and their High Mightinesse, and that it shall be required of him by the said Powers.

3 N II.

Troops.

Hessian

Troops.

n.

This Body shall consist of Nine Battalions, and Sixteen Squadrons; videlicet, the Nine thousand Men, stipulated by the Convention of the Seventh of,

One thousand Seven hundred and Two; one Battalion, of Eight hundred and Seventy Men, by the Convention of the Thirty-first of Marche One thousand Seven hundred

and Three j and Four Squadrons, making Seven hundred and Twenty Horse, which shall be forthwith added thereto by his most Serene Highness.

m.

For the Augmentation of the said Two Regiments of Horse, which his most Serene Highness will make, there shall be paid to his most Serene Highness, by her Britannic Majesty, and their High Mightinesse, a Subsidy of Fifty thousand Crowns.

IV.

Her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse engage themselves to make good to his most Serene Highness the Overplus of the Price of Bread and Forage, if it shall exceed that, which the Troops would have paid in Brabant; as also of the extraordinary Charges, or Contingencies, whereof Proofs and Vouchers shall be produced.

V.

the Loss, that may happen by the Change of Money, shall likewise fall upon her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse; which shall be proved by the Bills of Bankers, attested.

V!.

And his most Serene Highness judging it necessary, for the Preservation of his Troops, that the Body be provided with Waggons, for the Carriage of the Bread, without depending upon Chance in that respect; her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse oblige themselves to maintain Sixty Waggons for that Purpose.

VII.

Her Britannic Majesty, and their High Mightinesse shall likewise take upon themselves the Charges of the Hospitals for the tick of the said Body, either in erecting them, and providing, to that End, each Regiment a Waggon, for the Carriage of the Sick, and the Necessaries for the Hospitals, or by giving Four Sous a Day for every tick or wounded Person, that shall be brought into the Hospitals, erected by his most Serene Highness: in which Cafe, nevertheless, the Charges of 16 Waggons shall be borne by her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse.

yin.

Whereas the indemnifying his most Serene Highness, as stipulated in the 6th and 7th Articles preceding, comes to an uncertain Sum, his most Serene Highness is willing to charge himself therewith for a Subsidy of 70,000 Crowns per Annum, of Holland Money; but, as in this he has not any Regard to Profit, he is willing likewise, in order to give a Proof of his Difintcreftedness, and that he does not enter into this Convention, but with a Prospect of advancing the common Cause, and to improve more and more the Friendship of her Britannic Majesty, and their High Mightinesse, that the said Powers shall take upon themselves the Care of the two foregoing Articles, and to that Purpose fend Commissaries, and Officers, with the Troops of his most Serene Highness; in which same his most Serene Highness will quit all Pretentions to the Subsidy stipulated in this Article.

DC.

Whereas his most Serene Highness the Landgrave had a Right by the Convention of February 7th, 1702, to bring back the 3,000 Men, paid by Subsidy, to winter in his own Estates, and by this March it will be impossible for him to enjoy that Right; her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse oblige themselves to indemnify his most Serene Highness for the Loss, that there will be in the Exchange of the Money of Germany into that of Italy, during the Six Months of Winter Quarters.

*5

A. 170

x.

The Money for Waggons, Recruits, and all other Advantages, which the Troops have hitherto enjoyed, shall be continued to them, and paid to these 16 Regiments, upon the Foot and the Practice of former Conventions.

XL

In order to enable his most Serene Highness so much the more to make the Augmentation now stipulated, and also to encourage his most Serene Highness to engage in the present Convention, there shall be paid to his most Serene Highness forthwith, and within three Weeks after the Approbation of this Convention, the Remainder of the Subsidy of the Year 1705, due from her Britannic Majesty, and the Year 1706, payable beforehand, according to] the Convention of the 7th of February, 1702, amounting together to 80,802 Florins, ir Sous; and by their High Mightinesse the like Sum, on the Arrears due from them.

xn.

His most Serene Highness the Landgrave having in-fifted, and still infilling, positively, that the Arrears of the last War, remaining due to him on the Part of England, to be paid Half at present, and the other Half at the End of the Year, my Lord Prince and Duke of Marlborough, promises to make the most preflingInstances to her laid Britannic Majesty, that the Payment may follow in the Manner aforementioned.

XIII.

Whereas there has been no exact Account given, of what is due to the Officers, either for Recruits, Remounting, Waggon-money, or other Advantages, a List thereof shall be made forthwith; and her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse shall pay them as soon as possible, in order to enable thereby the said Officers to support their extraordinary and necessary Charges in this March.

XIV.

Their High Mightinesse promise, not only that they will continue their Offices, and earned: Instances, with the Province of Zealand, for Payment of the Arrears of the Regiment of General Spiegel, and of the Commission Officers of that of Rechteren; but his most Serene Highness being informed, that the said Province has made over what is due to it from the Provinces of,

Utrecht, and Overyejfel, upon the Charges of the Sea Service, for the Payment of the said Arrears; their High Mightinesse promise, that they will employ the like Offices with the said three Provinces, and that the Money which shall arise from thence, shall be applied to this End, and that they will give Order, that, from the present Month, henceforward those Regiments, and Commission Officers, be regularly'paid.

XV.

Whereas his most Serene Highness will be disfur-nished by the said March of his Troops, her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse promise, not only tohaften to, and assist, his most Serene Highness with their Forces, in case of an Attack by the Enemies, but also to secure him from any Insults of his Neighbours, either for Winter Quarters, or otherwise, without Exception.

XYL

The Payment of the Subsidy, stipulated in the third Article, for the Augmentation, shall commence from the Day of the Conclusion of the present Convention; as also that mentioned in the Articles 6, 7, and 8th, if her Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse agree to indemnify his most Serene Highness from the Charges, mentioned therein, by Way of Subsidy, payable every three Months.

xvii.

Her Britannic Majesty shall engage in the Payment of all the Charges, which shall arise from the present Convention, for Two Thirds, and their High Mightinesse for the 3d Third.

Mr. Secretary Harley presented to the House, fade with A Representation from the Lords Commissioners of Finders. Trade and Plantations, relating to the Trade with

Flanders:

And, Extracts of Letters from Mr. Stepney, her Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary at relating to Trade.

And the Titles thereof were read.

And the said Representation, and Extracts, are as follow; viz.

The laid Representation.

To the Queen's most excellent Majesty:

May it please your Majesty:

IN Obedience to your Majesty's Commands, signified to us by the Right honourable Mr. Secretary that

we should examine several Extracts, and Papers, received by him from Mr. Stepney, your Majesty's Minister then.

Vol. 15.

at Bruxells, relating to the opening and erico'uraging the Trade with Flanders-, and consider, what may be done therein, either by your Majesty alone, or by your Majesty in Parliament;

We have been attended by divers Merchants, and have examined several Particulars in that Trade, and especially the repealing the Act, prohibiting the Import of Bone Lace from Flanders; and do find, that the said Prohi-' bkion of their Lace having occasioned a like Prohibition of our Woollen Manufacture, it would be very advantageous to our Trade, that the Act be repealed; as, on the other side, the taking off the said Prohibition of Lace from Flanders will be very acceptable to the PecK pie of that Country: Upon which we humbly offer, that the Parliament, by an Act, passed in the nth and 12th of his late Majesty's Reign, did provide, that at the End of three Months, to commence from the Time of taking off the Prohibition of the Woollen Manufactures in Flanders, a former Act, made in the 9th and 10th Year of his said Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " rendering the Laws more effectual, for preventing the " Importation of foreign Bone Lace," should be repealed; but upon Consideration hereof, and the Opinion of your Majesty's Attorney General, it appearing unto us, that the said last mentioned Act would be in no wife sufficient, for allowing the Importation of Bone Lace from Flanders, unless another Act, made in the 13th and 14th of King Charles the 2d, intituled, "An Act pro-' " hibiting the Importation of foreign Bone Lace, Cutwork, Embroidery, Fringe, Band-strings, Buttons, and " Needle-work," be likewise repealed;

We are thereupon most humbly of opinion, that, whereas the States of the Spanish Low Countries have already taken off the Prohibition of our Woollen Manu* fasture there, in Expectation, that the Trade of their Bone Lace be likewise opened, it will be for your Majesty's Service, and a great Encouragement of the Woollen Trade of England, that both those Acts afore-mentioned be together repealed, and that the Importation of Bone Lace from Flanders be permitted, under a moderate Duty; wherein we are the more confirmed by a Computation, that the Value of Bone Lace, which was formerly imported from thence yearly into England, did not exced £. 30,000 Sterling; whereas by an Estimate made of English Goods, imported into the Spanish Low Countries in the Year 168 r, it does appear, that they amounted to £. 400,000 Sterling, and that the Woollen Manufacture alone did amount to £. 160,000 Sterling; by which your Majesty may please to judge, how advantageous it will be to your Majesty's Subjects, that the Trades between England and Flanders be mutually' laid open.

As to other Particulars, and chiefly that of settling the Tariff, or Book of Rates, which has been lately renewed in Flanders, in favour of your Majesty's Subjects, as it flood in the Year 1680, and also the altering the Book of Rates in England, mentioned by Mr. Stepney, in reference to fbme Parts of the Trade from,

we have consulted the Merchants, concerned therein, who have wrote to their Correspondents, on several Heads, and are expecting their Answer thereunto;

We are therefore humbly of opinion, that at present the repealing the Acts before mentioned be offered to the Consideration of the Parliament, if your Majesty shall so think fit, as a Matter of great Importance to the Trade of this Nation.

All which is most humbly submitted.

Dartmouth,

Ph. Meadows,

fVm.

John,

Mat. Prior.

Extract of a Letter from Mr. Stepney to Mr. Secretary Hedges, dated at Brujfells, 4 November, 1706.

I received, some Days ago, the Honour of your Letter of the 8th pall, but have forbore acknow-leging it, till I had informed myself, in the bed manner 1 could, according to your Directions, what Progress has been made in these Provinces, towards renewing the Commerce between her Majesty's Dominions and these Countries.

I am now to assure you, that the Magistrates and People of Brabant and Flanders seem to desire nothing more passionately, than the opening such a Trade; which Blelfing the y hope to receive from her Majesty 3 Goodness, as they on all Occasions gratefully acknowlege their Deliverance to be chiefly owing to her Miajedys Power.

They have already made the most essential Step toward this Intercourse, by taking off the Prohibition of our Woollen Manufactures, as well as of our other Commodities; which Circumstances I perceive was not yet come to your Knowlege, though Orders were issued- to . that Purpose, on the 7th of June last, by a cir-

cular Letter from the Ptefidtent and Chamber of Accounts here to the Officers of the several; Tolls, that they should receive the usual Duties, according to the Tariffs and'Ordinances of 1700, which were in Force to the Day of his late Catholick Majesty's Death; which short and general Terms they judged' to be a sufficient Publication, that the Trade is opened into these Parts, n In consequence whereof I am to acquaint you, that Eight Days ago 17 English Vessels, laden with ploth and other of our Merchandizes, entered-at Ostend, and have been allowed' to proceed1 towards- How-

ever, to avoid all dark and equivocal Expressions, I desired the President of the Chamber to give me a

P more dear and authentic Declaration, which you

find in the Paper here inclosed; whereby there is no doubt, but the Trade is redored, and our Merchants are now to examine, whether the Tariff be according to their Wish.

The States General objected against that of 1700 D ‘ above mentioned, JubLit. A; and their Deputies

here proposed, the Regulation of 1680 should be observed, and that all Innovations, made since that Time, might cease, and be abolished.

£ The President endeavoured to prove, that Tariff was both improper, and prejudicial to these Countries: However, the Dutch Deputies infided there-

F. upon, by a 2d Memorial; whereby the President

G. was obliged, the Day following, to publish the fame, at their Desire; and, upon that Footing their Commerce remains at present, except in the Article of Draperies, the Value thereof not being taxed equally enough, pj and in proportion to their several Degrees, by the

Tariff of 1680. A new Ordonance has been pub-liflied here, in that Particular, by the Council of State and Finances, referring to the Rates, settled by-a former Tariff of 1669.

I am now to acquaint you, what the Magistrates and People of these Countries expect, for the Advantage of their Commerce in her Majesty's Dominions: id, That the drift Prohibition of their Laces be taken off;

2. That their Manufactures of Damask. Diapers, and other Linens, which, since the Reign of King Charles the ad of England, have been charged with such heavy Duties, as amount to a Prohibition, may be entered at the same Rates with the Linens, imported from France and Germany: 3. That the Duties on Tapedry may be likewise lowered. There are some other Merchandizes, and Commodities, of the Growth of these Countries, such as Camblets, raw and wrought Silks, Fudians, Hops, &V. which might be received more favourably j but of these I shall make no further mention at present.

The fird of these Articles above-mentioned is the mod, material one; to which, I under and, the Parliament has provisionally consented; and I humbly conceive, it may be seasonable, for her Majesty to declare her Pleasure thereupon by an Order in Council, under the Signet to be sent to me in writing, or rather published in the

The other two Articles, arid whatever else shall appear to be of Benefit to both Nations, may be regulated hereafter, at Leisure, when the People, who are most knowing in Trade on each Side, shall have given their Opinion thereupon; whether it be necessary to renew the Treaties of Commerce, made in 1604, and 1630, which lad is thought here most reaforiable; or, to settle a new Tariff, more suitable to the present Juncture, than any of the former; or, ladly, till that be done, that all Goods, imported on both Sides, may be taxed ad valorem, at the rate of Four or Fi veperCent.

A PETITION of Benjamin Nicoll, Citizen, and Nicoll'*D*bt late Merchant, of London, was presented to the to th. Crown. House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioner hath for many Years been a great Importer of Wines here, and other Commodities, for all which (except Wines) he paid the Duties in ready Money, amounting to many thousand Pounds: That all his Bonds for Wine Duties before the 10th of April, 1702, are discharged, and, since that Time his Bonds standing out amount to £.,3995 6r. 8 d. and no more: That, when he failed, and, since, the Commissioners of the Customs have, by Extent, and otherwise, reduced his Debtto about£.2,000.

That by the Petitioner's Losses in Shipping, Merchandize, Correspondents, and Shopkeepers breaking, he has, within four Years last, loft above £. 15,000, and he is now a Prisoner in the Fleet, and he, and his Sureties, are prosecuted on the Bonds (though they are Persons of mean Circumstances) and in danger to be ruined; and the Petitioner hath nothing left, to maintain himself, and eight Children; yet hopes, by the charitable Contributions of Friends and Relations, to pay some Part of the Debt due to the Crown, if he, and his Sureties, may be admitted to a Composition: And praying, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Lord High Treasurer to compound with the Petitioner, and his Securities, for the Debt by him owing to her Majesty.

Translation of Count Briangon' % Memorial,

March 31, 1706.

Madam,

THE underwritten Envoy Extraordinary of Savoy has received Orders from his Royal Highness, his Matter, to inform your Majesty of the deplorable Condition, to which he is reduced, and the imminent and unavoidable Danger of seeing himself belieged in his Capital, not only with a Number of Troops quite disproportioned to the Defence of it, but, what is (till worse, intirely ex-haufted of Money, which is the rr.oft certain and effectual Means of sustaining the Siege long enough, to give the Time, which is necessary, for the Arrival of those Succours, which your Majesty's generous Goodness has been pleased to provide, in order to put Prince Eugene in a Condition to act.

He has ordered me most humbly to represent to your Majesty the prodigious Expences, and extraordinary Efforts, he has been obliged to make in all the Fortifications, that he has raised, and which 'tis necessary to keep

up, without Intermission, in so many different Places, and at so great a Charge; by the Maintenance, the Pay, and Subsistence, which he has furnished the Imperial Troops, ever ftnee their coming into Piedmont, and Hill actually fumilhes to the Remainder of them, without which they would absolutely perish, being so intirely abandoned, as they have been, by the Imperial Court; nay more, he has remounted Part of their Cavalry, and made the utmost Efforts for recruiting, as much as it was possible, his own Troops; but Money growing scarce, and the Dearness of Provisions increating at whilst there

is Plenty in the Enemies Quarters, the Desertion begins to be very great, and it is impossible to prevent it, but with Money, which he absolutely wants.

He is likewise obliged to get all his Com from Abroad, for the Subsistence, not only of the Troops, but of the People too, there being none in his own Country: as also the Ammunition; and all at excessive Rates.

The small Space of Country he has remaining, is lo ruined by the perpetual Inroads of the Enemies, and the exhorbitant Contributions they exact from it, that he cannot raise any more Imposts, or have the lead: Assistance from it; so that he has no other Support left him, but the Subsidies, which your Majesty is pleased to furnish him, in Conjunction with the States General.

He has hitherto made use of all the Means, that have been in his Power, having borrowed considerable Sums, pawned all his Jewels, and melted down the greaceft Part of his Plate; but now he has no Supply of that Kind remaining; and in the extreme Diffrds he suffers, being forced to redouble his Expences, and provide for lb many different Things, in order to enable himself to re-fist the extraordinary Preparations of the Enemies, and finding himself under an absolute Impossibility of doing it in any Degree, he has recourse to your Majesty's generous Protection, and most earnestly beseechcs you, that you will be pleased to grant him an extraordinary and immediate Subsidy of Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling, which is the Sum, that is indispensably necessary for him to maintain himself, till the Arrival of the expected Succours.

The signal Marks your Majesty has hitherto given him of your powerful Protection, and the hearty Concern you have been pleased to shew for what regards him, give him a just Assurance, that you will be graciously pleased to let him (till feel the Effects of it, by granting him this new Favour, in the most pressing and most important Occasion, that he ever had, since his Preservation depends upon it, and 'tis the Determination of his Destiny.

I need not enlarge upon the fetal Consequences, that would follow from the intire ruining his Royal Highness, my Matter, which, without this Supply, is unavoidable j and this may not only prevent it, but will render the glorious Efforts, your Majesty makes for the publick Good, extremely useful and advantageous, which by his Destruction would be made ineffectual.

All the solid Reasons, that may be produced to this Purpose, cannot escape your great Wisdom and Penetration; and, besides, your Majesty's great and generous Soul will be engaged by a yet stronger Motive to grant him this Favour, since upon the Resolution, you are pleased to take in this Affair, depends either the Preservation, or the Ruin, of a Prince, who has fecrificed so much for the Service of the Alliance, and whose Con-stancy has been invincible, and above all Temptations, by the settled Confidence, which he has intirely placed in your Majesty's powerful Protection, from whom he thinks himself assured of receiving this generous Assistance, in such extreme and urgent Necessity; which will enable him to give more and more Instances of the inviolable Passion, which he shall always have for the Glory and Interests of your Majesty.

The Count de Briangon,

March31, 1706.

Translation of a Letter from Mr. Secretary Harley to

Count Briancon, Envoy Extraordinary from the Duke

of Savoy, dated April the 2d, 1706.

Sir, Whiteha, the 2d April, 1706.

HER Majesty having thoroughly considered your Me-riiorial, of the 31st past, has commanded me to make you the following Answer:

That the Queen has very much at heart the Interests of his Royal Highness of Savoy, whose unshaken Firm-ness, in the most dangerous State of his Affairs, has so sensibly touched her Majesty, that she is disposed to make the utmost Efforts to succour a Prince, who has shewn his Zeal for the publick Good, in so signal a Manner.

His Royal Highness will have seen, by the Proofs he has already had of her Majesty's Friend ship, that no body could be more concerned at the Misfortunes, that have happened to his Royal Highness, than her Majesty has been.

To support so brave and so faithful an Ally, her Majesty has already this Year remitted 200,000 Crowns for the Army in Italy: Soon after that was done, (lie entered into Treaty with the States General, to maintain Ten thousand Men more for the same Service.

Her Majesty has lately granted a Loan of above a Million of Crowns, for the Payment of the Army under Prince Eugene: She has likewise made pressing Instances to the King of Spain, to fend some Troops to Oneglia; and given Orders to Sir John Leake, to transport them thither.

And since, you have presented another Memorial to her Majesty, deliring her to grant an additional Subsidy of £. 50,000 to his Royal Highness, which is hardly

practicable, according to the Custom of this Country, when the Parliament is not assembled; nevertheless, her Majesty, as an Effect of her Zeal for the Security of the States of his Royal Highness, is willing to advance the said Sum of£. 50,000, reserving to herfelfa Right to de-

duct the said Sum out of the Subsidies, which shall hereafter become due, at such a Time, as the shall judge most proper.

You will be pleased to represent this to his Royal Highness, as a Mark of the great Esteem her Majesty has for his Royal Highness, and the Regard she has for his Alliance.

Copy of a Letter from Mr, Secretary Harley to the Lord Treasurer, April 13 th, 1706.

My Lord, Whitehall, April y, 1706.

THE Count de Briangon, Envoy Extraordinary from the Duke of Savoy, having presented the indofed Memorial Jo the Queen, her Majesty, with the Advice of the Committee of the Lords of the Council, ordered me, in the Absence of Mr. Secretary Hedges, to return an Answer, whereof there is a Copy inclosed.

And I am commanded to transmit both to your Lordship, and to signify her Majesty's Pleasure, for advancing to the Duke of Savoy the Sum of £. 50,000 by way of Anticipation of the Subsidies, which shall grow due to him from her Majesty, as more at large doth appear by the said Answer.

I am, my Lord,

Tour Lordship's, &V.

Ro. Harley.

Translation of a Memorial to her Majesty from the Imperial Envoy, August 24th, 1705.

Madam,

THE underwritten Envoy Extraordinary of his Imperial Majesty has received Orders, by these last Mails, most humbly to represent to your Majesty, that his Imperial Majesty was no sooner entered upon the Government, but he employed his first Care and Application upon the Affairs of Italy; which he found reduced to such a Condition, that, without a speedy Remedy, they must, without fail, be intirely ruined, and the Interest of the common Cause thereby suffer an irreparable Lois; which has obliged his Imperial Majesty, not only

to fend thither immediately a great Number of Recruits, but to order a new Levy, which is to be ready by the End of October next.

But being lately informed by Prince , that,

unless there be two Bodies of Tloops, one on each Side of the Po, it would be impoflibie for him to penetrate into the Heart of the Mi/aueze, since , notwith-

standing all these Recruits, would (till keep the Superiority there; where, on the other Side, if he might ex-pedf, by the Month of October, a good Body of regular Troops, he hoped, by the means of Defcrtions, and Dif-tempers, by which the Enemy's Army suffered very much, to have the Superiority then of his Side, to presently re-establish Affairs in that Country, and to save his Royal Highness of Savoy, whose Ruin, without it, was unavoidable:

His Imperial Majesty, being most sensibly affcdVed, as well with the Condition, to which his said Royal High-ness is reduced, as with the Consequences, that his Ruin would infallibly produce, has resolved to make the utmost Efforts, for preventing so fatal a Blow to the common Cause, and to form, with all Speed, the Body of Troops, which Prince Eugene requires; for which Purpose he makes u(e of the 4,000 Men of the Bifttop of

Wurtjbourg's Troops, and has, for the same End, concluded a Treaty with the Duke of for 1,600

Men; to which his Imperial Majesty will add, besides the Recruits he is raising, as many as he can spare of the Troops in Bavaria: And, since all this cannot make that Body so considerable, as is requisite, his Imperial Majesty has desired the States General to let him have the 4,000 Men of the Duke of Wurtember s, which are in their Pay, for the same Service, which was no sooner asked, than granted by the said States; there being nothing now to be done, but toperfuade the Duke of Wurtemberg to it, to whom Instances have been already made for that Purpose.

With all these Troops his Imperial Majesty hopes to form a Body of about 20,000 Men, and to have it in Italy by the Month of October; but as Experience has but too evidently shewn, that it is not enough to get Troops, if you have not the Means to put them in Motion, and Action, for want of which, it has been seen these last Years, that his Imperial Majesty's new Levies could not befent into Italy, and what is worse, dwindled away as fall as they were made; and his Imperial Majesty, in the Condition he is in at present, deprived of his Revenues of Hungary, of and the

greatest Part of his hereditary Countries, which have been ruined, some by the Bavarians, and others by the Rebels, and not daring to over-charge even the Provinces, that have been exempted from these cruel Invasions, for fear that this Spirit of Sedition, which possesses the Hungarians so much, may not, by the Neighbourhood, be communicated thiiher too; not knowing, where to find a Fund, ready enough, and sufficient, to supply so urgent Expences, as the March of these Troops into Italy, and their acting the re, requires with so much Expedition; he finds himself obliged to have recourse to your Majesty's great Generosity, and that of the States General, desiring you to advance him the Sum of 400,000 Crowns, which his Imperial Majesty promises faithfully and punctually to repay out of the Contributions, which are due to him from the Princes of Italy, and which is a Fund, that cannot fail, as soon as ever there is a Superiority of Forces.

The underwritten Envoy Extraordinary hopes, that, if your Majesty, according to your great Wisdom, will please toconsider the Effort his Imperial Majesty designs to make, and the great Advantage, that may arise from it, you will find, that the desiring of these 400,000 Crowns is in itself a very small Thing, but very important in regard that they are the principal Foundation of the whole l'rojedt: For though all this Reinforcement of the Troops afore-mentioned, or of any other, that might be employed there, were now ready, it would be impoflibie for his Imperial Majesty to find in

his

his hereditary Countries all the Money, requisite for their March.

Wherefore, as his Imperial Majesty has (b many Proofs of the ardent Zeal, which your Majesty signalizes, upon all Occasions, by such great and generous Efforts for the Advancement of the common Cause, he allures himself, that your Majesty will make no difficulty of granting the Two Thirds of this Sum, for your Part j and at the same Time beseeches, you will employ your most powerful Offices with the States General, that, on their Part, they may agree to the other Third: But the Constitution of their Government not admitting of the Dispatch, which should be given to this Affair, your Majesty is most humbly desired to extend your Zeal and Generosity so far, as to advance the said Two Thirds, in Expectation, that your Interposition with the States General will prove effectual, to whom this ready Compliance of your Majesty's will further serve as an Encouragement, and Example; whereas, if, contrary to all Expectation, your Majesty should think fit to refer yourself to the positive Consent of the said States General, before you please to grant your Part of the Sum, the same Thing would happen, as did two Years ago, when Count Wratijlaii fohcited for a like Sum for , which, for want of the Concurrence of the States General, was not obtained, and reduced Affairs to the Extremity, we fee them in; which is such, that, if the Assistance, which his imperial Majesty now desires, should likewise fail, the Consequences of it would be much more fata!; since, at present, the Question is about intirely re-establishing the Affairs of Italy, and saving his Royal Highness, as it were besieged in his Capital, or the seeing them ruined, past Recovery; whereby France will be in a Condition to employ against the High Allies 120 Battalions, and 160 Squadrons, which it now has in , will ruin all the Benefit of the mighty Victories, which the glorious Arms of your Majesty have obtained, and elude all the Efforts, that can be made for the future.

Your Majesty will be graciously pleased to take into Consideration all these powerful Motives, which the under-witten Minister has the Honour to represent to you, and to return him an Answer, agreeable to the great Desire his Imperial Majesty has to contribute, all that is possible for him, towards the freeing from Oppression a Prince, who, by an unexampled Firmness and Constancy, has deserved so much of the common Cause, and whose Ruin would give a fatal and irreparable Blow to

Answer to Count Gallas*s Memorial, 29th 1705-

Sir,

THE Queen, having upon all Occasions given Marks of the Regard she has for the Duke of Savoy, will not be wanting to do her utmost to maintain and support a Prince, whose Merit is so much advanced by the Vigour, and Firmness, he has lately shewn against tho common Enemy. The Queen having the refore considered, with a great deal of Attention, your Memorial, dated the 24th Instant, concerning the Succours, necessary for his Royal Highness, her Majesty has commanded me to return you the following Answer:

That her Majesty has already long ago given such Orders, as might have furnished his Imperial Majesty with the Means (had he been pleated to make use of them) to cause the Troops, that are intirely at his own Disposal, to march into Italy, which being nearest that Country, are only capable of being at present useful to his Royal Highness. It was with that View, that her Majesty consented, that the Prussian and Palatine Troops, which were to decamp from the R, to join the Duke of Marlborough, should remain with the Margrave of Baden, to supply the Place of those, that were to be detached from his Army for that of Italy j since they, Vo 1. 15.

being nearest to that Country, might march thither in less Time, and with greater Ease, than any other, and by that Means be in a better Condition to answer the End, for which they were designed j and, as that was the bell Method, for the speedy succouring his Royal Highness, the Allies had reason to hope, that, when those Troops were actually on their March, they should not have been diverted, to serve elsewhere. But the Thoughts of the Imperial Ministers seem to be at present intirely bent upon the War of Hungary; whereas, if they had applied themselves with the same Diligence to the carrying-on that of Italy, the French had been in all likelihood driven out of that Country, which consequently would have brought the War in Hungary to a happy Issue; but*, as Italy is neglected, and left to Chance, there is reason to fear, both those Wars will have the same Faie.

Her Majesty therefore thought, she could not give a better Testimony of the great Esteem she has for the Duke of Savoy, whose constant Zeal and unshaken Firmness have been so conspicuous to all the World, than by concerting proper Measures fur his most speedy and effectual Relief; and her Majesty, after mature Consideration, is of opinion, that nothing can be done byway of Negotiation, for relieving of him this Year: Therefore her Majesty does not doubt, but that his Imperial Majesty will give the necessary Orders, that such of his Troops as are nearest to Italy, do immediately march thither: When that is done, her Majesty will be willing to hearken to what reasonable Propositions can be made to her.

I am.

Sir, your, &c.

Ro. Harley.

A Petition of divers miserable Bankrupts, on behalf Bankrupt*, of themselves, and great Numbers of others, who have surrendered all they have in the World for the Use of their Creditors, on the Penalty of Death, under the Encouragement and Directions of the late Bankrupt Act, who have yet had no Benefit thereby, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have in all things complied with the said Act, thinking to enjoy Liberty, and the Benefit thereof, as they were advised they ought to have, even beyond any Objection

5 Ann. 22,0 — 23°

of their Creditors; yet tome Words in the said Act seeming obscure to the Judges, the Petitioners are con-ftfued not to be within the meaning thereof, and some of them (though they have their Certificates from the Lord Keeper, and the Judges, as the Act directs) are since taken up, and put into Newgate, and otheF Gaols j so that, presuming on a parliamentary Security for their Liberty, they are reduced, with their Wives and Children, to a Milery past all Example: And praying, that such Bankrupts, as have surrendered their Effects, according to the said Act, may be immediately relieved by some short Bill, or Clause, to explain the said Act, in Favour of the Petitioners.

Resolved, That the Petition be rejected.

Sir William AJbhurJi reported from the Committee, Luftring to whom the Petition of the Royal Luftring Company Company* was referred; that the Committee having heard the Petitioners, the Committee had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That by the Encouragement of the several Acts of Parliament, made for the Benefit of the said Luftring Company, the said Manufacture doth equal, if not exceed, that of France.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, since the making of the late Act, in the 3d and 4th Years of her present Majesty's Reign (for prohibiting all Trade and Commerce with France) the said Manufacture hath been under great Discouragements, by Doubts, which have arisen, whether the Act of Prohibition has not repealed, or made ineffectual, the said several Acts of Parliament, relating to the Luftring Manufacture in this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That some Provision be made, to put the Royal Luftring Company in as good a Condition, as they were before the making of the said late Act of Prohibition.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Rye EledHo* Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Port of Rye, in the County of Sussex, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the feme were read, and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Charles Fagg, and Philip Gibbon, Esquires, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of Edward Southwell, and Philip Herbert, Esquires, to serve in Parliament for the Port of Rye:

That, upon the Poll, the Numbers were.

For the Petitioners - 19:

For the Sitting Members - 21.

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayor, Jurats, and Freemen, paying Scotland Lot, resident within the Port, or who had been resident within twelve Months before the Election.

That the Petitioners Counsel infilled, that one Person, who polled for the fitting Members, had no Right to vote j and that Six others, who were refused by the Mayor (as not qualified according to the Statute of 13* Car. 2*', for the well governing and regulating Corporations) ought to be added to the Petitioners Poll j which would give them a Majority.

As to the Person, that polled for the fitting Members, viz.Mr. Martin, the Petitioners Counsel gave Evidence.

That he had not lived in Rye for above Mr. Tho. ni e. twelve Years: That he did not pay Scotland Lot, nor had any House there: But the Evidence admitted, that, when he left the Town, he went to Sea in the late King's Service, and was employed in a Custom-house Sloop, during the Peace; and that he did not know, that he had a Settlement in any other Place; and that he had a Daughter, that had lived at for three Years last pad, but that Ihe was only a Lodger.

As to the Six Persons, that were refused by the Mayor, viz.

John Young, Thankfull Bishop, Robert John

Dadd, Jof. Breades, Geo. Burwafh;

The Petitioners Counsel produced the Assembly Book; by which it appeared, they had all Six been made free:

And called several Witnesses; viz. Mr. Gribble, Jof.

Tucker, Wal. Walters, to prove, that they offered their Votes for the Petitioners, but were refused by the Mayor; who said, they might be free to some Purposes, but not to chuse Members to Parliament; and, if he admitted them to poll, he could not return the Sitting Members:

And one of the Witness'es: viz. Walter Walters, feid, that in March, 1704, the Mayor said, they should be free, or not, according as they voted, notwithstanding their Mandamus.

And the feme Persons gave Evidence, that the Six Persons in dispute were warned by the Serjeant to the Election; and that they were warned, and had appeared, at the next Assembly, that was held after the Election; and that Thankful Bishop one of the Six, had paid half Duties to Mr. Mamouch, the Mayor, for Hops; and all, that are not Freemen, pay whole Duties.

Jof. Breades, one of the Six, said, he was warned by the Serjeant to the last Election; and that the Mayor asked his Vote for Mr. Southwell, and Mr. Herbert; and that he has been at several Assemblies, since the last Election; and that the Mayor declared, be it how it would, the Sitting Members should have it.

That, as to these Six Persons not having qualified themselves according to the Act, passed 13 Car. the Petitioners Counsel produced the Resolution of the House of Commons, 12 November, Y WiHielmi et Maria, in the Cause between Caleb Banks, and Tho. Frewen, Esquires, Petitioners, and Sir John Aujlen and Sir John Dorrell,

Sitting Members; viz. "Resolved, That Thomas ble, Thomas Tutty, and Samuel Joke, senior, being discharged

5 Ann. i 3° Januarii. 25 i

" discharged by the Commissioners, appointed by the " Act for regulating Corporations, have a Right to vote " in electing Barons, to serve in Parliament for the Port of Rye."

That then the 4th and 12th Sect. of the Act, passed 13* Car. 2di, for the well governing and regulating Corporations, were read, relating to Persons, concerned in the Government of Corporations, qualifying themselves, by receiving the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, according to the Rights of the Church of ,within

one Year next before their Election.

That the Counsel for the Sitting Members admitted, that the Six Persons above mentioned did offer their Votes for the Petitioners, and were refused by the Mayor; but they infilled, that the said Six Persons had no Right to vote, because that they, as well as several others, who voted for the Petitioners, were not duly elected Freemen.

And, to make this appear, they alleged, that by the Constitution of the Port of Rye there are two Courts, the one called the Assembly Court and the other the Hundred Court: That the Assembly Court confided of the Mayor, two Jurats, and eight Freemen at the lead; and that at this Court Freemen are chose. Bylaws made, and Leases are let; and that at the Hundred Court, confiding of the Mayor, Jurats, and all the Freemen, the Mayor, and other Officers, and also Parliament-men, are chosen.

That the Counsel for the Sitting Members alleged likewise, that there are three Ways of admitting Persons to their Freedom in the Port of

id. The elded Sons of Freemen at 21 Years of Age have a Right to their Freedom:

adly. Every Mayor has a Right to make one Person free in his Mayoralty:

3dly, All other Persons, to be made free, mud be. proposed by the Mayor at the Court of Assembly, and approved by a Majority of the Freemen present.

And thus much of the Conditution was admitted by the Petitioners Counsel.

But the Counsel for the Sitting Members infided farther, that the Freemen, affidingattheCourtof Assembly, being of the Nature of a Common Council, ought to qualify themselves according to the Corporation Act} and also, that, by the Cudom of the Port, if any Person has been proposed, to be made free, to the Assembly Court, and rejected, he cannot be proposed again in the same Mayoralty.

And as to the First of these two controverted Points, the Sitting Members Counsel called several Witnesses: And fird,

Robert Meadow; who laid, he had known Rye 26 or 27 Years; and that he always looked upon it, that no Person, that had not qualified himself, by receiving the Sacrament, could vote in the Assembly Court, but in the Hundred Court they might; and that himself, and Four others, went 15 or 16 Miles to receive the Sacrament, to qualify themselves to vote at the Assembly Court.

Allen Olive, Mich. Cadman, said, it was not usual to

come to the Assembly Court, without receiving the Sacrament: And Cadman said, that one , being at the Assembly Court, would not aft, because he had not qualified himself.

That the Sitting Members Counsel also to this Point produced an Entry in the Assembly Book; where at a Court, held 6* Dec. 1690, it was proposed, whether Mr. Thomas Ttttty had a Right to fit, and aft, being a Person expunged by the late Act of Parliament; and it was carried, he had a Right.

That, as to the other Point, the Sitting Members Counsel called Robert Meadow, John , — knew

Rye 35 Years; Allen Olive, Thirty-five Years; Mich. Cadman, free almost eight Years:

Who said, that the Custom was, that, if a Person had been proposed to the Assembly Court, to be made free, and rejected, he could not be proposed again in the same Mayoralty; but that they never made an Entry V o l. 15,

of a Negative. Arid Meadow said, that himself having Ry«ElefU , been put up, and rejected, 25 Years ago, was refused to be put up again the same Year; the Mayor saying, it was contrary to Custom; And Jeremiah Cribble was refused about four Years ago, on the feme Account.

That the Sitting Members Counsel then called a Wit-nels, William Easter, who had been Chamberlain of the

Court; who said, that four Persons, infilled to be added to the Petitioners Poll, viz. John Young, and Bishop, and likewise two others, who polled for the Petitioners, viz.Walter Walters, and Thomas Hills, were

rejected several times in Mr. Francis Young's Mayoralty, but were at last elected in the same Mayoralty.

That the Sitting Members Counsel also objected, and gave Evidence (Wm. Easter) to other three (of which Wm. Chiswell, Edward Whelmand polled for the Petitioners, and the other, viz. George Burwa/h, was one of the Six, infilled to be added to the Petitioners Poll) as being chose by Persons, made free contrary to the aforesaid Custom.

That the Counsel for the Sitting Members also read the Report 19th December, in the first Year of her present Majesty, as an Evidence of the Opinion of that Parliament.

That the Sitting Members Counsel called one Witness, in relation to the Mayor, viz. Step. Odiarne; who said, that he took the Poll at the Electlon; and that the Mayor refused the Votes in Question, and gave this Reason for it,

That, if he admitted them, he mull makea Return against-the Act of Parliament; and that the Report of the controverted Election in the last House of Commons was read.

That the Petitioners Counsel was heard by way of Reply.

And they admitted, that the Four Persons abovementioned were put up in the Assembly Court and that they were rejected, and chose again in the same Mayoralty; but denied, there was any Custom against it.

And, as to this Point, the Petitioners Counsel produced an ancient Book of the Customs of the Corporation; and called a Witness (Mr. Toumay) who had been Town Clerk in 1672, and Mayor in 1681; who laid, he knew no Custom, that, if a Man had been rejected in an Assembly Court, he could not be put up again the same Mayoralty; and, though he had examined the ancient Book, or Customacy, he could find no such Custom.

That the Petitioners Counsel also produced the Copies of three peremptory Mandamus's, with their Returns, brought by Walter Walters, Geo. Burwa/h, and Edward Wilmhurst, 40 of this Queen, for restoring them to their Freedom, three of the Persons objected to by the Sitting Members Counsel; and the Mayor and Jurats returned those Mandamus's, that the said Persons were never amoved, but enjoyed all the Privileges of Freemen.

That they also produced the Copy of the Record of an Action, brought in the Queen's Bench, 3* of her pre--lent Majesty, by Morgan Warner against Mr. Mannouch, the Mayor, and feme of the Jurats, viz. Robert,

Allen Olive, and Mick. Cadman, for a false Return to a Mandamus, brought by the said Warner, for restoring' him to his Freedom. The Return was, that Mr. -tier was not elected: And Mr. Warner had a Verdict, and recovered Damages, and Colls, in that Action.

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Relating Poor, and other ancient Inhabitants, of the several nightly Hamlets of the Parish of St. Dunsta Stepney, was pre-. " atcJl-fented to the House, and read setting forth, that there is a Bill in the House, for regulating the nightly Watch:

That the Petitioners have always provided an able and sufficient Watch in their Hamlets, in so much that, for a long time, they have not had any Robbery, or House-breaking, nor the lenft Complaint; yet the Petitioner* are willing to increase their Watch, if the Inhabitants desire it; but hope, they shall not, by the said Bill, be compelled to an unnecessary Charge, considering the Security they now enjoy, by the good Orders, and Care, observed in the said Hamlets, relating to the nightly Watch: And praying, that they may be exempted out of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

And that afterwards her Majesty was pleased to make this most gracious Speech to both Houses j viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

HAVING acquainted you, at the opening of this Session, that the Treaty, for an Union between land and Scotland, which had been concluded here by the Commissioners appointed for that Purpose, in pursuance of the Powers, given by the Parliaments of both Kingdoms, was then under the Consideration of the Parliament of Scotland, 1 can now, with great Satisfaction, inform you, that the said Treaty has been ratified by Act of Parliament in Scotland, with some Alterations, and Additions.

J have directed the Treaty, agreed to by the Commissioners of both Kingdoms, and also the Act of Ratification from Scotland, to be laid before youj and I hope, it will meet with your Concurrence and Approbation.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

It being agreed by this Treaty, that is to have

an Equivalent for what that Kingdom is obliged to contribute towards paying the Debts of England, I mull recommend to you, that, in case you agree to the Treaty, you will take care to provide for the Payment of the Equivalent to Scotland accordingly.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

You have now an Opportunity before you of putting the lait Hand to a happy Union of the two Kingdoms; which, 1 hope, will be a lading Blelfing to the whole Wand, a great Addition to its Wealth and Power, and a firm Security to the Protedant Religion.

The Advantages, which will accrue to us all from an Union, are so apparent, that I will add no more, but

14

Articles of Union.

AGREED on the Twenty-second Day of July, in the Fifth Year of the Reign of her most excellent Majesty Anne, by the Grace of God Queen of England, Scotland, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, (Ac. and in the Year of our Lord 1706, by the Commissioners, nominated on the behalf of the Kingdom of England, under her Majesty's great Seal of England, bearing date at Westminster the Tenth Day of April lad pad, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, made in England, in the Third Year of her Majesty's Reign, and the Commissioners, nominated on the behalf of the Kingdom of Scotland, under her Majesty's great Seal of Scotland, bearing date the 27th Day of February lad pad, in pursuance of the 4th Act of the Third Session of her Majesty's current Parliament of Scotland, in the 4th Year of her Majesty's Reign, to treat of and concerning an Union of the said Kingdoms; which Articles are in all Humility to be presented to the Queen's most excellent Majesty, and offered ro the Consideration of the respective Parliaments of both Kingdoms, pursuant to the said Acts, and Commissions:

1. That the two Kingdoms of England and

shall, upon the fird Day of May next ensuing the Date hereof, and for ever after, be united into one Kingdom, by the name of Great Britain; and that the Ensigns Armorial of the said united Kingdom be such, as her Majesty shall appoint; and the CroHes of St. and

St. Andrew be conjoined in such manner, as her Majesty shall think fit, and used in all Flags, Banners, Standards, and Ensigns, both at Sea and Land.

2. That the Succession to the Monarchy of the united Kingdom of Great Britain, and of the Dominions thereunto belonging, after her most sacred Majesty, and in default of Issue by her Majesty, be, remain, and continue, to the most excellent Princess Scphia, Fleet refs and Duchess Dowager of Hannoverand the Heirs of her Body, being Protedants, upon whom the Crown of England is settled by an Act of Parliament, made in

in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, "An Act for the " further Limitation of the Crown, and better securing the Rights and Liberties of the Subjectand that all Papids, and Persons marrying Papids, shall be excluded from, and for ever incapable to inherit, possess, or enjoy, the Imperial Crown of Great Britain, and the Dominions thereunto belonging, or any Part thereof; and in every such Case, the Crown, and Government, shall from time to time defeend to, and be enjoyed by, such Person, being a Protedant, as should have inherited and enjoyed the lame, in case such Papist, or Person marrying a Papist, was naturally dead, according to the Provision for the Descent of the Crown of England, made by one other Act of Parliament in England, in the fird Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, intituled, "An Act, declaring " the Rights and Liberties, of the Subject, and settling " the Succession of the Crown."

3d. That the united Kingdom of Great Britain bere-presented by one and the same Parliament, to be (tiled the Parliament of Great Britain.

4th. That all the Subjects of the united Kingdom of Great

5 Ann. 28° Januarii. £59

Great Britain shall, from and after the Union, have full Freedom and intercourse of Tradeand Navigation to and' from any Port or Place within the said united Kingdom, and the Dominions and Plantations thereunto belonging; and that there be a Communication of all other Rights, Privileges, and Advantages, which do or may belong to the Subjects of either Kingdom, except where it is otherwise expressly agreed in these Articles.

5th. That all Ships, belonging to her Majesty's Subjects of Scotland at the time of signing this Treaty, for the Union of the two Kingdoms (though foreign-built) shall be deemed, and pass, as Ships of the Built of Great Britain, the Owner, or (where there are more Owners) one or more of the Owners, within twelve Months after the Union, making Oath, that at the time of signing the said Treaty, the same did belong to him, or them, or to some other Subject, or Subjects, of Scotland, to be particularly named, with the Places of their respective Abodes, and that the same doth then belong to him, or them, and that no Foreigner, directly or indirectly, hath any Share, Part, or interest, therein; which Oath shall be made before the chief Officer or Officers of the Customs in the Port next to the Abode of the said Owner, or Owners: And the said Officer or Officers shall be impowered to administer the said Oath; and the Oath, being so administered, shall. be attested by the Officer or Officers, who administered the fame; and, being regiftsred by the said Officer or Officers, shall be delivered to the Matter of the Ship, for Security of her Navigation; and a Duplicate thereof shall be transmitted by the said Officer or Officers to the chief Officer or Officers of the Customs in the Port of Eden burgh, to be there entered in a Register, and from thence to be sent to the Port of London, to be there entered in the general Register of all trading Ships, belonging to Great Britain.

6th. That all Parts of the united Kingdom, for ever, from and after the Union, shall have the same Allowances and Encouragements, and be under the same Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Regulations of Trade, and liable to the same Customs and Duties, on Import and Export; and that the Allowances, Encouragements, Prohibitions, restrictions, and Regulations, of Trade, and the Customs and Duties, on Import and Export, settled in England, when the Union commences, shall, from and after the Union, take place throughout the whole united Kingdom.

7. That all Parts of the united Kingdom be for ever, from and after the Union, liable to the same Excises upon all excisable Liquors; and that the Excise, settled in England on such Liquors, when the Union commences, take place throughout the whole united Kingdom.

8th. That from and after the Union, all foreign Salt, which shall be imported into ,shall be charged,

at the Importation there, with the same Duties, as the like Salt is now charged with, being imported into England j and to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner: But Scotland shall, for the Space of Seven Years, from the said Union, be exempt from the paying, in,

for Salt, made there, the Duty or Excise, now payable for Salt, made in England; but, from the Expiration of the said Seven Years, shall be subject and liable to the same Duties for Salt, made in Scotland, as shall be then payable for Salt, made in England; to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner, and with the like Drawbacks, and Allowances, as in England: And, during the said Seven Years, there shall be paid in England for all Salt, made in Scotland, and imported from thence Into England, the same Duties, upon the Importation,

as shall be payable for Salt, made in; to be

levied, and secured, in the same Manner, as the Duties on foreign Salt, are to be levied, and secured, in England: And that, during the said Seven Years, no Salt whatsoever be brought from Scotland to England by Land, in any manner, under the Penalty of forfeiting the Salt, and the Cattle and Carriages, made use of in bringing the same, and paying Twenty Shillings for V01. 15.

every Bnfliel of such Salt, and proportionably for a greater or Idler Quantity; for which the Carrier, as well as the Owner, shall be liable, jointly and severally; and the Perffins, bringing or carrying the fame, to be imprisoned by any one Justice of the Peace, by the Space of Six Momhs, without Bad, and until the Penalty be. paid: And that, during the said Seven Years, all failed Flelli, or Fish. exported from Scotland to England, or, made use of for victualing of Ships in Scotland, and all. FJefli put on hoard in Scotland, to be ex;>orrcd to Parts beyond the Seas, winch IhaM be salted wuh Scotch Salt, or any Mixture therewith, shall be forfeited, and may be seized: And that, from and after the Union, the'. Laws and Acts of Parliament in Scotland, for pining, curing, and packing, of Herrings white lr:fh, and Salmon, for Exportation, with for ign Salt only, and for preventing of Frauds in curing and packing of Fiffi, be continued in force in Scotland, tubied to such Alterations, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain: A-d that all Fish, exported from Scotland to-Parts beyond the Seas, which flv-.il be cured with foreign Salt only, shall have the tame Ealies, Premiums, and Drawbacks, as are or shall be allowed to such Persons, as export the like Fish from England: And if any Mat-, ters, or Fraud, relating to the said Duties on Sait, shall hereafter appear, which are not sufficiently provided against by this Article, the same shall be subject to such further Provisions, as shall be thought fit by the Parliament of Great Britain.

9th. That, whenever the Sum of One million Nine hundred Ninety-seven thousand Seven hundred Sixty-three Pounds, Eight Shillings, and Four Pence Half-peny, shall be enacted by the Parliament Britain

to be raised in that Part of the united Kingdom, now called England, on Land, and other Things, usually charged in Acts of Parliament there, for granting an Aid to the Crown by a Land Tax, that Part of the united Kingdom, now called Scotland, shall be charged by the same Act with the further Sum of Forty-eight thousand Pounds, free of all Charges, as the Quota of Scotland to such Tax, and so proportionably, for any greater or lesser Sum, raised in England by any Tax on Land, and other Ttiings, usually charged, together with the I.and; and that such Quota for Scotland, in the Taxes aforesaid, be raised and collected in the tame Manner, as the Eels now is in Scotland, but subject to such Regulations in the Manner of collecting, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain.

10th. That, during the Continuance of the respective Duties on stampt Paper, Vellum, or Parchment, by the several Acts now in force in England, Scotland shall not be charged with the same respective Duties.

nth. That, during the Continuance of the Duties, payable in England, on Windows and Lights, which determines on the First Day oiAuguft, 1710, shall not be charged with the same Duties.

12th. That, during the Continuance of the Duties, payable in England, on Coals, Culm, and Cinders, which determines the 30th Day of September, 1710, Scotland shall not be charged therewith, for Coals, Culm, and Cinders consumed there; but shall be charged with the same Duties, as in England, for all Coal, Culm, and Cinders, not consumed in Scotland.

13th. That, during the Continuance of the Duty, payable in England, on Malt, which determines the 24th Day of June, 1707, Scotland shall not be charged with that Duty.;

14th. That the Kingdom of Scotland be not charged with any other Duties, laid on by the Parliament of

England before the Union, except those consented to in this Treaty; in regard it is agreed, that all necessary; Provision shall be made by the Parliament of for the publick Charge and Service of that Kingdom, for the Year 1707: Provided nevertheless, that, if the Parliament of England shall think fit to lay any further Impositions, by way of Customs, or such Excises, with which, by virtue of this Treaty, Scotland is to be charged

17th. That, from and after the Union, the same Weights and Meafores shall be used throughout the united Kingdom, as are now established in; and

Standards of Weights and NIcafures shall be kept by those Boroughs in Scotland, to whom the keeping the Standards of Weights and Measures, now in use there, does of special Right belong; all which Standards shall be lent dawn to such respective Boroughs from the Stand* ards, kept in the Exchequer at subject ne-

vertheless to such Regulations, as the Parliament of Great Britain shall think fit.

18th. That the Laws^concerning Regulation of Trade, Customs, and such Excises, to which Scotland is, by virtue of this Treaty, to be liable, be the same in Scotland, from and after the Union, as in England; and that all other Laws, in ule within the Kingdom of Scotland, do, after the Union, and notwithstanding thereof, remain in the same Force,.as-before, except such, as are contrary to, or inconsistent with, the Terms of this Treaty, but alterable by the Parliament of; with

this Difference betwixt the Laws, concerning publick Right, Policy, and civil Government, and‘those, which concern private Rights that the Laws, which concern publick Right, Policy, and civil Government, may be made the same throughout the whole united Kingdom, but that no Alteration be made in Laws, which concern private Right, except for evident Utility of the Subjects wirhin Scotland.

19th. That the Court of Session, or College of Justice, do, after the Union, and notwithstanding thereof, remain in all Time coming within , as it is now

constituted by the Laws of that Kingdom, and with the same Authority and Privileges, as before the Unions subject nevertheless to such Regulations, for the better Admin ill rat ion of Justice, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain: And that the -Court of Justi-ciary do alfc, after five Union, and notwithstanding thereof, remain in all Time coming within as k

now is constituted by the Laws of that Kingdom, and with the same Authority and Privileges, as before the Union; subject nevertheless to such Regulations, as shall be made by the Parliament of and with-
