24th. That, from and after the Union, there be one Great Seal for the united Kingdom of Great , which shall be different from the Great Seal, now used in either Kingdom; and that the quartering the Arms, as may bell suit the Union, be left to her Majesty; and that, in the mean Time, the Great Seal of England be used as the Great Seal of the united Kingdom: And that the Great Seal of the united Kingdom be used, for sealing Writs, to cledl, and summon the Parliament of Great Britain, and for sealing all Treaties with foreign Princes and States, and all publick Acts, Instruments, and Orders, of State, which concern the whole united Kingdom, and in all other Matters, relating to England, as the Great Seal of England is now used: And that a Seal in Scotland, after the Union, be always kept and made use of in all things, relating to private Rights, or Grants, which have usually passed the Great Seal of Scotland, and which only concern Offices, Grants, Commissions, and private Rights, within that Kingdom; and that, until such Seal shall be appoimed by her Majesty, the present Great Seal of Scotland Hull be used lor such Purposes: And that the Privy Seal, Signet, Cachet, Signet of the Jufiiciary Court, Quarter Seal, and Sea's of Courts, now uled in Scotland, be continued; but that the said Seals be altered, and adapted to the State of the Union, as her Majesty shall think fit: And the said Seals, and all of them, and the Keepers of them, shall be subject to such Regulations, as the Parliament of Great Britain shall hereafter make.

25th. That all Laws and Statutes in either Kingdom, so far as they are contrary to, or inconsistent with, the Terms ofihele Articles, or any of them, shall, from and after the Union, cease, and become void; and shall be so declared to be by the respective Parliaments of the said Kingdoms.

8th. That from and after the Union, all foreign Salt, which shall be imported into Scotland, shall be charged, at the Importation there, with the same Duties, as the like Salt is now charged with, being imported into England , and to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner: But, in regard the Duties of great Quantities of foreign Salt, imported, may be very heavy on the Merchants Importers, that therefore all foreign Salt, imported into Scotland, shall be cellared, and locked up, under the Custody of the Merchant Importer, and the Officers, employed for levying the Duties upon Salt s and that the Merchant may have what Quantities thereof his Occasion may require, not under a Wey, or Forty Buftiels, at a time, giving Security for the Duty of what Quantity he receives, payable in six Months: But Scotland shall, for the Space of seven Years from the said Union, be exempted from paying, in Scotland, for Salt, made there, the Duty or Excise, now payable for Salt, made in England; but, from the Expiration of the said seven Years, shall be subject and liable to the same Duties for Salt, made in Scotland, as shall be then payable for Salt, made in England; to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner, and with proportional Drawbacks, and Allowances, as in England; with this Exception, that Scotland shall, after the said seven Years, remain exempted from the Duty of Two Shillings and Four-pence a Bushel on home Salt, imposed by an Act, made in England, in the ninth and tenth of King William the 3d of England; and, if the Parliament of Great Britain dial), at or before the expiring of the said seven Years, substitute any other Fund in place of the said two Shillings and Four-pence of Excise on the Buffiel of hofne Salt, Scotland shall, after the said seven Years, bear a Proportion of the said Fund, and hare an Equivalent in the Terms of this Treaty: And that, during the said seven Years, there shall be paid in England for all Salt, made in Scotland, and imported from thence into England, the same Duties, upon the Importation, as shall be payable for Salt, made in; to be levied

and secured, in the same Manner, as the Duties on foreign Salt, are to be levied, and secured, in England: And that, after the said seven Years, how long the said Duty of two Shillings and Four-pence a Buthel upon Salt is continued in England, the said two Shillings Four-pence a Bushel shall be payable for all Salt, made in Scotland, and imported into England; to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner: And that, during the Continuance of the Duty of two Shillings Four-peace a Buibel upon Salt, made in no Salt

That whenever the Sum of £. 1,997,763. 8r. 4f d. shall be enacted by the Parliament of Great Britain to be raised in that Part of the united Kingdom, now called England, on Land, and other Things, usually charged in Acts of Parliament there, for granting an Aid to the Crown by a Land Tax, that Part of the united Kingdom, now called Scotland, shall be charged by the same Act with a further Sum of £.48,000 free of all Charges, as the Quota of Scotland to f uch Tax; and so proportionally for any greater or Idler Sum, raised in England by any Tax on Land, and other Things, usually charged together with the Land; and that such Quota for Scotland, in the Cafes aforesaid, be raised and collected in the same Manner as the Cess now is in Scotland, but subject to such Regulations in the Manner of collecting, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain.

14th. That the Kingdom of Scotland be not charged with any other Duties, laid on by the Parliament of before the Union, except these consented to in this Treaty; in regard it is agreed, that all necessary Provision shall be made by the Parliament of Scotland for the publick Charge and Service of that Kingdom, for the Year 1707: Provided nevertheless, that, if the Parliament of England shall think fit to lay any further Impositions, by way of Customs, or such Excises, with which, by virtue of this Treaty, Scotland is to be charged equally with England, in such same Scotland shall be liable to the same Customs, and Excises, and have an Equivalent, to be settled by the Parliament of Great Britain; with this further Provision, that any Malt, to be made and consumed in that Part of the united Kingdom, now called Scotland, shall not be charged with any Imposition

upon Malt, during this present War. And seeing it cannot be supposed, that the Parliament of Great Britain will ever lay any forts of Burthens upon the united Kingdom, but what they shall find of Necessity at that Time, for the Preservation and Good of the whole, and with due Regard to the Circumstances and Abilities of every Part of the united Kingdom; therefore it is agreed, that there be it further Exemption infilled upon for any Part of the united Kingdom, but that the Consideration of any Exemptions, beyond what are already agreed On in this Treaty, shall be left to the Determination of the Parliament of Great Britain.

The Title of the Minute Book of the Proceedings of the Commissioners was read.

And the said Book is bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Saturday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Articles of Union, and Act of Ratification of them by the Parliament of Scotland.

Ordered, That the Articles of Union, and Act of Ratification, as also the Minutes of the Proceedings of the said Commissioners, be printed.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put. That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, that shewill.be pleated to give Orders, that the Minutes of the Proceedings of the former Commissioners, appointed in the First Year of her Reign, to treat of an Union, may belaid before this House;

The House divided:

The Yeas go forth:

Tellers forth. Yeas} 49-

Tellers for the

So it passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, returning her Majesty the humble Thanks of this House, for her most gracious Speech this Day to both Houses of Parliament, and for communicating to this House the Articles of Union, and the Act of Parliament in Scotland, for Ratification thereof.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty s most honourable Privy Council.

Ordered, That Mr. Thornb Mr. Skippott, Mr. Farter, Sir Robert Eden, Mr. Foley, Mr. Mompejon, Mr. Shepherd, Sir John Spencer, Mr. Clayton, Mr. Gwynn, Mr. Hampden, Mr. Winstanley, be added to the Committee, to whom the Petition of several principal Breeders of Cattle is referred.

Resolved, That the Bill for Sale of certain Houses near Aldgate, in London, late the Estate of WtUiams, Esquire, deceased, and for purchasing Lands in lieu thereof, do pass; and that the Title be. An Act for Sale of certain Houses near Aldgate, in late the Estate of William Williams, Esquire, and for purchasing Lands in lieu thereof.

Ordered, That Sir Francis Masham do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence thereunto.

Ordered, That Sir Henry Peachy have Leave to withdrawn his Petition, touching the Election for the County of SuJJ'ex.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the Clause, offered to the Bill for the further and better Relief, Employment, and Maintenance, of the Poor, be further adjourned rill Tomorrow Morning.

Ordered, That the Names of such Members, as made Default to appear, upon the Call of the House the 14th Instant, and were not excused, be called over on Saturday Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the City of Coventry, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House j which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of several Freemen of the City of Coventry, complaining of an undue Election of Sir Christopher Hales, Baronet, and Thomas Gery, Esquire, to serve in Parliament for the said City:

That the Petitioners Counsel alleged, that at the last Election of Citizens, to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry, Sir Chr. Hales, Baronet, Tho. Gery, Esquire, Sir Orlando Bridgman, and Edward Hopkins, Esquire, flood Candidates. They admitted, that the Majority of the Poll was with the two former; but infilled, that by the Riots and Tumults, before and at the Election, the Voters for the two latter were deterred and hindered from giving their Votes; and to this they examined several Witnesses. And first they examined

Mr. Samuel Billing, who was Mayor at the Time of the last Election: And he gave an Account, that Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins were invited down to Coventry, to Hand at the last Election of their Represen-tatives, to serve them in Parliament; and accordingly they came down on or about the Beginning of March, 1704; and there having been a Discourse, that the said Candidates did not intend to Hand, they desired Leave of the Mayor to walk the Streets, and declare the same Act the Cross: Accordingly they did walk on the 8th of March, and the same was declared at the Cross; but t'lat Day they walked there happening a great Riot, he ac'vised with his Brethren, the Aldermen, and they though it proper to fend a Letter to Mr. Secretary Harley, for the Queen's Directions in the keeping of the publick Peace; who returned an Answer, which was produced, and read; and thereby signified her Majesty's Pleasure, that they should do their utmost, according to Law, for that Purpose, as being answerable for the Peace of the City: That accordingly he, and his Brethren, in their Formalities, on a Market Day, caused Proclamation to be made by the Cryer, that no Person should appear at that Election, but such, as had Right to be there; and that none should come with Sticks: That afterwards Sir Chr. Hales and Mr. Gery came to *4

him; and Mr. Gery told him, he understood, he intended to busy himself at the Election; and that be had nothing to do there: That he was a Deputy Lieutenant, and had Power of the Pofle; and that their Men should come with Sticks; That he, the said Mr. Billing, for the better preventing Disturbance, proposed several Methods of polling to the Candidates, and, particularly, to poll by Wards; which Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins were willing to do, but the Sitting Members refused; but Sir Christopher Hales proposed to proceed by way of Ballot: That the Night before the Election he set a strong Watch, and about One or Two in the Morning, before the Election, himself took a Walk, and fee some Butchers, and others, rallying in the Butcher Row, with Sticks, which he took away: That afterwards, the Numbers increasing, and some having Sticks, he was called out again about Four; where he fee Stones flying about, and heard several cry out, A Hales, and Gery /" and he dispersed the Company: But half an Hour after he was called out again, they appearing again with Sticks, and having knocked down one William Mathews, a Watchman, and dragged him about in such manner, that some time after he died; and that himself attempting to take away a Butcher's Stick, a great Pebble was thrown at him, which cut him; and that between Four and Five he saw Mr. Mr. Robert Smith, and Mr. Burton, with them: That the Election began about Nine a Clock, and laited Three Days; That he appointed 30 or 40 Men, with Halberds to attend, without'Distinction of Parties: That, while the Poll was carrying on, he went several times into the Hall, but did not stay long, and did not fee any Disturbance, while he was there: That he was asked by Mr. Gery to poll, but declined it.

Isaac Bifaore said, he was commanded to carry an Halberd the Night before the Election, to keep the Peace; and one came up to him, and took away his Halberd, and told him, he had nothing to do with it; and he received several Wounds: That some, who carried Halberds, were in the Interest of the Sitting Members; and others, in the same Interest, refused to accept them.

John Wall laid, that he, being an Officer of the City, was in the Mayor's House, when Mr. Gery came to him, and told him, if he raised the Constables against his Men, he had an equal Share of Power, as Deputy Lieutenant, and would raise the Pofle; and on the Election Day, in the Morning, they threw Stones at the Mayor, and made the Mayor withdraw into his Parlour, whither Mr. Gety followed him: That one Chaplin, who would have voted for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins, was horsed, viz. carried bn a Cowle-llaff on two Men's Shoulders, by some, that appeared for the Sitting Members.

Wm.Wood said, he was commanded by the Mayor and Justices to aflill the Constables; and about Five in the Morning Mr. Gery's People appeared with Sticks; and that, offering to take away a Man's Stick, Mr. Gery said, They should carry Sticks; and took hold of the Stick, and said, he would do his Business.

Mr. Samuel Paul said that he was at Coventry in May was 12 Months; and he fee a great Number of People got together, between Three and Four a Clock in the Morning, several of them with Halberds; and that Mr. Gery was present; and a Party fell upon the Halberdeers, and took away their Halberds, and beat them.

Richard Benyon, Constable, gave an Account, that he was present on the Day of the Election; and about Five a Clock in the Morning the re was about 500 Men met together; and the Mayor endeavoured to break them; and they threw Stones at the Mayor; and wounded him; and afterwards Mr. Gery followed the Mayor to the Parlour: That he was, at the Time of the Poll, desired by the Mayor to keep the Peace; and that he brought up half a Score, to vote for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins, and they were abused, and driven back, there being about 500 Persons assembled; and that one getting up to the Poll, they cried, "No Freeman

A Horse ! aHorse!" and that, attempting to bring up the Men the second Day of the Poll, there was one Wm. Sheers horsed, and dragged in the Dirt: He said, some of Sir. Chr. Hales and Mr. s Side would not

appear to watch though warned by the Mayor: That Mr. Wright, Mr. Bttgg, and Mr. Bryon, and others, were appointed Inspectors for the Sitting Members.

Richard Launder said, that the Mayor and Aldermen ordered, that they should bring no Sticks to the Election; but Mr. Gery bid his Men bring Sticks, and said, he would stand by it: That things were quiet when they polled for the Sitting Members; but when any offered to poll for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins, they were ready to eat them; and, particularly, one a Butcher, coming to justify a Man's Vote, they said, he had polled before, and Tho. Grajcomhe cried out for a Horse for him.

Richard Phillips said, that on the Election Day he was lent by the Mayor, to keep the Peace: That in the Morning he heard Murder cried; and his Maid told him, if he went out he would be knocked of the Head: That he went out, and fee the Mayor, Constables, and Watchmen, engaged, and several had seized upon one Mathews, and knocked him down; That another Parcel, and Mr. Gery, seized upon one JJaac Bifcaore; but he did not fall, till one Onyon kicked him: That Mr. Edward and Mr. Stephen Hales were present there.

That he went to poll, and they cried out, " Here is Phillips ! A good Horse!" and he went back, and did not poll: That Mr. Gery made a Speech at the Cross, and bid his People bring Sticks; and said, he would stand by them.

Edward Shaw gave an Account of Mr. Gery's speaking to his Men at the Cross, to bring Sticks: That he was present, when the Mayor was wounded; and amongst the Company there was Mr. Steph. Hales, and Mr Humphry Burton, junior, the last of which {truck at the Mayor: That they got down, and wounded, several of the Watchmen, which was the Occasion of the Mayor's appearing: That he went up several times, to poll, and they cried," No Halberds 1" and drove him back; and one saying, "Take care of they knocked him

down: He owned, that afterwards he was told, he might poll quietly.

Tho. Newcomhe said, that he attempted several times on Wednesdayto poll, and could not get into the Hall;

but on Thursday Morning he polled for Sir Orlando

Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins: That Mr. Wade, who repre-' fented Mr. Hopkins, was drove back on Wednesday to Saint Mary Hall.

Colonel Davenport gave an Account, how lie was coming through Coventry, and went to the Hall, to speak with Sir Orlando Bridgman, to know, if he had any Service for Mr. Hopkins, then at London j and that the Mob used him in a very rude manner, holding Sticks oyer his Head, and telling him, he should declare, who he was for, though he told them, he had no Vote: And he said, he believed, he had been knocked down, but for one Man.

Mr. Richard Barnes said, he was at the Election on the 22d May, 1705, and was at the Mayor's, when he, Mr. Gery, said, he was a Deputy Lieutenant, and had the Power of the County, and would be obeyed; and was also present, when the Mayor, in his Formalities, read the Secretary's Letter, and forbid Sticks; and one Dines said, That was the Devil and all; but they would bring Sticks: And Barnes said, he was an Inspector of the Poll for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins; and that he was very much abuted, and at last put out of the Hall by Sir Christopher Hales; who said, " Down " with himand that he would cure him of coming from London to Elections: And that the Poll was carried on very partially for the Sitting Members; and, particularly, Mr. Benyon, Mr. Bofwand others of the Inspectors for the Sitting Member, polled for them several, without the Content of the Sheriff; and that

Vo t. 15.

Michael Lawrence, Inspector for the Sitting Member, Coventry polled, and rejected, whom he pleased: That he did not Election, vote at this Election, his Friends not thinking it safe for him so to do; and 'that, when they came from London, they were assaulted at two Places by the Sitting Members Men; and that he himself was committed to Prison by Catefby Oadham, on the Pretence of an Assault on Dines Six Days before.

Abraham Ellin laid, he went to poll for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins; and they pulled his Cloathes almost off his Back, and pushed him out of the Hall; and afterwards Mr. Catejby Oadham committed him to Bridewell, on pretence of a Bastard Child; whereas he had none.

Nathaniel Chambers also said, that he went to the Poll for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins; and was pudied back, and knocked over the Pate, and carried to Alderman Oadham's Shop, who sent him to Bridewell.

Wm. Bales said, he attempted to poll three several times; the 2d of which times he went to the Mayor, and the Mob abused both; and the 3d time they let him poll; but afterwards they fell upon him, and one took him by the Collar, and, as he thinks, had strangled him, if his Collar had not broke: He laid, he lay eleven Weeks, before he could help himself; is since in the Hospital.

Tho. Bedford said, that the First Day of the Election he endeavoured to have brought up some Men to be polled for Bridgman and Hopkins, and he could not:

That, when the Sitting Members Men thought they should lose the Election, they called for Horses, particularly Mr. Gery himself, Mr. Tito. Wjunior, and Mr. Jof. Meak, who were Inspectors, and Agents, for the Sitting Members.

Henry Ligburne said, he was refused to poll for Sir.

Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins; was knocked down* and carried lor dead, and laid on a Tomb in the Churchyard.

Mr. Jof. Cater was also examined; who gave a general Evidence to the Effect, that several Witnesses had spoke before: Said, he attended the Pol! for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins; and asking the Sitting Members, who were their Inspectors, Mr. Gery, pointing to the Mob, said, " There are our Inspectors."

Mr. Tho. Cliifwellsaid, he was one of the Sheriffs at

the Time of the Election; and denied, that he had any Security, to save him harmless.

The Clerk of the Assizes Clerk attended with several Records of Conviction of Riots, Assaults, and Batteries:

The Records being long and numerous, they were admitted, and so not read; but Mr. Cater, by Consent of the Sitting Members, was allowed to give an Account thereof; who gave an Account of several convicted on both Sides, upon whom small Fines were set; but the Mayor and Aldermen took their Trial, and w'ere acquitted.

The Sitting Members Counsel observed, that the Sitting Members had served in three Parliaments for the City of Coventry; and if ever there was a fair Election for the City, the last was one, upon the Poll their being,

to fall on the Sitting Members Men, and kill them; and that my Lord Leigh's Man, with Letters, was seized by those Men; and that many of the Halberd-men were drunk: That the Poll began, and proceeded, very fairlyj and that for 20 Years there had not been so fair an Election, though the utmost Endeavours of the other Party were used, to make a Riot; and a great many of the Charity-men made a great Noise to be polled: That on Wednesday Morning Sir Orlando Bridgman made a publick Declaration, that he never fee an Election in Coventry so peaceably carried on; and that on Sir

Orlando Bridgman wrote a Letter, he would give no further Trouble to his Friends: That he never knew any Poll by Wards,'or otherwise, than at this Election: Said, that he remembered Mr. Fielding's Election; and, that he is about 30 Years of Age.

Job Haycock said, he was present at the Election, on the 22d of May: That at Five he was ordered to attend the Mayor, being a Constable; and about Two of the Clock Two of the Halberd-men came, and broke his Door, being fuddled: That the Sitting Members Men would have avoided the Halberd-men, but the Halberd-men were ordered to meet them; and that Mr. Edward Owen bid them charge the Peace with them; and, if they did not obey, to knock them down: That all was peaceable at the Poll, and any one might have polled; and, that Abraham Ellin was committed for leaving his Family, who thereupon received weekly Collection; and that, before closing the Poll, the Bell-man was sent to all the Streets, to summon Persons to come and poll.

John Tippin said, he had taken the Poll at all the Elections for 10 or 12 Years: That he took the Poll for Sir Orlando Bridgman, and voted for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins: That he could not fee above a Third Part of the Hall, but, so far as he could fee, this Election was the most peaceable of any.

Tho. CUavor laid, that Mr. Edward Owen ordered him to bring a Stick, three Quarters long, and, if he could not reach their Heads, to strike their Faces; and that he give him Four Tickets for his Vote for Sir Orlando Bridgman and Mr. Hopkins.

Mr. Lloyd said, he was present all the three Days of the Election; and he fee the Mayor assault Mr. by llioving him; and that Mr. Gory bid his Men be quiet, and easy: That he had seen five or six Elections, and it was never so quiet, as now: Fie said, ‘Mr. Samuel Cater assaulted a Constable, and said, he was a Rogue, having taken Sir Orlando Bridgman and M r. Hopkins' Money; and that the Bell-man gave Notice to Persons, to come, and vote, before the Poll wasclosed.

That the Trustees for Irish Forfeitures did not make any Conveyance of a House, and Lands, granted to the Petitioner from the Earl of Clancarty, for the Term of 99 Years, and confirmed by Act of Parliament, in the first Year of her Majesty's Reign.

That the Petitioner, for want of fdch Conveyance, hath received no Benefit by the said Act of Parliament; and therefore, in Companion of her Circumstances, 'tis thought requisite, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill for impowering her to enter upon the Premisses, and to receive the Rents and Profits in Arrear, and now in the Tenants Hands; with a Clause, reservtng the Right of any Person or Persons, lawfully claiming under any Contraft or Bargain, made by her the said Katherine Harris, since the passing of the said Act, any Contract or Bargain to the contrary, made by any other Person, than the Petitioner, notwithstanding; and to enable the Petitioner, by Sale, or Mortgage, of the Premisses, to raise Money, to pay off the just Debts, contracted by her in these her Sufferings, and Disappointments.

A Petition of several Merchants, in behalf of themselves, and others, trading to Portugal, was presented to the House, and read; fetfing forth, that the Trade to Portugal is of great Advantage to England, by the vast Exportation of Corn, and our Woollen Manufactures; but, for want of Convoys, the said Trade is very much discouraged, to the great Lois of the Traders thither, and Returns from thence, their Goods lying sometimes nine Months aboard, for want of Convoy, which could never be obtained otherwise than by taking the Opportunities of failing with her Majesty's Ships on the publick Expeditions; when a neighbouring Nation, by due Care, manage this Trade to Advantage: That, for the Encouragement of the Portugal Trade, 'tis necessary, that Bated Convoys be appointed; viz. the first to fail the 15th of August, to carry out the Ships ready; the next, to fail the 15th of November, to bring the Trade back; the next to fail the 15th , to bring home

the Ships failed the 15th of November', and then there will need no odier Convoy until August again; by which

1706.

means this Trade may be encouraged, and carried on with Advantage to England:And praying, that Consideratiort may be had, how the Petitioners may for the future have Redrels in respect of Convoys, that so important a Trade to this Nation may be secured, and encouraged.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, and Bailiffs, of the Borough of Clifton Dartmouth Hardnesse, in the County of Devon, relating to the Trade to Newfoundland, is referred; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the lame, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Draper, Assignees of the Estate of John Aynsworth, late of London, Merchant, on behalf of themselves, and the Majority of his Creditors, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in January, 1705, the said Ainfvmth became a Bankrupt, owing above £.18,000, and, proposing to pay down 8 s.in the Pound, and the remaining ia*. in three Years after, to which most of his Creditors had agreed, did not come in before the 24th of June, 1706, to take the Benefit of a Clause in an Act to prevent Frauds, frequently committed by Bankrupts; and, before all his Creditors had signed the said Agreement, Aynsworth had great Losses, and thereby became incapable to perform the Agreement, and fled into foreign Parts, concealing his Effects so as not to be recovered by his Creditors, without his Assistance: That he now offers to return, and conform himself to the said Act, if he may be allowed some short Time for Performance thereof: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to allow the said John Aynsworth convenient Time, for returning from beyond Sea, and surrendering himself, and his Estate, and in all things conforming to the several Statutes, made concerning Bankrupts, under such Encouragements for Discovery, and Penalties upon his Refusal, as shall be thought meet.

Mr. Compton (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred the Consideration of the Articles of the Commissioners for the Union between the Kingdoms of England and Scotland, and the Act of Parliament of Scotland, for Ratification thereof, the Resolutions, which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be one of the Articles of the Union of the Kingdoms of England and Scotland,

1. That the two Kingdoms of England and Scotland shall, upon the first Day of May, which shall be in the Year 1707, and for ever after, be united into one Kingdom, by the Name of Great Britain; and that the Ensigns Armorial of the said united Kingdom be such, as her Majesty shall appoint; and the Crosses of St. George and St. Andrew be conjoined, in such Manner, as her Majesty shall think fit, and used in all Flags, Banners, Standards, and Ensigns, both at Sea and Land.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

t. That the Succession to the Monarchy of the united Kingdom of Great Britain, and of the Dominions thereunto belonging, after her most sacred Majesty, and in default of Issue of her Majesty, be, remain, and continue, to the most excellent Princess Sophia, Electrels and Duchess Dowager of Hanover, and the Heirs of her Body, being Protestants, upon whom the Crown of England is settled by an Act of Parliament, made in England, in the twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the 3d, intituled, An Act for " the further Limitation of the Crown, and better fe-Vol. 15.

" curing the Rights and Liberties of the Subject;" and that all Papists, and Persons marrying Papists, shall be excluded from, and for ever incapable to inherit, possess, or enjoy, the Imperial Crown of Great Britain, and the Dominions thereunto belonging, or any Part thereof; and in every such same the Crown and Government shall from time to time defrend to, and be enjoyed by, such Person, being a Protestant, as should have inherited and enjoyed the fame, in same such Papists, or Person marrying a Papist, was naturally dead; according to the Provision, for the Descent of the Crown of England, made by another Act of Parliament in England, in the first Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, intituled, "An Act, declaring the Rights and Liberties of the Subjects, and settling the Succession of the Crown."

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

3. That the united Kingdom of Great Britain be represented by one and the same Parliament, to be stiled the Parliament of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

4. That all the Subjects of the united Kingdom of Great Britain shall, from and after the Union, have full Freedom and intercourse of Trade and Navigation to and from any Port or Place within the said united Kingdom, and the Dominions and Plantations thereunto belonging; and that there be a Communication of all other Rights, Privileges, and Advantages, which do or may belong to the Subjects of either Kingdom, except where it is otherwise expressly agreed in these Articles.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

5th. That all Ships or Vessels, belonging to her Majesty's Subjects of Scotland at the time of ratifying the Treaty of Union of the two Kingdoms in the Parliament of Scotland, though foreign-built, be deemed, and pass, as Ships of the Built of Great Britain; the Owner, or (where there are more Owners) one or more of the Owners, within Twelve Months after the first of May next, making Oath, That at the Time of ratifying the Treaty of Union in the Parliament of Scotland, the same did, in whole, or in part, belong to him, or them, or to some other Subject or Subjects of Scotland, to be particularly named, with the Place of their respective Abodes; and that the same doth then, at the time of the said Deposition, wholly belong to him, or them; and that no Foreigner, directly or indirectly, hath any Share, Part, or Interest therein: Which Oath shall be made before the chief Officer or Officers of the Customs in the Port next to the Abode of the said Owner, or Owners; and the said Officer or Officers shall be impowered to administer the said Oath; and the Oath, being so administered, shall be attested by the Officer or Officers, who administered the lame; and, being registered by the said Officer or Officers, shall be delivered to the Matter of the Ship, for Security of her Navigation; and a Duplicate thereof shall be transmitted by the said Officer or Officers to the chief Officer or Officers of the Customs in the Port of Edenburgh, to be there entered in a Register, and from thence to be sent to the Port of London, to be there entered in the general Register of all Trading Ships, belonging to Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union.

6th. That all Parts of the united Kingdom for ever, from and after the Union, shall have the same Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks, and be under the same Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Regulations, of Trade, and liable to the same Customs and Duties, on Import and Export; and that the Allowances, Encouragements, and Drawbacks, Prohibitions, Restrictions, and Regulations, of Trade, and the Customs and Duties, on Import and Export, settled in England, when the Union commences, shall, from and after the Union,

take place throughout the whole united Kingdom; excepting and reserving the Duties upon Export and Import of such particular Commodities, from which any Persons, the Subjects of either Kingdom, are especially liberated and exempted by their private Rights, which, after the Union, are to remain safe and inti re to them, in all respects, as before the same: And that, from and after the Union, no Scotch Cattle, carried into shall be liable to any other Duties, either on the publick or private Accounts, than those Duties, to which the Cattle of England are, or shall be, liable within the said Kingdom: And seeing, by the Laws of , there

arc Rewards granted, upon the Exportation of certain Kinds of Grain, wherein Oats, grinded or ungrinded, are not expressed, that, from and after the Union, when Oats shall be sold at Fifteen Shillings Sterling per Quarter, or under, there shall be paid Two Shillings and Six Pence Sterling for every Quarter of the Oatmeal, exported in the Term of the Law, whereby, and so long as. Rewards are granted for Exportation of other Grain; and that the Beer of Scotland have the same Rewards, as Barley: And, in respect the Importation of Visual into Scotland, from any Place beyond Sea, would prove a Discouragement to Tillage, therefore, that the Prohibi-. tion, as now in force by the Law of Scotland, against Importation of Victuals from Ireland, or any other Place beyond Sea, into Scotland, do, after the Union, remain in the same Force, as now it is, until more proper and effectual Ways be provided by the Parliament of Great Britain, for discouraging the Importation of the said , Victuals from beyond Sea.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

7th. That all Parts of the united Kingdom be for ever, from and after the Union* liable to the same Excises upon all-excitable Liquors, excepting only, that the Thirty-four Gallons English Barrel of Beer, or Ale, amounting to twelve Gallons Scots present Measure, fold . in Scotland by the Brewer at nine Shillings Six Pence Sterling, excluding all Duties, and retailed, including Duties, and the Retailers Profit, at Two Pence the Scots Pint, or eighth Part of the Scots Gallon, be not, after the Union, liable, on account of the present Excise upon excisable Liquors in England, to any higher Imposition, than Two Shillings Sterling upon the aforesaid Thirty-four Gallons English Barrel, being Twelve Gallons of the present Scots Measure; and that the Excise, settled in England on all other Liquors, when the Union commences, take place throughout the whole united Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

8th. That, from and after the Union, all foreign Salt, which shall be imported into , shall be charged,

at the Importation there, with the same Duties, as the like Salt is now charged with, being imported into England -, and to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner: But, in regard the Duties of great Quantities of foreign Salt, imported, may be very heavy on the Merchants Importers, that therefore all foreign Salt, imported . into Scotland, shall be cellared, and locked up, under the Custoiiy of the Merchants Importer, and the Officers, employed for levying the Duties upon Salt; and that the Merchant may have what Quantities thereof his Occasions may require, not under a Weigh, or Forty Bushels, at a time, giving Security for the Duty of what Quantity he receives, payable in Six Months: But Scotland shall, for the Space of Seven Years from the said Union, be exempted from paying, in Scotland, for Salt, made there, the Duty, or Excise, now payable for Salt, made in England; but, from the Expiration of the said Seven Years, shall be subject and liable to the same . Duties for Salt, made in Scotland, as shall be then payable for Sait, made in England; to be levied, and secured, in the same Manner, and with proportionable Drawbacks, land Allowances, as in England-, with this Exception, that Scotland shall, after the said Seven Years, remain

-exempted from the Duty of Two Shillings and Four Pence the Bushel on home Salt, imposed by an Act, made in England, in the 9th and 10th of King William the Third of England; and, if the Parliament of Great Britain shall, at or before the expiring of the said Seven Years, substitute any other Fund in place of the said Two Shillings and Four Pence of Excise on the Bushel of home Salt, Scotland shall, after the said Seven Years, bear a Proportion of the said Fund, and have an Equivalent in the Terms of this Treaty: And that, during the said Seven Years, there shall be paid in England for all Salt, made in Scotland, and imported from thence into England, the same Duties, upon the Importation, as

shall be payable for Salt, made in England to be levied and secured, in the same Manner, as the Duties on foreign Salt are to be levied and secured in England: And that, after the said Seven Years, as long as the said Duty of Two Shillings and Four Pence a Bushel upon Salt is continued in England, the said Two Shillings and Four Pence a Bushel shall be payable for all Salt, made in Scotland, and imported into England-, to be levied, and secured in the same Manner: And that, during the Continuance of the Duty of Two Shillings Four Pence a Bushel upon Salt, made in England, no Salt whatsoever be brought from Scotland to England, by Land, in any Manner, under the Penalty of forfeiting the Salt, and the Cattle and Carriages, made use of in bringing the same, and paying Twenty Shillings for every Bushel of such Salt, and proportionably for a greater or lesser Quantity; for which the Carrier, as well as the Owner shall be liable, jointly and severally; and the Persons, bringing or carrying the fame, to be imprisoned by any one Justice of the Peace, by the Space of Six Months, without Bail, and until the Penalty be paid: And, for establishing ari Equality in Trade, that all Flesh, exported from Scotland to England, and put on board in Scotland, to be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, and Provision for Ships in Scotland, and for foreign Voyages, may be salted with Scots Salt, paying the same Duty for what Salt is so employed, as the like Quantity of such Salt pays in England; and under the same Penalties, Forfeitures, and Provisions, for preventing of Frauds, as are mentioned in the Laws of England: And that, from and after the Union, the Laws and Acts of Parliament in Scotland, for pineing, curing, and packing, of Herrings, White Fish, and Salmon, for Exportation, with foreign Salt only, without any Mixture of British or Irifk Salt, and for preventing of Frauds in curing and packing of Fish, be continued in force in Scotland, subject to such Alterations, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain: And that all Fish, exported from Scotland to Parts beyond the Seas, which shall be cured with foreign Salt only, and without Mixture of British or Irijli Salt, shall have the same Eases, Premiums, and Drawbacks, as are or shall be allowed to such Persons, as export the like Fish from England: And that, for the Encouragement of the Herring Fishing, there shall be allowed and paid to the Subjects, Inhabitants of Great Britain, during the present Allowances for other Fishes, Ten Shillings Five Pence Sterling for every Barrel of White Herrings, which shall be exported from Scotland: And that there shall be allowed Five Shillings Sterling for every Barrel of Beef, or Pork, salted with foreign Salt, without Mixture of British or Irish Salt, and exported for Sale, from Scotland, to Parts beyond Sea, alterable by the Parliament of Great Britain: And ifany Matters,"or Fraud, relating to the said Duties on Salt, shall hereafter appear, which are not sufficiently provided against by this Article, the same shall be subject to such further Provisions, as shall be thought fit by the Parliament of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

19th. That the Court of Session, or College of Justice, do, after the Union, and notwithstanding thereof, remain in all Time coming within Scotland, as it is now constituted by the Laws of that Kingdom, and with the same Authority and Privileges, as before the Union; subject nevertheless to such Regulations, for the better Administration of Justice, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain: And that hereafter none shall be named by her Majesty, or her royal Successors, to be ordinary Lords of Session, but such who have served in the College of Justice, as Advocates, or principal Clerks of Session, for the Space of Five Years, or as Writers to the Signet, for the Space of Ten Years; with this Provision, that no Writer to the Signet be capable to be admitted a Lord of the Session, unless he undergo a private and publick Trial on the Civil Law before the Faculty of Advocates, and be found by them qualified for the said Office, two Years before he be named to be a Lord of the Session; yet so, as the Qualification, made, or to be made, for capacitating Persons to be named ordinary Lords of Session, may be altered by the Parliament of Great Britain: And that the Court of Judiciary do also, after the Union, and notwithstanding thereof, remain in all Time coming within Scotland, as it is now constituted by the Laws of that Kingdom, and with the same Authority and Privileges, as before the Union; subject nevertheless to such Regulations, as shall be made by the Parliament of Great Britain, and without Prejudice of other Rights of Justiciary: And that all Admiralty Jurisdictions be under the Lord High Admiral, or Commissioners for the Admiralty of Great Britain, for the Time being: And that the Court of Admiralty, now established in Scotland, be continued; and that all Reviews, Reductions, or Suspensions, of the Sentences in maritime Cafes, competent to the Jurisdiction of chat Court, remain in the same Manner after the Union, as now in Scotland, until the Parliament of Great Britain shall make such Regulations, and Alterations, as shall be judged expedient for the whole united Kingdom; so as there be always continued in Scotland a Court of Admiralty, such as is in England, for Determination of all maritime Cales, relating to private Rights in Scotland, competent to the Jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court; subject nevertheless to such Regulations, and Alterations, as shall be thought proper to be made by the Parliament of Great Britain: And that the heretable Rights of Admiralty, and Vice Admiralties, in Scotland, be reserved to the respective Proprietors, as Rights of Property; Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Article of the said Union,

24th. That, from and after the Union, there be one Great Seal for the united Kingdom of Great Britain, which shall be different from the Great Seal, now used in either Kingdom; and that the quartering the Arms, and the Rank and Precedency of the Lyon King of Arms, of the Kingdom of Scotland, as may belt suit the Union, be left to her Majesty; and that, in the mean Time, the Great Seal of England be used as the Great Seal of the united Kingdom; and that the Great Seal of the united Kingdom be used, for sealing Writs, to elect, and summon, the Parliament of Great Britain, and for sealing all Treaties with foreign Princes and States, and all publick Acts, Instruments, and Orders, of State, which concern the whole united Kingdom, and in all other Matters, relating to England, as the Great Seal of England is now used: And that a Seal in Scotland, after the Union, be always kept, and made use of in all things, relating to private Rights, or Grants, which have usually passed the Great Seal of Scotland, and which only concern Offices, Grants, Commissions, and private Rights, within that Kingdom; and that, until such Seal shall be appointed by her Majesty, the present Great Seal of Scotland shall be used for such Purposes: And that the Privy Seal, Signet, Caflltt, Signet of the Justiciary Court, Quarter Seal, and Seals of Courts, now used in Scotland, be continued; but that the said Seals be altered, and adapted to the State of the Union, as her Majesty shall think fit: And the said Seals, and all of them, and the Keepers of them, shall be subject to such Regulations, as the Parliament of Great Britain shall hereafter make: And that the Crown, Sceptre, and Sword of State, the Records of Parliament, and all other Records, Rolls, and Registers whatsoever, both publick and private, general and particular, and Warrants thereof, continue to be kept, as they are, witlvn that Part of the united Kingdom, now called Scotland -, and that they shall so remain in all Time coming, notwithstanding of the Union.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be another Articleof the said Union,

25th. That all Laws and Statutes in either Kingdom, so far as they are contrary to, or inconsistent with, the Terms of these Articles, or any of them, shall, from and after the Union, cease, and become void; and shall be so declared to be by the respective Parliaments of the said Kingdoms.

[Frauds by Bankrupts.]

Sir Gilbert Heathcott reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to consider of the Abuses relating to, or arising from, the Act, of the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act to prevent Frauds, frequently committed by Bankrupts, the Examinations, which the Committee had taken, and directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

That the Petitioners, Merchants, and Traders, of the City of London, acquainted the Committee with the Abuses, and ill Practices, arising from the said Act; viz.

Mr. Walker, Citizen, and Linen-draper said, that this Act was made upon the account of that notorious Fraud of one Pitkyn; but that it is found by Experience to be deficient, and the same Cheat may be still acted:

1st, In not providing Penalties upon such Bankrupts, as shall remove any Goods or Effects, from off the Premisses:

2dly, By not giving sufficient Power, for the detesting, and punishing, Concealers of Bankrupts Effects; which is avoided under the Umbrage of the 30 Days Notice, allowed them by this Act to come in, to discover, after such Commission is issued forth: And,

3dly, By the Abuses, and ill Practices, of several of the Commissioners, appointed for putting the Act in Execution.

In order to the proof of these Assertions,

Mr. Walker said, that one James Stone carried off Effects to the Value of £.3,000, and has not surrendered himself, though a Reward of 50 has been published in the Gazette; and, as the Act Hands, had he been taken

within the limited Time, he must have been allowed the Benefit of this Act, without Punishment for his Villany, as if he had voluntarily surrendered his Effects to his Creditors.

Mr. Mount said, that one , formerly Apprentice to a Woollen-draper, turned Merchant, and tailing, carried off his Effects, to the Value of £. 4,000, and, when this Act was passed, he returned, to take the Benefit thereof, and, to that End, surrendered what he called his All; viz. A Silver-hilted Sword, a Pair of Pistols, two-Guineas, Six Pence, and Seven Farthings, a False

7'urky Stone Ring; and had a Certificate thereupon, signed by the Commissioners, though he is Son to a Gentleman at this Time of £. 700 per Annum.

And that the Numbers of Commissions, taken out against Butchers, Alehouse-keepers, and such Sort of Tradesmen, are very pernicious, the Expence of the Commissions generally exceeding what is left of their Effects for their Creditors.

That, upon passing this Act, one Green surrendered himself, and gave in an Inventory of his remaining Effects; but therein omitted a Bond 50 owing to him, since paid to the Assignees by the Person, and another Debt of Value, not mentioned, and after was paid for the Benefit of his Creditors.

That there can be no Conviction of a Bankrupt's Perjury, pursuant to the Act, without there had been a positive Oath appointed, by reason of the Evafiveness of the Oaths, now administered to them; such positive Oaths being always the Method prescribed in Acts of Grace.

That the Commissioners, for putting the Act in Execution, being under no Oath, exercise very extraordinary Po wers over the Subject.

Mr. Egg/eton said, that Wm. Peel, Silkman, removed

himself, and Goods, from his Shop in the Poultry, into the Mint, about the beginning of 1705.

That a commission was awarded against him, dated Vox- 1&.

the nth Day of July, 1706, Eight Months after his Removal. *

That the first Notice, most of his Creditors had thereof, was from an Advertisement in the Gazette, of the 25th of July, 1706, giving an account, that the Commissioners intended to meet at the Two fighting Cocks in the Mint, the 9th Day of August following, in order to finish the Examination of the Bankrupt.

That the Bankrupt, Peel, sent a Letter, dated the next Day, on the 10th of August, 1706, to Mr. Anth. Beckwith, one of the Commissioners, containing several extravagant Articles of Losses, and Expences, to near £. 300, for Nine Months Expences, that he had been in the Mint: Which Letter was produced to the Committee.

notwithstanding this Letter, the acting Commissioners, by a Certificate, bearing Date Seven Days after, viz. the 17th August, 1706, do certify to the Right honourable the Lord Keeper, that they found, that the said William Peel became a Bankrupt since the 24th Day of June last; and that he did on the 23d Day of July last past, voluntarily surrender himself to them; and that in all things he had conformed to the several Statutes, formerly made against Bankrupts, and to the late Act,

This Procedure, with some other Particulars, relating to the Execution of this Commission, seems very extraordinary:

That there was but one Advertisement published, of the Meetings of the Commissioners, and that in the Mint;. where few Creditors were willing to appear, for fear of being insulted:

Tliofe, that did appear, were not suffered to ask the Bankrupt any Questions, being check'd, as impertinent therein, and told their Business was to give Reasons, why a Certificate should not be signed, in order to his Discharge:

That they signed a Certificate, that he became a Bankrupt since the 24th June last? when they knew (Mr. Beckwith at lead) that he had been Seven Months before that Time in the Mint:

That the said 24th of June appears in the original Certificate to be interlined, but owned by Mr. Beckwith to be done before signing:

That, notwithstanding the Bankrupt was a Angle Person, and his Accounts so extravagant, yet the Commissioners (although defiled) would not grant Time, for the Creditors to make Objections:

That Mr. Beckwith went out of Town, and locked the Bankrupt's Depositions up, that no Copy could be had till after the Time, the Lord Keeper had set for Appeals to be made:

That this Mr. Beckwith appeared as Attorney for the Bankrupt, at an Hearing before the Lord Chief Baron Ward and Mr. Justice Powell.

Mr. Wright said, that about four Years since one Stroud broke, and carried off all his Effects; and about two Years after he offered his Creditors is. and 6d.per. Pound; which not being accepted, he surrendered himself, summoned his Creditors to Brown's Coffee-house, the 13th of November, at Five a Clock; and, though the Commissioners did not meet till Nine a Clock that Night, he had the Benefit of the late Act, and his Certificate signed by the Commissioners, one Mr. Mead being then the acting Commissioner.

Mr. Walker said, that one Stanton set up but in October last, and had then received £.156 of his Wife's Portion, and procured to himself£. 1,800 Credit, and run out, and broke on the 23d Jati. last, and carried off his Effects; but upon his Apprehensions of this Committee's fitting, he has promised his Creditors, he will return the remaining Effects, and come in to have the Benefit of the late Act.

Mr. Wilson said, it is not uncommon now for Bankrupts to get their own Assignees appointed: That one Majon, a Surgeon, owed him £. 86 and then broke; and he took out a Commission of Bankrupt, proved his Debt, and applied to the Assignee for Payment: who

[Frauds by Bankrupts.]

told him, he had contracted with another Creditor, to pay him the Bankrupt's Effects; but, upon his threatening him, to petition the Lord Keeper for Relief against his Frauds, the Assignee paid him.

Mr. Dowfe, and Mr. Mtwo of the Commissioners in a Commission of Bankrupt, awarded against one field, laid, that the Bankrupt being got into the Mint) they went to the Sign of the Two fighting Cocks to examine; who told them, that he had contracted a Debt with one Rogers, a Taylor, to the amount of £. 58, upon which he bad obtained a Judgment against him, and, upon the Execution thereof, paid himself ,£. 40, and then offered him, as a fresh Credit, the Redemption of a Mortgage, he, the said Rogers, had upon five or six small Houses, that might prove of some small Advantage to the Bankrupt; and then took out a Statute against him.

That, upon examining Rogers upon Oath, he at first confessed, that the Debt from was but 48, but

afterwards he produced Bonds from the Bankrupt, for above £. 80, and swore, the Consideration of the said Bonds were due to him, without including any Interest upon the Account of the Redemption of the aforesaid Mortgage; and that, from the said Rogers swearing backwards and forwards, they, the said Commissioners had a great deal of Reason to believe, that it was a Contrivance between Rogers and the Bankrupt, to have a Statute taben out, to screen the Bankrupt from his just Debts.

Mr. Rogers, appearing, said, the reason of his prevaricating was, by being aflced too many Questions by the Commissioners; and owned he had obtained £.38 of his Debt, before the Statute, upon his Execution, which he took out for or £. coo.

That the Charge of the said Commission amounted to about £. 60.

That it appeared to the Commissioners, that the said Rogers and Blumfield had arrested a Debtor of the said Bankrupt's j and the Commissioners are often some Years, before they make a Dividend among the Creditors, and sometimes none at all.

And an Expedient, for remedy therein, was offered, that for the future the Majority of the Creditors may elect the Assignees.

Mr. Huggins, an Attorney, said, that he had known several Commissions of Bankrupt taken out for very small Debts, to defeat their just Creditors; particularly, a Statute was taken out against one Charles Evans by his Barber, who at the same time owed his Client £. 1,000, and when the Bankrupt surrendered himself, to take the Benefit of the late Act, all, that he surrendered, for the Satisfaction of his Creditors, did not amount to above £. 5, and that the Charge of the Commission, amounted to £.30.

Mr. Walker said, that another Mischief attends the Creditors, from the Necessity the Commissioners are obliged to make three Sittings, though neither the Effects are removed, nor the Bankrupt absent; which occasions the Increase of the Charge of the Commission, to the Disadvantage of the Creditors.

One Christopher Gold, said, that when he was in Holland, a Commission of Bankrupt was taken out against him by three of his Creditors, whose whole Debts did not amount to above 45, under the Hardship whereof his Goods, and all his Effects, were seized, and fold, to the Ruin of himself, Wife, and Children

Mr. Wallis said, that he was summoned to the Two fighting Cocks in the Mint; upon a Commission against one of his Debtors; where one Beckwith, an Attorney, was fitting Commissioner, assisted by two others; and, upon his Delire of knowing, what the Bankrupt had surrendered, was sufficient to pay his Creditors, Beckwith, told him, he was very impertinent: They came there, to discharge the Bankrupt, and not to answer such Questions; and would sign their Certificate: Upon which he desiring some Time, that he might detect the Bankrupt's Discovery; but it was denied him; and by the

Usage Beckwith treated him, had it not been by the Interest of the other two Commissioners, the said Mr.

Wallis (as he was threatened) had underwent the b'caluy Usage, which they there call the Law of the Mint.

Mr. Walker said, that many Commissions of Bankrupt are taken out against Bankrupts, whole Effects have not answered the Charge of the Commission; and it's reasonably believed, four in five Commissions are taken out by the procurement of the Bankrupts themselves.

One Grevill, a Bankrupt, said, he was indebted to one Mr. Brand, in Lombard-street, in £.80, for securing where-ofhe left in his Hands the Leases of two Houses, worth £. 300, and gave him his Bond and Judgment, and 5 Procuration, and a Guinea per Month, whilst he had the Money; and having bought Ten Ton of Coffee, at £. 24. 7/. 6d. per Hundred, he was offered £. 200 for his Bargain; which he refilling, it proved afterwards worth £. 600, and, because he would not fell it. Brand took out a Commission of Bankrupt against him, and seized upon the Coffee, and kept it, till he brought to account but £.$o to the Commission; whereas, if the said Grevill might have disposed of his Bargain in a proper Time, he should have been able to have paid ics. per£. and, for want of Money, the Commission is delayed, and no Dividend yet made, but the Effects remain in their Hands; and they yet keep an Officer in his House, though the Money has been offered to be laid down.

That the last Money he could raise, was £. 4. is. which he paid for the last Sitting of the Commissioners; and Mr. Cole's Clerk (which Mr. Cole was acting Commissioner) told the said Grevill, if he expected any Fruit from the said Commission, he should have secreted £. 50 of his Effects, to have born the Expences thereof.

[Newfoundland Trade.]

A Petition of the Merchants of Bideford, concerned in the Importation of Salt, for the carrying on the Newfoundland Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Act of Parliament, obliging the Importers of Salt to pay down the great Duty thereon, within Six Months after Importation, has so discouraged all Traders from bringing any foreign Salt into the said Port, that the Petitioners are wholly incapacitated to supply their Ships with Salt for Newfoundland, inso much that of at least 40 Sail, employed in that Trade, they cannot now send above four or five small Vessels: And praying, that a longer Time, than Six Months, be allowed, for paying the said Duty upon Salt, for the better encouraging the Trade to Newfoundland.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Trade of this Kingdom.

[Ways and Means.]

The House (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

Year of his late Majesty's Reign, the Petitioner, who was then an Infant, in Kindness to his Sifter Barbara Byde, did voluntarily submit to charge his laid Estates with the Payment of £. 3,000 for her Portion, whereof £. 1,000 was to be paid, with Interest, upon the Petitioner's purchasing in of his Mother's Jointure (which by the Act he was enabled to do) or upon her Death, and the other £. 2,000 and Interest, on the Death of his Grandfather: That, although the Petitioner hath no other than the so settled Estate, he finds, by the said Act, that he is wholly restrained, from doing any Act to bar, or prejudice, any of the Uses, or Remainders, limited by the said Settlement, without any Recompence to the Petitioner, for disabling himself to dispose of his said Estates, or so much as making any Provision to raise his Sifter's Portion, or any other Money whatsoever, save only £. 4,000 for younger Children, if he should have any:

Byde died, and left the Estate, and the Mansion-house, wholly unfurnished, and very much out of Repair; so that the Petitioner has and must expend great Sums . of Money in necessary Repairs and Furniture; and his Sifter has brought a Bill in Chancery for the £. 2,000,

Residue of her Portion, which, if decreed, can be raised no otherways, than by sequestering the Rents of the Pe-tioner's Estate; whereby he will be deprived of Subsist-ance: That it is much doubted whether, if the Petitioner should have Daughters, or one only Daughter, the Provision in the said Act for younger Children is not defective: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to amend the said Defect, and to repeal in part the restraining Clause in the said Act, and to enable the Petitioner, by Mortgage, or otherwise, to raise Moneys, to discharge his Sifter's Portion, and a reasonable Sum for the Petitioner's other necessary Occasions.

And the same was read, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Petitioners, the Six Clerks, by their Counsel alleged themselves to be the only Attorneys of the Court of Chancery; and that they, and their Predecessors, amongst other Fees and Perquisites, were intitled to the

ancient Tcrmly Fee of 3/. 4 and that their Fees hare often been inquired into, and found reasonable.

To prove which, they produced an Act, made in the 31st Year of Hen. VIII. whereby their Predecessors, the Six Clerks, were incorporated; and also an Ordinance, of Michaelmas, 11® Car. I. wherein the Six Clerks are called the only Attorneys; as also several other ancient Preferments, Ordinances, and Orders, of that Court, for their Establishment; and particularly a Preferment in the 40 Year of Queen Eliz. by which the said Termly Fee of 3 s. and and the Fees of the small Writs, are presented, as the Six Clerks Fees; as aHo a Decree, made by. the Lord Keeper Bridgman, Amo 1668, was read; whereby it appeared, that the under Clerks, therein directed to be sworn, shall and may have, receive, detain, and keep, to their own IJfes, 1 s. and 4 d. out of every Termly Fee of 3 s. and and likewise a Share and Part of several other Fees, as is therein particularly mentioned, and a Moiety of all other Fees for all other Writs, usually dispatched by the Clerks in their Clients Causes; and the under Clerks respectively shall be accountable to the Six Clerks only for 2 s. of the Termly Fee of 3 s. and 4 J. and likewise for such Share of all other Fees, as therein is particularly mentioned: And it is expressed in the said Decree, that the under Clerks should duly account with, and pay to, the Six Clerks the residue of the Fees, in regard they abated much of what heretofore they used to receive.

That a Copy of another Presentment of Fees was produced, made in the Year 1689 to the House of Peers, and ligned by Mr. Derbyshire and Mr. Slater (then two of the Senior under Clerks) intituled, " The ancient " Fees of the Six Clerks of the Court of Chancery, " usually taken in the Six Clerks Office ;" wherein the said Termly Fee of 3 s.4 d. and the rest of the Fees, mentioned in the 40th of Eliz. are enumerated; and at the End of the said Presentment are these Words; " There hath been an Allowance out of the Fees abovementioned to the under Clerks, who dispatch the Bu-

finess of the Client in that Office; and by a Decree, " made by the late Lord Keeper Bridgman, and the then " Master of the Rolls, the 18th Day of June, in the " 20th Year of King Charles the 2d, the same are settled between the Six Clerks and the under Clerks, and have " been ever since observed.'*

By their Counsel they further insisted, that, time out of mind, they have had under Clerks under them, at such Allowances, as they thought fit.

To prove which,

Mr. Bladen produced two Papers, found in the Six Clerks Office, purporting to be two Petitions in the Year 1627, from some of the under Clerks to the then Six Clerks, for an Increase of their Allowance of 2 d. per Sheet to 3 d.which, upon due Examination of their Employments, the then Six Clerks granted: And further laid, that he had searched the Register Books, from the Year 1660 to this Time; and that he found great Numbers of Orders, made by the Court, for admitting Suitors in forma Pauperis; by all which the Six Clerks were appointed to be Attorneys, or Six Clerks, for such Paupers; and that he did not find any one Pauper Order directed to an under Clerk in all that Time: And the Register Books being produced, several of the said Orders were read, wherein the Six Clerks were stiled Attorneys.

By their Counsel they further insisted, that the Reason, why the Sixty Clerks became to be called fivorn Clerks, was from the Oath they were obliged to take, not to cmbezil, or deface, the Records of the Court; and that the Equivalent, given those under Clerks, in lieu of the Tenor of the Bill, taken away by the late Act of Parliament (for the Amendment of the Law) is become a Yery great Advantage; the Attorneys Fee, and all final! Writs, given them by way of Compensation, exceeds their Lois above Eleven hundred Pounds in every Six hundred Causes.

To prove which.

Mr. Jojlua Hinton said, that he had made a Search into the Records, hrought to him into the Six Clerks Hall, for the four Terms before Erin, last, and found Twelve hundred Eighty-six Bills filed, whereupon were 538

Dedimus's.

Mr. Samuel Ehroughton said, that he had made the like Search; and that what Mr. Hinton had declared, was true: But neither of them knew, or could say, that they were all the Records of those Terms.

Cha. Ehetford, Porter to the Six Clerks, said, he

carried the Bundles out of the Six Clerks Studies into their Dining Hall, in order to examine the Dedimus Caules: And being asked, whether those Bundles contained all the Records in those four Terms, said, he could not tell: And being further asked, whether he had not been frequently sent by the Six Clerks to their Studies, to deliver out Bills and Answers to thefworn Clerks, said, he had; and that he believed, many Answers of those Terms were in the Custocly of the fivorn Clerks at that time.

Mr. Wright, Attorney at Law, produced a printed Paper, importing a Calculation of the Six Clerks Lois, sustained from the Equivalent; from which he supposed, that the Compensation given to the sworn Clerks, does considerably exceed the Loss they sustained by taking away the Tenor of the Bill; but could not affirm the fame, otherwise, than from the said printed Paper.

Mr. Milner, one of the Petitioners, produced his Book of Entries; and said, that the Six Clerks made Entries of the Names of all Plaintiffs and Defendants in all the Bills and Answers, brought to them to be filed; and that they gave their Attendances in the Afternoons for that Purpose, and in the Mornings, in Term-time* at Westminster, to read the Pleadings of the Court there.

Then the sworn Clerks, by their Counsel, in answer to what had been offered by the Six Clerks, did admit, that the Six Clerks were ancient Officers, and that their Predecessors, at their pnmilive Institution, were Men of great Abilities and Judgment in the Practice thereof; but that now, and for many Years past, the Six Clerks have proved to be just contrary, whereby the Business, done by the Six Clerks anciently, is now devolved upon, and dispatched by the sworn Clerks; for the Performance whereof they are sworn into their Employments, and have settled Fees allowed them by the Court; and instead of receiving from, they pay to, the Six Clerks what Fees they receive by virtue of their Office; which, notwithstanding their Complaint, and though they do so small a Share (if any thing) towards the Performance of, and carrying on, the Proceedings of Causes in that Court, their Offices are worth to them, by the Receipt of the various Fees and Perquisites, they now enjoy,/.600 per Annum respectively, one with another.

To prove which,

Mr. Bez. Knight, Attorney at Law, produced a Decree of the Court of Chancery, in the Year 1663, for the regulating the Six Clerks Office, and settling and establishing the sworn Clerks, and all Fees to be paid in that Office: And further {kid, that he had been a Practitioner in that Court for 20 Years past, and always applied himself to some of the sworn Clerks, for the carrying on and dispatch of his Clients Causes; and always found, that they went through the fame, without the Six Clerks being any way concerned therein.

Mr. George Eduards, feniur, Deputy Register' of the Court of Chancery, proved* that the whole Course of Proceedings in that Office went through the Hands of the sworn Clerks; and that he did not apprehend, the Six Clerks to be any ways concerned therein, nor did they ever come to his Office, upon any Business of that Court; And said, that all Notices of Motions, and Orders, are given to the fivorn Clerks only; and that the Suitors are m all Cafes bound by the Consent of the fivorn Clerks.

Air. Nicholls, Barrister at Law, laid, that he came into

the said Office 26 Years ago, and was there bred up; and that it was the Practice of the Six Clerks then, for

18 tW9

5 Ann.

i 3° Febru

*95

two of them, in Term-time, to attend the Court at Westminster j and, upon their Return, they dine at their Hall, and in the Afternoons should give their Attendances in their Studies} but they so often omit their Duty therein, that many Causes have been ruined by their neglect of Attendance, because Recourse cannot be had to the Records in their Absence.

He further said, that formerly the Six Clerks were Men of that Ability, that the Court, upon Complaints of Irregularities in Practice, usually referred the same to the two senior Six Clerks, who used to hear them in the Hall, after Dinner, gratis; but, as those Abilities proved deficient in their Successors, the Court, for many Years pa ft, have fen t such References to Matters inChanceryj which is great Expence, and Delay, to the Suitor.

He said further, that, whilst tie was a Praftifer in the Court, he paid above £.1,500 in Fees to one of the Six Clerks, then present at the Committee j and appealed to him whether ever he knew the Merits of any one Caule: To which the Six Clerk made no Reply.

He also said, that in his Time he has often made out 50 Dedimus's in one Term; and the Equivalent of a

whole Year would not make good the Loss of that Term.

He said further, that he has had three or four Score Causes begin in one Term, and not three Hearings; and that, if one of the sworn Clerks die, a Writ ad faciendum Attornat' issues forth, before the Cause can proceed; but no such Writ, or any other, ever issues, when any of the Six Clerks die; and, upon issuing such Writ-, a new iworn Clerk is appointed, and the same Six Clerk remains.

He also laid, that, if a Defendant be brought, to the Bar by Habeas Corpus, for want of an Appearance, the Court directs a sworn Clerk to appear, and not a Six Clerk, though present in Court.

He further said, that the Six Clerks are named Attorneys of that Court in Pauper Causes, to indemnify the sworn Clerks from paying Fees to the Six Cleks in such Causes: and that he has applied himself with a great deal of Consideration of several other sworn Clerks Circumstances in Business, as well as the Experience of his own, in respect to the Recompence, given by the late Act, for the Amendment of the Law, to the sworn Clerks, in lieu of the Tenor of the Bill, thereby taken away; and does find, that their said Recompence falls Very short, in proportion to the Lois they have sustained thereby.

He said further, that, when he left his Business, he had owing to him, on his Book, about £.4,000 for Business done in the Office; and offered it to his late Six Clerk, then present, for £. 2,000, and would give him Seven Years to pay it.

And being asked, what was the present yearly Value of the Six Clerks Places; he said, at least£. 600. And being further asked, what was the Value of their Places before the late Act of Parliament; he said, he did not know, but they formerly might have been worth £.1,000 Annum.

Mr. Turner, Barrister at Law, brought up in the said Office ever since the Year 1665, and practised therein to the Year 1696, said, that he, being concerned in Town Causes, knows, that they amounted to about an 8th Part with the Country Causes; whereby he calculated that the Recompence, given to the sworn Clerks, by the small Writs, and Term Fee, falls very short of the Loss they have, in taking away the Tenor of the Bill; for that the Fees in Dedimus's, in his own Practice, usually amounted to £.100, and those of small Writs, and Term Fees, to not near so much.

And that, upon Consideration of the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolution following:

Resolved, That, it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners, the Six Clerks in Chancery, have not made good the Allegations of their said Petition.
