Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, that her Majesty having received from Scotland an Extract of an Act, settling the Manner of electing the Sixteen Peers, and Forty-five Members, to represent Scotland in the Parliament of Great Britain, (he had commanded him to lay the same before this House.

And he delivered the same in at the Clerk's Table} where the same was read, and is as followeth j viz.

Act, settling the Manner of electing the Sixteen Peers, and Forty-five Members, to represent Scotland in the Parliament of Great Britain.

AT Edinburgh, the fifth Day of February, 1707 Years.

Our sovereign Lady considering, that by the 22d Article of the Treaty of Union, as the same is ratified by an Act, passed in this Session of Parliament upon the 16th of January last, it is provided, that, by virtue of the said Treaty, of the Peers of Scotland at the Time of the Union Sixteen shall be the Number, to fit and vote in the House of Lords, and Forty-five the Number of the Representatives of Scotland in the House of Commons, of the Parliament of Great Britain; and that the said Sixteen Peers, and Forty-five Members in the House of Commons, be named, and chosen, in such Manner, as by a subsequent Act, in this present Session of Parliament in Scotland, should be settled, which Act is thereby declared to be also valid, as if it were a Part of, and ingrossed in, the said Treaty: Therefore her Majesty, with Advice and Consent of the Estates of Parliament, statutes, enacts, and ordains, that the said Sixteen Peers, who shall have Right to fit in the House of Peers of the Parliament of Great Britain, on the Part of Scotland, by virtue of this Treaty, shall be named by the said Peers of Scotland, whom they represent, their Heirs or Successors to their Dignities and Honours, out of their own Number, and that by open Election, and Plurality of Voices, of the Peers present, and of the Proxies for such, as shall be absent, the said Proxies being Peers, and producing a Mandate in Writing, duly signed before Witnesses, and both the Constituent, and Proxy, being qualified according to Law; declaring also, that such Peers, as are absent, being qualified, as aforesaid, may send to all such Meetings Lists of the Peers, whom they judge fittest, validly signed by the said absent Peers, which shall be reckoned in the same Manner, as if the Parties had been present, and given in the said Lift; and, in case of the Death, or legal Incapacity, of any of the said Sixteen Peers, that the aforesaid Peers of Scotland shall nominate another of their own Number in place of the said Peer or Peers, in Manner before and after mentioned: And that of the said Forty-five Representatives of Scotland in the House of Commons, in the Parliament of Great Britain, Thirty shall be chosen by the Shires, or Steuartries, and Fifteen by the Royal Burrows, as follows; viz. One for every Shire, and Steuartry, excepting the Shires of Bute and Cathness, which shall choife one by Turns, Bute having the First Election; the Shires of Nairn and Cromarty, which shall also choife by Turns, Nairn having the First Election; and in like Manner the Shires of -

*5

manan and Kinross shall choife by Turns, Clackmanatt having the First Election; and, in case of the Death, or legal Incapacity, of any of the said Members from the respective Shires, or Steuartries, above-mentioned, to fit in the House of Commons, it is enacted and ordained, that the Shire, or Steuartry, who elected the said Member, shall elect another Member in his Place: And that the said Fifteen Representatives for the Royal Burrows be chosen as follows; viz. That the Toun of Edinburgh shall have Right to elect, and fend, one Member to the Parliament of Great Britain; and that each of the other Burghs shall elect a Commissioner in the same Manner, as they are now in use to elect Commissioners to the Parliament of Scotland-, which Commissioners, and Burghs (Edinburgh excepted) being divided in Fourteen Gaffes, or Districts, shall meet at such Time, and Burghs, within their respective Districts, as her Majesty, her Heirs or Successors, shall appoint, and elect one for each District; viz. The Burghs of Kirkwall, Week, Domock, Dingwall, and Taine, one; the Burghs of Nairn, and Forrefs, one; the Burghs of Elgin, Cullen,

Banff, Inverury, and Kintore, one; the Burghs of Aberdeen, lnverbervy., Montrose, Aberbrothock, and Brochine, one; the Burghs of Forfar, , Dundee, and St. Andrews, one; the Burghs of Craill, Kilreunie,

Anstruther Easter, Anstruther Wester, and one; the Burghs of Dyfart, Kirkaldie, and

Bruntisland, one; the Burghs of lnnerkithen, Dunfermline, Queensferry, Culrefs, and Sterling, one; the

Burghs of Glasgow, Renfrew, Ruglen, and Dumbarton, one; the Burghs of Haddington, Dunbar, North Berwick, Lauder, and Jedburgh, one; the Burghs of Selkirk, Peebles, Linlithgow, and one; the Burghs

of Dumfries, Sanquhar, Annan, Lochmaben, and Kirkcudbright, one; the Burghs of Wigtoun, New Galloway, Stranraver, and Whitehern, one; and the Burghs of Air, Irvin, Rotbefay, Campbletoun, and Inverary, one. And it is hereby declared, and ordained, that, where the Votes of the Commissioners for the said Burghs, met to choife Representatives from their several Districts to the Parliament of Great Britain, shall be equal, in that same the President of the Meeting shall have a calling or decisive Vote, and that by and attour his Vote, as a Commissioner from the Burgh, from which he is sent; the Commissioner from the eldest Burgh presiding in the first Meeting, and the Commissioners from the other Burghs, in their respective Districts, presiding afterwards, by Turns, in the Order, as the said Burghs are now called in the Rolls of the Parliament of Scotland; And in case that any of the said fifteen Commissioners from Burghs shall decease, or become legally incapable to fit in the House of Commons, then the Town of Edinburgh, or the District, which choifed the said Member, shall elect a Member in his or their Place. It is always hereby expressly provided, and declared, that none shall be capable to elect, or be elected, for any of the said Estates, but such, as are Twenty-one Years of Age compleat, and Protestant, excluding all Papists, or such, who, being suspect of Popery, and required, refuse to swear and subscribe the Formula, contained in the third Act, made in the 8th and 9th Session of King William's Parliament, intituled, " Act for preventing the Growth of PoperyAnd also declaring, that none shall be capable to elect, or be elected, to represent a Shire, or Burgh, in the Parliament of Great Britain, for this Part of the united Kingdom, except such, as are now capable, by the Laws of this Kingdom, to elect, or be elected as, Commissioners for Shires, or Burghs, to the Parliament of Scotland. And, further, her Majesty, with Advice and Consent aforesaid, for the' effectual and orderly Election of the Persons, to be chosen to fit, vote, and serve, in the respective Houses of the Parliament of Great Britain, when her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors, shall declare her or their Pleasure for holding the first, or any subsequent, Parliament of Great Britain, and when, for that Effect, a Writ shall be issued out under the Great Seal of the united Kingdom,

That the Sixteen Peers, iand : Forty-five Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, who shall be chosen by the Peers, Barons, and Burghs, respectively, in this present Session of Parliament, and out of the Members thereof, in the same Manner, asi Committees of Parliament are usually now chosen, shall be the Members of the respective Houses of the said first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of Scotland;: which Nomination, and Election, being certified by a Writ under the Lord Clerk Register's Hand, the Persons, so nominated, and elected,.shall have Right toifit and, vote in the House of Lords, and in the House of Commons, of the first Parliament of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to her Majesty, a Sum, not exceeding^. 1,120,000, be raised by Sale of Annuities for the Term of Ninety-nine Years, to commence from Lady-day, 1707.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Impositions, granted by an Act of Parliament, of the 4th Year of their late Majesties King William and Queen Ma, of glorious Memory (intituled, An Act for granting to their Majesties certain additional Impositions upon several Goods and Merchandizes, for prosecuting the present War again!! France) and which by an Act, of the first Year of her Majesty's Reign (intituled, An Act for making good Deficiencies, and preserving the publick Credit) are already to continue until the first Day of , 1710, shall be further continued, from the last Day of July, 1710, for the Term of Ninety-six Years from thence next and immediately ensuing.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rates and Duties, granted by an Act of Parliament, made in the 5th Year of the Reign of their said late Majesties (intituled, An Act for granting to their Majesties several Duties upon Vellom, Parchment, and Paper, for four Years, towards carrying on the War again!! France) and which by the said Act of the first Year of her Majesty's Reign, are already granted to continue till the first Day of , 1710, shall be further continued, from the last Day of 1710, for the Term of 96 Years from thence next and immediately ensuing.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Impositions on Goods and Merchandizes, and the said Rates and Duties upon Vellom, Parchment, and Paper, to be granted, as aforesaid, when the same shall respectively commence, be appropriated and applied to make good the Fund for Payment of the said Annuities.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a further Sum, not exceeding Thirty-five thousand Pound, be raised by Sale of Annuities, as aforesaid, to discharge the two first quarterly Payments, to grow due on the 24 th Day of June, and the 29th Day of next, respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Impositions on Goods and Merchandizes, and the said Rates and Duties upon Vellom, Parchment, and Paper, to arise by virtue of the said Act, of the first Year of her Majesty's Reign, (after all the Principal and Interest, thereby charged thereon, shall be paid and satisfied) be applied towards

satisfying the quarterly Payments, which at or before the Feast of Saint Michael, the Archangel, 1710, shall be grown due, and unsatisfied, for the said Annuities, to be purchased as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion-of this Committee, That, for completing all the Moneys, which shall grow due, for the quarterly Payments of the said Annuities, at, or at any Time or Times before, the said Feast of St. Michael the Archangel, 1710, so much as shall be sufficient for that Purpose, be taken, and applied, out of the overplus Moneys, which shall arise from Time to Time by the Funds, formerly settled for the Payment of Annuities, granted before this Session of Parliament, the said overplus Moneys being such, as are disposable for the publick Service by the several Acts of Parliament relating the reunto.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

That the said Mr. Dann being present, the Committee ordered, That Mr. Dann do lay before the Committee, all the Particulars of the joint Account between Mr. Brerewood, Mr. Pitkin, himself, and Partner; as also the Particulars of the separate Account between the said Brerewood and Dann; together with what Securities he now hath, or hath had, in his Hands, upon either of the said Accounts; as also the Bill of Sale, made of the Goods he took upon an Execution of some Goods, he had in his Power, for securing part of his Money he advanced to Brerewood.

That the said Mr. Dann being asked, what Time he desired to comply with the said Order, he undertook to do the same in four Days; which Time being granted him, he then produced an Account, which appeared to be very unsatisfactory to the Committee, and evasive to their Order: And as to the Bill of Sale, he had mislaid it, and could not make up the said Account, to the Satisfaction of the Committee, considering the Business he has upon his Hands, under ten Days time.

That he owned all the absolute Notes, made payable to the said Mr. Elias Rich; and that, as to the accountable Notes, he was ready to comply to the Conditions therein mentioned; and as to what Effects he had from Pitkin, he keeps as a Security for what he has suffered upon Pitkin's Account; for that he has paid, and is obliged to pay by the Articles of Agreement, to the Debts proved, and claimed, £. 25,000 to the Charges of the Commission of Bankrupt, before those Articles were,

A Petition of the Drugget-makers, Serge-makers, Fullers, Dyers, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Taunton, in the County of Somerset, and Parishes adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that within four or five Years last the Weavers (who are very numerous) have in most Towns, where the Woollen Manufactures are made, formed themselves into Clubs, particularly at Taunton, and have a common Seal, Tipstaffs, and Colours, which they display at Pleasure, and meet, as often as they think fit, at their Club-house, being an Inn at Taunton; and four or five Persons, appointed as their Supervisors (if any of their Club are about to be prosecuted) give them a Certificate under their Hands and common Seal, and Money out of their Common Stock, to travel from their Families, whereby their Families have become chargeable to their several Parishes; and by their arbitrary Proceedings they hinder many honest Labourers, who refuse to join in their Club, from using their lawful Employments, whereby they might get a comfortable Maintenance for their Families: That the said Taunton Club have committed many Outrages and Riots, and put many of her Majesty's Subjects in great Danger of their Lives, forced many from their Habitations, broken the common Gaol, and also private Houses, and refeued several Persons, who were committed for the said Crimes: And praying the House to consider of feme effectual Method to suppress these riotous Clubs, and the future ill Consequences that may attend them.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Capital Burgesses, and Assistants, of the Borough of Tiverton, in Devon, together with other the Merchants Clothiers, and other principal Traders, of the fame, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Combinations, or Clubs, into which the Labourers in the Woollen Manufactures have of late formed themselves, is a growing Complaint at Tiverton, and, after a great deal of Forbearance from their Matters, are become so infelent, as to oblige them to comply with whatever their Clubs shall determine; and assemble themselves, when they please, in a riotous Manner, abusing their Mailers, intuiting Justice, and daring all Authority, that opposes them: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think fir.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Robert Davers reported from the Committee of the State of whole House, who were to consider of the Trade of this 1 Kingdom, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table j where the same were read, and are as follow;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all foreign Salt, imported into England, , or Berwick upon Tweed, after the first Day of May, 1707, shall be cellared and locked up under the Custody of the Merchant Importer, and the Officer employed for levying the Duties upon Salt; and that the Merchant may have what Quantity thereof his Occasions may require, not under a Weigh, or Forty Bushels, at a time, giving Security for the Duty of what Quantity he receives, payable in six Months.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That for all English Salt, which from and after the first Day of May, 1707, shall be shipped, to be carried Coastwise, the Duties having been paid, or secured, according to former Laws, there shall be an Allowance made of the Duties of so much of such Salt, as shall be actually wasted in the Carriage, for Wastage, upon Certificates, to be given Gratis by the proper Officers at the Port of Lading, of the true Quantity of Salt, laden or put on board, and a Certificate of the proper Officers, at the Port of Discharge, of the Quantity of the said Salt, which shall be there discharged, and upon Proof made upon Oath, to verify the said Certificate; which Proof, and Certificates, being produced to the propec Officer of the Salt Duties, by whom the Duties of the said Salt, so carried Coastwise, was paid, or secured, he shall be allowed upon the Security, or repaid (in case the Duties be actually paid) io much, as the said Allowance for Wastage shall amount to, as aforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That fiorn and after the first Day of May, 1707, there shall, upon the Exportation of White Herrings from England and Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed, be the like Allowances, as are to be made, upon the Exportation of White Herrings from Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there shall be allowed for every Barrel of Beef, or Pork, felted, and exported from England, Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed, after the first Day of May,

1707, for Sale, the like Allowances, as are to be allowed upon Exportation of such Beef, and Pork, exported from Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there shall be the like Premium given for all Oatmeal, and Grain called Bear, alias Bigg, upon the Exportation thereof, exported after the first Day of May,

1707, from England, Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed, as are to be given upon Exportation of Oatmeal and Bear from Scotland.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said Resolutions; and that Sir Robert Davers, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr, Lowndes, Mr. Scobell, Mr. Carr, and Mr.

Clayton, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Saturday Morning Ditto, next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Trade of this Kingdom.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A. 1706,

them, touching the Complaint of a Breach of Privilege against IVyriott Owen, Esquire (a Member of this House)

and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the , Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the Complaint of a Breach of Privilege, in arresting John Higgins, Steward to IVyrriot , Esquire (a Member of the House) by Joseph Tivycr, Samuel 'Thomas, and Jan.es IVUffin, at the Suit of Thomas Christopher

Coke, and Thomas Kilpin.

That the Fact was admitted, as to the Arrest.

That, to make good the Complaint, several Witnesses were examined, to prove John Higgins Steward to Mr. Owen.

Mr. John Griffith laid, that on , the 8th

of January last, he gave Notice to the Bailiffs (having then in their Custody the said Mr. Higgins) that Mr. Higgins was Mr. Owen's Servant; and the Bailiffs said they could not discharge him, without Mr. Ford's Order: And that afterwards he went to Mr. Ford, and informed him, as he had done the Bailiffs; and Mr. Ford refused to give any Order for his Discharge, laying, Mr. Higgins might take his Course; or Words to that Effect.

Mr. Griffith, Mr. Cozens, said, that they did know, that Mr. Higgins had lived with Mr. Owen, and his Father, Sir Hugh Owen, as their Servant, for 15 or 16 Years last past, and particularly with Mr. for two

Years last past: And Cozens laid, before he came to Town, he had gone with Mr. Higgins to several of Mr. Owen's Tenants, and fee him receive the Rents.

That it was admitted, that Mr. Higgins did not live with Mr. Owen at the Time of Ins being arrested.

That, on the other Side, tojuftify the Persons complained against, several Witnesses were called:

Mr. Richard Natt; who laid, he had known Mr. Higgins 5 or 6 Years; and that he had a House, ever since October was 12 Months, in St. JM«'s Court, and lived there: That he always looked upon him as a Merchant, he appearing every Day upon the Exchange; and that they had been concerned together in a Sloop; and some time since Mr. Higgins told him, he was going to Wales, to remove his Effects.

That, to corroborate his Evidence, two Letters of Mr. Higgins were produced; in one of which he desired Mr. Natt to insure£.1,200, in the other 300 upon two Ships at Sea.

That a Bill of Loading was also produced, by which. Mr. Higgins had Goods assigned to him.

Mr. IVII/iam Carwitty ttlbfied, that he fee a Gold-smith's Bill, for £. 100 delivered to Mr. Higgins-, and, he believed Mr. Higgins received the Money.

Mr. Roger Aldy was also examined, who gave an Account, that Mr. Higgins was arrested on the first of January; and on the 3d he went to him: That Mr. Higgins said, he had a Paper amongst Mr. Owen's Writings, by which he had Privilege; but he did not care to make the Matter publitk, and so desired Mr. Aldy to procure him Bail. Mr. Aldy said, accordingly he did procure two sufficient Persons to be Bail to the Action; but then the Bailiffs produced two other Warrants; and then Mr. Aldy advised him to send to Mr. Owen.

And that, upon this Evidence, the Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Higgins is such a Servant to Wyrriott Owen, Esquire (a Member of this House) as is intitled to Privilege of Parliament.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Thomas Ford, Christopher Coke, and Thomas Kilpin, in causing the said John Higgins to be arrested at their Suits, in the Time of Privilege of Parliament, are guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

And the said Report is as followed); viz.

To the honourable the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled:

IN Obedience to an Order of this honourable House, of the 28th Day of February last, directing the Commissioners of the Customs to lay before this House, an Account of the Drawbacks and Allowances, which have been made upon the Exportation of Dying Goods, Naval Stores, French Wines, and Brandy, imported between the 25th Day Of December, 1702, and the 25th Day of December, 1705, which pay the additional Impositions, granted by an Act, in the 4th Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, and continued by an Act, of the first Year of her present Majesty's Reign, we have directed such Accounts to be drawn out; but, lead (as it requires a great deal of Time, and Labour, to do it exactly) they should not be perfected soon enough, to answer the Expectation of this honourable House, we pray Leave to offer, in the mean time, the Abstract, annexed of the net Payment into the Exchequer, from the Custom-house, on the said additional ImpoGtions, in the four Years last past, with a Medium of the Whole, and how much thereof received in London, and how much in the Out-ports; as also, what Debentures, Allowances, and other Payments, have been made in London out of this Branch, during the said four Years: And admitting, that the Sum of £. 26,583. 6s. lid. mentioned in Dr. Account, lately

presented to this honourable House, has been the gross annual Produce of the four enumerated Articles only of the French Wine, Brandy, Naval Stores, and Dying Goods, in this Branch, and that the Debentures, and Allowances, in the Out-ports, answer in the like Proportion, as the same Payments have done in London, or not of the whole Receipt s we are humbly of Opinion, that the leaving out these four Articles (if that should be thought of in the Continuation of this Fund) would be such a Diminution of it, that the rest would not suffice to answer the Credit of the Annuities, now proposed to be raised thereupon for the publick Service.

Which is humbly submitted to this honourable House.

Jo. Werden,

Custom-house, London. C. Godolphin,

4 March, 170-f. Sam.

An Act for an Union of the two Kingdoms of England and Scotland; and to the several publick and ptivate Bills following:

Esquire, Remembrancer of the said Court, the usual Oaths for the due Execution of his Office, and to enable him to take the Oaths, and subscribe the Declaration, in the Court of Chancery in England, instead of those re-quisite to be taken, and subscribed, by the Laws of England and Ireland, in order to qualify him to execute the said Office:

And afterwards to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament; which he had obtained a Copy of, and he read as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

IT is with the greatest Satisfaction, that I have given my Assent to a Bill for uniting England and Scotland into one Kingdom.

I consider

QueenV

p«ecli.

Address on

Queen's

Speech.

Queen's Speech to be confide red.

Rich's Debt to the Crown.

\ Copy Right of printed Rooks.

5 Ann. 6° — 79 Martii. 327

I consider this Union as a Matter of the greatest Importance to the Wealth, Strength, and Safety, of the whole Island, and at the same time as a Work of so much Difficulty and Nicety in its own Nature, that, till now, all Attempts, which have been made towards it in the course of above a Hundred Years, have proved ineffectual; and therefore I make no doubt, but it will be remembered and spoke of hereafter to the Honour of those, who have been instrumental in bringing it to such a happy Conclusion.

I'desire, and expect, from all my Subjects of both Nations, that from henceforth they act with all possible Respect and Kindness to one another; that so it may appear to all the World, they have Hearts disposed to become one People.

This will be a great Pleasure to me, and will make us all quickly sensibleof the good Effect of this Union.

And I cannot but look upon it as a peculiar Happiness, that in my Reign so full a Provision is made for the Peace and Quiet of my People, and for the Security of our Religion, by so firm an Establishment of the Protestant Succession throughout Great Britain.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I take this Occasion to remind you of making effectual Provision for the Payment of the Equivalent to Scotland within the Time appointed by this Act; and I am persuaded, you will thew as much Readiness in this Particular, as you have done in all the other Parts of this great Work.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Season of the Year being now pretty far advanced, I hope you will continue the same Zeal, which has appeared throughout this Session, in dispatching what yes remains unfinished of the publick Business before you.

The laid Address was twice read, with a Blank, and is as followeth; viz.

Die Sabbati,8* Martii, \ 706.

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal

in Parliament assembled, return our most humble Thanks to your Majesty, for your gracious Approbation of the Share we had in bringing the Treaty of an Union, between your two Kingdoms of England and Scotland, to a happy Conclusion; a Work, that, after so many fruit-less Endeavours, seems designed by Providence to add new Lustre to the Glories of your Majesty's Reign. The Success of your Arms having secured us from all Attempts from Abroad, and the Care, your Majesty has taken of the firm Establishment of the Protestant Succession, having given a great and lasting Security to our Religion, as in the Church of by Law

established; we beg Leave humbly to allure your Majesty, that our Endeavours shall never be wanting to support your Government at Home, and so to establish the Peace of this Island, that no Dispute may remain among us, but how to acknowlege, in the most dutiful Manner, the auspicious Conduct of so great and so renowned a Queen.

Resolved, That the Blank in the said Address be filled up with the Words " and Commons."

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Address, so amended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 13th and 14th Years of the Reign of King Charles the 2d, intituled, "An Act for " the better Relief of the Poor of this Kingdom," which was enacted to have Continuance (except what related to the Corporations therein mentioned, and thereby constituted) until the 29th Day of May 1665, and from thence to the End of the First Session of the next Parliament; which said Act, by an Act, made in the first Year of the Reign of the late King the

ad (except what related to the Corporations therein mentioned, and thereby constituted) was enacted to be in force from the first Day of , 1685, and so to continue for the Space of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the next Sessions of Parliament: And whereas by an Act, made in the 3d and 4th Years of the lteign of his late Majesty King William, the said last mentioned Act (as to what therein related to the Settlement of the Poor) was enacted to be in force from the first Day of May, 1691, but no Provision was thereby made, for continuing of divers other Parts of the said Act: Which said Act, for the better Relief of the Poor of this Kingdom, as to all Parts thereof, not mentioned and continued in and by the said Act, made in the 3d and 4th Years of the Reign of their late Majesties (other than except what relates to the Corporations mentioned in the said Act, for the better Relief of the Poor of this Kingdom, and thereby constituted) was by an Act made in the 4th and 5th Years of the Reign of their late Majesties, continued for the Space of Seven Years, from the 13th Day of February, 1692, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament i which said Act afterwards by an Act, of the nth and 12th Years of King William, intituled, "An Act for " continuing several Laws therein mentioned," was continued for Seven Years from the 29th Day of tember, 1707, and is now near expiring, is fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That so much of the Act, made in the 22d and 23d Years of King Charles the 2d, intituled, "An Act to " prevent Frauds in the buying and selling Cattle in " Smithfe/d, and elsewhere," which relates to the preventing Butchers within the Cities of London and West-tniujler, or Ten Miles thereof, to buy fat Cattle, and fell the same again to any other Butcher; as also so much, as relates to the preventing fat Cattle, bought in Smithfield, in one Market to be sold there again alive; which, was continued by an Act, in the 4th and 5th Years of King William and Queen Mary, for Seven Years, from the 13th of February, 1692; and by another Act, made in the nth and 12 th Years of King Withe said Act was continued for Seven Years, from the 29th Day of September, 1700, which is now near expiring, is fit to be continued.

A Petition of Thomas Br Gentleman, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioner, being concerned in cloathing Part of the Army, had great Dealings with Thomas Pitkin, who was a generalTrader, and reputed to be a rich Man, intending to leave off his Trade, (as he told the Petitioner) and proposed to fell his whole Stock at a Rebate of £. 15per Cent* from the prime Coil; to which the

Petitioner agreed, and gave him Notes, at his Request, in the Name of Elias Rich, Esquire, (his Wife's Brother) for the Payment thereof, at 6, 12, and t8. Months after the Date; and the Petitioner took good Discharges from Pitkin for the Goods so bought: That soon after Pitkin failed, and fled into Holland; but an Act of Parliament being passed, for punishing him with perpetual Imprisonment, and Pillory three Times a Year, in case he did not surrender by a certain Time, he surrendered himself in Holland before the time limited, but did not arrive in England till after; and he, being under the Threats of his Creditors, and the dreadful Apprehensions of the Penalties of the said Act, was prevailed on to depose whatever his Creditors pleased to charge the Petitioner with, the Truth whereof he hath since often denied: That Pitkin delivered up to the Creditors all the Petitioner's Notes (which although not due) yet they brought an Action against the Petitioner for f. zo, oco, on which he long lay a Prisoner, not being able to find Bail for such a Sum, and was obliged to comply with certain Articles of Agreement, made upon long Deliberation, with the Advice of Mr. Attorney General, and Mr. Serjeant Broderick, whereby the Petitioner was to pay much more, than he was indebted to iV/C/Vs Estate; under which there has been an Acquiescence of near two Years, and a Session of Parliament intervening; yet now the Creditors of Pitkin have brought a Bill into this House, to subject the Estate of the Petitioner to the Creditors of Tho. Pitkin, notwithstanding any Agreement, or Composition, made with the Creditors of the said Pitkin-, whereby the utter Ruin of the Petitioner is contrived, and to strip him, and his Son, of their Employments; *tis to punish ex post; and is grounded on the Suggestions of Pitkin, a Bankrupt, only, although the Petitioner has performed the said Articles of Agreement: And praying, that he may be heard by his Counsel at the Bar of the House, or otherwise, against the said Bill.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That it shall not extend to avoid any annual Sum, Pension, or Annuity, heretofore granted out of the Revenues of First-. fruits and Tenths; but if, by discharging small Livings, the First fruits and ioths in any one Diocese shall not be sufficient to pay such annual Sums, then the whole Revenues shall be liable to make good such Deficiencies.

And the same was twice read, and amended; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That the same shall not affect any Grant, Exchange, Alienation, or Incumbrance, made of the Revenues of First fruits and Tenths, or any Part thereof.

And the same was once read, and, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

The House being informed, that Two of the Six Clerks attended, they were called in, and, at the Bar, presented to the House, The Six Clerks Report of the Value of their Office, and the Survey of the Building of the Office.

And then they withdrew.

And the Title of the said Report, and Survey, were read.

And the said Report, and Survey, are as follow;

In humble Obedience to the Order of the honourable

House of Commons, of the 11th Instant, that the

Six Clerks do lay before the House, an Estimate of the

Value of their Offices, and of their House, and Ground

belonging thereto.

THE Six Clerks do humbly represent, That their Offices (wherein they have a Freehold) with their House, Ground, and Fees, and Perquisites, thereto belonging, have usually been estimated worth about £. 6,000 each.

That their laid House was built by the Six Clerks, purposely for the keeping the Records of the Court of Chancery, and for other the publick Use and Business of the Office, for the Dispatch whereof the same is very conveniently situated, and accommodated j and in which, and in the said Ground thereunto belonging, they have an Inheritance by Act of Parliament; and which they have caused to be surveyed by two able Workmen, who have valued the feme, in the Condition it now (lands, and for the Purposes aforesaid, at £. 6,120, as by the annexed Estimate, under their Hands, appears.

Bazill Herne,

13 th March, 1706. John Sufi eld.

The said Survey.

WE, whole Names are under-written, having carefully surveyed the Building called the Six Clerks Office, in Chancery Lane, and the Ground belonging thereto, are of Opinion, that the fame, in lire Condition it now is, and to be continued, to be used for the same Office, is worth £.6,120. Witness our Hands this 12th Day of March, 1706.

Tho. Denning,

Tho. Dennett.

Sir William Ashhurst reported from the Committee, Foreip. to whom the Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Com- made pany, of Gun-makers, of the City of London, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to the said Committee, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the said Petition being read at the Committee, the Commissioners of the Ordnance did admit, that there was a Debt due to the Petitioners, of about £.30,000, and that 10,000 Arms were bought in Holland, for the Lord Rivers' Expedition, which cost about £ 8,000, and would haVecoft about £. 11,000 here; and that 10,000 Arms more were bespoke for the Service of Ireland.

That then the Petitioners proceeded to prove the other Allegations of their Petition; and for that Purpose called,

John Sibley, late Master-of the Gun-makers Company; who said, that the said Company have made 70,000 Arms in a Year, and can furnish the Government with 30,000 Arms every six Months; and the said Company will contract so to do; and, when sent for to the Ordnance Board, offered to supply those Arms, that were bought in Holland, provided they might be paid their laid Debt, or some Part, thereby to enable them to pay their Men, and have such Encouragement, as the Merchants give.

That the said Company always used to furnish England and Ireland with Arms; but since her Majesty's Accef-lion to the Crown have had but one Year's Work for her Service, although they made 40,000 Arms for the King of Portugal the last Year, by Leave of the Board of Ordnance; and that their Work has been at a Hand for a Month or six Weeks together, for want of a Proof by the proper Officers, who have alleged, other Business, hindered them from Dispatch therein; and this within six Months last: And said, they do not find fault with the Government's Pay, but, if they had Interest for their Debts (in like manner as the Navy's) they could the better be able to carry on their Work, and tell cheaper.

Mr. Hawkins, Gunsmith, said, he was put out of the Queen's Work, and afterwards, upon his Application to the Duke of Marlborough, he was permitted to make 100 Guns; and that he has (laid three Weeks for a Proof.

Mr. Barber, Gun-maker, laid, that several Regiments have been furnished with Dutch Arms, particularly the Lord Mordaunt's. Lord Essex, and Colonel Langston's,

as he was informed; but the Lord Mordaunt told him, he bought Accoutrements in Holland for his whole Regiment.

That the Petitioners produced to the Committee an Act, made in the First Year of her Majesty's Reign, for punishing Mutiny or Desertion; wherein there is a Provilb, That all Cloathes, Arms, and Accoutrements of War, belonging to the Horle, Foot, and Dragoons, in her Majesty's Pay and Service, who receive English Pay, shall be bought in the Kingdom of England, Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed, and not elsewhere; and every Officer, or Person, who shall offend herein (upon Proof made ip that behalf) shall be cashiered.

That then the Petitioners called Evidence to other Matters relating to their Petition;

Mr. Vaughan, Gun-maker, said, that about a Year ago, he made a Lock by a Dutch Pattern, with Improvements, for the Surveyor of the Ordnance, to send to Holland, as Mr. IVoulrich and Mr. Crips, Clerks of the Ordnance Office, told him; but, he iupposes, the Lock was bespoke, in order to make such in;

and that no Price was put to him for the Lock.

Mr. Woolrich and Mr. Crips, laid, that Vaughan did

make a Lock from a Dutch Pattern; but that it was not lent to Holland; and that three Locks were made from that Pattern.

Mr. Sibley said, he made a Pattern of a Gun, and asked the Surveyor of the Ordnance 2 for it; but he bid him nothing, and told him, he should hear further from him; which he has not yet done.

Mr. Huggins, Gun-maker, laid, he saw two Dutch Pattern Guns, which were both defective, and would blow in the Britch; and the Cocks being too short, would miss Fire, as often as hit.

Mr. Nutt said, he had the Queen's Mark in his Hand, which was to be put on Guns, made in Holland, as Mr. Eyres, the Surveyor's Clerk, told him.

Mr. Brush said, that Mr: Eyres sent for him, and Huggins, and others, to the Ship Tavern in Water; where he asked them several Questions, for the making and proving of Guns; and he took Directions in Writing, in order to lay them before the Ordnance Board, for the Service in H as Mr. Eyres said; and that he asked Brush, if he would go into Holland, to view and try Arms there; and, if he would, that he would endeavour to contrail with the Board for ioj. a a Day: to which Brush laid, he would go on those Terms.

Huggins said, that he was at the Tavern with Mr. Eyres and Brush; and Mr. Eyres took Instructions for trying and viewing of Arms; which he carried away, saying, it was for fume Service Abroad; but did not hear any Talk of the Proposal to Brush.

Mr. Phillips, and Mr. Britain said, they were at the Ship Tavern with Mr. Eyres and Brush; and that Mr. Eyres did take Instructions for making and trying of Guns; and he said they were to go for Holland.

Lewis Barber laid, that one Barryon, a Gun-lmith, was sent over into Holland, to view Arms there j and believes, he is an Armourer for Ireland.

Mr. Eyres said, he believes he might draw up some Method for proving of Arms, and might alk the Petitioners Directions therein, as also, how to examine a Lock; which was to improve his Judgment, that he might be more serviceable in his Station: That he did give those Instructions to Mr. Bridges; but denies, he laid, that they were to be sent to Holland; nor does he know, they were lent; nor did he treat with Brush about his going, nor had any Directions so to do.

Colonel Burr said, that in his Service at , his

Regiment was furnished with English Arms from the Tower of London, many whercofwere very bad, and burlt

in firing; since which he has bought 400 Muskets of Mr. Hawkins aforesaid, at 2ir.a-piece, whichhaveproved very good Arms.

Mr. Lacock said, that at the Siege of Carrick Fergus he was Lieutenant of a Company, which bore Dutch Arms j and cut of 50, 25 burst in firing; in one Night; and believes, Dutch Arms will not hand the English Proof.

That the Petitioners having finished their Evidence;

The Commissioners of the Ordnance affirmed, as Fact, to the Committee, that the io, oco Arms, for the Ex-, pedition of the Earl of Rivers, were procured from the States of Holland, out of their Arsenal at at

the Instigation cfColonel Blood,_ by the Direction of her Majesty, and not by any Order of the Ordnance Board; and they were paid for by Order of the Lord . Treasurer, by Direction under her Majesty's Signjma-

Yon. 15.

nual; and that they were not for the Use of any Forces in her Majesty's Pay.

That the said 10,000 Arms for Ireland, were bespoke in Holland by Lieutenant General Ingoldsby, Mailer of the Ordnance in Ireland, and Major Comptroller of the Irish Ordnance, by Order of the Queen and Council, and are paid for out of the Revenue of Ireland.

That the Petitioners have been paid in Course, and are no more in Arrear, than other Artificers.

And to justify their Proceedings in the other Matters, charged upon them, produced several Witnesses; viz.

Major General Wythers, and Colonel Tatton; who laid, that about four Years ago there was a general Complaint-of the Colonels in Flanders, that their Mea were afraid to fire their Arms (which were English, marked with King William's and King James's Marks) by reason of their frequent burlting; and thereupon the Duke of Marlborough appointed them to view the Arms in the Tower of London; which they did accordingly; and found many of them defeClive, both in the Locks and Barrels; but since that time such Care hath been taken, that the Arms, marked with Queen Anns Mark; have proved very good, and no Complaint made.

Mr. Gardner, Storekeeper of the Tower small Arms, produced a State of small Arms in the Tower on the 26th of January, 1705; viz.

Snaphance Muskets - 7,695.

Carbines three Foot - 1,356.

Pillols - - - - 722 Pair.

And said, that about January, 1705, the Board of Ordnance ordered the Gun-makers to attend then?, and told them, they had great Occasions for Arms; and the Board urged them to use their utmost Diligence; and that as soon as they had finished one Contrail, the Surveyor ordered another Contrail for more Work, some whereof are not yet completed; and never heard the Gun-makers say, they could riiake above 10,000 Arms in Half a Year, such as the Service required.

Mr. Eyres and Mr. Mercato, Clerks of the Ordnance; laid, that the Gun-makers were summoned to attend the Ordnance Board in January, or February, 1705 j who told them, the Government had great Occasions for Arms, asking what Quantity they could make: Whereupon they made many Demurrs; and laid, they could not answer the Demand, by making such, as the Service', required by the Standard Pattern, because they could not get Locks; but could make enough of such, as they formerly made; and the most they proposed to make, was 10,coo Arms in six Months.

That from April, 1705, to September last, the Gun-makers were fully employed, and might have had more Work, if they would have done it, being often pressed to dispatch what they had in hand, and to enter into new Contrails; but several of the chief Gun-makers-said, they had rather work for the Merchants, than the Queen; and that the greatest Part of the Arms made in the Time aforesaid, was done by the younger. Mailers of the Trade, some of whose Contrails are not yet finished; and that the Queen's Arms are much better, than those made for Portugal, or the Merchants.

Mr. Towle, a Gun-maker, said, that from 1705, to September last, he had as much Work as he could do;

but that, ifhehadhad more Money, he could have made more Arms.

Mr. Huggins, Gun-maker, said, that the Gun-makers had as much Work, as they could do, between April, 1705, and September last; but they often complained, that they could not get Pattern Locks enough, for want of Money, which hindered them from making a greater Number of Arms, than they did: And believes, some had not finished their Warrants in September last; and that the Queen's Arms are better, than those made for Portugal, or the Merchants, by near one Half,

Mr. Eyres said, that a Pattern Gun of Lieutenant General Engoldsby's, bought in Holland for about 20

That Mr. Sibley, being again examined, confirmed what he laid before: And further said, that before 1705 the Gun-makers Company petitioned the Ordnance Board for Work; and from.April, 1705, to September lad, bad full Employment; and be made 1,500 Arms in the Time of his Contract.

That by their Charter they are obliged wholly to apply themselves to the Service of the Government, if required.

That by employing Blackliniths, and unskilful Per-(ons, at Portsmouth, and other Places, for fixing up of

A Petition of Michael Miles was presented to the House, and read , setting forth, that the Petitioner having on his own Account, as also by Commission from Abroad, bought divers Goods and Merchandizes of several Persons, and shipped them for foreign Parts, one Tho. Pitkin failing, several of his Creditor violently seized the Goods, and stopt the Ships, until they had taken out the Goods; for which the Petitioner might bring an Action of Trover, to recover the Value, and also of Trespass, for the Damage, but was prevailed on by one Brerewoodto enter into Articles of Agreement

between Brerewood, and the said Creditors, and others, upon Assurance, that the Petitioner should receive full Satisfaction for his Goods out of Pitkin % Effects, after Payment of 8 s.6d. in the Pound to his Creditors: That the 8j. 6 d.per Pound has been paid, and the Petitioner ought to have Satisfaction for his Goods 5 but by the Violence of the said Creditors he is utterly ruined, and is now a close Prisoner in the Bench; where he is-

informed, the Creditors have brought a Bill into this House, to subject the Estate of Tho. Brerewood to the Creditors of Thomas Pitkin, notwithstanding any Agreement, or Composition, made with the Creditors of the said Thomas Pitkin; which is a great Surprize to the Petitioner, whose utter Ruin, and perpetual Imprisonment, is thereby intended, if the Bill should pass: And praying to be heard by Counsel against the fame.

Resolved, That the Petition be rejected.

An ingrafted Clause was offered, as a Ryder, That no Rectory, or Vicarage, shall be discharged of First fruits and Tenths, when the Incumbent holds more than one Rectory, or Vicarage, at a time, or has any other ecclesiastical Preferment of per Annum.

And the same was twice read, with a Blank; and the Blank ivas filled up with £. 80.

And then the Question being put, That the Clause be read the Third time;

It passed in the Negative.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered, as a Ryder, to be added to the Bill, That it shall not extend to discharge any Benefices, with Cure of Souls, the Tenths whereof were granted by any of her Majesty's Predecessors to any Person or Persons, Bodies politick or corporate.

And the same was once read.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Clause be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

Frauds by The House resumed the adjourned Consideration of Bankrupts, the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill to explain and amend an Act, of the last Sessions of Parliament, for preventing Frauds, frequently committed by Bankrupts, was committed.

And the Amendments, made by the Committee to the Bill, being once read throughout, and then (as far as Clause C) a Second time, one by one, the same were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Clause C, being read a Second time, That where an Oath is required by the said late Act, the Affirmation of the Quakers shall be instead of an Oath;

And the Question being put, that the House do agree with the Committee, in the said Amendment;

It passed in the Negative.

Clause D, being read a Second time. That all such Persons, against whom Commissions of Bankruptcy were awarded before the 25th of December, 1706, who surrendered themselves, and Effects, as in the said Act is appointed, shall have the Benefit thereof; and that such Certificates, as have been, or shall be, granted them, shall be effectual, in case four Fifths of their Creditors in Number and Value do allow of the same;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee, in the said Amendment;

It passed in the Negative.

Clause E, being read a Second time, That no Farmer, Grazier, or Drover of Cattle, shall be entitled to any of the Benefits, given by this or the said late Act, nor be deemed a Bankrupt, within the same, or any former Acts, made against Bankrupts, any Law, or Custom, to the contrary notwithstanding;

The Clause was amended: And then the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Clause F, being read a Second time, That, if a Bankrupt be a Prisoner at the Time of obtaining a Certificate, or at any time after, for any Debt or Damages, due before the Date of his Commission, the Judge of the Court, out of which Process issued for his Confinement (upon proving such Certificate to be duly signed) shall grant a Su/er/edeas to the Bankrupt, for his Dil'charge, upon his entering or filing common Bail, or a commonAppearance, except for criminal Matters;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee, in the said Amendment;

It passed in the Negative.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That absent Persons beyond the Seas, being Bankrupts, shall have the Benefit of the Ad within a certain Time after their return.

And the Question being put, That the Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That no Person shall be obliged to repay any Sum of Money, that was actually paid to, or received from, any Bankrupt before the time of suing out a Commission of Bankruptcy against such Person; and that all Contracts, and Sales, before that time made, shall be good, notwithstanding any Act of Bankruptcy within the Meaning of the Statute, of the 2 ill of King James the First, touching Bankrupts.

And the Question being put. That the Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That no Book-keeper, Calli-keeper, or Servant, or any other Person by their Order, shall remove, conceal, or imbezzle, any of the Goods, Money, Books, or Effects, wherewith they are entrusted, or alter any Book, with a Design to defraud; with a Blank for the Penalty.

And the Question being pur, That the Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Another CJaule was offered, to be added to the Bill, That the Ad shall continue in force for Years,

and from thence to the End of next Session of Parliament, and no longer.

And the same being twice read, with a Blank; the Blank was filled up with " Three."

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

And several other Amendments were made by the House to the Bill.

Sufferers in Nevis and St. Christophers.

Mr. Comptroller reported to the House, that their Address, in relation to the Plantations of Nevis and St. Christophers, having been pre fen ted to her Majesty;

her Majesty was pleased thereupon to return this most gracious A nfwer:

That Ihe is very well pleased, to find the House of Commons has so compassionate a Sense of the Losses of her Subjects in Nevis and St. Christophers, as also with the Concern they ftiew, upon this Occasion, for the Plantations, which are so justiy entitled to their Care, by the large Returns they make to the Publick; and her Majesty will give the necesiary Orders for what the House has desired in this Matter:

And also, that their Address, in relation to the buying, in England all Cloathes, Arms, and Accoutrements of War, for the Army in her Majesty's Pay, or Service, having been presented to her Majesty; her Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

That file will endeavour to give Encouragement to the Manufactures of England, upon all Occasions, where it may consist with the publick Service.

Sir Richard Onslow reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Lords at a Conference, for difigreeing to the Amendment, made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highway between Fornhill, in the County of Bedford, and the Town of Stoney Stratford, in the County of Buckingham; that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were twice read, and (with some Amendments) agreed unto by the House; and are as follow:

The Commons cannot agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highway between Fornhill, in the County of Bedford, and the Town of Stoney Stratford, in the County of Buckingham, in Pr. 2. Line the

>5th;

1 ft, Because there is no Coertion on any Person to pay the Toll, charged for repairing of the said Ways, but on such, who make use of the same for their own Advantage, or Conveniency, and that without any Restraint, or Limitation, whatsoever. The Commons therefore are of an Opinion, that the Payments ought to be without Distinction, to prevent the Differences, that unequal Assessments frequently occasion between her Majesty's Subjects.

The Commons cannot agree to your Lordships Amendment; for this 2d Reason;

Because it may be an Encouragement to many PersonSi to evade the very Intent of the Bill, by pretending to be of those Places, which by your Lordships Amendment are to be eased, and thereby escape the Payment of the Toll, without which there may not arise Money sufficient to repair the Roads, so.necessary for the publick Service.

The 3d Reason, the Commons give, is, Because those, who are entitled by the Amendment to the Exemption, may not be known to be so; which will unavoidably occasion Disputes, Breaches of Peace, and Obstructions on the Highways,* which ought to be free and easy to her Majesty's Subjects.

The Commons decline at this time offering any other Reasons; believing, what has been said may be sufficient to prevail with your Lordships not to infill on your Amendment, that a Bill, so necesiary, may not be loll.

Resolved, That a Conference bedefired with the Lords upon the Subject-matter of the said Amendment.

Ordered, That Sir Richard Onslow do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

" And whereas great Trouble has been ocealioned to " Shopkeepers, and others, by common Informers, who are Persons of mean Reputation; be it enacted by the " Authority aforesaid, that only such Person or Persons,

" shall and may seize any Luftrings, or Alamodes, with*

" in the Cities of London and and the Bills " of Mortality; any thing herein, or in any former Act,

" to the contrary notwithstanding. And whereas by an ,r Act, made in the 9th and 10th Years of the Reign of " his late Majesty Ring W the third (intituled, An Act for the better Encouragement of the Royal Luftring Company, and the more effectual preventing the fraudulent Importations of Luftrings, and Alamodes) it is, amongst other things, enacted, that,

" before any Person or Persons shall be admitted to claim " any of the said Silks, they shall give good Security,

by Recognizance, in the Court, where such Claim " shall be entered, not only to pay the Costs of Suit, in ' " case such Ciaimer or Ciaimers shall be cast, but also to " answer and pay the Penalties and Forfeitures, incurred " by the said Act; and the Security on such Claim 41 cannot be discharged by yielding the Claimer's Body " to Prison; which is found a great Discouragement to " fair Traders.dealing in Alamodes and Luftrings:

" Fr remedy whereof, be it enacted by the Authority " aforesaid, that, when any Person or Persons claim " any Alamodes, or Luftrings, seized, it shall be sufficient, that such Person or Persons give good Security " in the Court, where such Claim shall be made, to " answer and pay the full Costs of Suit only, in case a " Verdict shall pass against him, her, or them, or the " Ciaimer shall be nonsuited, or a Judgment pass by (f Default. And whereas, since the making the said " Act of Prohibition of Trade and Commerce with Vo l 15.

" France, Thirty-three Pieces of foreign Luftrings have

** been seized, and condemned, being imported contrary " to the said Act, and sold to Mr. David Martin, Merchant, to be used in England, and have not been " sealed and marked with the Custom-house Sea) and " Mark; it is hereby further enacted, that the said Thirty-three Pieces of foreign Luftrings may be used " in England; and that the feme shall not be seized, or " forfeited, provided that the Possessors thereof respectively do, on or before the first Day of May,

" One thousand Seven hundred and Seven, bring the " laid Thirty-three Pieces of Luftring, or such Part " thereof, as remains undisposed of, to be sealed and " marked at the Custom-house with the Seal and Mark,

" used for sealing Alamodes and Luftrings imported j " and Oath being made, that such Silks are the feme " individual Thirty-three Pieces of Silks, or Part thereof,

" so sold at the Custom-house: And the Commissioners of her Majesty's Customs are hereby impowered " and required (such Oath being made) to cause the " said Silks to be sealed and marked accordingly; any *5 Law to the contrary in any wise notwithstanding."

Captain Thomas Green late Commander, seized and condemned in Scotland, was referred.

And the said Report, and the Refutations of the Committee thereupon, were read, and are as follow; viz.

That, upon hearing the Petitioners, many of their Witnesses, and Proofs in Writing,

It appeared to the Committee, that the Petitioners, by Licence from one of the Proprietors of the separate Stock, allowed by Law to trade to the East Indies, did fend the said Ship Worcester-, where ftie having traded successfully, upon her Return came round by the North of Scotland, to avoid the French, and put into Leith Road, to wait for a Convoy to England, the aSth 1704; where a Seizure was made upon the said Ship and Cargo, in a very extraordinary, and violent Manner, as appeared by John Eagle, Carpenter of the said Ship, and several other the Sailors on board of the fam§ at the Seizure thereof.

Who being examined, laid, that on the 12th 1704, one Mr. Roderick Mackenfy, Secretary to the African and East India Company in Scotland, with several other Scotch Gentlemen, and Servants, came on board her, pretending to see the Ship.

That the Boatswain invited them (the Captain and Mates being then ashore) and treated them with Punch

in

6 Ann. 310 Marliu — i* Ap369

in the great Cabbin; wherewith, and with drinking Wine, and Brandy, which Mr. Mackenzie brought on board with him, the Ship's Crew were very merry, and, at Mr. Mackenzie's Request, several of them did sing Songs.

That, during their Mirth, a Scots Man of War, then at Anchor near the Worfired a Gun with Shot; upon which Mr. Mackenzie immediately rose up, and told the Ship's Crew in the Cabbin, that, for their Civility, he would sing them a Song, had he been used to singing; but that his Song was in Writing: Upon which he pulled out a Paper, which, he told them, was a Warrant from the African and East India Company to seize their Ship, for llcprizal for their Ship nandale, seized in England. Thereupon all the Scots on board drew their Swords, and told the Ship's Crew, they were their Prisoners; and that Night turned Part of the Crew on Shore, and detained five of them Pri-loners on board, where they were so kept about 18 Weeks; and afterwards 15 of the Crew, with their Captain, were tried, and condemned, for Piracy and Murder; and the Captain, his Chief Mate, and Gunner, were executed, upon the Evidence only of a Black, who died (as is supposed by Poison) before the Day of Execution; it appearing afterwards by the Oaths of two of Captain Drummonds Ship's Crew, some Time after, being in London (for robbing and murdering of whom the said Captain, Mate, and Gunner, were executed) that they never saw the Worcej in all their Voyage; and that Drummond was turned Pirate; and when they left him, to return home, he made to Madagascar with two Moco Ships, he, and another Pirate, had taken in the East Indies.

That, soon after the aforesaid Seizure, the was proceeded against in the high Court of Admiralty in

Scotland, as appeared by a large Extract of those Proceedings, under the Hand of Mr. Daniel,

Clerk of that Court j and on the ajd of March last Sentence of Condemnation was given against the said Ship, in Reprizal for the A and ordered the

Worcester, and her Cargo, to be sold, for Satisfaction of the same; which, in August and September following was done accordingly.

That, upon Application to her Majesty for Relief in the Premises, the whole Matter was stated and reported to her Majesty by her Attorney and Solicitor General, Sir John Cook, Knight, her Majesty's Advocate, and Doctor Brampston, Judge of the Court of Admiralty.

Which Report was read to the Committee 5 whereby, upon strict Examination, it appeared, the Petitioners Damages, being particularly estimated, upon account of the said Ship, amounted to 23,975. os.

That the Owners have been at Charges since the said Report, by their Endeavours to come at Relief, £. 400.

Which, with Interest of the 23,975. or. 10 d. for two Years f, at £. 6 per Cent, being £. 3,596. 5 o

makes the Petitioners total Loss amount to£. 27,971.

Also, the Lords have commanded us to acquaint this House, that their Lordships having under Confederation a Bill, lent up from this House, intituled, An Act for obliging John Rice to account for Debentures, granted to him in the last Session of Parliament; and the said Rice having petitioned to be heard on the said Bill, and to have Liberty to attend his Counsel in the mean Time; their Lordships desire, that the said John Rice (who, as they are informed, is in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House) may be permitted, and ordered, to attend his Counsel accordingly, and to appear at their Bar, when desired; and that this House will iransmit to "their House such Papers, as are now before this House, relating to the Matter of the said Bill.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do permit John Rice to attend his Counsel, and to appear at the Bar of the House of Lords, when the Lords do desire it.

The House was informed by the Clerk, that the Papers, which were before the House, relating to the said Bill, have been delivered (by Order of the House) to the respective Parties, who delivered the same in.

The Messengers were called in again, and acquainted with the Matters aforesaid.

A Petition 0 f Samuel Powell, Esquire, Serjeant at Arms

attending this House; praying, that his Circumstances may be taken into Consideration, in relation to the great Charges lie has been at in fending his Messengers to most Parts of the Kingdom (in Obedience to the Orders of the House) to apprehend Persons ordered into his Custody; but that such Persons absconded to the End of a Session, whereby they clcaped with Impunity, and evaded the Justice of the House; and also in relation to some few, who have been taken into Custody, and have lain to the End of a Session, and not paid any thing; and such, as did p3y, paid only what they thought fit; and that he may be relieved therein, as shall be thought meet.

And the House taking into Consideration the several Contempts of their Orders by Persons who have justly incurred the Censure of the House, and the great Charges, the Serjeant at Arms, attending the House, hath been at, in endeavouring to execute such Orders, for which he has had no Satisfaction, some of the Persons having absconded from Justice, and others, who have been in Custody, having their Liberty at the End of a Session, upon a Prorogation, have refused to pay the Officers their just Fees; and likevy ife considering the ill Consequences of such Contempts of the Authority of the House;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That when any Person,

ordered to be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Anns, shall either abscond from Justice, or, having been in Custody, shall refuse to pay the just Fees; that, in either of those Cafes, the Order for Commitment shall be renewed the Beginning of the next Session of Parliament; and that this be declared to be a Handing Order of the House.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom it was referred to enquire into Frauds, committed by Drawbacks of Goods and Merchandizes exported.

And the same was read, and is as follows, viz,

Mr. Pitkin, being examined, laid, that, for five Years before he broke, he was concerned in the Practice of defrauding the Government of high Drawbacks upon Goods, falsely entered for such, upon which those Drawbacks are allowed; and that he was induced into such PraAices by Mr William Lucy, and Charles ittgbam, who told him, they had followed that Practice a considerable time, before, very much to their Advantage $ and was offered to be a Partner with them in such their Profit; which he agreed to accordingly.

That, upon his Engagement with Lucy and ham, they entered great Quantities of low Goods, inclosed in the outward Wrappers, called Gunnills,-for high Goods, and, according to the Direction of Law, sometimes swore themselves, at other Times procured their Brokers, or others, to swear, the Goods were such, as those Wrappers imported, and their prime Cost, as high Goods, and thereupon they received from time to time Drawbacks, from 50 to too per Bale, which they had Persons to swear for ioj. or 15 s. That it was usual for them to ship off from two toseven Bales at a time, lb sworn to, and have received 500 upon one Drawback, at the Rate of £. 15 per Cent, according to the prime Cost of the Goods, so sworn to; and when the said Bales have been put on board such Ships, as they had contracted with the Captains to compleat their Designs (who were Mr. Magnus Mason, Mr. Charles Lovefetto, and Mr. Ralph Selby) those Captains used to lay their Ships so near their own Houses at St. Katherines, that, by laying a Plank from their back Doors, they could go into and from their Ships, and in the Nighttime, when all was safe, they used to cut off the said Gunnels, and Wrappers, and convey the Muslins, and other Goods, into their Houses from the said Ships j and after they were so secured there at proper Times, they were conveyed at Midnight by an old Woman, with Bags, from the said Captains House to one Mr. Chad-well's, a Goldsmith, in Cornh5 and when at Times, the old Woman had brought all their Goods to Chad-welts, they, the said Pitkin, Lucy, and Beckingham, used to fend their Porters thither, to fetch their said Goods to their own Shops.

That the said Captains were paid Ten Guineas for every Bale of Goods they so re-landed, as aforesaid; and were privy to the false Entries, and Practices of Drawbacks, made use of by the said Pitkin, Lucy, and Beckingham.

That he believes, the Custom-house Officers are not capable of detesting such Practices j for that the Law requires only the Oath of the Exporter as to Goods, and Value, for Exportation; and, should the Officers open any of their Bales, they do not know the Difference of Goods between 40 s.and £.4/rr Piece; and, without

they can justify a Distinction, the Goods are packed up again at their own Charge; and therefore is satisfied, that very few Bales are opened, without particular Grounds of Suspicion, by the Custom-house Officers.

But the said Lucy and Beckingham telling Pitkyn, that, as they had, so he must continue to make Matters ealy with one Mr. Car case, a Custom-house Officer, who was their very good Friend, and whose Business it was to examine the Merchants Certificates of Goods, bought at the publick Sale, and who, they told him, was privy to their aforesaid Practices; and accordingly they used to make the said Carcase, and his Wife, Presents, and Treats, by Turns; particularly, he, the said Pitkin, at Lucfs Request, consented, Lucy should present her with a Gold Watch, which cost Pitkin about £. 38, which

Frauds in Drawbacks.

Lucy told him, would stop Car case' % smoking their Practices.

That the said Carcase was, in a manner, a Stranger to Pitkin; but there was a very great Intimacy between Lucy and him, and their Wives, who were seldom asunder.

That, since his, the said Pitkin's, failing, he applied to Lucy, for an Allowance out of the £.6 per Cent, that

he had received for what Effects Pitkyn had discovered himself; and, upon Pitkyn's threatening to make a Discovery of the aforesaid Frauds and Practices upon the Government, Lucy agreed to allow him £. 50 Annum, for Seven Years.

The said Pitkyn further said, that, upon one of their Attempts for a Drawback, they were detected by Mr. Bertie, a Custom-house Officer, upon a false Entry; upon which the Goods were seized, to the Value of £. 1,300, and it cost them £. 500 to retrieve them; the Merchants, upon a Seizure, paying only what Goods seized are valued at, and not what they cost, whereby their Competitions are made easy.

And such Seizures being kept private by the Officers, the Exporters Reputations, not being exposed, are not prejudiced by such Practices.

Mr. Bertie, one of the Custom-house Officers, laid, he had seized some Goods, that Pitkin was endeavouring to export by false Entries, and in another Person's Name, to the Value of about £. 800, and the tame were condemned, and fold; and does not remember, any Person appeared to be concerned with Pitkin, other than one Peirce, who was his Solicitor.

Mr. Peirce said, he was concerned for in that

Seizure; and Mr. Beckingham was concerned with Pitkin.

Mr. Walker, to prove the Partnership between Pitkyn, Lucy, and Beckingham, upon Goods for Exportation,

said, he had seen several Bills of Parcels of Goods, of a very great Value, that has been made in their three Names jointly: To which Mr. Lucy said, that, though there might be such Bills of Parcels, yet they used to divide the Goods, as soon as they were brought Home, and gave their separate Notes for paying for the tame.

Mr. Carcase, attending, was examined touching a

Gold Watch, said by Pitkyn to be presented to Mr. Carcase's Wife by Mr. Lucy, at s Charge, of about

1-38.

Mr. Carcase owned, Mr. Lucy had presented his Wife with a Watch; but, that it was not on account of private Business, but only the Friendship and Intimacy, that was between their two Families; and that he had presented Mr. Lucy's Family with Presents, more than an Equivalent for what he had received from Mr. Lucy, and that he never received any Gratuity from Pitkyn in his Life; and was never privy to any of their Transactions.

Mr. Lucy owned, he had presented a Watch to Mrs. Carcase, which he bought, and paid £.32 for it; but that it was not for any Business done, but the Friendthip between their Families; and had received several Presents from Mr. Carcase.

To which Pitkyn laid, that, though Mr. Lucy bought the Watch, he allowed him the Money it cost, upon Account, out of the Divisions, made between them upon the account of Drawbacks: Which Lucy denied.

Mr. Pitkyn further said, that Mr. Lucy put a Parcel of prohibited Silks on board a Vessel, whereof one Cook was Master, for Exportation for Holland, of the Value of £. 900 or thereabouts, and Pitkyn gave Bond at the Custom-house, that none of those Silks should be relanded; but, notwithstanding, the said Silks were relanded, and he saw them afterwards in Lucy's Ware-house.

Mr. JVatkinson said, that he having bought two Bales of Betillys of Mr. Newman, who bought them at the East India Sale, which, he lupposes, Mr. Lucy did not imagine he intended for Exportation, for that, when he

came to the Custom-house, to enter them for Exportation, he found, Mr. Lucy had writ off about 160 Pieces of the same Goods in his Name; upon Complaint whereof, that Entry was rectified by Mr. Carcase, otherwise Lucy must have received the Drawback.

Mr. Carcase (according to Order) laid before the Committee an Account, to what Head the Goods, so writ off by Lucy, were placed, upon his rectifying Mr. Watkinson's Entry.

Mr. Edward Loveybond, formerly Apprentice to Mr. Pitkyn, said, that, whilst he was in Mr. s Ser-

vice, though he was often sent out of the Way, yet he has observed, when Goods have been sent, to be shipped off from the Shop, he has seen, in a few Days after, 40, 50, and 100, Pieces in a Day, of the same Goods, so said to be shipped off, to be brought into the Shop again; and believes, the Goods, so said to be shipped off, and re-landed, were in Partnership between Lucy, Beckingham, and Pitkyn, having seen great Quantities of Goods brought from their Shops to s for flapping, and, upon their Return to s, they have been

sent back to Lucy and Beckingham

Mr. Dawbus, who had been an Apprentice to Beck-ingham four Years, and three Years a Journeyman, laid, that he did not know of any Goods re-landed by his Master, lent on board; but owned, he often suspected, there had been such Practices; for that, when Goods are shipped for Holland, they usually had Orders to deface the Marks, put upon the Sample Pieces by the East India Company; and yet when such Goods have been sent from the Shop, for Exportation, he has afterwards found those Sample Pieces, with other Goods, as he might suspect were sent with them, brought back again to the Shop; and has observed Goods, so brought back again several Times, divided between Lucy, Beckingham, and Pitkyn-, but knew nothing of their Practices in re-landing Goods, of his own Knowlege.

Mr. Whetberley, Servant to Mr. Beckingham about

two Years since, laid, that he had shipped off many Parcels of Goods for his Master, but knows nothing of their re-landing any of them.

Mr. Selby, one of the Matters of the Ships (Mason and Lovefetto, the other Matters, being now in Holland) was examined, and accused of re-landing of Goods: Said, that about Seven Years ago, a Dutch Ship lying along-fide by his Ship, Mr. Lucy and Beckingham came to him, and desired him to let them hand a small Box over his Ship ashore; which he consenting to, became acquainted with them; and they afterwards, about the Year 1701, sent him several Bales of Goods, with Coc-kets for Exportation; and when his Ship was cleared, they sent him Word, that they had sent some Goods to him by Mistake, and desired, such Bales, as they deferred, might be re-landed, and they would fend him other Goods, to make up his Freight, and would gratify him for his Trouble; upon which he re-landed the Goods desired, and which were put on board a Wherry, and sent through Bridge at Midnight, by Lucy's Direction.

And being asked, whether he did not use to give Receipts for what Goods he received on board, and, if so, how he re-landed Goods, without the Delivery of his Receipts, especially after the Ship's being cleared;

The laid Selby said, that he did not re-land Goods, till his Ship was cleared, to save his Oath, as Master; and that as to his Receipts, he gives for Goods, they are Handing out against him, though re-landed; and that in Smuggling Affairs there are no Notes passing among them, but deal with one another upon Honour.

That he has not yet received his Gratuities, promiied him, there being an open Account between him and Lucy; and Lucy has preferred a Chancery Suit against him.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of- this House as are of hef Majesty's moll honourable Privy Council.

John Earl of Southerland was pleased to inform the Committee, that about a Year and an half ago, at burgh, Captain Breholt told his Lordship, that his Mate and Ship's Crew cut the Cable of his Ship, and run away with her to Madagajcar, leaving him behind on Shore: That afterwards several of his said Men applied to him, to procure their Pardons, they being desirous to return into England; and informed the said Breholt, that the PiraUs at Madagajcar were a Thousand strong, and worth three Millions of Money.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a great Number of Pirates have settled themselves in the Island of Madagajcar, from whence they have committed many great Piracies, Robberies, and Depredations, very ruinous to the Trade, and whereby the Lives of many of her Majesty's good Subjects have been destroyed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, that she would be graciously pleased to take into her royal Consideration, how the said Piracies may be suppressed, and their further Piracies, Robberies, and Depredations, may be effectually prevented.
