My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I was willing to give you an opportunity of coming together again, to consider, if any thing can properly be done, to prevent the Inconveniences, that may happen to our Trade by too great an Interval between the riling of the Parliament and the first of May; and I need not add, that whatever is to be done of that kind, will require to be dispatched in a little Time.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election for any Member, to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in case it shall appear, any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, as a Member of this House, or endeavoured lo to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear, any Person hath been tampering with any Witnesses, in respect of their Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly endeavoured to deter, or hinder, any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Mifde-. meanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear, any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, That for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Election of Members, to serve for the Commons in Parliament, the same is a high Infringement of the liberties and Privileges of the Commons of England.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do from time to time take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

[f/] By the QUEEN: A Proclamation,

Containing her Majesty s Declaration, that it is expedient, that the Lords of Parliament of England, and Commons of the present Parliament of England, should be the Members of the respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England.

A N N E, R.

H ERE AS by the Two-and-twentieth Article of the Treaty of Union of the two Kingdoms of England and Scotland, as the same have been ratified and confirmed by two Acis of Parliament, the one passed in the Parliament of England, the other in the Parliament of Scotland, it is agreed, that, if we, on or before the first day of May next, on which Day the Union is to take Place, mould declare, under the great Seal of England, that it is expedient, that the Lords of Parliament of England, and Commons of the present Parliament of End a ml, should be the Members of the respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England, then the said Lords of Parliament of England, and Commons of die prelient Parliament of England, should be the Members of the respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England; and that the Time and Place of the Meeting of the first Parliament of Great Britain being appointed by us, by our royal Proclamation, under the great Seal of Great Britain,' the Lords of Parliament of England, and the Sixteen Peers of Scotland, who are, by virtue of the Articles of Union, to fit and vjrte in the House of Lords, and the Members-of the lfoule of Commons of the said Parliament of England, and the Five-and-forty Representatives of Scotland in the House of Commons of the Parliament of Great Britain, should assemble and meet respectively in the respective Houses of the Parliament of Great Britain at such Time and Place, as should he lb appointed by us, and should be the two Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain: And we, having taken into our royal Consideration the present Circumstances of Affairs, do judge it to be for the Good of our Kingdoms, that the Lords of Parliament of England, and the Commons of the present Parliament of England, should be the Members of the respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England; and we do, pursuant to the said Articles of Union, hereby declare, under our great Seal of England, that it is expedient, that the Lords of Parliament of England, and Commons of the present Parliament of England, which now Hands prorogued to the Thirtieth Day of this instant April, should be the Members of the respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England; and the Lords of Parliament of England, and Commons of the present Parliament of England, are accordingly to be the Members of the respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the Nine-and-twentieth Day of April, Anno Dom. 1707, in the Sixth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen.

By the QUEEN: A Proclamation,

Declaring her Majesty's Pleasure for holding the first Parliament of Great Britain, and appointing the Time and Place of meeting thereof.

A N N E, R.

'!A/rHEREAS, in pursuance of the Two-and-twentieth Article of the Treaty of Union, as the same hath been ratified and confirmed by two Acts of Parliament, the one

{►ailed in the Parliament of England, and the other in the ^liament of Scotland, we, for many weighty Reasons, have thought fit to declare by our royal Proclamation, issued under our great Seal of England, on the Twenty-ninth Day of April last, that it was expedient, that the Loras of Parliament of England, and Commons of the Parliament of England, which then ltood prorogued to the Thirtieth Day of April aforesaid, should be Members of die respective Houses of the first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on the Part of England: And whereas, in pursuance of an Act, passed in the Parliament of Scotland, for settling the Manner of electing the Sixteen Peers, and Forty-five Members, to represent Scotland in the Parliament of Great Britain (which Ad is by the Two-and-twentieth Article aforesaid declared to be as valid, as if the same had been part of, and ingrossed in, the said Treaty) Sixteen Peers, and Forty-five Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, have been chol'en to be the Members of the respective Houses of the said first Parliament of Great Britain, for and on die Paxt of Scotland: We do by this our royal Proclamation, under the great Seal of Great Britain, with the Advice

[a] At the Beginning of this Journal are inserted th§ three follow* printed Proclamation*.

of our Privy Council, declare and publish our Will and Pleasure to be, and do hereby appoint, that our first Parliament of Great Britain shall meet, and be holden, at our City of Well-minder, on Thursday, the Twenty-third Day of October next; whereof the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of our said first Parliament of Great Britain, and all others, whom it may concern, are hereby required to take Notice.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the fifth Day of June, 1707, in the Sixth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen.

Given at our Court at Windsor, the eighth Day of September, 1707, in the Sixth Year of our Reign.

HE It Majesty having by her royal Declaration and Proclamations (hereunto annexed) declared, appointed, and culled, her first Parliament of Great Britain, to meet on this Day, the most noble Duke of Devonshire, Lord Steward of her Majesty's Houshold, came about Eleven a Clock into the Rooms belonging to the Cletk of the House of Commons, called the Inner Court of Wards, the usual Place to administer the Oaths, appointed to be taken by the Members, returned to serve in Parliament; and George Wright, Esquire, Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, having before delivered to Paul JodreH, Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons, a Book of the Return of the Names of the Knights, Citizens, Burgefi'es, and Barons, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the said Parliament; and the said Mr. Jodrell, and Mr. Needier, his Clerk Assistant, and other his Clerks, attending, according to the Duty of their Places; the Lord Steward administered the Oaths appointed to several of the Members appearing, and afterwards made a Commission, or Deputation, under his Hand and Seal (hereunto also annexed) to several Members, to administer the said Oaths to the rest of the Members returned; who administered the feme accordingly to so many, as appeared: Which being done, the Members repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons: After which,

A M ffage was brought from the Queen by Mr. Aston, Deputy Gentleman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her Majesty immediately in the House of Peers.

And accordingly the House went up, to attend her Majesty; who was pleased (by the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain) to command the Commons to return to their House and chuse their Speaker.

And the House being returned;

The honourable Langham , Esquire, took notice, that her Majesty had, by the Lord Chancellor, directed them to chuse a Speaker; and therefore he hoped, he should propose one, that every body would agree with him in; one, that they had the Experience of the last Session; and that he need say no more in his Commendation, for that it was fresh in every one's Memory, how impartially all things were then carried on: And desired, that the Right honourable John Smith, Esquire, might be called to the Chair.

And being seconded by Mountgomery, Esquire; who added, that Mr. Smith had contributed much to the advancing of the Union of both Kingdoms, which, he hoped, would be to their Advantage; and therefore he seconded the Motion, That Mr. Smith might take the Chair, as Speaker:

And Mr. Smith being generally called upon j he, in his Place, humbly thanked the Gentlemen, that had proposed him; but, in regard he had had the Honour of serving the House once already, and that there were a great many Gentlemen in the House, more fit than himself, desired, that he might beexcufed, and that they would make Choice of some other Gentleman.

But the House unanimously calling upon him to take the Chair, he was conducted by Mr. Booth and Mr. Mountgomery up to the Chair; and, being upon the first Step thereof, desired again, that the House would please to re-consider their Choice, and the ill Consequences of that Place being not better supplied; and to excuse him, and think upon chusing some other.

Vot,. 15.

But they crying, " No, No!" Mr. Smith fat down in the Chair; and the Mace (which before lay tinder the Clerk's Table) was by the Serjeant at Arms, attending the House, laid upon the Table.

To which some Gentlemen took Exceptions; alleging, The Mace the Mace ought not to be put upon the Table, until laid on the the Speaker was approved of by her Majesty. Table.

Whereupon the Journal for the Year 1661, was called for; and what related to that Matter was read: And also the Journal for the Year 1694, was produced; wherein is entered what passed on the Election of Paul Foley, Esquire, Speaker, and also a Report from a Committee then appointed to draw up the Proceedings of the House in relation to the Election of a Speaker.

Whereupon the Mace remained upon the Table.

The Queen's Mr. Speaker reported, that her Majesty was pleased Speech on Thursday last to make a most gracious Speech to both

reported. Houses of Parliament; and, in regard of the Length of

it, and the Noise, when it was spoke, and for the better help of his Memory, he had procured a Copy thereof; which he read to the House, and is as follows;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

IT is with all humble Thankfulness to Almighty God, and with intire Satisfaction to myself, that I meet you here in this first Parliament of Great Britain; not doubting, but you come with Hearts prepared, as mine is, to make this Union so prosperous, as may answer the well grounded Hopes of all my good Subjects, and the reasonable Apprehensions of our Enemies.

To this End nothing is so immediately material, as to convince, as soon as is possible, both our Friends, and our Enemies, that the uniting our Interests has not only improved our Abilities, but our Resolutions also, to prosecute this just and necessary War, till we obtain a safe and honourable Peace for ourselves, and for our Allies.

In so great and extensive a War, as this is, many things may be usefully undertaken, which are not fit to be communicated before-hand. The attempt upon Toulon was of this Nature; and, though it had not wholly its desired Effect, has nevertheless been attended with many great and obvious Advantages to the common x Cause in this Year, and has made our Way more easy, I

hope, to greater in the next.

As the French have gained Ground upon us in Spain, lo they have been wholly driven out of Italy; by which it is become more easy for all the Allies to join their Assistance next Year, for enabling the King of Spain to recover his Affairs in that Kingdom, and to reduce the whole Spanish Monarchy to his Obedience.

The Weakness and ill Posture of Affairs upon the Rhine, in the Beginning of the Year, has given an

t o° Novembris. A. 1707.

Opportunity to the French to make themselves stronger in all other Parts; but this Defect seems in a very promising Way of being fully remedied, against next Campaign, by the Conduct and Authority of the Elector of Hanover, whose seasonable Acceptance of that Command has strengthened, and obliged, the whole Confederacy.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons.

The just Application of the Supplies, given me by former Parliaments, the plain Necessity of continuing this War, the reasonable Prospect of putting a good End to it, if we be not wanting to ourselves, and the Honour of the first Parliament of Great Britain, are, I make no doubt, sufficient Arguments to incite you to provide the necessary Supplies, which I am obliged to desire of you, for the ensuing Campaign in all Parts, and particularly for the timely Support of the King of Spain, and the making good our Treaty with Portugal, as also for strengthening the Confederate Army under the Command of the Duke of Savoy; all which Services I don't doubt but you will think so necessary, that they ought not to be neglected, even though they should require an Augmentation.

The Sums, already expended in this War, have been very great; and they are sufficient Proofs, how well (a-tisfied my Subjects have always been with the Ends of my Government, of which I am so sensible, as never to ask any Supplies from them, but what are absolutely necessary for the Preservation of their Religion and Liberty; and I look upon it as my great Happiness, that I have not the lead Interest separate from that of all my good Subjects.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

In a Work so great, and new in its Kind, as that of the Union, it is impossible, but that some Doubts and Difficulties mull have arisen; which, however, I hope, are so far overcome, as to have defeated the Designs of those, who would have made use of that Handle to foment Disturbances.

There are several Matters expressly made liable, by the Articles of the Union, to the Consideration of the Parliament of Great Britain; which, together with such others, as may reasonably produce those Advantages, that, with due Care, must certainly arise from that Treaty, I earnestly recommend to your serious Consideration.

On my Part, nothing shall be wanting to procure to my People all the Blessings, which can follow from this happy Circumstance of my Reign, and to extinguish, by all proper Means, the least Occasions of Jealously, that either the civil, or religious, Rights of any Part of this my United Kingdom can suffer by the Consequences of this Union.

Such a Suggestion shall never in my Time have any Foundation, how restless soever our Enemies may be in their Endeavours, and Artifices, to disturb our Peace and Happiness: Those great and valuable Blessings cannot but be always secure to us, if we heartily endeavour to confirm, and improve, our present Union. I hope therefore, you will suffer nothing to prevail with you to disunite among yourselves, or abate your Zeal in opposing the common Enemy.

Resolved, Nemitie contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, returning the Thanks of this House for her Majesty's most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament; and to allure her Majesty, that the Commons of Great Britain will effectually enable her to carry on the War with Vigour, and do all, that in them lies, to improve the mutual Advantages of the happy Union.

Fleet Prison, November 7th, 1707.

Sir,

I think it my Duty to make known to the House, that I am detained, from attending their Service, in the Prison of the Fleet, by reason of two Judgments, executed upon me by procurement of John Rice, and Hezekiah Ben/on, his Attorney, the one at the Suit of John Holland, and the other of Thomas Mathews and John Wetton, Trustees for the said Rice, of Lands by him purchased with Debentures, granted him by Parliament, and, as such, since veiled in her Majesty, and of some other mesne Process, from which I had delivered myself by Bail, if not disabled by these Executions.

I am advised, the proper Method of advertising the House is by Letter to yourself; but if, upon communicating of this, they should please to signify their Plea-sure for any other way of Address, my Obedience is ready for their Commands. Sir,

Your most humble Servant, John Afgill.

To the Right honourable John Smith, Esquire,

Speaker of the honourable House of Commons.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up an humble Address, to be presented to her Majesty, that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the feme was twice read, and is as followeth j viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great in Parliament assembled, do, with all Thankfulness and Humility, acknowlege the divine Goodness in making your Majesty the glorious Instrument of uniting your two Kingdoms.

And: we shall never be so wanting in our Duty to your Majesty, and to the Trust reposed in us by those we represent, as not to embrace all Occasions of confirming, and improving, the Advantages of this happy Union.

As this cannot fail to strengthen your Majesty's Government at Home, and answer the well-grounded Hopes of all your good SubjtCh, so your faithful Commons are resolved to exert the united Strength of this Istand in such a Manner, as shall make it a Terror to your Enemies.'

The Elector of Hanover being at the Head of the Army on the Rhine, gives us the greatest Hopes of Success on that Side, from his Conduct, and Authority.

And though your Majesty's great and wife Designs, for the Advantage of this Nation, and the Good of the common Cause, have not had all the desired Effects in the last Campaign, yet we beg Leave to affine your Majesty, that no Difeppointments shall distourage us from making our utmost Efforts to enable your Majesty, in Conjunction with your Allies, to reduce the whole Spanish Monarchy to the Obedience of the King of Spain, to make good the Treaty with Portugal, and to strengthen the confederate Army under the Command of the Duke of Savoy.

Your Majesty has shewn, throughout the whole Course of your Reign, that you have no Interest separate from that of your People; who have been so sensible of the many Blessings they have enjoyed under your Administration, as never to be wanting on all Occasions to express their Gratitude to the best of Queens.

And we, your united Commons of this Parliament, do faithfully promise your Majesty, that we will proceed upon publick Business with Unanimity and Dispatch, and give such effectual Supplies, as may carry on the War with Vigour, and, by the Blessing of God upon your Majesty's Arms, obtain an honourable and lasting Peace.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That this House doth agree to the said Address, to be presented to her Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Mr. Speaker reported, that he, with the House, did Yesterday present their humble Address to her Majesty; and that thereupon her Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer:

Gent'einen,

I thank you very kindly for this Address. The Desires you express, of taking all Occasions to improve the Advantages of our happy Union, are extremely agreeable to me.

As you cannot give me a more sensible Proof of your Loyalty and Affection to me, and my Government, than by your Assurances of supporting me effectually in a vigorous Prosecution of the War, so I make no doubt, but that these Assurances will have their due Weight Abroad, and be of the greatest Advantage imaginable to the common Cause.

'That the Committee had examined the Matter of the Complaint, and also searched Precedents} and that the Cafe, and Precedents, are as follow;

That it appeared, upon the Examination of the High Bailiff, and Keeper of the Westminster, one

Elderlon, a Bailiff, and the Warden of the Fleet, that a Warrant was sent from the Sheriff of to the

High Bailiff of Westminster, dated the 11 th of June, 1707, for arresting the - laid Mr. AJgill, at the Suit of John Holland, for 6,390 Debt, and at the Suit of John Tayler, for £. 2,500 Debt.

That, pursuant to the said Warrant, Mr. AJgill was arrested the 12th of June aforesaid by one a

Bailiff to the said High Bailiff of Westminster, and by him detained till the 14th of the said June-, and then he delivered Mr. AJgill to the Custody of the Gate-kouse Prison, charged in Execution at the Suit of the said John Holland and John Tayler.

That the said Mr. AJgill, the 23d 1707,

was removed by Habeas Corpus from the Gate-house to the Prison of the Fleet, then charged with Actions upon mesne Process, at several Persons Suits,' in the Sum of £. 2,284, and on Executions in the Sum of 9,890, as by the original Return, and annexed to the said Writ of Habeas Corpus, appeared.

Then the Committee proceeded to search for Precedents of the Method of Proceedings, which this House has used in Cafes of Privilege, and the Method of freeing their Members under Arrests -, which, in Point of Time, as they Hand upon the Journals of this House, are; viz.

The first Precedent is the same of Sir Tho. Shirley in i° Jacobi, as follows; viz.

The Parliament 1° Jac. was summoned to meet on the 19th of March; and on the 15th of March (four Days before the Parliament met) Sir Tho. Shirley, who was elected Burgess for Steyning, in Sussex, was arrested, and committed to the Fleet.

Upon a Motion made on his behalf, the House or-tlertd a Warrant should be directed, under the Hand of Mr. Speaker, to the Clerk of the Crown, for a Writ of Habeas Corpus, to bring the Body of Sir Tho. into the House upon Tuesday following. 22 Mar. 1603.

It appeared, upon Examination of the Fad, that the Execution was taken forth the 30th January, 1603, a Day before the Tejle of the Writ, and was delivered to the Serjeant the nth of February, before Sir Thomas was elected. The Heads of the Debate upon this Oc-calion appear upon the Journal, and concluded with ap-22

pointing a Committee, to confidey ;of all the Queliions and Doubts, in this Cafe. 27 March, 1604.

Upon Report of the Committee, the House ordered, that Sympjon, at whose Suit'Sir Thomas was committed,

and the Serjeant} that arrested him, llibuld be committed to the Tower j and that they would hear Counsel on all Parties on these Points:

1 ft, Whether Privilege were to be allowed, since the Execution was taken forth, before the-Parliament fat: 2d, Whether the Action was discharged:

3d, Where the Loss should lie. 1604.

The Argument of the Counsel, and the Precedents they used, appear in the Journal; That of Hyde, 14th Edw. IV. of Larke, 8° Hen. VI. and of Clark, 29° Hen. VL

Upon reading these Precedents, three Questions were Put:

ift. Whether Sir Tho. Shirley should have Privilege: 2dly, Whether presently, or deferred till further Order:

3dly, Whether we shall be Petitioners to his Majesty, according to former Precedents, for feme Course of securing the Debt of the Party, and laving harmless the Warden of the Fleet.

Which were all resolved in the Affirmative.

A Bill for securing Sympjon % Debt, was twice read, and committed.

The feme Bill read a Third time, and passed: — Sent up to the Lords.

A Bill for the Relief of Plaintiffs, where the Defendants in Execution are set at Liberty, altered in the Stile, and ordered to be ingrossed.

On the 2d of May a Motion was made, to appoint a Committee, to consider of all such Precedents, as shall be offered in the Particulars of Sir Tho. Shirley's same of Privilege; and there are the Copies of several Records in your Journal.

Upon the 4th of May a Petition was tendered, and read in the House, to be exhibited to his Majesty, for the Royal Assent to Sir Tho. Shirley's Bill presently to be had.

Upon the reading, it was not approved, nor thought fit by the House to proceed-in that Manner, being, as was conceived, feme Impeachment to the Privilege of the House: The Petition itself is entered in the Journal, and is according to the Form of those Acts, that passed in the Time of Edw. the 4th: But the House resolved, that a Habeas Corpus be awarded, as before.

But the Warden of the Fleet denied to execute the Writ of Habeas Corpus, before the King's royal Assent was procured to the Bill, for the Security of Sympjon', and himself; and was committed to the Serjeant. 7 May, 1604.

The same Day an Act, for new Executions to be feed after the Parliament, when the Defendants, &c. was read a Third time, and passed.

and A Petition of several Merchants of London, on behalf of themselves, and others, trading to foreign Parts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners at the Beginning of the War reaped great Benefit by the extraordinary Care, then taken, to pre-lerve the Petitioners Ships from the Enemy, in their return Home from the West Indies, Straits, 6*by appointing a sufficient Number of clean Cruizers in the

A Petition of divers Clothiers of the County of cejier. in behalf of themselves, and divers others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that a Stop is put to the Exportation of white Cloths by the Commissioners of the Customs, upon the Expiration of a Patent, formerly granted, for Payment of a Duty upon the Exportation of such Cloths, to the great Impoverishment of the Petitioners, and many others, who have large Stocks upon their Hands, and cannot otherwise dispose of them: And praying Relief therein by such Ways, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion therein, to the House j

Sir,

I expect, you'l immediately fend me Word, when and where you'l meet me, to give me a Gentleman's Satisfaction. In the Interim

I am, Sir,

From Mr. Pralfs Your injured humble Servant,

Ordered\Th.it the Consideration of the said Lifts* and Accounts, be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to take into Consideration the State of the Navy of this Kingdom.

Supply* Mr. Conyers (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Forty thousand Men be employed in the Sea Service for the Year 1708, including Eight thousand Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pound a Man per Menjem, be allowed for maintaining the said 40,000 Men for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Twenty thousand Pounds, be allowed for the Ordinary of the Navy, for the Year 1708.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon* agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of several Merchants of that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by the Articles and Acts of Union, the Subjects of the united Kingdoms of England and Scotland should, after the ift of May 1707, have a free Trade to and from any Place within the united Kingdom; and the Petitioners having, before the said first of May, imported into Scotland divers Merchandizes, and paid the Duties there due, they did since import many of those Commodities into London, and other Parts of England, as by the Union they are advised, they might lawfully do; yet the Petitioners Commodities have been seized in and they have been

obliged to consent to appear, this present Michaelmas Term, in the Exchequer, to a Prosecution for the Value of the said Merchandizes, altho' several Commodities, of the Product of England, have been brought into-Scotland since the Union, without interruption, which before were prohibited: And praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and relieve the Petitioners therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee.

Ordered, That the Consideration thereof be referred to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Saturday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee of the whole House.

Ordered, That the Consideration of those Parts of her Majesty's Speech, which relate to the Union of the two Kingdoms, be referred to the said Committee of the whole Eloufe.

A Petition of several Merchants trading t6 Portugd, Italy, and Spain, on behalf of themselves, and other Merchants trading to those Parts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that a collusive Trade has been carried on in French Wines, and other Goods, for several Years past, notwithstanding the high Duties thereon; and this pernicious Trade has much increased since March last, when part of the Duty (£. 15 per Tun) determined, which makes the said Duties lower, than those on Portugal Wines, Spani/fi, and Italian: That French Prize Wines having this Advantage in point of Duty, great Quantities have been brought in, in foreign Ships, under pretence of legal Capture, though the Privateers, that took them, were fitted out by Consent of the Parties; and the Petitioners have reason to believe that great Quantities of French Goods will speedily be brought in by the like Collusion, if immediate Care be not taken to prevent it j and should these clandestine Practices be continued (the Goods being paid for in Money) would be a great Detriment to Navigation, and our Manufactures, aleffening of her Majesty's Customs, and the Impoverishment of the Nation: And praying such speedy Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

Cloth. and Owners of Lands, husbanded and employed for breeding and railing of Sheep and Wool, in the County of Wilts, in behalf of themselves, and many thousand others, concerned in the lame, was presented to the House, and read; felting forth, that an Act of Parliament, prohibiting the Exportation of white woollen Cloth, hath been lately put in Execution, which hath hundred the Exportation of such vast Quantities of the said Cloth, that the Clothiers, for want of Vent, cannot go on to buy Wool, and make the wonted Quantities; whereby the Price of Wool is much fallen, many of the Manufacturers turned out of their Employments, and the Wages of such, as have Work, are so lessened, as not to afford a competent Maintenance for themselves, and Families: And praying the House to apply such speedy Remedy for Redreis of their said Grievances, as shall be thought meet.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Landholders, Clothiers, Exporting and others, concerned in the Woollen Manufacture in the Cloth. Borough of Chippenham, and Places adjacent, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, by Force of several obsolete Laws, there has been lately a very great Stop put to the usual Exportation of rough white woollen Cloth, which has occasioned a great Fall in the Price of Wool, and Prejudice to that Part of the Woollen Manufactory; which Grievance, if not speedily remedied, will tend to the utter Destruction thereof, as well as many poor Families, formerly employed therein: And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises, by repealing those Laws, or otherwise, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of divers Clothiers in the County of Gloucester, is referred,

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that he had received a Letter from Mr. AJgill, in relation to the Book under Examination: And the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Sir, Fleet, November 26, 1707.

Observing your Votes, for enquiring into the Author of a Book, signed with my Name; I think it my Duty to prevent the House loss of Time in that Enquiry.

What I wrote, I am ready to produce and recognize, whenever the House pleal'e to admit me to answer it in my Place; and not doubting, but they will adjudge my Right to that Admission, I hope, they will pleal'e to relpite ar.y further Cenlure upon it till then.

To the Right honourable Sir,

John Smith, Esquire, Your most humble Servant,

A PETITION of John Graves, Col left or of her Majesty's Customs in the Bahama Islands, in the behalf of himself, and others, her Majesty's distressed Subjects in New Providence, and the rest of the Bahama Islands, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in February, 1705, the Petitioner presented a Memorial to most Members of this House, relating to the said Islands, and hath ever since constantly attended the Commissioners of Trade, and been by them examined; yet nothing has been further done in relation to the said Islands, tho' the Petitioner has had fresh Advice, that the French and Spaniards have lately twice plundered New ProvidenceAnd praying, that the de-

plorable Condition of the Inhabitants of the said Island

may be taken into Consideration, and speedy Relief granted unto them.

A Petition of Francis Anncjley, Esquire, was presented to the' House, and read; setting forth, that by an Act of Parliament, passed in the eleventh Year of the Reign of the late King William, all the forfeited Estates in Ireland were veiled in Trustees, to be sold, for Payment of the publick Debts; and every Person, having an Interest in those Forfeitures, were to enter their Claims by the i oth of Atiguft, 1707, and, in Default thereof, to be lor ever barred; and the Decrees of the said Trustees were to be final: That Robert , Esquire, entered his Claim for -J- Parts of the Lands of Tippenan, in the County of Kildare, as defeended from his Ancestors, and no Part of the Estate of the late King James-, and the Trustees, on hearing the said Claimant, decreed one Moiety to him, and dismist his Claim for the other Moiety, as being the Estate of the late King James: That the Petitioner, being Tenant to that Parc of the Lands (the Estate of the.late King James) and not doubting, but' that all-Purchases under the Sanction of an English Law should be safe, did bid, upon the

Cant, for the same £.600; the Agent for Mr. Dixon bidding only £. 595, and the Petitioner was declared the Purchaser, and had the said Moiety of 7 conveyed to him according to the Directions of the said Act: That the said Dixon brought his Ejectment for the Moiety, conveyed to the Petitioner, and had a Verdict and Judgment for all, except ten Acres thereof; and the said Judgment was affirmed, on a Writ of Error, in the Queen's Bench at Westminster, and, on another Writ of Error, affirmed in the Lords House; whereupon Dixon executed a Writ of Enquiry of Damages, and had a Verdict and Judgment for £.404 id. and also, upon an Habere facias , directed to his

Brother, Sir Kildare Burrowes, then Sheriff of the County of Kildare, turned the Petitioner out of Possession, not only of Tippenan, but also out of the ten Acres, and also of a considerable Part of the Petitioner's ancient Estate; and, by reason of Privilege of Parliament in Ireland, the Petitioner has not been able to get his own ancient Estate again: That the Petitioner has taken all the Steps he was advised to, which has been very expensive, even to the almost Ruin of himself, and Family: And praying, that the House will take his Calc into Consideration, and grant him such Relief therein, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same to the House;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that he had received another Letter from Mr.; which was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Sir, Fleet, December 9*, 1707.

I Hope the Call of the House (or the Report on my Book) will occasion the Judgment of the House, in calling me to my Place.

As an additional Help to obstruct that, I understand, there is a close Application made against me, as being guilty of a Breach of Trust in Purchaseof Lord Ken-mare's Estate in Ireland.

Against this I have no way of Defence, but by Letter to your Chair; which yet I should not have done, had not some Members been plealed to declaim, what Influence this hath had on them in the Matter of my Privilege, now depending; which I hope will plead my Pardon for the following Narrative.

Several Years since I was expelled the House of Commons in Ireland, on Pretence of the Book, now to be reported.

But about three Days after, the true Cause of this Vet. 15.

Expulsion appeared, by delivering a Petition into that House against me, for Breach of this Trust, which was heard at the Bar of the House; where there appeared against me four Witnesses, two Counsel at the Bar, and four Managers in the House, who bad been chief Sticklers for my Expulsion.

Against these I made my Defence alone, having my1 Innocence for my Counsel, and the Contradiction of their own Witnesses for my Evidence; and after the Petition had been exposed to be as ridiculous, as it was false, it was rejected.

Ever since that I have offered them to wave my Privilege to any Bill.

And having been lately shewn a Petition, prepared (as is said) for this House, 1 have pressed them to deliver it, flattering myself,' that the hearing of the Cause may prove some Diversion to the House for all the Trouble (so unwillingly) occasioned to them by.

To the Right honour- Sir,

able the Speaker of Your most humble Servant, the House of Commons. John AJgill.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take Exporting . into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to cloth.* whom the Petition of divers Clothiers in the County of Gloucester, complaining of a Stop being put to the

Exportation of white Cloth, and other Petitions, was referred.

And the Report was read, and the Resolutions thereupon; which Report, and Resolutions, are as follow; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, that, since the Month of May Iaft, the Officers of her Majesty's Customs have put a Stop to the Exportation of all white woollen Cloths, without making any Distinction between such, as are dressed, and such, as are not dressed: That this they had done by refuting to suffer any Entries to be made of any such Cloths, in order to Exportation; by giving general Notice, that they would seize upon any. such Cloths of the aforesaid Sorts, as should be shipt; and by seizing divers such Cloths, as aforesaid, as were shipt, or shipping, in order to be exported.

To all which the Commissioners of her Majesty's Customs have given to the Committee an Answer, in Writing, in these Words;

Whereas by an Act of Parliament, made in the 14th and 15th Hen. VIII. Cap. 3. it is enacted, that no Person or Persons convey or transport into any Parts beyond the Seas any manner of Cloths, or Worsteds,

made 27 Hen. VIII. Cap. 13. it is enacted, that no white Cloth, above the Value of £.4, or coloured Cloth, above the Value of £. 3,shall be exported to Parts beyond the Seas, unrowed, unbarbed, or unihorn, under the Penalty of forfeiting the said Cloths; which said Act is confirmed by another Act, made 33® Hen. VIII. Cap. 19. And whereas there was a Patent granted by the late King Charles the ad, bearing date at the 15th Day of April, in the 28th Year of his Reign, to Sir James Hayes and Sit Peter , their Executors and Administrators, being a Licence to export white woollen Cloths, with a Non-objl to the several Acts of Parliament for prohibiting the fame; which laid Patent was reserved to the Proprietors by a Clause in an Act of Parliament, made in the 11th and lath Years of the late King William 3d, Cap. aoth, intituled, "An Act for taking away the Duties upon the Woollen Manufactures, exported," there being then about Eight Years to come in the said Grant; but the said Patent expiring in or about the Month of May last, the said Acts of Prohibition are in full Force.

That the Committee think it their Duty to take Notice of a Mistake in this Answer: The same being given to the Committee, as the Officers of the Customs Answer to the Petition of the Gloucestershire Clothiers, before the Wiltshire Petitions were presented to this House, the Officers of the Customs could not reasonably allege the Statutes of the 27th and 33d Hen. VIII. which only prohibit the Exportation of Cloths of above a certain Value, unless they be barbed, rowed, and (horn; for the Complaint of the Glouceft Clothiers Petition is, that they are stopt from exporting their white Cloths, which are all barbed, rowed, and (horn.

That the said Officers of the Customs are also mistaken, in laying in their Answer, that the Penalty of the said Statutes is Forfeiture of the Cloth; for the said Statutes say, that the Exporter shall forfeit the Value of the Cloth; but the Cloth itself is not declared to be forfeited by any Statute, unless in that of the 33d Hen. VIII. which is only as to Cloths, which were not barbed, rowed, and lhorn.

That, upon Perusal of the Statutes, referred to by the Officers of the Customs in their said Answer, and of all other Statutes (as far as this Committee is informed) relating to the Exportation, or Limitation of Exportation, of woollen Cloths, if. appears to the Committee,

That it has been provided by the Statute, of the 7th of EHw. IV. Cap. 3d, that no Cloth should be exported, before it be fulled, and fully wrought.

Now what is meant by being fully wrought, is particularly explained by the 8th of Queen Eliz. Cap. 16th, viz. barbed, rowed, first-coursed, and (horn.

That by the Statute of 3 Hen. VII. Cap. 11, it is provided, that no Cloth be exported, before it be barbed, rowed, and (horn: Then follow some Exceptions, which relate not to the Subject of any of the Petitions, referred to the Committee.

By the 5th Hen. 8th, Cap. 3d, that white woollen Cloths, not exceeding each the Value of five Marks, may be exported, tho' not barbed, rowed, or (horn: So that hitherto there was not any Restraint from exporting of white woollen Cloths, which are barbed, rowed, and (horn; which is the Cafe* in which the Gltucester-shire Petition craves Relief.

That the Statute of the 14th and 15th Hen. 8th, Cap. 3d, referred to by the Officers of the Customs in their aforesaid Answer, is intituled, " Touching Worsted " Weavers of Yarmouth and Lynn The Preamble, and the whole Body of the Act, expressly relates to Stuffs, Cloth of Worsted, Sayes, and Stammills, only, and made only at Lynn, and Yarmouth; but the last Clause in the said Act is in these general Words: " That any Vol. 15.

" Person, who shall export any inanner of Cloth, or Worsteds; before the same be (horn, dyed, co oured,

and calendered, shall forfeit the Value, half to the Crown, and half to the Informer.*'

That the 27th Hen. VIII. Cap. 13th (to which the Officers of the Customs refer in their said Answer) takes Notice, that the Price of Wool is much increased since the aforesaid Statute, of the 5th of Hen. 8th; and therefore allows of the Exportation of white woollen Cloths* of £.4 Value, and under* and of coloured Cloths of £. 3 Value, and under, tho' not barbed, rowed, or (horn, but that the Exporter of white woollen Cloths, of above £. 4 Value, unless barbed, rowed, and shorn, and coloured Cloths, of above £. 3 Value, uless first barbed, rowed, and (horn, shall forfeit the Value of what he exports, half to the Crown, half to the Informer.

That the 33d Hen. VIII. Cap. 19. (which is also referred to in the said Custom-house Officers Answer) is pursuant to that of the 27th Hen. VIII. last mentioned; only it enacts further, that the Time of incurring the Penalty shall be upon shipping, in order to export, tho* there be no actual Exportation; and the Forfeiture is the Cloth, or the Value.

That the Statute, of the 14th and r 3 th Hen. 8 th, aforementioned, being temporary, was continued in the 21 Hen.

8th; afterwards it expired, and was again revived, ind perpetuated, by the Statute of 26. 8th, Cap. 16.

And the last Clause thereof, already recited, is thelole Foundation (as far as appears to this Committee) upon which the Officers of the Customs can any ways pretend to hinder the Exportation of such white woollenCloths, as are barbed, rowed, and shorn; which is the same of the Gloucestershire Petitioners, whose Cloths are stopt by virtue of the last Clause of the said Statute, of the 14th and 15th Hen. VIII. only for not being dyed; which Clause fays, that any Person, who shall export any manner of Cloth, or Worsted, before the same be shorn, dyed* coloured, and calendered, shall forfeit the Value, tec.

That the Committee think it their Duty to represent* that they very much doubt, whether the said Clause ought to be construdd to extend in general to woollen Cloths i 1 ft. For that the Title, as well as Preamble, and Body, of the Act do shew, that the same was made particularly as to Cloth of Worsted, and Stuffs, tec. as the Manufactures of Lynn and Yarmouth:

2dly, Because the Words of the said last Clause of the said Act, prohibiting Exportation, are, " unless, or " before, the same be first lhorn, dyed, coloured, and " calendered;" which Word " calendered" being joined to the preceding Words by the Copulative " and, " if this Statute be interpreted to relate to woollen Cloth in general, there appears as good a Reason for Hopping the Exportation of woollen Cloth, for not being calendered* as for not being dyed; which cannot be; because it is well known, that Stuffs and Worsteds are calendered* but woollen Cloth is never calendered:

3dly, All the other Acts of the same King's Reign* peruled by the Committee, being Four or Five in Number, relating to the Exportation, or Limitation of the Export of white Cloths, do always use the Expression of woollen Cloths; but the Expression in this Clause, of the 14th and 15th Hen. 8th, is Cloth and Worsteds; which* it is conceived, may relate only to another Sort of Cloth, made at Lynn, and Yand not to woollen Cloths: And this the Committee the rather conceive, because the Body of the same Act mentions particularly Cloth of Worsted, Sayes, tec. but doth no where mention woollen Cloth; and it appears, there was a Manufacture called Cloth of Worsted, otherwise called Cloth Rash, and Cloth Serge, which were all one and the same Thing:

Lastly, The Acts of the 17th and 33d Hen. 8th (both which were made after the perpetuating of that of the 14th and 15th of the same King) which provide, that white woollen Cloths of £. 4 Value, and under, may be exported* tho' not barbed, rowed, or lhorn, but

But, notwithstanding all the aforementioned Statutes, it appears to the Committece, that white woollen Cloths from Wiltshire, rough, and not barbed, rowed, or (horn, as well as the Gloucestershire white woollen Cloths, barbed, rowed, and (horn, have been allowed to be exported ever since the Beginning of the Reign of Queen Eliz. or longer, by Licence of Patentees of the Crown, the Exporters paying a Consideration.

That by the Act, of the 8th of Queen Eliz. Cap. 16. (which was two Years after granting the said Patent to the Hambrough Company) it is enacted, that, for Relief and Employment of Multitudes of the Queen's Subjects, using the Art and Labour of Cloth-working, that for every nine Cloths unwrought, hereafter to be exported, contrary to any of the Statutes now in being, by Force of any Licence, hereafter to be granted, one Cloth, of the same Size, and Goodness, shall be exported by the same Person, ready wrought, and dressed, that is to say, rowed, barbed, first coursed, and (horn, und^r Pain of forfeiting £. 10 for every Nine Cloths; with a Proviso, that the said tenth Cloth, ready wrought, shall not be accounted one of the Number licensed, but that such Person, as shall have such Licence, may transport, according to such Licence, the full Number of Cloths unwrought, mentioned in the same Licence, over and above the Number of the 10th Cloth, which the y re compelled to export by this Statute; and a Proviso, that no Licence shall extend to Kentish or Suffolk Cloth.

And it appeared to the Committee, that it is upon this Point alone, that the Legality, or Illegality, of flopping the Cloths of the Wiltshire Petitioners, offered to be exported by the Hamborough Company, or their Order, doth depend.

And it further appeared to the Committee, that in the 28th of Charles the 2d, another Patent was granted to Sir James Hayes and Sir Peter Apjley, in Trust for the Countess of Portland, to licenso the Exportation of all manner of woollen Cloths, white as well as coloured, tho' not barbed, rowed, (horn, or dressed, without Limitation as to Price, or Number, and this for 31 Years, with Power to agree and compound, as they could, with Merchant, or Exporter, for the Quantum to be paid for the Licence; a Non-objlante to all Acts to the contrary; with an Exception to Kentish and Suffolk Cloth, and a Prohibition for exporting, without Licence from the said Patentees, and a Reservation to the Crown of all Customs due.

That the Hamborough Company, who before this Patent did export the Wiltshire Cloths according to their own limited Patent, did agree to pay 3 s. 4 per Cloth to the said new Patentees, for their Licence for such woollen Cloths, as by their own limited Patent they could not export; but that Disputes arising about the Number of Cloths, of this and that Quality, between the Company and the Patentees, it was agreed, that the Hamborough Company should pay to the Patentees, for their Licence of Exportation, 1 s. 4 d. per Cloth for every Cloth, exported by the said Company, of the 30,000 Cloths, limited by this Grant; but all other Exporters of white Cloths paid 5 s.per Cloth to the said Patentees, for their Licence.

That the Hamborough Company making use of the Licence of the said Patentees, upon Exportation of the Wiltshire white rough Cloths, as did also all other Exporters of white Cloths, already dressed, until the Expiration of the said Patent, whiefe ended in or about May last, the Officers of the Customs have (rom thenceforward refilled to admit of the Exportation of the white Wiltshire Roughs in such manner, as if the Hamborough Company's Power of exporting such Cloths had depended upon the Licences', which they formerly took under the Patent, which is expired.

That it was further alleged by the said Dyers Petition, that, whilst the aforesaid Duties were paid upon Exportation of white Cloths, dressed, and undressed, there was hevertheless asufficient Exportation of such Cloths; for that foreign Merchants, to whom they were exported into foreign Parts, could, by the Cheapnefe of Dying Materials, and of Labour in dressing and dying the said Cloths, in their own Countries, employ their Poor, and then fell the said Cloths, totally manufactured, in the proper Markets (being the same Markets used by our own Merchants) as cheap, or cheaper, than our own Merchants could fell the same Cloths in the same Markets, when totally manufactured; so that the Duty, paid upon Export of our white Cloths, did not hinder a sufficient Vent for them; but, if there be a free Exportation of white Cloths rough, and undressed, without paying some Duty, the Loss to the Nation in Labour, as to the WiltshireCloths, is about I2r. 6d. in the Article

of dressing, if rowed in the Gigg-mill, but, if dressed fully, is more; besides the Expence of Materials for dying, and Labour in dying, and packing, and the like.

That the last Dressing of a Long Cloth

(which comes to London barbed, rowed, and shorn) together with Materials for dying, and Labour in dressing,. dying, pressing, packing, and the like, is from 30 to £.3. That near one half thereof is Labour; but that this Calculation is made as to dying in Grain, and the most chargeable Colours.

That we have now a Trade to with our own Cloths, fully manufactured, and dyed, and our Ships return with naval Stores, and our Seamen, and Navigation, is increased thereby; but, if we send out our Cloths undressed, and undyed, the Dutch will dress and dye them, and be the Carriers to , as well as other Parts, and we lose the Advantage of returning vt'xthRuffia Goods, as well as lose so much of the Manufacture of our own.

That the Lose, on Exportation of the fine shire Cloths undressed, and undyed, was represented to be much greater, namely, Cent, per Cent, but that was not taken notice of by the Committee, because not before them by any Order of Reference from the House.

That several Merchants appeared, to support the Petition of the Dyers, and others; and alleged, that the French have got from us a great Part of our Trade in the fine Sort of Cloths: That the Dutch, and People of Flanders, are advanced a great way in the Trade of Medleys: That the Glocester and Cloths being of

a coarser Sort, and made of our own Wool, it is our ln-terest to manufacture them totally, and dye them, at home; and we may find sufficient Vent for them folly manufactured, for that no other Country can fornish those Cloths, but ourselves; and that, by exporting the IViltshire Cloths rough, and undyed, we lose £.15 Cent, and by exporting the Gloucestershire dress'd white Cloths, undyed, we lose £. 10 per Cent, per Cloth: That Dying Materials, and Labour, are cheaper in,

than here; and that, if, they buy our Cloths white, they will, when they have dyed them in their own Country, undersell us in Turkey, and other Markets, unless some Duty be paid upon Exportation of the Cloths undressed, and white: That 5 s.paid here upon each Cloth exported undressed, or white, is more significant towards preventing the Mischiefs apprehended, as the consequence of a free Export, than if no Duty were paid upon Dying Materials.

All, that appeared at the Committee, to support the Petition of the Dyers, and the Merchants, did all agree, that, if the IViltshire white rough Cloths, and the Gloucestershire white.dressed Cloths, had been still exported, paying first 5J. per Cloth, as the Gloucestershire Cloths Voi. U.

did pay till May last, they should all have been satisfied; and thought, they had no Reason to complain; and that our own Merchants would then think, they had reasonable Encouragement to buy, dress, and dye, our Cloths here, and export them to foreign Markets totally manufactured.

That, in Answer to all the before-mentioned Allegations, the Gloucestershire Clothiers do say, that they conceive, there is no Law to hinder the Exportation of their white woollen Cloths, they being barbed, rowed, and shorn, which, according to the Letter of the Statutes, is as much as to fey, fully manufactured: That the Expence of Labour upon each of their Cloths, in barbing, rowing, and sheering, if rowed with the Gigg-mill, is from 15 to 20 s.in each Cloth, and, if rowed by Hand* 23 or 2 6s.per Cloth: That many of their Cloths are used abroad white, without dying.

That one Gloucestershire Clothier hath now here at London £. 2,000 worth of that Country white Cloths; barbed, rowed, and shorn, of which he cannot fell one* because of the Stop put upon Exportation:

That another has 200 Cloths of the same Sort, manufactured as aforesaid, which he cannot export, because the Officers of the Customs told him, they would not enter them, and others, that they would be seised:

That the Hollanders have, with repeated Instances, made Demand of Quantities of our white Cloths, declaring, that, if they be not speedily supplied, they will seek ell'ewhere.

The IViltshire Clothiers, and several of the Hamhrough Company, who deal with them, do likewise fey, in Answer to the Officers of the Customs, and to the Dyers, and others, that they conceive, that the Hamborough Company's Patent doth authorize the Exportation of the IViltshire rough white Cloths, as ufoally:

That one Trader has now 1,000 Pieces of white Wiltshire woollen Cloths, which he has in vain fought In' export for several Months together, in order to fornish his Correspondent, who has contracted to cloath several Danish Regiments; and that his Correspondent has lately sent him Notice, that he cannot be delayed any longer, and, if not speedily supplied from hence, will fend for his Quantity to Silesia:

That Silesia increascs upon us in making and vending the coarle Sort of white Cloths rough, which will be bought abroad instead of those of Wiltshire, unlefe these be exported rough, and undyed:

That another has 200 white Wiltshire rough Cloths lying by him, in order to export, but is not permitted to enter them: That this Sort of Cloths will quickly be spoiled by lying, as they are: That the Clothiers can fell no more:

That the Exportation of the Witshire white rough Cloths by the Hamborough Company is much diminished of late, and the Use of such Cloths, made in Silesia, does daily increase; and that we are in danger of losing that Part of our Trade to Hamborough.

And the Clothiers of both the aforesaid Counties do aver, that the Stop upon the Exportation, since the first , of May last, has been £. 20,000 Damage to the Clothing Trade.

That it appeared to the Committee, that the Damage had been very great: That there is almost a total Stop to the making of the aforesaid Sort of white Cloths in Willshire and Gloucestershire, and (as a Consequence thereof) of the Sale of Wool, and of Employment of the Poor.

- That the better Sort of Wool in the County of Gleu-cester is fallen, in nine Years last past, from £. 1 s.

-to 13 s.per Tod, which is 28 pound Weight, and the common Field Wool from £.1 to its. or thereabouts; and that since the Stop of Exportation, from May last, it is fallen 2s. per Tod.

That the Hamborough Company carry thither a greater Number than of undressed Cloths, although the Statute of 6* Queen Eliz. aforementioned, which seems to be a Regulation, or Restraint, upon their Patent, requires only, that, for nine of the rough white undressed Cloths, one Cloth, fully manufactured, should be by them exported.

That the Hollanders have for a long Time also refused to allow of any of our plain dyed Cloths (other than Medleys, which are all dyed in the Wool) to be imported there.

So that the Clothier can find no Vent for his rough white, or dressed white, Cloths (since the aforesaid Stop) of which so very great a Quantity lie upon their Hands, already brought to London, as well as remaining in the Country, that a Multitude of substantial Clothiers must probably break forthwith, and many Families starve, unlets they be very speedily relieved against the present Stop of exporting their Cloths.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners, the Clothiers, have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Nation will be very great Sufferers, unless some very speedy Remedy' be found, to take off the Stop, which is at present put to the great Number of Cloths, ready to be shipt off, and exported.

The ad Resolution being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That the Nation will be very great Sufferers, unless some very speedy Remedy be found, to take off the Stop, which is at present put to the great Number of Cloths, ready to be shipt off, and exported.

That the Committee, having examined into the Allegations, contained in the said Petition, do find, that by an Act of Parliament, made in the nth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William, all the Estates in Ireland, forfeited for the late Rebellion, as also the

Estate of the late King James, were veiled in certain Trustees, in the said Act named, to be sold, for the Payment of the publick Debts.

That by the said Act it was enacted, That every Person, having any Estate orlnterest in the said Forfeitures, or Estate of the late King James, were to enter their Claims with the said Trustees on or before the loth of August, 1700, and, for Default of such Entry, their Estates and Interest were for ever to be debarred, and without Remedy; and the Decrees of the said Trustees were thereupon to be final, and to be obeyed by all Persons; and, after Determination of the Claims, the Trustees were impowered to fell by Cant the said Estates, so veiled iu them, and to convey the same to the best 20

Bidder; the PilrChafer to hold the fame, dischlrged of all Claims and Demands, except such, as were allowed by the Trustees; as appears by the said Act.

That on or about the 7th Day of August, 1700, Robert Dixon, Esquire, did enter his Claim before the said Trustees for \Parts of the Lands of in the County of Kildare, in the said Kingdom, as defeended from his Ancestors, and that the same was no Part of the lata King James' Estate; and, upon hearing the said Claim before the said Trustees, they did decree one Moiety to the Claimant Dixon, and dilmified his Claim for the other Moiety, as being the Estate of the late King James; as appeared by an attested Copy of a Decree by the said Trustees, dated the 5th of September, 1700, which was produced, and read to the Committee, and proved to be a true Copy of the original Decree by Thomas George.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that the Petitioner before the passing the said Act was Tenant to the said Moiety of the Lands of and paid Rent

of October, in the sixth Year of her Majesty's Reign, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Conservators of the River Tone, appointed by an Act of Parliament, of the 10th and nth 3", for making and keeping the said River navigable from Bridgwater to Taunton, have effected the Navigation from Ham Mills to the Town of Taunton, which hath proved a considerable Advantage to the said Town, and Places adjacent; yet the good Intents of the said Act are not likely to be obtained, unless there be some Increase of Toll at a Place called Knaps Bridge, below which Place it will be necessary to erect an half Lock, or Turnpike, and to scour a Shoal, which will be very expensive: That the Petitioners are well allured, the granting some Increase of Toll at Knapps Bridge will enable the Conservators to perfect the Navigation from Bridgwater to Ham Mills, which will tend to a publick Good: That the Petitioners therefore offer the Conservators same to the House, for fufch Relief, as shall be thought meet.

A Petition of several of the Members, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the Corporation and Town of Taunton, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read j setting forth, that several Persons of Taunton, known by the Name of Conservators, did,

in the 10th and nth Years of the Reign of the late King William (under some plausible Pretences) get an Act of Parliament, for making the River Tone navigable from Bridgwater to Taunton, paying a Toll of per Weigh on Coals, and id. per Ton, for all other Goods, at a Place called Coal Harbour, below Knap Bridge, and 4s. per Weigh, and is. per Ton, at the first Lock above Coal Harbour i That the said Conservators do receive the said full Duty at Knap Bridge, but not one fourth Part at the said Lock 1 so that the Traders at Coal Harbour, and Ham Mills, pay their full Toll, and the Traders at Taunton pay very little; by which Means they will in Time ruin the Traders at Coal Harbour and Ham Mills, and so monopolize the Trade into their own Hands, and make the Petitioners pay for their Coals, and Salt, and other Goods, at the Will oif the said Conservators: That-the Petitioners have always been well served with Coals and Salt, from Coal Harbour, at very reasonable Rates, to which Place the said River was ever navigable, and Taunton, and Country adjacent, are generally supplied with Coals by Land Carriage, the said Conservators neglecting to make the said River navigable from Bridgwater to Taunton; yet (out of some fimfter Ends) have petitioned the House to have a further Toll, payable below Coal Harbour 1 which, if granted, will be a great Grievance to all the Inhabitants of Taunton: And praying, that there may be it further Toll granted, than what is already laid by Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be brought in.

As also an Account of all such Commissions, as have been gramed to Privateers for two Years last past, and their Securities in £.1,500 Penalties; which is marked C.

Upon which the Merchants did observe, that many of the Persons, therein named as Securities, were insolvent, or Persons of little or no Worth, and were not prol'e-cuted.

That the Merchants, in Proof of a collusive Trade, did produce several Instances of Ships, taken under Pretence of legal Capture, when in truth the Privateers, that took them, were fitted out by the Consent of the Parties: To which Facts they called

Mr. John Glover', who delivered in a List of Ships, which he informed the Committee the same were taken by Collusion; which Paper is marked D: And likewise informed the Committee, that two of the said Ships, called by the Names of the Pearle, and

Rapbell, wherein he had a 16th Part, were taken by the Diligence Privateer, about three Years since, collusively, and by the Consent of the Parties concerned.

And as to the Ship E uMargaretta, taken by the Wellcome Gaily, John Watler Commander;

Mr. George Meter, If;, Solicitor of her Majesty's Customs, informed the Committee, that about three Years since the same was seized by Order of the Commissioners of the Customs, and brought to a Trial in the Exchequer, where a Verdict pafl'ed for the Queen.

That the said Mr. Metcalf did likewise deliver to the Committee an Account of the Trial of the Ship, called the Prince Charles, Martin Peterson Commander, taken by the HannikallPrivateer, Captain fbmpfon Commander; by which it appears, the same was a collusive Capture: Which Paper is marked E. And the Record was also produced, on which the Verdict was entered for the Queen.

And Mr. Charles Carcajfe, Under Secretary to the Commissioners of the Customs, laid before the Committee the Commissioners Report to the Lord Treasurer, relating to collusive Captures, marked F.

That by the Evidence of Captain John Tkompfon,

John Huggins, Esquire, and the said Mr. Metcalf, the Ship, called the Stadt,o{ Rotterdam, taken by the

garettaPrivateer, Captain Pigram Commander, it appeared, that the said Ship was brought in as Prize, and condemned in the Court of Admiralty, and afterwards prosecuted. by one Mr. Scott in the Court of Exchequer, and found to be a collusive Capture.

Captures.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that the Ship, called the Liberty, laden with French Wines, to the Value of £. 5,000, taken by a small Fiftier Boat, called the May Flower, Captain Edward Slaughter Commander, was a collusive Capture.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that a Duty of £.15 per Tun on all French Prize Wines, did determine in March last.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee

came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Merchants have fully made out the several Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,;

That the preserving the Portugal Trade is of the utmost Concern to this Nation, being at present the greatest Mart for Vent of our Woollen Manufactures, Corn,

Fish, and other British Commodities.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there was a considerable collusive Trade in French Prize Wines, carried on before, and more increased since, the falling of the £. 15 per Tun.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That except effectual Provision be made, to prevent the like Practices, with relation to the collusive Trade of bringing in French Wines, as if they were Prize Wines, it will not only be a great Discouragement to the gal Trade and Traders, but endanger the intire Loss thereof.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, the three last were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Papers, referred to by the Report, are bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill upon the last Resolution; and that Sir IVm. Ashurst, Lord ningsby, Mr. Conyers, Sir Gilbert Heathcot, and Mr. Ward, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Declaratio facta ex parte Ducis Ebor. contra delibera-tionem predicti Prolocutoris. 26.

Item, the Friday, the 15th Day of February, it was opened and declared to the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, being in the Parliament Chamber, by the Counsel of the Duke of York, That where Thomas Thorp, the Monday, the Day of the Month of the

Year of the Reign of King Henry the 6th the 31st, came to the Place of the Bishop of Durham, and thence and there to be and bear away certain Goods and Chattles of the said Duke's, against his Will and Licence; and thereupon the same Duke tamed, and took an Action by Will, in Michaelmas Term last past, against the said Thomas, in the Court of Exchequer, according to the Privilege of the same Court, for so much that the same Thomas was one of the Court, by which Privilege he ought to be enpleted in that Court of Exchequer in such Cases, and in none other Court: To the which Bill the said Thomas wilfully appeared, and had divers

Days to imparle, at his Request and Desire; and to the said Bill and Action answered, and pleted Not guilty: Whereupon there was awarded in the said Exchequer a Venire facias to the Sheriff of , retornable in the said Exchequer; and there by the Jury, that passed between the said Duke and the said Thomas, it was found, that the same Thomas was guilty of the Trespass contained in the said Bill; and the same Jury assefited the Vot. 15.

Damages to the said Duke, for the said Trespass, to Privilege of a M.li. and for his Costs/. 10, and thereupon Judgment was given in the said Exchequer, and the said according to the Course of Law, was committed to the Fleet, for the Fine belonging to the King in that behalf:

And thereupon it was prayed humbly on behalf of the said Duke, that it should like their good Lord ships, considering, that the said Trespass was done and committed by the said Thomas since the Beginning of this present Parliament, and also, the said Bill and Action were take and tamed, and by Process of Law Judgment thereupon given against the said Thomas, in time of Vacation of the same Parliament, and not in Parliament time; and also, that, if the said Thomas should be released by Privilege of Parliament, or the Time, that the said Duke be satisfied of the said Damages, and Costs, the same Duke should be without Remedy in that behalf; that the said Thomas, according to the Law, be kept in Ward to the Time that he hath fully content and satisfied the said Duke of his said Damages, and Costs: The Lords Spiritual and Temporal, not intending to impech or hurt the Liberties and Privileges of them, that were Commons for the said Commonalties of this Land to this present Parliament, but legally, after the Course of Law, to minister Justice, and to have knowledge, what the Law will wey in that behalf, opened and declared to the Justices the Premisses, and axed of them, whether the said Thomas ought to be delivered from Prison by force and virtue of the Privilege of Parliament, or not: To the which Question the Chief Justice, in the Name of all the Justices, after fadd Communication, and mature Deliberation, had among them, answered, and said, that they ought not to anfiver to that Question; for it hath not yet been used aforetime, that the Justices should at any time determine the Privilege of this high Court of Parliament; for it is so high, and so mighty in this Nature, that it may make Law, and that, that is Law, it may make no Law; and the Determination of that Privilege belongeth to the Lords

of the Parliament, and not to the Justices: But as for

/ t #

Declaration of Proceeding in the lower Courts in such Cases, as Writs of Supersedeas of Privileges of Parliament be brought, and delivered; the said Chief Justice said, there be many and divers Supersedeas of Privilege of Parliament brought into the Courts, but there is no general Supersedeas brought, to lurceafe all Procelies; for, if there should be, it should seem, that this high Court of Parliament, that ministreth all Justice and Equity, should lett the Process of the common Law; so it should put the Parties Complainant without any Remedy, for so much as Actions at common Law be not determinable in this high Court of Parliament; and if any Person, that is a Member of this high Court of Parliament, be arrested in such Cases, as be not for Treason, or Felony, or Surety of the Pleas, or for a Condemnation had before the Parliament, it is used, that all such Persons should be released of such Arrests, and make an Attorney, so that they may have their Freedom and Liberty, freely to entend upon the Parliament.

After which Answer, and Declaration, it was throughly agreed, afiented, and concluded, by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, that the said Thomas, according to the Law, should remain dill in Prison for the Caules abovesaid, the Privilege of the Parliament, or that the same Thomas was Speaker of the Parliament, notwithstanding; and that the PremifiTes should be opened and declared to them,♦that were comen for the Commons of this Land, and that they should be charged and commanded in the King's Name, that they, with all goodly Hade and Speed, proceed to the Election of another Speaker.

The which Premisses, for as much as they were Matters in Law, by the Commandment of the Lords were opened and declared to the Commons by the Mouth of Walter Moyle, one of the King's Serjeants at Law', in the Presence of the Bishop ot Ely, accompanied with other Lords in notable Number; and there it was charged and commanded to the said Commons by the said Bishop

That this was the same of Thomas Thorpe: And there are several other Precedents in the Time of Hen. VI. and Edw. IV. where Members, arrested, and taken in Execution, fating the Parliament, were obliged to procure Acts of Parliament for their Enlargement; viz.

William Lark, menial Servant, an Attendant on Wm. Milrede, one of the Citizens of London for the Parliament of 8° Hen. VI. was arrested at whilst attend-

ing the re on his Master, fitting the Parliament; and, upon the Petition of the Commons, there was a special Act of Parliament for his Enlargement. Rot. Parl. 8 Hen. VI N°. 57.

That there was a like Act of Parliament for the Enlargement of Walter Clark, Burgess of Chippenham, in Wiltshire. Rot. Parl. 39 Hen. VI. N\ 9.

Another for William Hyde, Burgefle of Chippenham. Rot. Parl. 14 Edw. IV. N°. 55.

All which were arrested, and taken in Execution, during the Sessions of Parliament, and their Attendance on this House, yet released by Special Acts of Parliament.

But in the Time of Henry the 8 th the House proceeded in another Manner; as in the same of who, being arrested, during the Parliament 34 Hen. VIII. was let at Liberty by the Serjeant; and the Sheriff's of London, refuting to deliver him, were lent to the Tower. Holinshed, p. 1582.

Another Precedent, that the Committee considered, was the same of diamond, 3^ Hen. VIII. as it is reported by my Lord Dyer, as follows:

35 Hen. VIII. Freziinard was arrested upon an Exigent, at the Suit of Skewis;and a Writ of Privilege of Parliament issuing forth to diamond. Sheriff of Cornwall, setting forth, that Frewinardwas a Burgefle, and declaring the Custom of the Privilege of Parliament, the Sheriff* set him at Liberty: Upon this the Executors of Skewis brought an Action against diamond, the Sheriff?: To this he demurred; and upon this Demurrer these three Points were argued:

1 ft. Whether Privilege be grantable in this Cafe, where a Burgefle of Parliament is arrested in an Exigent:

2dly, Whether, if Privilege be grantable, the Party, so set at Liberty, shall be for ever discharged from the Execution of the Plaintiff, or only during the Parliament:

3dly, Admitting, that Privilege is not allowable in this Cafe, whether the Writ and Warrant of the King, proceeding from Parliament, be not a sufficient Excule and Discharge for the Sheriff against the Plaintiff.

For the first it was alleged, that, for as much as the King, and the whole Realm, had an Interest in the Body of every one of the said Members, the private Interest of every particular Man ought not to be regarded; for it is a Maxim, Quod majus dignum trahit ad fe minus dig-num; as was adjudged in the same in 6" Edw. IV. That if a Man was condemned in a Trespass, or Redifeifine, and in Execution for a Fine to the King, if he was outlawed of Felony, his Body should not be imprisoned at the Suit of the Party, because the King had an Interest in his Body.

And it is concluded, that the Court of Parliament is the highest Court, and has more Privileges, than any other Court of the Realm:

And that in every Cafe, without any Exception, every Burgefle is privileged against Arrests at the Suit of any Subject: And this same is the better, for as much as the Execution was sued during the Parliament; in which same the Plaintiff was at Liberty to sue Execution of his Body, or of his Lands or Goods: And also, every Privilege is by Prescription, and every Prescription that is for the Advantage of the Common Weale, is good, although it be prejudicial to any private Person.

Therefore in the Time of Edw. IV. it was held a good Prescription to dig in the Ground of any Man near the Sea, to make Bulwarks against the King's Enemies.
