My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I AM very well pleased with the Occasion of my coming hither at this Time, and desirous to take this Opportunity of expressing to you the Satisfaction I have in seeing so good a Progress made in the publick Business.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I am extremely sensible of the Readiness and Affection, with which you have provided so considerable a Part of the Supplies.

As I am fully persuaded, it must needs give the greatest Satisfaction to all our Allies, so I look upon it as a sure Pledge of your being disposed to make good those hearty Assurances, which you gave me in the Beginning of the Session.

I told you at the opening of this Parliament, that I did hope, you would look upon the Services, relating to Spain, Portugal, and the Army under the Command of

the Duke of Savoy, to be of so much Importance in the Prosecution of this War, that they might deserve an Augmentation; which I cannot but think will be of the greatest Use to the common Cause, both with regard, to those particular Services, and to the putting ourselves in a Condition to improve such favourable Opportunities, as may arise in the ensuing Year.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I shall only add, that, as nothing is more essential to my own Quiet, and the Happiness of all my good Subjects, than the bringing this War to a lafe and honourable Conclusion; so I must think myself obliged to look upon all those, who are willing and desirous to support me in it, for attaining that End, as the most proper Objects of my Favour and Encouragement.

I cannot conclude, without once more recommending

Resolved, That this House will, upon , the Union with

Thirteenth Day of January next, resolve itself into a Scotland. Committee of the whole House, to consider further of those Parts of her Majesty's Speech, which relate to the Union of the two Kingdoms.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of Benjamin Joules was presented to the Portsmouth House, and read; setting forth, that, by Order of the Harbonr. Navy Board, 23 Jan. 1702, it was referred to Samuel Atkinson, Esquire, to survey Porlfmouth Harbour; who 7th Febr. 1702, reported, that the Bank, called the Middle Bank, and the Shoal on Gosport Side of the Harbour, was very much increased; and his Opinion was, that the Queen should employ Vessels, and Men, to remove the said Shoals, which would be a great Advantage to the Harbour; and upon a subsequent Survey of the said Harbour, Henry Greenhill, Esquire, reported the 27th March, 1703, to the like Purpose; adding, that by taking Ballad from Block-house Point, it had wasted that Point 20 Yards, by which means a Capftern, set up for a Boom a-thwart the Harbour, to prevent an Enemy's coming in, was rendered unserviceable: That, upon these Reports, the Commissioners of the Navy published, that they would contract with any Person, to serve her Majesty's Ships there with Ballast, but uot from Block-house Point; That ever since the 6 th of Sept.

1703, the Petitioner, by Contract, hath served the Navy there with Ballast from oft his own Ground; That the Petitioner proposes to remove the said Shoals out of the said Harbour, at his own Charges, provided (as the Report of Mr. Atkinson faith) it is fitting for Ballast, but if not, then tobe allowed nine Pence pfr Ton, which is 4 d. per Ton cheaper, than the Queen paid for the same Work at Chatham Harbour; and the Petitioner be obliged sufficiently to supply both Men of War, and Merchant Ships, with Ballast, in such Time after Notice, as to be no Prejudice to their Service; and that the Boys, employed in the Ballast Work, after they have served one Half of their Time, shall, if Occasion be, serve the other Half in any of her Majesty's Ships of War; And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for settling a Method at Gosport, near Portsmouth Harbour, for the better ballasting her Majesty's Men of War, and other Ships and Vessels, and also for removing and preventing, the Shoals within the said Harbour.

12 j. 5 d.as appeared to the Committee by a Report of the said Trustees to this House in 1704.

Great Bedwin Mr. Qompton reported from the Committee of Pri-Elettion. vileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Borough of Great Bedwin, in the County of Wilts, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were . read, and are as follow;

Upon the Petition of Nicholas Esquire,

complaining of an undue Election and Return of Tracey Pauncefort, Esquire, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Great Bedwin, in the County of Wilts:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Freeholders, and the Inhabitants of ancient Burgage Messuages.

That, upon the Poll, the Numbers were.

For the Sitting Member - - 68:

For Mr. Edward Pauncefort - 29:

For the Petitioner - - - - 22.

But the Petitioner's Counsel infilled, that several, who had voted for the Sitting Member, had no Rightj and that all the Sitting Member's Votes were gained by Bribery and Corruption; and that Mr. Edward Pauncefort' % Votes were gained in the same Manner, and with a Design to prevent any Petition.

A. 1707.

That, as to the Sitting Member's unqualified Votes, it was admitted, that Eight, viz. Jof. Bally, Edw. Batt, John Sindall, Tho. Mundy, John Collins, Anth. Collins, John King, and John Sheppard, who voted for the Sitting Member, did live in Houses crofted upon new Foundations:

And that Isaac Gilbert, who voted for Mr. Edward Pauncefort, was under the like Disqualification.

That, as to the Bribery, several Witnesses were called; viz.

Richard Bartholomew; who said, he was called out of his Bed on Sunday Night, the 23d of Novem. to go to the King's Head, kept by Mundy, and, when he

came, he found many of his Neighbours there; and it was proposed to set their Hands to a Writing, to join in the Election of Mr. Tracy PauncefortThat £.3 a Man was offered ;. but (ome infilled to have 4, but it was answered that £. 3 was a pretty deal of Money for the Time this Parliament was like to continue j and so £. 3 a Man was agreed to:

That Captain Hall and Mr. Hall were in a Room above Stairs; and several Persons, who were called, went up to them, among whom were Richard Earley, junior. Rich. Cope, and John; who owned, they

received Money above Stairs; and that William and Edward Tidcombe, who were two of the Bar-

gain-makers, went up, and Simon Payne; who owned, that he received Money for his Father-in-law, Richard Burger: But of his own Knowlege he could give no Account of their receiving any Money, he Haying below Stairs.

He further said, there were several Voters below Stairs, who drank there, as well as himself; and that he did not pay, nor fee any body else pay.

He laid further, that the Sitting Member had lent him, and one Bushell, half a Guinea a-piece; and told him, that, if he, the said Bartholomew, would vote for him, it should not be demanded; but not voting for him, he had been threatened, if he did not pay it.

William Nalder, Edward John Nutley,

Richard Talmage, Richard Langfeild, John Spreadberry,

John Talmage, and James Bezant, being severally examined, gave an Account, that they were sent for on the 23d Day of November, between Two and Three a Clock at Night, to Mundy's House, and were called up Stairs, and a Writing was offered them to sign, to chuse Mr. Tracey Pauncefort: That there was in the Room the two Halls (mentioned by BartholomeJohn Long, and a Person, whose Name they did not know: That they received two Guineas, and 17 in Silver, from this nameless Person; and that, when they received their Money, they saw a great Sum of Money on the Table, divided into Parcels. One of these Witnesses, viz. Richard Talmage, voted for Mr.; of the Seven

others, fix voted for the Sitting Member, and one for Mr. Edward Pauncefort; but most of them deplared, they would have voted for Mr. Pollexfen, if they had not had the Money. And Bezant laid, there were about Threescore called up into this Room, one by one; but said, that some, that were called of, voted for Mr. Pollexfen.

And then the Petitioner's Counsel produced a Note under the Sitting Member's Hand, of the Date, and in the Words, following:

November 26th, 1707. I promise to pay to Mr.

Bushell, or Order, the Sum, of Forty-nine Pounds, on " demand: Value received. T. ."

A Message from the Lords, by the Lord Chief Baron Ward anc! Mr. Baron Smith:

Mr. Speaker,

We are commanded by the Lords to acquaint this House, that the Lords have agreed upon an Address, to be presented to her Majesty; to which they desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

And then the said Address was twice read, with a Blank, and is as followeth; viz.

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and obedient Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, having been always fully persuaded, that nothing could restore a just Balance of Power in Europe, but the reducing the whole Spanish Monarchy to the Obedience of the House of Austria, and having seen several great Parts of that Monarchy, by the Blessing of God upon the victorious Arms of your Majesty, and your Allies, already in the Possession of that House, do think it not only seasonable, but necessary, at this Juncture, humbly to offer this^ur unanimous Opinion to your Majesty, that no Peace can be honourable, or safe, for your Majesty, or your Allies, if Spain, the West Indies, or any Part of the Spanish Monarchy, be suffered to remain under the Power of the House of Bourbon.

When we consider, what Efforts this Kingdom has continued to make from the Beginning of the War, we cannot but think, a much greater Impression might have been made upon the Enemy before this Time, if feme of your Allies, who l'eem principally concerned, and have reaped the most immediate Advantage, had seconded your Majesty with like Vigour, whereby France might have been equally press'd on all Sides.

We are obliged to return our humble Thanks to your Majesty, for the Care you have taken, and the Instances you have used with his Imperial Majesty, for lending a considerable Force to the Relief of Spain, under the Command of Prince Eugene, as being certainly the most likely Method to restore the Affairs of the Confederacy in that Country.

But the frequent Disappointments we have observed on the Part of the Emperor, and Empire, to the great Prejudice of the commonCaule, makes us think it our Duty, in order that the War may be brought to a speedy and happy Conclusion, to beseech your Majesty to make

6 F the

Address on State of the War.

48* a 2® — 23 0 Decwbris. . 1707.

the most prefling Instances to the Emperor, that he would, with all Expedition, tend powerful Succours to his Brother the King of Spain, under the Conduct df that great and successful General; that he would timely and cfle&ually make good what has been concerted, for his putting Twenty thousand Men under the Command of the Duke of Savoy j and would also make use of his utmost Power and Interest, for strengthening the Army upon the Rhine, which is now happily put under the Command of that wife and valiant Prince, the Ele£torof Hanover.

We believe, no Part of this can be refused, upon your Majesty's earned Interposition, who have done such great Things for the House of Austria j and this being complied wiA, we may reasonable hope, by God's Assistance, the next will prove a happy and glorious Campaign.

Resolved, That the said Blank be filled up with the Words of and Commons."

Woollen Sir Humphry Mackworth reported from the Committee, »i»uifatiur«j. to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and also of the Merchants, Clothiers, and other Traders in the Woollen Manufactures, within the City of Exon, and Parts adjacent, and several other Petitions, wt re referred, relating to the Prohibition of the Importation of the Woollen Manufactures into Jlria and Stiria, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, by the Represen-tations of the Commissioners of Trade, and also by Copy of an Edict, or Grant, made by the Emperor of Germany, and proved by Mr. Bartholomew dated the 7th of April, 1707, reciting another Patent, dated the 13th of October, 1700, made to Dominico Koll, for a long Term, that the same did, in Effect, amount to a Prohibition of the English Woollen Manufactures within Austria and Stiria.

Mr. Gulicker likewise proved, that the said Koll is endeavouring to obtain the like Patent for Moravia, Bohemia, Hungaria, and Silesia.

Mr. Gulicker, Mr. Edw. JVootton, Mr. Nich. -Jons, Mr. Ben. Heath, Mr. Jacob Row, proved the Consumption and Sale of our Woollen Manufactures much lessencd since the said Patents, to the Value of £. 1,000 a Week in Exon, and proportionably in other Places.

r That it further appeared by the said Representatiopi

from the Commissioners of Trade, that the substantial Merchants of Austria and Stiria do look upon this Undertaking of Kolb as a Monopoly, destruftivp to the general Liberty, formerly given to all Merchants there, to trade in Englishi Woollen Goods.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, that both Houses did, the Z3d Day of December last, present their humble Address to her Majesty; and that her Majesty was thereupon pleased*to give this gracious Answer j viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am fully of your Opinion, that no Peace can be honourable or safe, for us, or our Allies, till the intire Monarchy of Spain be restored to the House of; and very well pleased to find, that the Measures I have concerted, for the Succour of the King of Spain, are so well approved by both Houses of Parliament.

I shall continue my most pressing Instances with the Emperor, for the hastening of farther Succours, and that they may be commanded by Prince Eugene, as also upon all the other Particulars, mentioned in your Address.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other capital Inhabitants, of the Parishes of Sand ford, near -diton, Morchard-bishop, Crews-morchard, and Fitz-pain, and other adjacent Parishes, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have, ever since the War, 20

been supplied with Lime, for improving their Land, from the Parishes of Holcomb Regis and in

Devon, by Persons, who have their Coals and Culm from a Place, called Coal Harbour, on the River Tons, in Somersetshire, where a Toll is payable, by Act of Parliament, to the Conservators of the said River, who are endeavouring to obtain another Act, for a further Toll: That, if a further Toll should be granted, the Persons, concerned in the Lime Trade, have declared, they will leave off the same; whereby the Petitioners, and all the North-eastern Parts of the County of Devon, will be deprived of the Means of improving their lands, and lay down the greatest Part of their Tillage: And praying, that no further or other Toll be laid below Coal Harbour, than is already granted by Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for perfecting the Navigation of the River Tone, be brought in.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Lime-burners, Farmers, and Workers in the Lime Trade, within the Parishes of Holcombe Regis and Burlifcombe, within the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, and Places adjacent, have always been supplied with Coals, Culm, and Salt, from a Place called Coal Harbour, in Somersetshire, at reasonable Prices: That the Conservators of the River Tone (with other Gentlemen, who are not concerned, nor can be burthened thereby) are endeavouring to get a further Toll, than is already payable by Act of Parliament, which comes to about £. 60 per Annum, and where to the Petitioners are the greatest Contributors, the Culm, they use in burning of Lime in the said Two Parishes, amounting to above £. 1,800 per Annum, the Lime mostly used in improving the Lands near 20 Miles West of 'em, and employs daily several hundred Horses: That, if a further Toll should be granted, it will be very prejudicial to their Tillage, a great Fall to all their Estates, their Pastures generally being fed by Horses, employed in carrying Lime, and the Ruin of the Labourers, employed in the Lime Trade, which the Petitioners will not be able to carry on: And praying, that the Petitioners may not be made Contributors to the extravagant and unnecessary Charges of the said Conservators, and that no further Toll be granted below Coal Harbour, than is now payable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for perfecting the Navigation of the River Tone be brought in.

A Petition of several of the Grand Jury at a Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held at Taunton, in and for the County of Somerset, on Tuefdathe 7th Day of 0Bober, in the Year of our Lord 1707, was prefonted to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, being 12 of the said Grand Jury (the whole being but *7) upon the Requestof Christopher . , their Foreman, (who is one of the Conservators of the River Tone) together with some Justices of the Peace of the said County, did sign a Petition to this House, that a further Toll might be granted at a Place called Coal Harbour, more than is now payable by Act of Parliament to the Conservators; but the Petitioners having since informed themselves of the Nature and Design of the said Petition, do find the same (if granted) will be a great Charge on all the Towns lying at least 20 Miles South and South-weft of Coal Harbour, from whence they are all now supplied with Salt, Coals, and other Goods, at reasonable Rates: And praying, that there may be it further Toll payable below Coal Harbour.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon t he Table, until the Bill for perfecting the Navigation of the River Tone, be brought in.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of Bristol, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read -f

Januarii. 1707.

setting forth, that the Conservators of the River Toni, by Act of Parliament, have cotnpleated the Navigation on the said River from Taunton to Ham Mills, to the great Benefit of the adjacent Country, in lowering the Carriage of Tonnage Goods to half the Price of Land Carriage, and in preserving the Highways; yet, because the Navigation is not finished below Ham Mills to Bridgwater, Boats can come up but at feme Times, for want of Depth of Water; so that, by reason of the Uncertainty, Merchants fend their Goods by Land Carriage at some Times, to the great Prejudice of the Roads; and, if the Navigation aforesaid were compleat, it would be a further Benefit to the Country, and supply Bristol with Timber for Shipping, and otherwise: And praying the House to encourage the Conservators to finish the said Navigation, by granting such Increase of Toll, as shall be thought reasonable for that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for perfecting the Navigation of the River Tone, be brought in.

A Petition of the Bailiff, Capital Burgesses, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough of Ivelchester, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Conservators of the River Tone, appointed by Act of Parliament, for making and keeping the River Tone navigable from Taunton to Bridgwater, have been at great Expence in erecting Locks, and other Works, on the said River, from Taunton to Ham Mills, which hath proved a considerable Benefit toTrade, and Preservation of the Highways; and, if the Navigation from Ham Mills to Bridgwater was perfected, it will be a further Advantage, and answer the good Intent of the said Act, but will be a further great Charge to the said Conservators: And praying, that they may have all fitting Encouragement to compleat the said Navigation.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for perfecting the Navigation of the River Tone, be brought in.

A Petition of the Merchants within the City of Bristol was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Conservators of the River Tone, by Act of Parliament, have compleated the Navigation on the said River from Taunton to Ham Mills, to the Benefit of the adjacent Country, in reducing the Carriage of Tonnage Goods, bought at Bristol, and carried up by Water from Bridgwater to Taunton, to Half the Price of Land Carriage in the Summer, and much less in Winter, by reason the Highways are then hardly passable; yet, because Boats cannot come up at some Times, for want of Water below Knap Bridge, Merchants are much discouraged to fend their Goods by Water, and are forced to lend them by Land Carriage, to their great Loss, and Damage of the Ways; which Inconveniences would effectually be remedied, were the Navigation from Bridgwater to Ham Mills perfected: And praying the House to encourage the said Conservators to finish the said Navigation, by granting them a Toll at Knaps Bridge, or otherwise, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for perfecting the Navigation of the River Tone, be brought in.

His Majesty having proposed, that, seeing God was pleased to bless his Arms with such Success, and it being necessary to pursue the Advantage, before the Enemy should have Time to gather fresh Forces, he had called together the Persons present in Council, to deliberate with them about the most important Operations, and the easiest Method of putting them in Execution; desiring all their Opinions in a Matter of so great Consequence, as likewise in the following Proposals:

«ft. Whether the Campaign shall be carried on in the Kingdom of Aragon, or Valencia ? tdly, Which and what Troops ought to be employed in the Campaign, and will be sufficient to leave in Catalonia for its Defence ? jdly, What Train of Artillery is proper, and how the Baggages should be regulated

4thly, How and what Places will be most proper for Magazines

5thly, What Operations may be pitch'd on with Hopes of Success

6thly, Where his Majesty shall be

7thly, Where the Army shall rendezvous

His Majesty concluding with Expressions of his Confidence in the known Valour and Application of all the Generals by whole Conduit he expected a most advantageous Progress to the common Cause.

Admiral Leak declared, that the Dispositions for the Operations of the Fleet were of a different Nature of those by Land, but he assured, in the Name of the rest, that they would comply with their Obligations and Services to his Majesty, to the utmost of their Power, in what belonged to the Sea Service; and having shewn his Majesty their Opinions in a Council of War, held on board, he referred himself to that, as his Sentiment, seeing no Reason to alter his Opinion.

His Majesty having heard the Discourse of every one, it was the unanimous Opinion of all, that, considering the present Circumstances of Affairs, it would be belt to carry on the Operation in the Kingdom of Valencia, where we should not only enjoy the Advantage of the Assistance of the Fleet, which would save great Expences and Troubles, which the Army would be liable to in a March to Arragon, but there being no other Body in Spain, that could embarrass the speedy Conquest of that Kingdom, but that small one of the Count De la Torres, routing this, the Kingdom of Valencia would be free, Murcia brought to submit, and the most convenient Way would be open, to proceed with the Army towards the Capital of Madrid, besides the Advantages gotten by inclining towards the Portuguese Army, being able to refill any Force the French can make, in order to hinder the intire Conquest of the Continent of Spain.

As to the 2d Point; it being of the highest Consequence to preserve this Principality from the Insult and lnvafions of the Enemy, leaving to this End a considerable Garison in Gerona, altho' it is thought the Enemy is not in a Condition to besiege any other Place this Summer, nor effect any thing against Barcelona, while the Fleet are in these Parts of the Mediterranean, it is thought fit to make the Dispose of the Troops, as followeth:

D" Anth. Paguera, his Majesty's -It was agreed to take into the Field the following-Train:

Fourteen Field Pieces, four Half Canon, two Mortars, with Powder, Shot, Bombs, and other'Necessaries, proportionable. And it being of Consequence to regulate the necessary Baggage, it was left to some Generals to regulate, and concert a Contrail at the most moderate Rate it can be performed for.

About the 4th Proposition, of the Magazines, and Provisions, my Lord Peterborow declared, he had in the Fleet Wheat enough for three Months, for 20,009 Men; and it was proposed to make another Contrail for Bread and Barley, that should be necessary for the Campaign; always providing Magazines in the most convenient Places. The Operation by Sea and Land ought to be accommodated to the Motions and Dispositions of the Enemy, endeavouring always to frustrate his Designs, that he may not have any favourable Opportunity of Advantage against us.

Where the Residence of his Majesty should be: — Altho' he declared his Mind, that he would be at the Head of his Army, it was thought more proper by his Council, that his Majesty should proceed to , that he may be on the Borders of Anagon and Valencia, to animate with his Presence the general Inclination of his Subjects of putting themselves under his Obedience, and to forward the Disposition of the Campaign, towards the speedy bringing the Army together; and, when so, and fit for Service, that they may be in the neighbouring Towns, that they may have immediate Notice, and that his Majesty may the more easily issue out those Orders^ that any Occasion may require.

Touching the last Proposal, where the Army ought to join; 'twas the common Opinion, that the most convenient Place for the Rendezvous, 'twould be nigh Valencia, for the fake of fending by Land, or Sea, with greater Conveyance, all Necessaries for the Camp, and for being the more at hand for the preventing any Attempt 01 the Enemy.

A Petition of the chief Inhabitants of the Parishes of North Curry and Gregory Stoke, in the County of set, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they find by the printed Votes of this House, that the Justices of Peace of the said County, and Grand Jury, with the Conservators of the River have

petitioned this House, to have a new Lock below Knap Bridge on the said River, paying a certain Duty to the Conservators for the Passage of Boats through the same: That the Petitioners conceive, the same will be an Op- ' pression to them, and contrary to the Laws, made for the Relief of the Poor, which direct, that the Poor of each Parish shall be relieved by Assessments on the Inhabitants in each particular Parish; and the Petitioners think it hard, that Taunton should be exempted from such Assessment, by laying a Burthen on the whole Country by a Duty on Goods, passing through a Lock five Miles distant from them in another Parish, to wit, North Curry, who rather ought to have the Benefit arising by such Duty, than the Town of Taunton: That the Petitioners are also possess'd of 400 Acres of Meadow, lying near the said River, worth £.600 per and also of two

Commons, lying on each Side the said River, which will be more liable to be overflown, as often as the Water shall be check'd at the said Lock; and, besides, the Inhabitants in the West and South Parts of Somerset/hirt will by this Project of the Conservators, for their own private Interest, have the Price of Coals and Salt advanced to an excessive Rate, beyond other Parts of the Nation 1 and this River has been always navigable as far as a Place called Coal Harbour, from whence the Country, and Town of Taunton, have been supplied as cheap, or cheaper, by Horse Carriage, than by Water Carriage; and a Lock having been erected by one Mr. Mallet below the said Knap Bridge, the same being found prejudicial to the Lands, and no ways advantageous to the Navigation, the same was quickly disused: And praying, that the House will not grant the said Conservators the Liberty of erecting a Lock below Knap Bridge, nor grant any other Duty, than what is already payable by Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the more effectual making and keeping the River Tone navigable from Bridgwater to Taunton, in the County of Somerset, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the ancient Boatmen trading on the River Tone, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have always been employed on the said River between Bridgwater and Coal Harbour, and never knew of any Toll, until Mr. Mallet's, Heirs demanded Six-pence per Boat; but the same being refused to be paid, they sued for the lame, but could not recover it; and the Conservators of the said River, having purchased s Interest, obtained an Act of Parliament, for laying a Duty at Knap Bridge, and now endeavour to get another Act, for laying a further Toll, and erecting another Lock, below Coal Harbour; which will be no way beneficial to the Navigation of the said River, but will overflow the Lands adjoining, and be prejudicial to the Petitioners, and all their Neighbours: And praying, that the House will not grant thelaid Conservators any other Toll, than is now payable on the said River.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the more effectual making and keeping the River Tone navigable from Bridgwater to Taunton, in the County of Somerset, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Dean and Chapter of the Cathedral Church of Wells, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that certain Persons, known by the Name of Conlervators of the River Tone, in the said County, have petitioned this House, under Pretence of making the said River more compleatly navigable, by erecting a Lock below Knap Bridge: That the River has been always navigable as far as Coal Harbour, and there can be no Occasion for a

Lock below Knap Bridge, but the plain Design is to enrich the Conservators; and if such Lock should be ereCled, it would drown or 500 Acres of Meadow, worth £ 600 per Annum, belonging to the Church of Wells, lying in the Parishes of North Curry and Gregory Steak: And praying, that the House will not pass any Bill for erecting a Lock below Knap Bridge, which will be Damage to the Petitioners, and no Advantage to the said Navigation; and that they may be heard by Counsel therein.

A Petition of William Thomffon, Esquire, was pre- ThompW* fented to the House, and read; fitting forth, that King Grant* Charles the 2d, by Letters Patents, dated the 27th of May, in the 14th Year of his Reign, did grant unto the Petitioner's Ancestors, and their Heirs, a certain Rent, and other Things, issuing out of the Manor of -

ton, in lieu of a Surrender, made to his Majesty by the Petitioner's Ancestors, of the Site of the Castle of Scarborough, and Lands therewith held, of about the same Value, and have ever since been enjoyed by the Crown;

That the said Grant, by Reason of some Mistake, is void in Law; and the Petitioner, as Heir at Law to his Ancestors, is intitled to the Benefit intended by the said Grant; yet, by Reason of the said Mistake, his Estate became chargeable with a great Arrear of the said Rents, and her Majesty, being sensible of the Justice of the Petitioner's Cafe, upon his humble Application to her, was pleased by her Privy Seal to release the fame; but the said Mistake cannot be intirely rectified, but by Act of Parliament: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making good to the Petitioner the Benefit intended his Ancestors, upon their granting to the Crown the Site of the Castle of Scarborough, and Lands therewith held, which have been enjoyed accordingly.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir Richard Onslow, Mr..Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Lowndes, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

And the said Representation and Account are as follow; viz.

The said Representation,

IN Obedience to her Majesty's Commands, signified by the Right honourable Mr. Secretary Harley, by his Letter of the 13th Instant, upon an Address from the honourable House of Commons, directing the Commissioners for Sick and Wounded to lay before that House an Account of all Sea Officers, and Seamen, which have been taken Prisoners by France, and of the Method observed in exchanging Prisoners, and what .6 K Numbers

if N umbers of Prisoners are in we, the said Commissioners, do humbly represent, as follows;

As to the Method of exchanging Prisoners of War, we humbly beg Leave to inform this honourable Houfo, that about December, 1702, we were impowered by her Majesty, to treat with the Count de who was

then Prisoner of War in England, and received Instructions from Monsieur Pont chartraine, Secretary of State in

France; and he came to an Agreement with us, to exchange Man for Man, and Officer for Officer, of equal Rank; and, where there were not Officers of equal Rank to exchange, it was agreed to accept of twenty Men for a Captain, and ten for a Lieutenant; and, pursuant to this Agreement, the Exchange has been carried on ever since.

The Account of Exchange of Prisoners, from the Commencement of this War to this present Time, is contained in a Sheet of Paper, which we herewith humbly lay before this honourable House; in which general Account the Number of EnglijkSea Officers, exchanged

to the 5th of December, is included, being as follows; viz.

Captains - - 14:

Lieutenants - - 19:

Marine Lieutenants 3.

Till the taking the three last Men of War, viz. Cumberland, Chester, and Ruby, we are well allured, there were but very few of our Seamen at St. Malo, and thereabouts; but Monsieur the Commis-

(ary there, in his last Letter to us, of the 26 Novem. last, acquaints us, that at that Time of his writing the re were above 1,200 Prisoners in those Parts; and by Lieutenant Collier, of the Severn Man of War, who lately came from Dunkirk, we have been informed, that they had above 200 at Abeville, and about 120 at Calais; in the whole, according to an Expression in the said Monsieur L'Empereur's Letter, we had then in several Parts of France near 2,000.

It is to be observed, that the French Commissaries do not think themselves obliged to fend us an Account of the Numbers of Seamen they take from time to time, tho' we have often desired it; and it is very rare they do; nor could we ever know, what Numbers they have of our Prisoners, but when they were pleased to mention it in their Letters, or by the Report of the Seamen exchanged; both which are very uncertain, and not to be relied upon; for we have always found the Numbers to be much less, than what was reported.

Since Monsieur L'Empereur's Letter, before-mentioned, we have received home from Calais 197 Seamen; and when we get home by the three Vessels, now sent over, the 1,039 (the Balance, which will be due to us, upon the Arrival of the said Vessels in France) we are humbly of opinion, we shall not have above 600 or 700 remaining the re.

All which is most humbly submitted to this honourable # House, this 16th Day of January, 170!.

R. Adams, Tho. Lawrencet P. Silvejre, Plumptre.

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to her Majesty, a Duty of Five Shillings be laid upon every Cloth, commonly called Broad Cloth, exported white.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to her Majesty, a Fund, not exceeding Forty thousand Pound per Annum, be charged upon, and made payable, during the Term of Ninety-nine Years, from Lady-day next, out of the overplus Moneys of the Funds, settled for Payment of Annuities for Ninety-nine Years, purchased in the Years 1706 and 1707, which overplus Moneys are reserved for the publick Nfe and Disposition by an Act, made in the fifth Year of her Majesty's Reign, and also to be charged upon, and payable out of, the overplus Moneys of that particular Branch of Excise, which was granted to the Crown in the fourth Year of King William and Queen Mary (of glorious Memory) for Payment of Annuities, with Benefit of Survivorship.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the better making good the said Fund, not exceeding £. 40,000 per Annum, during the said whole Term of Ninety-nine Years, for which the same is to be settled, the Duties on low Wines, and Spirits of the first Extraction, and the Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen, and the Stamp Duties, and the additional Duties of Tonnage and Poundage, commonly called the One-third Subsidy, mentioned in the said Act, of the fifth Year of her Majesty's Reign, be severally granted to her Majesty for one Year more after the Expiration of the present Terms therein respectively; and that the Duties on Sweets, granted by the said Act, of the fifth Year of her Majesty's Reign, be granted for two Years more after the Expiration of the present Term therein; and that the said particular Branch of Excise, which was granted in the said fourth Year of their late Majesties Reign, be granted for Fifteen Years after the present Term of and in the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Fund, not exceeding Forty thousand Pound per Annum, be applied to the Payment of Annuities for Ninety-nine Years, from Lady-day next, which any Person will voluntarily purchase, towards railing any Sum,- not exceeding Six hundred and Forty thousand Pound.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That out of the said Purchase-money Provision be made of so much, as shall be necessary to be reserved, to make good the Payment of the said Annuities, so to be purchased, until and for Micha 1710; and that the residue of the said Purchase-money be applied towards her Majesty's said Supply, for carrying on the War.

Y ol. lb.

was (according to Order) read; setting forth, that the said John Lord Bophin, being attainted of high Treason, and his Estate forfeited, made Application to the Parliament of England, for reverlal of his Attainder, and in the first Year of her Majesty's Reign obtained an Act of Parliament, to restore him to his Blood, and Estate, upon Payment of £.25,000 for the publick Service, at such Times, and in such Manner, as the Act directs: That the Lord Bophin, and Trustees, did expose to Sale a sufficient Part of the said Estate, and by publick Sales to the Petitioners did raise £.10,384, which was paid into the Exchequer of Ireland', but were not able to raise the intire £.25,000 within the Time limited by the said Act; and thereupon the Lord Bophin the next Session of Parliament procured another Act, for further Time to raise the said £.25,000, with Interest after the rate of£.6 per Cent, at certain Payments, and to-be made in English Money; and, in case of Failure, the Estate was vested in the Queen: That, upon the Security of the said Two Acts, the Petitioners did purchase a considerable Parc of the Lord Bophins Estate, and did in due Time pay into the Exchequer in Ireland£.26,344. 2 6d. as Money is valued in Ireland; and the Lord Bophin, and his Trustees, did affine the Petitioners, that they would pay a considerable Sum, more than sufficient to answer any Mistake, that might happen in the Difference betwixt English and Irish Money: That the Petitioners thought the said Acts had been fully complied with, but are now informed, there is about £.681 short of what ought to be paid; and they being apprehensive, that their Titles might be drawn into question, by reason of the said Failure, are informed by Mr. Pratt, Deputy Receiver General of Ireland, that he had Directions from England to allure the Petitioners, that no Advantage should be taken, more than to enforce the Payment of what was really due: The Petitioners therefore pray, that, for avoiding Disputes, that may arise, by reason of the said Failure, they may have such Relief, for making their said Pilrchafes as valid, as if the said £.25,000 and Interest, had been intirely paid, they offering to pay what remains due.

The House being informed, that the Commissioners Exchange of of the Sick and Wounded, and for Exchange of Prison- Pfi(‘>ner*> ers, attended, they were called in, and, at the Bar, presented to the House, a Translation of the Letter to them from Monsieur L'Empereur, the French Commissary at Saint Maloes.

And then they withdrew.

And the Title thereof was read.

And the said Translation is as followeth; viz,

St. Malo, 26 November, 1 yoy.

Gentlemen,

I received by the Transport, commanded by Captain.

Marlow, the Letter you gave yourselves the Trouble to write to me, of the 4th of October, with a new Account of the Exchange inclosed; by which I am very well pleased to fee, that at last you agree to allow us all the Articles, that are in Dispute between us, except the 1,755 Prisoners, taken at Nevis; and, altho' you have no just Reason to dispute that with us, and we have a. great deal on our Side to infill upon it, yet, to shew you, how desirous I am to entertain a good and sincere Correspondence with you, I will agree, that it shall be struck out of the Account, since you will have it so: And, since you have nothing to fiiy for yourselves, but that they were Prisoners taken at Land, I mud at the same time demand, that they be accounted for in the Exchange at Land, without which, we mud set aside the whole Commerce and Exchange; for, since we are engaged in a Treaty, made in Form with the Inhabitants of that Island, it mud one way or other have its Effects I ‘lo are also,

6 N that

510 a 2° Januarii. 1707.

Exchange of that I will not leave it, till it be done: Therefore you Prisoners. may choose which of the Alternatives you please, either the Exchange at Sea, or at Land, and let me have a positive Answer thereupon: But, to tell you the Truth, it seems as convenient for you, as for us, to agree to what I propose: Moreover, 1 allure you, upon the Word of a Man of Honoui, I do not seek to make any Advantage, which the great JNI umber of Prisoners, and those since taken by Monsieur Fourbin and Du Guay, might give us over you, to do you any Injury or Injustice; therefore, if you would but use the same Sincerity, as I do, the Exchange would be carried on with all the good Correspondence, that ought to be between ho-nest People, who are Enemies no otherwise, than being of different Nations.

If the two Courts.could be disposed to agree to a general Exchange, such as we have with the it

would be a great Benefit to both Nations. I do not despair of bringing ours to it: It is your Part then, Gentlemen, to infuse the same Sentiments into the Court of England; and I am persuaded, it will not be disagreeable there.

As to the other Articles, which 1 found joined to your Account, either for the Prisoners tent back by Mr. Methwen, or by my Lord , or sent by the

Orange Transport; altho' I have a gieat deal of Reason to dispute it with you, nevertheless, I agree to allow them in the Account; but as it is not reasonable, that you should fend us back only the Angle Letters and Certificates, which don't determine precilely the Number, you mull not take it ill, if, in allowing them, I desire you to fend me back the Rolls, that the Truth may appear in the Maratime Provinces, where they were sent, as we do to you on the same Occasions. Besides, Gentlemen, you must have ill interpreted or explained the Terms of my Letter, if you understood, that I pretended, at your Desire, to remit the Prisoners, sent by Captain Henry Vernon: I only said, it was to do you Service; and that is quite different; but since you account for them, that Explanation is useless.

I every Day expert the Answer you promised me to my Letter of the 3d of ;but, to tell you ingenu-ously, it is not impossible, but that Letter being given to the Captain of the Transport, who did not part from hence till the 4th or 5th, my Lord 5 might

write the 6th of the same Month, in Answer to that Letter, to Mr. Ponchartraln, nor that his was sent, as you observe, to Mr. ChatSo it is certain, that Minister did not receive it; and he has writ himself a Letter to my Lord Sunder, here inclosed, which I must desire you to give him.

I don't understand, how Mr. Pearfe can say, that he is not paid the Freight of his Transports, or at least, that we give him nothing but Bills of Exchange at so long a Time, that the Discount thereof would ruin him; since there is not one Farthing due to Captain Masters, and all the Bills of Exchange, which Mr. nish'd him with, were at most but at ten Days Sight, and were punctually paid. As to Captain , it is true, there is still due to him about 2,000 Livres; but since Mr. Maget has given him his Bill, it is not our Business, but Mr. Maget'$ if the Treasurer does not regularly perform his Orders, to apply himself to me, to be indemnified for the retarding the Payment.

Moreover you know, as well as I, that the transporting of Money into strange Countries being forbid, I can make no other Payments, than by Bills of Exchange and it seems to me, that, instead of complaining, Mr.; Pearce ought to take it kindly, that he has his Money brought home to him.

As to Mr. James Pulleyn, whom you have given Leave

to come over, you must have forgot. Gentlemen, that in speaking formerly of the Sieur La to whom

I had given the same Leave, for an extraordinary Affair he had at Jersey, you took it so outrageously, as if he was sent to disturb the State; and, after having detained him above two Years, it was with a great deal of Diffi-ao

culty he was then released, notwithstanding the many pressing Solicitations I was obliged to ule on that Account. He may think himself very happy, that I am of an easy peaceable Temper; for, without that, he had run the Risque of suffering for the Injustice done to La Lande: But I cannot punish him for a Fault, he had no Hand in; and he can tell you, that I have not only not used him as a Criminal, but with all the Regard that can be.

I must thank you for what you have done on my Account to Captain Adams, for his Neglect: His Example will at least caution others, and we shall be much better served.

As we have now more than 1,200 Prisoners, it is not necessary to fend the Transport to Calais. 1 have given him only expecting, that you would have sent us back all ours, which are at Kinfale, and Dublin, and that I may-find, how you are disposed to regulate the Matters, as well as to the Prisoners at Nevis, as the detained at Dublin, and Jersey, and the Exchange of the Bishop of Quebec, and the Ecclesiasticks; for if there is no Hopes of agreeing, it is not convenient/ as you yourselves lay, to think to continue Exchange; and you can't take it ill, if I follow the Example you have given me, of fending me back but twelve. I would not do so, if I were not obliged to it; and I desire you to consider of it.

I desire also, in case you will not consent to the Exchange of the Bishop of Quebec, nor to that of the Ecclesiasticks, which are with him, to give Orders to the Officers (a List of whom I fend herewith) to come back, according to their Parole of Honour, by the first Transport, except Sir Hugh , to whom the King, upon Mr. Harley's Account, has shewn Favour.

I know, how uneasy it will be to them, and I am very sorry to make them such a Compliment. It is not my Fault: It is the Court of England, that must obtain their Liberty, by releasing the Bishop of or the

Ecclesiasticks with him.

There is just now fallen into our Hands an Exchange for that Bishop, by the taking of Mr. Robert,

Governor of Virginea; and, that he may endeavour it, the King has let him pass into England by this Transport. As he is Governor of a Province on the tame Continent, where Monsieur Quebec is Bishop, per- haps may make some Equality between these two Prisoners, and by Consequence little Difficulty in the Exchange; at least, I hopefo: And I desire you to consider what may be for your Interest on this Occasion, since you value the Liberty of one Man more, than thac of 2,000 unhappy Men, whom you expose to die in Mi-fery in our Prisons by your Refusal.

I will say no more of the cruel Usage of our Prisoners in the Prisons at Jamaica, tho' I receive fresh Complaints every Day, because I am.assured, that the Court of England has given Orders therein; but I must desire you to give such, as are necessary to obtain the Liberty of Mr. Makan, who has been detained there by Force a long Time, without which I cannot but make a Re-prifal. I desire also, as I have oftentimes done, that you will fend back Mr. Creanton, upon his Parole. You know how ingenuously I have dealt with all your Prisoners; and 1 really deserve, that you should have more Regard to me.

We have in the Prisons of Guernsey an Hostage of the Parish of St. Mary Du Monte, in Normandy, which a Privateer of that Island brought in, for Security of the Sum of 500 Livres, for which they ransomed some Fith-ermen; and, as the People of that Pavifh are in a very poor Condition, and not capable of paying his Ransom,

I desire you to give Orders to fend him us back: Besides, the Custom is not to take and ransom Fishermen. We always do the same by the like Hostages, when we . find them uncapable of paying; and I can aflfure you, that just now, by the King's Order, we have sent back two from Dunkirk, who were brought in there as a Scotch Prize, called the Marie Bertonne, in 1705, and ransomed for a hundred Pound Sterling.

and the said Manager and purchasing Trullee are now publickly fdliciting to get an Act of Parliament, for confirming the said Purchases, which, if obtained, will tend to the Ruin of the Petitioner, and his Brothers and Sifters, and the Evasion of the said Act } who conceive, that the Remainders, decreed to them by the said Trustees, were never deligned to be sold, for raising the said £.25.000, thereby to punish them who were guiltless, for their Fathers Crimes, the Lands restored only being liable to that Charge, and the Petitioners could not be restored to what they had before: That all the said Transactions were done, while the Petitioner Michael was a Minor, at Eaten College, and Oxford, and his Estate is so clogg'd with Incumbrances, that, unless the Petitioner, and his Brothers and Sifters, be relieved, by and Explanation of the said Act in their Favour, there will be little or nothing left for their Support: That Michael, being lately come of Age, went into Ireland, and his Father being convinced of several Mismanage-ments in relation to his Estate, he articled with the Petitioner, to convey all his Estate to him, in case it were recovered, reserving only to himself a competent Maintenance, with a Power to charge thereon Portions for younger Children: That the Petitioner has brought into England the Eldest of his younger Brothers, to be educated a Protestant, whom he cannot maintain, without the Relief of this House; and can expect no Support from his Father, he being taken away unknown to the Petitioner, and against his Consent: That the Lord Bophin's said Manager (who had the foie Prosecution of the Petitioners before the said Trustees for Irish Forfeitures) did enter a Claim for their Remainders to several Lands, and particularly for the Manor of Dunfandell, which was allowed } but, for private Ends of his own, left it out of the Decree, on purpote to defeat the Petitioners thereof, the said Remainders being all they have for their Support: And praying, that the Petitioners may be heard by Counsel before the Committee, to whom the said Petition of John Lord Archbishop of Tuam, Sir John King, Baronet, and others, is referred; and that they may not be deprived of their Remainders decreed to them, as aforesaid; and that they may be relieved as to the Manor of Dunfandell, omitted out of the said Decree; and that the said Agreement between the Lord Bophin, and the Petitioners, may be confirmed.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of John, Lord Archbishop of Tuam, Sir John King, Baronet, and others, is referred; and that the Petitioners be heard before the said Committee by their Counsel, if they think fit.

I shall lose no time in giving Order for a Proclamation, pursuant to your Address, nothing being more essential for the publick Service, than the immediate providing of the necessary Recruits for the Army. 1 cannot but hope, you will take care it be done in such a Manner, as may be efflftual.

A Petition of Robert Stayner, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Corporation of Droitwich had for many Years monopolized the making of Salt there, and fold it at 1 to d. per JBulhel; and the Petitioner being advised, the said Monopoly was against Law, did, by l'everal expensive Suits in Law and Equity, which colt him above £.5,000, ascertain his Right of making Salt in his Freehold Lands there; which he hath quietly done for several Years since, and thereby reduced the Price of Salt from 1 s, 10 d.to 5 4 the Bushel; which is for the Eale of the Subject, and great Increase of the Duty thereon, being now Twenty times as much made on Freehold Lands, as while the said Monopoly continued: But the Petitioner seeing by the Votes of this House, a Bill is now depending, for the better preserving the ancient Salt Springs in Droitwich, in the County of and the Rights of the Proprietors thereof, he conceives, the same is with intent to have some new Brine Pits con-.firmed by Act of Parliament, thereby to encompass, and ruin, the Petitioner's Salt Springs aforesaid: And praying, that he may be heard by his Counsel against the said

Bin.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be heard by his Counsel before the Committee thereupon, if he think fit.

ported here (except Pepper) but what comes from Holland ready garbled, and, if garbled here again, 'cwould greatly damnify them: That the Duty, demanded by the Garbler on all Spices, is very high, tho' he does nothing to 'em, and consequently very oppressive, and an unnecessary Burthen on Trade: And praying such Relief in the Premifts, as the House shall tnink fit.

Sir Edward Irby reported from the Committee, to Molloy's whom the Petition, of Margaret and Mary Motley was Eftat*. referred; the Matter, as it appeared to them, which they had directed him to report to the House; and which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the said Petition, it appeared, that Charles Molloy, the Petitioners Grandfather, was seised in Fee of a eonfi-derable Estate in Ireland, who had Issue Charles die Petitioners Father.

That Charles, the Grandfather, in Jan. 1 did devise the same in Fee to his only Son Charles, and his Heirs; whereby the said Charles, the Son, the Petitioners Father, became seised and possessed thereof; after whole Death the same defeended to his Son, and Heir, Arthur Molloy, who continued seised and possessed thereof until his Death, and left no Issue.

After whose Death the Petitioners, being Sifters of the whole Blood, and and consequently Heirs at Law to the said Arthur, entered, and had quiet Possession of the said

Estate, till such Time as the same was seized, upon pretence of the Attainder of one Geoghegan, who claimed under a Deed, made in 1663 by Charles, at such Time as he was a Lunatick, as was fully proved to the Committee.

That it appeared to the Committee, that the said Geoghegan never enjoyed, nor had any Possession of, the said Estate.

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, that the Petitioners exhibited their Claim to the said Estate before the late Trustees; yet they thought fit to dismiss the fame, and fold the Estate for about £. 6,034. 5J.

Whereupon the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of the Petition; and that they are real Objects of Companion, and justly deserve the Favour of the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Relief of the said Margaret and Mary Molloy; and that Sir Edward Irby and Sir Henry Dutton Colt do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of the Scarlet and other Dyers of Cloth and Stuffs, Cloth-workers. Setters, Cloth-drawers, Pressers, Tiljet-painters, and Packers, in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; felting forth, that their Families are wholly maintained by the finishing and making merchantable the substantial Woollen Manufactures of Cloth and Stuffs of this Kingdom, chiefly in Grain Colours, dyed with Cochineal, which is at a high Price of 26 per Pound, but fold in Holland under 20s. per Pound; whereby our Neighbours the Dutch, are enabled to dye much cheaper, than the Petitioners can, and consequently furnish foreign Markets cheaper with our Woollen Manufactures, which are likely to be exported white, to the great Prejudice of the Nation in general, and to the Petitioners in particular; which they conceive may be prevented, if Cochineal might be imported from Holland, and other Parts, into England, without incurring the Penalties in the Act, made in the 1i° Car. for the Encouragement and Increase of Shipping and Navigation: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Importation of Cochineal from foreign Parts, not of the Growth thereof, during this present War, in such Manner, as shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill,- according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir Richard Onslow, Sir Godfrey , Mr. Ward, Sir Davall, Sir William Ashhurfi, and Mr. Scobell, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

but his late Majesty granted him his Pardon, and the Petitioner reverled his Outlawry in this Kingdom by a Writ of Error; but never having been in Ireland since his Outlawry and Attainder there, the same stands Chill in force against him, to his great Prejudice and Inconvenience: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to reverie the Outlawry and Attainder against him in Ireland, provided, that no Estate of him, or any Estate, sold by the Trustees of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, shall be liable, or any ways impeached, charged, or affected, thereby.

Regulating A Petition of divers Merchants, and other Traders,

Brokers. jn (he City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners are informed, a Petition has been presented-to the House, praying, that an Act for limiting the Number of Brokers in the said City (now expiring) may be continued: That the Petitioners conceive, such a limited Number is a Prejudice to Trade in general, and to Traders in particular; for that they are necessitated, under a Penalty, to employ some of the limited Number, tho' others (not admitted) are more capable of serving the Traders in their several Negotiations; and such a Restraint is a great Hardship upon many Persons, who have been ruined by the War, not to allow them a Liberty of getting a Livelihood by such Means, as they are versed in: And praying, that the Number of Brokers may not be limited, but that every Trader may be at liberty to employ such Persons, as they think fit.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report shall be made from the Committee, to whom it was referred to examine, what Laws were expired, or near expiring, and to report, what were fit to be revived, and continued.

A Petition of the Grocers, Sugar-bakers, Distillers, Ditto. Shipwrights, Ironmongers, Soap-boilers, and other Traders in Tonage Goods, within the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, the Conservators, appointed by Act of Parliament, for making the River Tone navigable from Bridgivater to Taunton, have completed the said Navigation from Taunton to Ham Mills, to the Benefit of the adjacent Country, in that Tonnage Doods, bought at are carried up by Water from Bridgwater to Taunton for half the Price of Land Carriage in the Summer, and much less in Winter, by reason of the Badness of the Highways; but, because the Navigation is not finished below Ham Mills, towards Bridgwater, the Boats can come up but at feme Times, and are often detained, for want of Depth of Water below Knap Bridge, and Traders are forced to fend their Goods by Land Carriage, to their great Loss, and damage of the Highways; but, if the Navigation from Bridgwater to Ham Mills were made complete, those Inconveniences would be remedied, and prove advantageous for Bringing down Timber to Bristol, for building Ships, and otherwise: And praying, that the said Conservators may have such Encouragement to complete the said Navigation, by a further Toll at Knap Bridge, or otherwise, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the more effectual making and keeping the River Tone navigable from Bridgwater to Taunton, in the County of Somerset, be read a Second time.

Orders on Mr. Mo/esworth reported from the Committee, to Bills relating whom it was referred to consider of proper Methods, to to re and prQposed to the House, for giving Notice of private Bilk brought into this House, relating to Estates in -land-, that they had considered the same accordingly, and had come to two Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House r And which he read in, his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table 5 where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons, intending to apply themselves to the Parliament of Great Br, for obtaining private Acts, relating to Estates in Ireland, do from henceforth give publick Notice of their said Intention, by affixing printed Papers, setting forth their Pretensions, in each of the four Courts of Justice in Dublin, during the whole Term, which shall precede the Sessions of Parliament, as also in the Chief Town, wherein the Assizes are usually kept, of each County, where the Lands shall happen to lie, for one Month at lead before the Bill be brought in.

Exporting Sir William Withers reported from the Committee, to foreign whom the Petition of the Rope-makers of London, and Cordage. other Parts of Great B, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, which they had directed him to report to the House; and which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table j where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That, upon the Examination of Witnesses, it appeared to the Committee, that foreign Cordage, imported, pays a Duty of j s. per Hundred Weight to her Majesty, but, upon Exportation thereof, draws back 6 s. 8 per Hundred; so that there remains but 4 d. per Hundred of the said Duty.

That all Cordage made in Great Britain, pays, on Exportation, a Duty of 6d,per Hundred Weight, but, with the Duty on Hemp included, it pays 2 s. 10 d. per C. Weight more than foreign Cordage; which is £. a. 16 s.8 d.per Ton Loss to her Majesty in her Customs,

besides £. 6 per Ton Loss to the Nation in the manufacturing thereof, and Employment of our Poor.

That the Importation of foreign Cordage is a great Detriment to Navigation, for that one Ton of Hemp takes up the Stowage of two Tons of Cordage.

That the Rope-makers Trade in Great Britain is in great Measure loft, and Encouragement given to foreign Countries to manufacture the fame, and import it hither, for the Sake of the Drawback, on Exportation.

That, foreign Cordage is often made of damaged Hemp, and sold at 5 s. per Hundred Weight, whereby, 'tis feared, several Ships have been loft in the Plantations, our Cordage being better after twice made up.

And Mr. Lloyd, of London, Merchant, said, that he had been employed by Commission for several Dutch Merchants, to enter foreign Cordage at her Majesty's Custom-house, and to export the same again to New England, and other Parts.

And that he finds by the Custom-house Books, the Sid December, 1703, entered in and out the same Day,

So the Profit remaining to the Go-? , vemment is only - - j 2 1 4

That the Government gets more by 196 Tons of English Cordage exported, than by the like Quantity of foreign Cordage exported - 530 16 8

Mr. Wood, Rope-maker, also acquainted the Committee, that great Numbers of their Journeymen and Apprentices have, during the War, been impress'd for Service in her Majesty's Rope-yards, so that their Masters have been necessitated to take more Apprentices into their Trade; whereby in Time of Peace such Journeymen may want Relief from their respective Parishes, the Rope-makers not having Vent for their Cordage, nor Work to employ them.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Report be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Act, made in the eighth and ninth Years of the Reign of the late King William the Third (intituled, An Act to restrainthe Number, and ill Practices, of Brokers and Stock-jobbers) which was to continue for three Years, and from thence to the End of the next Sessions of Parliament; and which was further continued by an Act, made in the eleventh and twelfth Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty, for seven Years, from the Expiration thereof; which will expire at the End of this Session of Parliament, is fit to be continued.

Knightly, his Servant, and John Littlehale, employ themselves as Informers against the Petitioners, and have taken their Horses, and fell them to their own Accomplices for what they please; and who have now divers Warrants against the Petitioners: And praying, that there may be no common Informers allowed, but that the Parish Officer demand the Penalty, where the Offence shall be committed; and that the Petitioner* may go with five or six Horses in length, or seven or nine in Pairs, besides the Wheel Horse.

numerous Army of Irish Papists, by him then raised, the said Protestants took up Arms, to the Number of 32 Regiments, and fought the Irish Papists at Claudy!

Bridge, bpt y/anting Artillery, and Ammunition, they were totally defeated; after which several of the resolute Officers filled up their Regiments, and marched to Londonderry, being eight Regiments, making 9,000 Men, refolying to make the best Terms they could with their Enemies; bpt, upon their Majesties further Encouragements, and their. Declaration (partly annexed) of the 22d Ftbr. ;688, promising the Rebels Estates, and fending to the Garison a Supply of Ammunition, they rejected the great Offers made them by King James (who was then preparing to invade Scotland with a numerous Army, waiting only for the Reduction of don-derry) and declared for, and proclaimed, King William and Queen Mary, laid out their own Money in Provisions and Stores against a bloody Siege, which followed on the 16th Day of April by King James in Person, who sent the Garison a Chart blanche, to make their own Conditions, rather than delay his March into Scotland, where in all Probability, with the Assistance of the Lord Dundee, then in Arms, and successful, he would have carried all before him; but the Garison rejected it at a Time, when they were exhausted by Fire anti Sword, Dearth and Pestilence, and reduced to eat Horses, Dogs, falc Hides, Starch, and Tallow, and held out a, Siege of four Months, wherein they killed 10 or 12,000 Soldiers, and a great many Officers, and obliged the late fC*ng J notes to raise the Siege, baffled' his Army, and therewith was forced to quit that Part of the Country: That his Majesty King William was lbfen-fible of the Services done hiip>and the whole Kingdom, by the said Garison, that he acknowleges the same by his Letter (signed by the Duke of Shrewsbury, then Secretary of State) dated the 16th August, 1689, annex'd to the Petition, applauded their Bravery, and promised his royal Favour, and, as a Mark thereof, ordered the Accounts of the Garison to be stated by Mr. Fox, continued three Regiments of them, together with 214 fu-pernumerary Officers, in his Pay, during the War, whose Arrears he likewise ordered to be stated by Mr. Fox, which was also done, as by his Majesty's Letters (annexed) to Duke Schomberg may appear: That the said Gariion, by adhering to their said Majesties Interest, had their Hopfes and Plantations destroyed, and their personal Estates seized, to their Damage £. 200,000 at least, which has reduced them to a very indigent Condition: That, upon the Petitioners Application to the House of Commons last Session, for the Arrears of Pay due to the said Garison, the House appointed a. Committee to examine the Petition, and (late the FaCl; which accordingly they did; and reported the Arrears due to the Gariion, and that the Allegations of that Petition were true, as is upon the House Journals; but the Session then drawing near to an end, there was not Time to bring in a Bill for Debentures to be made out to the Petitioners, as to the rest of the Army, for the said Arrears of Pay: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in Bill for Debentures to be made out, and delivered to the Petitioners, for the Arrears of Pay due tp them, and for their Losses sustained on Account of their Loyalty, or such other Relief given them, as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Papers, laid before the House Yesterday, relating to the Officers and Soldiers, that served in the Defence of Londonderry, shall be taken into Consideration.

That the Hardship of gatbling lies only upon the Merchants and Traders, importing any of those Commodities into the City of London, and Liberties thereof; for^ if they are imported into Southwark, or any other Parts of this Kingdom, they may be again exported without the Garbler's Inspection.

Mr. Stewart, the Garbler, laid, that he never demanded to garble Indico, or any other Goods, not enumerated in the said Act, of the first of King James the first, unless the Merchants, or Traders, lent to him to garble the fame.

Mr. Kent said, that he has imported Indico, Pe-mento, and Ginger, for 11 Years part, and never knew them garbled, or liable to it; and therefore apprehends it very hard upon the Subject to lie liable to so vexatious a Law, that, in complying with it, does those Commodities no manner of good, and, in not complying, renders the Dealers liable to Ruin by the heavy Prosecutions, that may b£ brought by any Informer against Jtim.

Mr. Deputy Parrott said, that he has imported Indico, and Ginger, for 20 Years past, and never understood those Goods to be liable to be garbled, till lately an Information was brought against him by one a

p rfedt Stranger to him, and believes he is so to the Garbler: And produced a Copy of the Information to the Committee: So liable are the Merchants to vexatious Prosecutions by virtue of that Act.

That, upon the Petition of the Merchants trading in Spices:

Mr. Gough said, That, since the Law for garbling, the East India Spices are imported very clean from Holland; and that Mace in its own Nature is not capable of being garbled, and yet a high Duty is paid to the Garbler for not garbling thereof: That the Garbler receives 2 per Pound for Cloves, and 3s. per C. for Mace, and Nutmegs; for which he does no more than set his Seal upon those Goods, as garbled, without any In* speftion, they being imported ready garbled to his Hand.

That they are thus forced to submit to these needless Impositions, to save their Goods, and to avoid those vexatious Prol'ecutions, they are liable to by the aforesaid Act.

To which Mr. Stewart, the Garbler, said, there was a Necessity to inspect Mace; for that he has. known a Sort of wild Mace, that is brought from the East Indies, to be mixed with the good Mace, which is not discover-able by Colour, but by Taste only.

Mr. Crejfter said, that he pays £. 4. per Hog (head for Cloves to the GaTbler, for only his putting his Seal upon the lame, without any Inspection; and, notwithstanding, the Goods are liable to be seized by any Informer, by virtue of that Law, because not actually garbled.

That he has been a Trader for 15 Years last past, and never knew any such Thing as wild Mace imported from Holland: That the Hollanders, are so sensible of the Advantage of fending their Spices well cleaned, and in good Condition, to England, by the Advantage of Price, that there are none lent otherwise; And several Specimens of Mace, Cloves, and Nutmegs, were produced to the Committee.

That, upon the Salters Petition.

Mr. Ludlam said, That the Garbler demands a Duty for garbling of Argol, and Sal* Acmoniac, the' the same were never garbled in the Memory of Man; and that he receives 12 d.per for garbling Ginger for Exportation; and, when it is garbled, it is not 2 per C. the better; And produced a Table of Rates, which the Garbler demands for garbleable Goods, which were settled by the City in the Year 1599: And yet he now demands a Duty for Goods under the Notion of garbleable, that were not tlren known in England, under Pretence of Orders, made by the Lord Mayor Jeffryes, under whom he purchased his Place.

That Scammony, Sarsaparilla, Cassia fistula, are not in their Natures garbleable; and yet the Traders are

Mr. Stewart, the Garbler, said, that the aforesaid Rates were settled by Ad of Common Council in Queen Elix. Time, and by a Table of Rates in 1604, and Orders of the Court of Aldermen of the City of London thereupon.

Mr. Gough said, that tho' they buy their Pepper ready lifted, and cleaned, of the East India Company, yet they are liable to be seized, if the Garbler does not come and look upon it, for which he demands, and receives, as. per Bag; and i'ometimes there may be Rice mixed among the Pepper; yet he takes the Duty, tho' he does nothing for it.

To which Mr. Stewart, the Garbler, said, that he is at the same Trouble and Charge in the Maintenance of his Servants in the garbling of clean Goods, as well as foul; and, tho' Pepper may be clean, it is by Law liable to be inspected.

Mr. Dickenson said, that there is no Penalty in that Ad upon the Garbler, if he does not do his Duty, whereby a Forfeiture may be incurred: That the present Garbler is a Merchant, as well as Garbler, and had a Property in a Parcel of Turmerick, which is a garbleable Commodity^ which, to his Knowlege, was fold ungarbled, as must be believed, he being a Director of that Company, that fold the fame: Yet he afterwards seized the said Turmerick, because fold ungarbled, and has it yet in his Possession.

Mr. Stewart, the Garbler, being present, and deiiring to be heard in Answer to the Petitioners Allegations, said, that, by the Experience of 20 Years, he knows the Office for garbling to be of publick Use and Benefit, for the preventing and detecting of Frauds in the Sale of garbleable Goods, and to be a great Check upon unfair Traders.

He owned the Information brought against Mr. Millington, about 17 Years ago, for not garbling Cochineal > but compounded the feme, by Licence from the Exchequer, for his Fees and Charges.

That Cochineal is directed to be garbled by Order of the Court of Aldermen in 1618, and always comes over very foul, and frequently mix'd.

That the several Commodities mentioned in the Table of Rates, not enumerated in the Act, are in their Nature garbleable, and used to be garbled, and so directed to be by Act of Common Council, and Order of Court of Aldermen; yet are not infilled on, but when the Traders desire it.

A PETITION of the Grand Jury of the Court of Sewers for the River Tone, in the County of tnerjet, wasprclcnted to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Petitioners, pursuant to the Oath, taken upon their Admidion into this Trust, have made several Views yearly of the said River, in order to present all Annoyances they should find; but could never find, that the Locks, and half Locks, erected by the Conservators of the said River, did, or could, contribute to the Inundation of the adjacent Country, or the Prejudice of any Person, because the Top of ihofe Locks are much lower than the Banks of the River, and rather preserve the Lands adjacent from being Overflowed, and the half Locks only in use, when the Water is very' low; and, for that the now Navigation from Ham Mills to Taunton hath been a considerable Advantage to that Part of the Country, the Petitioners are well allured, that, if the said River were made compleatly navigable from Bridgwater to Ham Mills, it would be much more for their Advantage: And praying, that all due Encouragement may

be given to the said Conservators, for finishing the said Navigation.
