Hwhcnr. the Petition of Benjamin Joules was referred, the Mat-

Feiruarii. A. 1707.

ter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to; report to the House; and which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow;

That the Committee having examined into the Allegations of the said Petition,

It-appeared by a Report of Samuel Esquire,

to the Navy Board, dated the 7th of February, 170^, that the Bank, called the middle Bank, and the Shoal on Gosport Side of Portsmouth Hat boor, was very much increased; and that it would be of great Advantage to the Harbour, if Vessels and Men were employed to remove the said Shoals.

That the Petitioner produced another Report of Henry Greenhill, Esquire, to the Navy Board, w ho was

ordered to survey the said Harbour; who reported to the same Purpose; and further reported, that the taking up of Ballast from Blockhouse Point, the Ground is loll on, that Point about 20 Yard*, which hath very much damaged that Harbour, by stirring the Soil, a great Part _ _ of which hath lodged in the Bay, between Gosport and the Point.

Upon which said Reports, the Commissioners of the Navy ordered a Publication, for contrafting'with any Person to serve her Majesty's Ships with Ballast.

Accordingly the 6th of July, 1703, the Petitioner contracted with the said Commissioners to serve the Navy with Ballast; viz. to rransport and carry off to Spithead, or St. Hellens, if Occasion shall require, on board any of her Majesty's ships and Vessels, all such Ballast, as shall be required, finding Hoys, Ballast, and Men; to transport at the Rate of 12 d. pTon; and to trank port and carry Ballast on boat d, and receive the same* from, any of her Majesty's Ships in Harbour, finding Hoys, Men, and Ballast, at his own Charge, at Nine Pence per Ton; as by the said Contract (which was produced to the Committee) appears.

That it all'o appeared to the Committee, that the Petitioner, pursuant to the said' Contraft, hath served the Navy with Ballad ever since the 6th of 1703, from off his own Ground.

That it appeared also to the said Committee, by a Contrail, made the 21st of December, 1698, by Richard Arden, of London, Lighterman, who agreed with the Commissioners of the Navy for taking up of Ballast at Chatham, at the Rate of 13 d. p Ton, which is per Ton more, than the Petitioner proposes to have at PortJmoutH.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioner hath fully proved the Allegations of his Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it will very much conduce to the publick Service, if a Method was settled, for the better and more speedy ballasting her Majesty's Men of War, and other Ship?, as also for removing and preventing the Shoals within the Harbour of Portsmouth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved, for Leave to bring in a Bill for that Purpose.

The two first of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the Houfo.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the said Resolutions; and that Mr. Fulham and Mr. Jervois do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Pierce IValjh, Gentleman, his Guardian (presented to the House the sixth Instant) was read; letting forth, that in April, 1685, the Petitioner's Father, Sir Tho. Hacket, late of Dublin, deceased, being a clear Man from Debts, did, in pursuance of Articles made before Marriage, make a Settlement of his whole Estate, whereby a Jointure was secured for the Petitioner's Mother, Provision for younger Children, and Maintenance for the eldtft Son, and also for Payment of such Debts, as he should owe at his Death, by Judgment, or other Specialties, and was only Tenant for Life, with Remainders over in Tail Male: That afterwards the said Sir became indebted to several Persons, and in 1674, upon Appl cation of his Creditors, and with his own Corifent, an Act of Parliament passed in Ireland, for veiling his Estate in certain Trustees, to be sold, for Payment of his Debts; but the Saving in the said Act was sufficient to preserve the Petitioner's Title: That the Petitioner's Father died in 1706, leaving issue the Petitioner, his only Son, and "five Daughters, all unprovided for; after whose Death the said Settlement was found amongst his Papers; and several of the moll eminent Lawyers in England are of Opinion, that the Petitioner's Right was preservd by the said laving Clause, and that the Trustees Power by the said Act determined upon the Death of the Petitioner's Father: That in the lad Sc-ffion of Parliament in Ireland the Creditors applied for a Second, Act (as they pretended) to explain the former, and prevailed so far, as to obtain an Act, to set aside the said Marriage Articles, and Settlement, without the least Pretence of Fraud, or any Regard to the Petitioner's Title, or giving him any Opportunity of trying his Right, either in Law or Equity; so that he is utterly - reined iless, unless relieved by the House, who are the great Prclervers of the People's Property: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the said Acts, and to restore the Petitioner to such Estate and Right, as he had before the passing

thereof, subject to such Regulations, as shall leem reasonable, he being willing to pay his Father's Debts, according to the Settlement and Provision for that: Pur-pple.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee, and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the same to the House.

Sir Robert Eden reported from the Committee, appointed to inspect the Laws relating to Servants, and to consider, how the same might be made more effectual; that they had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House: And1 which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and areas follow; viz.

Resolved, Tint, upon perusal of the Statute of the 5th of Queen Elizabeth, relating to Servants, it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Testimonial, therein mentioned, is deficient, for that it does not certify the Fidelity and good Behaviour of the Servant, thereby licenlld to depart from his or her Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all menial Servants be obliged to proeme a Testimonial of their Fidelity and good Behaviour in their Service, from which they depart, before they are capable ofbeing retained in any other Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That proper Otlicers be appointed for the regillering and preserving such Testimonials.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, upon the* said Resolutions; and that Sir Robert Eden, Mr. Byer/cy, and Mr. Pocklington, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Stuff-makers, Weavers,. Importing Dyers, Salters, and others, concerned in the Woollen l*ith Yarn; Manufacture, in the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that they understand, the Prohibition of the Importation of Irish Yarn is attempted, which, if effected, will ruin the Petitioners for want of Work, because Hands cannot be found here, to spin the Irish Wool, if brought over unwrought, and consequently they cannot have Yarn to carry on their Trades; nor can it be any Advantage to the Nation, because, without it, we cannot make so great a Quantity of the Woollen Manufactures, as foreign Parts require; and if they should be made without it, they will be at so dear Rates, that Foreigners will undersell us abroad: And praying the Consideration of the House therein, so as not to suffer the Petitioners to be undone, and made miserable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Fund, not exceeding £.80,000 Annum,

be applied to the Payment of Annuities for the said Ninety-nine Years, which any Persons will voluntarily purchase, towards railing any Sums not exceeding One million Two hundred Eighty thousand Pound.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That out of the said Purchase-money Provision be made of so much, as shall be necessary to be reserved to make good the quarterly Payments of the said Annuities, lo to be purchased, till the said yearly Fund can take place for discharging the fame, and that the rdidueof the said Purchase-money be applied towards her Majesty's Supply, for carrying on the War.

A Petition of the Gun-makers, and Gun-lock-makers, in and about the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, on behalf of themselves, and many Hundreds of Workmen of the said Trades in and about the said Town, and Towns adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that upon false Suggestions a Charter was granted by King Charles the ad, in the 13th Year of his Reign, to such Persons, as did then, or should, use the Art of Gun-making within the City of London, and Liberties thereof, and four Miles Compass, and all such others, as should be admitted, pursuant to the Charter: That the said Company of Gun-makers have as much imposed upon their Fellow-subjects in the Exercise of their Charter, as they did upon the Government, when they obtained it, pretending, they made better Guns, and enough to supply all Exigences of the Government; yet, during the last and tins present War, the Petitioners have made great Quantities yearly, wherewith the Government and Merchants have been supplied; but the Gun-smiths of London (by reason all Fire-arms must be proved by their Proof'-master) put such Hardships upon the Petitioners, and so beat down their Prices, and totally obstruct their Trade to the Plantations, that they (besides their Dependents) being about 400, must remove into some other Nation, unless relieved therein: And praying, that

Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, or C-lause in a Bill, to relieve the Petitioners from the Discouragements and Hardships they labour under.

The Lord Coningsby, acquainted the House, that her Answer to Majesty had been pleased to fend by him her Answer to Address re-their Address, of the third Inltant, That her Majesty {peeling War would be pleased to order an Account to be laid before ,n bpdm* this House, how it came to pass, that there were no more English Forces in Spain and Portugal at the Time of the Battle of Almanza; and that her Majesty would be pleased to use her utmost Endeavours, that the War in Spain might be vigoroully and effectually prosecuted.

And he delivered the same to Mr. Speaker, who read the same to the House; which is as followethviz.

ANNE, R.

HER Majesty, having considered the Address of the House of Commons, presented to her the fifth Inltant, hath directed the following Answer to be returned:

In relation to that Part, which concerns the Prosecution of the War in Spain, her Majesty is pleased to acquaint the House, that, as the restoring the Spanijk Monarchy to the House of Austria, and thereby the Balance of Power in Europe, was the principal Inducement of the present War, so her Majesty is sensible, that on the Succels thereof, not only the Trade and Tranquillity, but even the Security, of Great Britain (subject to the divine Providence) do in a great Measure depend and therefore her Majesty can never be wanting to continue her utmost Endeavours (as her Commons have desired) to prosecute with Vigour and Effect a War of such a Nature and Consequence, or to excite her Allies, upon all Occasions, to concur with her Majesty's Endeavours in that behalf.

And as to the Account, how it came to pass, that there were no more English Forces in Spain and Portugal at the Time of the Battle of Almanza, her Majesty cannot but be very much concerned to find, that Matter has not been fully Hated to the House; and, to the end the same may be set in the clearefi Light, for the Satil-fastion of herself, and her Subjects, hath caused an Enquiry to be made of the Regiments, that were intended to compose the Number of Twenty-nine thousand Three hundred and Ninety-five Men, mentioned in the Address (in which Number are included Officers, and their Servants, making a full fourth Part of the Whole, according to the Establishment, and Allowance always made on the Mufiers) and how many of them were in Spain,

' or

X

552

18° Februarii.

A. 1707.

AnfW«r to or Portugal, in January, 1704, when the Resolutions Address re- were taken to make Provision for their Pay, and what jjf^War Regiments have been sent thither tinee that Time; wherein pain. it may appear, what Numbers of Men could rea-

lonably be expected to be in Spain or Portugal, on the 14th Day of April, 1707 (when the said Battle happened) and what Diligence hath been used towards making up the said whole Number, for which Provision was made by Parliament. Upon which Enquiry it appears.

That the said Body of 29,395 Forces were in-

tended to consist of One Regiment of Horse, Five Regiments of Dragoons, and One-and-thirty of Foot, in all, Thirty-seven Regiments.

That the said Thirty-seven Regiments were to be made up of One Regiment of Horse, Four Regiments of Dragoons, and Nineteen Regiments of Foot, which had served in Portugal and Spain under the respective Commands of the Earls of Peterborow and Galway, and would, if compleat, have amounted to 18,852 Men; and of One Regiment of Dragoons, and Ten Regiments of Foot, which had been sent the Year before to Portugal, under the Command of Earl Rivers, and, if they had arrived compleat in Spain, would have amounted to 8,833 Men; and of two Regiments, making together 1,710 Men, which were designed to be new-raised in England: So that, in case all these Thirty-seven Regiments could have been completed, they would have made up the said whole Number of 29,395 Forces, in-

cluding Officers, and their Servants.

Her Majesty is further informed by the Lord -ley, who was Lieutenant General, and Colonel (Fade, who was Adjutant General, that as to the said Regiments, which had served in Spain under the Earl of Peterborow, and those which had served in Portugal and Spain under the Earl of Galway, the Officers, and their Servants, with the private Soldiers, which remained in those Regiments at the Time of the said Provision made by Parliament, did amount in the whole to Twelve thousand and Seventeen, besides 1,790 Prisoners, which belonged to those Regiments, in all 13,807 Men, or thereabouts, and no more, altho* in the Years 1704, 1705, and 1706, several Recruits, amounting to 3,490 Men, had been sent into Spain and Portugal, by Draughts made out of the (landing Regiments of England and Ireland, as a particular Favour to the Service in Spain, and never practised in' any other Cafe, but once to the Indies.

That as to the said Regiment of Dragoons, and Ten Regiments of Foot, which Were sent in the Year 1706 under Earl Rivers into Portugal, and consequently were near at hand to be transported to Spain, for immediate Service, the said Earl Rivers received her Majesty's Commands lo timely, that he arrived'with them in the Kingdom of Valentia about the latter End of January, 170?-; and altho' these Regiments, when they (ailed from 7*or bay for Portugal, were, by Draughts, completed to the Number of 8,297 Men (including Officers, and Servants) and, if that Number had arrived in Spain, would have made up about 22,104 Troops; yet, loon

after the* Arrival of the said Forces with Earl Rivers in Valencia, they were found to be reduced by Death, or otherwise, to about 4,500 Men, including Officers, and their Servants; and therefore 'twas thought convenient, at the Beginning of the Year 1707, to take the common Soldiers, which remained in Six Regiments of Foot, then in Valentia and , and distribute

them towards tilling up several of the rest of the Regiments then there, and to fend the Officers of the said Six Regiments, with the Officers of the Earl of Barrymore's late Regiment of Foot (which had the Year before been converted into one of Dragoons by the Earl of Peterborow) into England, to raise their Regiments intirely of new Men; which Officers arrived in England about May, and June, 1707, and soon after had their Recruiting Orders, and have ever since been employed in that Service, except those of the Regiment of Barry-

more, which is some time since embark'd for Portugal: So that it was impossible, that the new-raised Soldier* of those Seven Regiments could be in Spain or Portugal at the Time of the said Battle.

That, upon duly weighing the Premises, it doth not appear to her Majesty, how there could reasonably be expected of English Forces in Spain or Portugal at the Time of the Battle of Almanza (which happened (o loon after the Provision made by Parliament) any more effective Men, than could be supplied by the said 13,807 Men, including Officers, Servants, and Prisoners, before commanded by the Earls of Peterborow and Gallway respectively, and by the said Number of about 4,500 (including Officers, and Servants) which remained of the Forces, that went under Earl Rivers, as aforesaid.

That as to the Two new Regiments, which were intended to be raised, and to make 1,710 Men, Part of the said 29,395 English Forces, it was found to be for the

Advantage of the Publick, in respect of the apparent Difficulties of railing them in concurrence with the Men of the said Seven Regiments, to apply the Money, given for the said Two Regiments, to other Uses of the War, according to the Libert}', given by Authority of Parliament in that behalf.

That, when the making of Recruits grew extremely difficult, if not impradlicable, and the making Draughts from Handing Regiments had been found ruinous to the Service, her Majesty caused four Regiments, which were on the Irish Establishment, to be completed, and the Levy-money for completing the fame, and the growing Charge of their Pay, to be placed on the Savings of the Non-effedlivcs of the Spanish Establishment; which four Regiments, as a Reinforcement, embark'd in April, 1707, and arrived in Portugal in June following, and ought to be reckoned as so many Recruits, towards making up the said Number of 29,395 English Forces.

That, since the Arrival of the said Four Regiments in Portugal, Three other Regiments have been prepared, to wit, that of Barrymore, upon the Spanish Establishment, that of Paston, taken from the Establishment of Guards in England, and that of Wynn, taken from the Establishment of the Forces in Ireland, which have been embarked for some time for Portugal, as another Reinforcement for the Service of the said War.

That, as soon as her Majesty had the News of the Battle of Almanza, (he applied herself immediately to obtain such foreign Troops, as were nearest at hand, to supply that Loss; and hath agreed for 7,000 Palatines, 3,000 Germans, and 1,200 Italians; the greatest Part of which have been embarked ever since November last for Catalonia, and the rest are ready for Embarkation, as soon as there is an Opportunity: Besides which, her Majesty hath made Application to the Emperor for 6,000 Germans more, with an Offer to pay all, or such Part of them, as his Imperial Majesty can spare for that Service.

And, upon the whole Matter, refledling impartially upon the Situation of this necessary War in Spain and Portugal, and upon the Difficulties, wherewith, for the Time pall, the Men have been supplied from England and Ireland, and considering the Losses and Accidents, which have attended the Service in Parts so remote, and the Provision made for foreign Forces for the future, her Majesty allures herself, it will be very evident, that no Care has been wanting to support the War in Spain and Portugal in the most effectual Manner.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morn-

ing next, take her Majesty's said Answer into Consideration.

Sir Humphry Maekworth (according to Order) re-

ported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, and also of the Merchants, Clothiers, and other Traders in the Woollen Manufactures, within the City of Exon, and Parts adjacent, and other Petitions, against the Importation of Irish Yarn, were referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Tablej where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, that great Quantities of Worsted Yarn, and also of Bay or Woollen Yarn, have lately been imported into Bristol, Minehead, and other Ports.

That Irish Bay or Woollen Yarn may legally be imported, paying but a small Duty; but yet great Quantities of Worsted Yarn are imported under the Denomination of Bay Yarn, paying the like Duty only, tho' it iseafy to distinguish the one from the other.

That Irish W ^rfted Yarn is fold cheaper 6 d. per Pound, than our English Worsted Yarn can be afforded, and of

equal Goocincfs; by which means the Weavers make up their Worsted Stuffs, without employing the poor Combers, Spinners, and other Labourers in the Woollen Manufactures, as usually, who are thereby reduced to great Necessities, for want of Work.

That combed Wool, imported from Ireland, is fold cheaper than our English Wool, by a Peny in the Pound.

That the Labour of Worsted Yarn is at lead 4^. per Pound cheaper in Ireland, than , for the middle

Sort, which is most used, and 6 8 10 and more,

for the finer Sorts, and Woollen Yam 2 d. per Pound.

That it appeared to the Committee by an Account, taken out of the Custom-house' Books at Bristol, that there had been imported there, between 1707, and the 24th of November following, 1,381 Packs of Woollen and Worsted Yarn, each Pack containing 240 lb. Weight.

That the Importation of Irish Worsted Yarn is a growing Evil, and yearly increases, and, if not speedily remedied, will utterly impoverish the Labourers in the Woollen Manufactures in the Western Parts of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Report be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Garbling A Petition of Thomas Peter , James

Spic«s. Birkell, and Nathaniel Candy, of London, Gentlemen* was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, observing, that the Act, made i° Jac. I. for the well garbling of Spices, was duly observed by all Persons in London, except the East India Company, with whom the City Garbler did not care to contend, brought several Informations in the Exchequer against the said Company, for Breach of the said Law, as by that Law they are authorized to do, and have been at great Charge in the Prosecution thereof, the said Company being a Body corporate, and no Process to issue against their Persons, thinking to weary out all Persons seeking Right by Law, and to bring them to their own Terms: That the Petitioners are informed, there is a Bill in the House, which will discharge the said Informations, if itfhould pass :That the Petitioners conceive, they have a Right to the Part given to Informers, for Breach of the said Law (which is very useful) and this House has always preserved to the Subjects their just Rights, even when the Execution of an Act has been thought a Grievance, as it fell out, when the Alnage Duty was taken away, and other Instances: That if the said Informations should (by Authority of Parliament, ex post fa SI o') be discharged, the same will discourage forever all Persons from bringing any Informations for the Breach of any Law; and particularly against the said Company, who would not scruple to break through their own Act, but all other Laws, with Impunity: And praying, that the Petitioners said Rights by Law, in nefpeft of the said Informations, may be preserved to them, and that they may be heard by their Counsel in Maintenance thereof.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Consideration of the Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for repealing the Act, of the first Year of King James the First, intituled, An Act for the well garbling of Spices, is committed;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Balloting Box, and Balls, be prepared.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That two Clerks attend the Balloting, one to deliver the Balls to the Members, the other to carry the Box.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That two Members of the House be appointed by the Speaker to attend the Box.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That each Member present his Hand bare and open, to receive the Ball, and that he hold it up between his Finger and Thumb, before he put his Hand into the Box: and that the Box be immediately after brought to the Table, and the Votes counted there by the Clerks, in the Presence of the said two Members.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Members fit in their Places, till the Votes are given, and the Affirmative, or Negative, declared by the Speaker.

The Lord Coningsby acquainted the House, that their Answer t* Addresses to her Majesty, of the eighteenth of Decem~ renewed ber and twelfth of January last, having been renewed, Adressu. according to their Order; her Majesty had been pleased to give the Answer following; viz.

That in relation to that Part of the Address, which concerns the Forces of the King of Spain, her Majesty has ordered to be laid before the House a List of the Troops, provided by the King of Spain for the Service of the Year 1707; and in relation to the Troops of Portugal, her Majesty has, ever since the Treaty with that Crown, given Directions to her Ministers there, to use all possible Means, that his said Majesty should furnish the whole Number of Men agreed for by the said Treaty; and her Majesty hopes, that those Instances have in a great Measure had their desired Effect.

At the same time her Majesty observes, that the Methods of Discipline there make it impossible to know the Number of those Troops with the same Exactness, as is practised in other Parts; and considering, with what Chearfulness, and Success, they marched through Spain to Madrid, and the Losses they sustained, and being very well allured, that the King of Portugal has lately raised, and is still raising, a considerable Number of Forces, her Majesty has not thought it adviseable to make too nice an Enquiry into the State of those Troops, especially since Ihe is very fenlible, how diligent the Enemy is in making continual Application to break an Alliance, of so great Importance to the common Cause.

Memorandum: That, since her Majesty's happy Accession to the Throne, there has been granted by Parliament in Land Taxes, exclusive of what was granted this Session, Eleven million Nine hundred Thirty-five thousand Three hundred Twenty-two Pounds, and Four Shillings; out of which there has been paid into the Exchequer Ten millions Six hundred Eighty-four thousand Seventy-one Pounds, Six Shillings, and Seven Pence, including Three-hundred Twenty-three thousand Two hundred Forty-eight Pounds, Six Shillings, and One 7 C Peny,

a3* Februarii.

Peny, being the Allowance of Six-pence Half-peny in the Pound to Receivers, Collectors, and Commissioners Clerks, and also including what the Land Taxes fell short in the Year 1702, and 1703, by Certificates in Abatement of the personal Estates, which were those Years charged in the Subsidy Acts.

And this honourable House may please to observe, that, except the Arrear of this Year 1707, which is now daily paying, and the lad Quarter not payable to the Receivers till Lady-day next, there is not unpaid to her Majesty, upon all the Land Taxes, above Ninety thousand Pounds; which is constantly bringing in, and in no danger of being loft.

Sir Robert Davers reported from the Committee, to Manner of whom the Petition of divers Waggoners, and Carriers of Goods, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to highway them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House:

And he read the same in his Place, and after delivered them in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, to whom the Petition of divers Waggoners, and Carriers of Goods, was referred, hav- ing heard the Petitioners and their Witnesses, the Matter of their Complaint, upon Examination, appeared to be as followeth; viz.

Mr. Henry Norman said, that one John , endeavouring to comply with the Clause in the Act, obliging Waggons to be drawn with double Shafts, or a Pole between the Wheel Horses, killed several of his Horses:

As also one Anthony Webb had three of his'killed in drawing with double Shafts; which is perfectly impracticable, it being impossible to turn in many Places upon the Roads, or into most of Inn Yards, without widening their Gates:

And that the Informers follow the Waggoners upon all the Roads, and have dogg'd his Waggon from London to BriJIol, tho' their Habitations are in of near

London:

And that about nine Months ago one William hampton, a common Informer, took away his Horses out of his Team near Twyford, in Parish, in

Berkshire, and the Beginning of Oft last did the fame

Thing at Hounslow, in HeJJien Parish, and the 23d of the same Month he took another Horse out of his Team, and demanded of him £.6 for three Defaults against the Act, tho' at those Seizures he had but five Horses in his Waggon, and therefore, he said, he seized, for that the Waggon was not drawn by double Shafts, or a Pole:

That his Waggon being in Company with fix more upon the Road, the said Polhampton obliged the Six to buy their Liberty of proceeding upon their Journey; and because he, the said Norman, would not so do, Polhampton seized, and took away, one of the Horses out of his Team.

Mr. Math. Lancaster said, that he, being desirous to avoid the vexatious Proceedings of the Informers, had a Pole fixed to his Waggon, according to the Direction of the Act, and, before he had drawn two Miles, the Pole broke one of his Horses Shoulders.

That the said Polhampton, flopping his Waggon at Enfeild, took away two of his Horses, because he had not double Shafts; whereby his Journey wa* stopt, till his Waggoner gave the said Polhampton a Note for the Payment of £. 12, and he afterwards arrested the Waggoner, and his Matter was forced to bail him.

Mr. Edward Edwards said, that upon the 12th of June last, Mr. Polhampton took away one of his Horses out of his Team, tho' he had but seven Horses, and those double to the Waggon.

Equivalent The House (according to Order) proceeded to take for Scotland. jn^0 Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Representation of the Commissioners of the Equivalent, and Papers and Petitions relating the reunto, were referred.

And the said Report was read, as is as. followeth; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, that by the Terms of the Treaty of Union the Subjects cf Scotland, for preserving an Equality of Trade throughout the united Kingdom, would be liable to several Customs and Excises, then payable in England, which would be applicable towards- Payment of the Debts of England, contracted before the Union; it was by the 15th Article of the Treaty of Union agreed, that ScotlandIhould have an Equivalent for what the Subjects thereof should be charged towards Payment of the Debts of England, viz. the Sum of £.398,085. ioj. together with the whole Increase of the Revenues, Customs, and Duties on Import and Export, and Excise on cxcifable Liquors in Scotland, to t lie Uses following;

1. To Losses, which private Persons might sustain

by reducing the Coin of Scotland to the Standard and Value of the Coin of En

2. In the next place, to the capital Stock of the African and Indian Company of Scotland:

3. In the third place, £.2,000 Annum, for Seven Years, to be applied towards encouraging the Manufacture of coarle Wool:

4. In the fourth place, Allowance for the Charge of the Commissioners, Secretaries, and Accornplants, to the last: two Treaties of Union.

Then the Overplus of the said Equivalent should be equally divided;

One hall to the Debts upon the Civil List,

The other half to the Debts due to the Army.

That, pursuant to the said 15th Article of the Treaty of Union, the Parliament of Scotland then being did by an Act, intituled, "An Act concerning the publick " Debts," declare, and ordain, that such Debts only, as were due to the Civil List, and Army, since the 27th of May, 1689, or such other Debts, as should be in-strudled to be publick Debts, in manner therein after mentioned, since the time aforesaid, should be understood publick Debts of the said Kingdom, payable out of the Funds therein mentioned.

That the Committee also took into their Consideration, how far the Commissioners for the Equivalent have complied with their Commission in the Disposition of the said Sum of £.398,085. ior.

In order to which, the Committee have examined into the several Particulars of the Representation, delivered to this House by the said Commissioners, and are as followeth; viz.

That as to what remains unpaid to the African Company, the Commissioners could not pay the same, by reason the Persons,' to whom the same was due, have not exhibited their Claim, or made good the fame, thereunto.

Upon this Head the Committee crave Leave to observe, that by the 15th Act of the last Session of the last Parliament of Scotland, on Payment of the said Sum of £.232,884. 5*. 4 \d. to the Company, all the

Goods of the said Company are declared to belong to the Queen, and appropriated to certain Uses in the Act mentioned; but the Commissioners for the Equivalent have not given any Estimate of the Value thereof, the same chiefly conlifting in decayed Ships, and bad Debts, so that no particular Account can as yet be taken; but the Commissioners do believe, the same will amount to a very inconsiderable Sum.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that there is £. 800 remaining in the Hands of the said Commissioners Out of the Sum, allowed for Payment of the African Company, which the Commissioners say, they cannot lafely dispose of, without a further Power.

That by the said 15th Act the Directors of the African Company are to make up several Accounts by the ift of May, 1707, and the Commissioners are to pay them £.300 for that Service, which they have accordingly done; but the said Directors could not make up the said Accounts in so short a Time, as the Act directed, but it took up Six Months more after the ift of , and the Directors demand £-500 more for that Service; but the Commissioners, tho they think it reasonable, the Directors should be paid for that Service, yet, being tied down by the aforesaid Act, they cannot relieve them, without further Power.

That by the 15th Article of Union, and by the Act passed in Scotland, concerning publick Debts, there is to be paid, for promoting the Manufacture of coarie Wool, £.2,000 yearly, for Seven Years; but the Commissioners for the Equivalent do say, that neither the Articles of Union, nor Acts of Parliament, have directed, to whom the said £. 2,000 per Annum should be paid; so that the Commissioners conceive, they cannot pay any Part thereof, without further Directions by Parliament.

That by the 15th Article of Union, and the aforesaid Act of Parliament, concerning publick Debts, it is provided, that after Payment of, t. The Loss on the Coinage: adly, The African Company:

The other half to pay the Debts due to the Army. And, in case such Overplus shall not be sufficient to pay the same, then the Increase of the Customs, and other Moneys, arising to Scotl, shall be equally divided, and applied, til! the said Debts be fully satisfied.

That the Overplus of the £.398,085. for. appears to be £. 70,681. 3 r. 2 d.which by the aforesaid Act is to be distributed in manner following:

lft. The Sum of £. 24,736. 12/. 2 to such as represented her Majesty, or the late King, being a preferred Debt on the Civil List:

Memorandum: This Article the Commissioners have paid:

ad'y. The Sum of£. 90,925. 4*. 8 for Fees, Salaries, Pensions, and other Claries, on the Civil List:

3<dly, The Debt £. 107,437, which is the Debt due to the Army in fevferal Claries.

That, as to the Debt upon the Civil List, the Lords of the Treasury of Scotland, delivered to the Commissioners for the Equivalent an Account of what was due to the Persons upon the Civil List, for the Term of 1707: in which said Account there are Blanks left for several Sums, and likewise they have not distinguished in the said Account, what Debts are due upon the several Claries; so that, till those Blanks are filled up, and the Debts upon the several Claries are distinguished, the Commissioners for the Equivalent cannot make any Payment upon the Civil List, or the Army: They do therefore desire the Direction of the House in that Matter.

That, as to the Debt due to the Army, which is to be paid in several Claries, pursuant to the 15th Article of the Union, and the 16th Act of Parliament in Scotland, the Lords of the Treasury there delivered to the said Commissioners an Account of Arrears due to the Army since the 27th of May, 1689; in which laid Account there are likewise Blanks left for several Sums, neither have they distinguished, what Debts are due upon the several Claries; so that the same Difficulty lies upon the Commissioners for the Equivalent in paying the Debt due to the Army, as upon the Civil List: They therefore crave the Direction of the House herein.

That the Reason, why the Lords of the Treasury have not been able to give complete Lifts, either of the civil or military Debts, being the backwardness of those Persons concerned to come in, and make good their several Pretensions before them, it seems necessary, there should be a Day appointed, betwixft and which, if the Persons concerned do not appear before them, and make good their Pretensions, their Lordships be impowered to close their Lifts, and give them in, so signed, to the Commissioners j who shall be warranted to proceed in Payment according to such Lift, without regard to such, as shall neglect to make good their Claims.

That the Commissioners for the Equivalent do represent, that by the 16th Act of Parliament in Scotland, if there shall be a Sum in their Hands, as will not compleatly answer the two Claries last mentioned, it does not thereby appear, that they are impowered to pay any of the said Claries, in Proportion to the Money in their Hands; so that the said Commissioners will be obliged to retain such Remainder in their Hands, till the other Moneys, arising to Scotland, coming in, shall make up a Sum sufficient to pay those Claries j which will be detrimental to the Persons concerned, without some Remidy be applied.

Vof.. IS.

That by the said 16th Act it is provided, that, after Equivalent Payment of Five Articles before-mentioned, the Com- for Scotland, missioners of the Equivalent shall pay such publick Debts, as are due by the Nation since May, 1689, which do neither fall under the Civilfor Military, Lift.

That the Committee do observe, that in the Account of the Civil List there is an Article, mentioning her Majesty's Bounty on the Charity Roll, but a Blank is left for the Sum; and the same being so far postponed, that there is no Probability of their getting Relief that way, the Commissioners for the Equivalent, out of Com-passion to the starving Condition of those poor People, do humbly represent their same to the House.

That the Commissioners do also crave the Direction of the House in relation to Salaries, and Pensions, due after the first of May (the Time, when the Union commenced) whether the Lords of the Treasury ought to have taken notice of those Pensions, and Salaries, due from the Term of Martinmas to which

was the 15th Day of May, 1707, and whether the Moneys upon the Equivalent shall answer what accrued due after the lft Day of May: But it was observed by some of the Committee, that the Salaries and Pensions, mentioned in the Lift delivered by the Lords of the Treasury, are therein certified as Debts charged upon the Equivalent, notwithstanding the re were Funds current for the Payment thereof.

That by the 15th Article of Union it is provided, that the Remainder of the said Equivalents, and other Sums arising to Scotland by the Articles of Union, be wholly applied towards the encouraging the Fisheries, and such other Manufactures and Improvements in Scotland, as may most conduce to the general Good of the united Kingdom.

That it appeared to the Committee, that the Commissioners for the Equivalent have expended considerabl©

Sums in executing their Commission, being necessary Allowance for Servants, and other incident Charges, amounting in the whole to £. 1,060, and there is no Provision made, neither by the Articles of Union, or any subsequent Acts or Orders of Parliament.

That the Committee, in pursuance to the Order of this House, took into Consideration the Petition of Captain Theodore Drury, her Majesty's chief Engineer in the North of Great Britain, also the Petition of Mr. Alexander Cunningham.

Sir Humphry Mackworth reported from the Committee, appointed to receive Proposals in relation to the covering the Cupolo of St. Paul's Church, London; that they had received Proposals accordingly, and had thereupon come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House: And which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered the said Proposals, and Resolution, in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as followeth; viz.

That the Committee had, pursuant to the Order of the House, received two Proposals, the one, for covering the said Cupolo with Lead, the other with Copper; which the Committee had dire died to be reported to the House, and are hereunto annex'd.

The Estimate of Joseph Roberts, Plumber, for covering the Cupolo of St. Paul's Cathedral, , with

Lead, according to his Contract with the Commissioners for rebuilding the said Church, hearing date the 29th of August, 1707.

THE Area of the said Cupolo (the Moldings being girt) is about 30,000 Feet; to cover which, and to make due Allowances for Lappings and Moldings, will require about 170 Tons of Lead to be call, at 12 to the Foot, and the Charge of Lead, Sodder, Tacks, and Workmanship, will come to about f. 2,500, and and may be performed before Christmas, 1708, if not obstructed. The said Plumber also is ready (if required) to give sufficient Security, that the whole Charge shall not exceed that Sum; and, as he has, in pursuance of his laid Contract, bought the whole Quantity of byshire Lead, pick'd, and of the bell Sort, and has laid Part, and call and raised more, he humbly hopes, that nothing will be done to vacate his said Contract, in the Performance whereof he has made so great a Progress. Witness,

Wm. Dickmfon, Jof. Roberts.

Tho. Cooke.

14th 1707.

IN Obedience to an Order of a Committee of this honourable House, made on last, we, Samuel

Davis, and Co. have taken the Dimensions of the Cupolo of St. Paul's, and find, by the bed Computation we could make, that it contains 16,087 square Feet; which we humbly propose to cover, at two Shillings and four Pence per Foot, with the bell and fined British Copper, of twenty Ounces to a Foot Square, all Charge of Metal, Workmanship, Nails, &c. except Scaffolds; the Metal to be measured, and weighed, before 'tis laid on.

And we are humbly of opinion, that the Laps, Seams, and Cuttings, called Shruff, may amount to about 3,900 square Feet; in which same there may be used Nineteen thousand and Nine hundred and Eighty-seven square Feet; which, at two Shillings and four Pence-per Foot, is Two thousand Three hundred Thirty and one Pound, sixteen Shillings, and four Pence; the Proposers to take back the Cuttings, or Shruff, at fourteen Pence per Pound; and the Weight in Copper will be eleven Tons, Three hundred Three Quarters, and Seven Pounds; The Payments to be made, when- there shall be one fourth Part of the Work done, and so proportionably, according to the Custom of the Building; and no Ornaments to come within this Proposal, but only the Covering } and the whole Work to be done for Three thousand and Fifty Pounds; and the Nails to be Copper, of the same Fineness.

Samuel , and Co.

May it please your most excellent Majesty:

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons in Parliament assembled, having examined the Complaints of several Merchants against Captain William Kerr, late Commander of a Squadron of your Majesty's Ships of Wat in the West Indies, do beg Leave humbly to represent toyour Majesty, that it hath been fully proved, that the Trade to the West Indies, (so beneficial to all your Subjects) has been greatly obstructed and prejudiced by the said Captain William Kerr's exacting Sums of Money from the Merchants for Convoys.

And we do also humbly represent to your Majesty, that the requiring or demanding of Money for Convoys! is illegal, opprcfiive to the Merchants, and destructive to Trade.

We therefore, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Commons, humbly desire, that yotir Majesty would be graciously pleased not to employ the said Captain William Kerr in your Majesty's Service for the future.

The laid Address being read a Second timej An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " desire that," and inferring " address ourselves to" in (lead thereof.

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by adding, at the End thereof, " and that your Majesty will be pleased to give Orders, that he may " be prosecuted according to Law."

Arid the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

May it please your most excellent Majesty:

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons, in Parliament assembled, having examined the Complaints of several Merchants against Captain William Ketr, late Commander of a Squadron of your Majesty's Ships of War in the West Indies, do beg Leave humbly to represent to your Majesty, that it hath been fully proved, that the Trade to the West Indies (so beneficial to all your Subjects) has been greatly obstructed and prejudiced by the said Captain William Kerr's exacting Sums of Money from the Merchants for Convoys.

And we do also humbly represent to your Majesty, that the requiring or demanding of Money for Convoys is illegal, oppressive to the Merchants, and destructive to Trade.

We therefore, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Commons, humbly address ourselves to your Majesty, that you would be graciously pleased not to employ the said Captain William Kerr in your Majesty's Service for the future, and that your Majesty will be pleased to give Orders, that he may be prosecuted according to L§w.

T H AT of Eight-and-twenty Dutch, and fix English and Scotch Regiments, who came over with the late King William (of glorious Memory) upon the Resolution, twelve Regiments were font back to Holland in March, 1684, folly paid and cleared, without any Deduction; and the fix English and Scotch Regiments were in 1692 transferred to the English Establishment, under the Care of the E^rl of Ranelagh, and since fully cleared in Debentures; and one Troop and one Regiment of Dutch Horse Guards, and three Battalions of Foot Guards, were in March, 1699, dismissed the English Service, and fully cleared their Pretensions, in ready Money, by Vote of Parliament.

Thus One-and-twenty of the said Four-and-thirty Regiments being paid, there remain only thirteen Regiments, who had the Misfortune to be dismissed the English Service, upon the Peace of Ryjwick, without being cleared their Arrears for their long and faithful Services.

That, upon several prefiing Instances of the States General, by Letters from time to time to her Majesty, the Auditors of the Imprest have been directed to examine, and state, the Account of Receipts and Payments, of Jacob Vander Efch, who was by his late Majesty's Order appointed Paymaster to the Dutch, and

To the Right honourable Sidney Earl of , Lord High Treasurer of May it please your Lord fh ip:

IN Obedience to your Lordship's Commands, signified to us by Mr. Lowndes, we have considered the Memorial of Jacob Vander Efch, Esquire, late Paymaster to the Dutch Forces, and of his Cafe, and the Opinion of his Counsel thereupon s and are humbly of Opinion, that the Clause relating to Mr. Vander Efch, contained in the Act, made in the first Year of her Majesty's Reign, for dating the publick Accounts, is not any Objection against making up, and declaring, the said Mr. Vander Efch's Accounts, according to the Course of the Exchequer.

But, notwithstanding his Accounts should now be made up, and declared, according to the Course of the Exchequer, yet no Sum of Money can be imprested, issued, or paid, thereupon, till Provision be made for that Purpose by Act of Parliament.

All wh ch is most humbly submitted to your Lordship. Sim. Harcourt,

June 13th, 1707.

To her most excellent Majesty the Queen of Great Britain: Some Answers to the Observations, made by the Auditors of the Imprest to the Abstract of the regimental Accounts of the Dutch and other Forces under Mr. Vander Efch's Care, during the late War, most humbly offered by John Hallingins, authorized, as well

by the Regiments, still in Arrears, as by the States General of the United Provinces:

Most humbly Iheweth,

THAT, since it hath pleased your Majesty to order the Auditors of the Imprest, that an Abstract of the Debts, due to the Dutch Regiments, should be laid before your . so as it (lands before them, and your Petitioner finding, that the same are charged with many Observations, whereof most Part belongs to some Dutch and other Forces, already cleared at their Dismission;

Your Petitioner most humbly craves Leave to offer to your Majesty a Reply to the following Observations, relating to the Regiments still in Arrear;

1 Observation: Why those Regiments were paid full, without Muster-rolis, or Refpits.

To which is most humbly answered, that his late Majesty considering the great Charges those Dutch and German Regiments were at in making their Recruits all beyond Sea, in Holland, Germany, Prussia, and his late Majesty, out of good Husbandry, rather chose to allow those Forces their full Pay, since it is evident, that the Charges of making the le Recruits in these foreign Countries, and the Transportations thereof, would have amounted to a far greater Sum, than those Refpits could have reached; and therefore his Majesty thought fit to order Mr. Vander Efch, that all those Regiments should be paid full, in Consideration of which they should be obliged to find the Recruits at their own

Charge;

6 Ann.

25° Febr

575

Charge; by which great Sums have been laved to the Publick, and therefore rather was a Burthen, than an Advantage, to those Regiments, his Majesty making at the Beginning of each Campaign a very exact Review of those Forces, that no Men, nor Horses, could be wanting.

2d Observation: Why the Deductions of one Day's and Poundage had not fully been made.

To this Article of undeducted Poundage, being made up to a great Sum of £.69,197. 12 is most

humbly replied, that when, after the happy Resolution, his late Majesty kept those Forces in England, it was by meer Connivance of the States General, who at that then dangerous Conjuncture of Time were uneasy to be deprived of their bed Forces, and therefore demanded their Forces back, which appears by the twelve Dutch Regiments that were sent them back in March 1684; and the Stay of the rest being uncertain, his late Majesty could not bring those Forces upon a regular Establishment, but caused their Pay to be made to them by monthly Orders under his royal Sign manual, without Direction of any Deduction of one Day's Pay, and Poundage (his Majesty seeming unwilling, that those Forces, who had been assisting in (b glorious an Expedition, and whose Stay was always uncertain, should be charged with any Deduction) till they were lent to Ireland, and then by the States General Permission were ordered to make Oath of Fidelity to the late King, and the Crown of England, the Stales General being then provided with other German Forces in the Room of these Regiments; till then, I say. Poundage was not deducted, First, because Mr. Fander Efck had no Authority nor Diretion for the same: And Secondly, it agrees with very good Reason, that those Forces, who never could expet the Benefit of a Charge, designedly made for that Purpose, ought not to be charged therewith: And since it is evident, that the one Day's Pay, and Poundage, is made on purpose for the keeping of old and disabled Soldiers in and about Chelsea College, and partly for the Expence of the Pay Office, and Exchequer Fees, it is, under Submission, thought, that th Forces ought

not to be charged with such Deductions, since their disabled and superannuated Soldiers have no Title or Admittance to Chelsea College; and sincealfo Mr. Vander Efcb, as Paymaster, has had his Allowance out of their own Pay, without any Allowance from the Crown; for which Reason all the Dutch Regiments applied to his late Majesty for Relief, when after the Reduction of Ireland, the Irish Paymasters charged them with one Day's Pay, and Poundage; and his late Majesty from time to time promised them, that at a general Clearing such Deductions should be allowed them, if not fully, at least one Half thereof,

Befid'es, it appears, that out of the abovesaid great Article of undeducted Poundage there belongs to the Regiments, paid and cleared already,

1. To the 12 Dutch Regiments, £. s. d.

sent away in March, i68f - - 1,349 6 8

2. To the fix English and Scots Regiments, who were taken from

under Mr. Vander EJch'sCare - - 8,537 16 il

3. To the Dutch Troop and Regiment of Horse Guards, and Regiment of Foot Guards, who were

lent out of England in March, 1699 - 44,999 5 ioj

These Guards were cleared in the Year 1693 of all their Irish Arrears; till the last of March, 1692; since which Time they continued in English Pay till 25th March, 1699; and it was then thought an Hardship upon his late Majesty to part with them:

So that it is, with Submission, supposed, that, for their long and faithful Service about his royal Person, his Majesty thought fit to pay them their last Clearings, without Deri uction of one Day's Pay, and Poundage, as a Mark of his royal Vot. \&.

Tenderness and Bounty, especially, when an express Vote of the honourable House of Commons had made Provision for their full Pay.

4. Remains therefore chargeable upon the 13 Regiments (till in Arrear, to compleat that above great Article, only - - - - 14,311 4

Arrears of Dutch Regiments.

£.69,197 12 ioi

And this only out of their Pay, and Clearings, made to them from the ift of January, 1684, to the sundry Times in the Year 1690, when sent to; since which 1

Times all Deductions have been made from them.

Here I take the Liberty most humbly to submit to your Majesty's Wisdom and Goodness, if it will consist either with Equity or Justice, that these poor 13 Regiments should now be charged with this Deduction, more than all the rest have been, and this to be taken out of their Arrears of the Year 1697, when it is evident, 1.

That these Regiments, from the Beginning of the Resolution till the End of the late War, have very faithfully served the Crown of England in all Actions, and great Part of them lost their Lives in this Service in Ireland, and in Flanders: Therefore, 2. It would be a very great Hardship to their Widows and Children, or Successors, if they should be made liable to a Deduction for the Year 1689, and this from a then compleat Pay, and Clearing, which Clearing was taken for granted, and never since thought of, 3. And this Hardship would be the greater to the Officers now in being, when it appears by Mr. Hills Account, that of this great Debt £.81,039. is. are barely Arrears of Subsiste nee; so that the Officers were obliged to take up Money on great Interest, to keep their Men from starving; which Interest amounted, from the Year 1697 to December, 1701, to upwards of £. 16,000, and far exceeds the Poundage claimed from them.

All which is most humbly submitted to your Majesty's Equity and Justice; hoping, that your Majesty will be moved by the Sufferings these 13 Regiments have been, and are still, labouring under by being detained so long from the Payment of these Arrears; and that your Majesty will be pleased to recommend this just Debt to your present Parliament, that at last they may be relieved, by receiving in Army Debentures an equal Payment with the rest of the Army, for their long and faithful Service.

And your Petitioner, as in most humble Duty bound,

shall ever pray. J. Hallangins.

Afliburton The House proceeded (according to Order) to the Election, hearing of the Merits of the Election for the Borough of Ashburton, in the County of Devon.

And Counsel on both Sides attending, they were called in, and heard, and several Witnesses examined on both Sides, touching the Right of Election of the Voters for Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough. Voi. 15.

And then the Counsel withdrew.

A Motion being made, and the Question being pro* posed. That the Right of Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Ashburton, in the County of Devon, is in the Freeholders, having Lands, of Tenements, holden of the said Borough only;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Word " only

Which being opposed by divers Members, the Ballot* ing was demanded.

And then the Question being put. That the Word " only" stand part of the Question;

The Balloting was prepared, according to the Orders of the House for that Purpose; and Sir Godfrey Copley and Mr. Henley were appointed by Mr. Speaker to attend the Box: And the Clerk, and Clerk-assistant, went with the Box, and Balls, and the said Two Members with them, round the several Benches of the House; and the Members fitting in their Places, took the Balls, and put them into the Box: After which th Box was carried to the Clerk's Table; and after counting the Balls at the Table by the Clerks, in the Presence of the said two Members (who flood one at e^ch End of the Table) the two Members went to the Bar, and came up to the Table (as usual, on other Occasions of reporting) and reported to Mr. Speaker;

That the Yeas were 189, and the Noes 148.

V/hereupon Mr. Speaker declared the Numbers, and that the Yeas had it.

Then the main Question was put; and it was

Resolved, That the Right of Election of Members, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Ashburton, in the County of Devon, is in the Freeholders, having Lands, or Tenements, holden of the said Borough only.

Then the Counsel were called in again, and Mr;

Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution:'

Upon which the Counsel for the Petitioners said, they would not give the House any further Trouble.

And thereupon the Counsel on both Sides withdrew.

Resolved, That Roger Tuckfield, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Ashburton.

Ordered, That Mr. Johnson, Sir Richard Onslow, Mr. Gun-mak»rs,

Bulteel, Mr. Scobell, Serjeant Whit acre, Mr. Clayton, Mf. ^c> Kent, Colonel Byerley, Sir Robert Davers, Mr. Heytham,

Mr. Harvey, be added to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gun-makers, and Gun-lock-makers, in and about the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, on behalf of themselves, and many hundreds of Workmen of the said Trades in and about the said Town, and Towns adjacent, was referred.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

A Petition of the People, called Quakers, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Act for the Affirmation, instead of an Oath, granted to the said People in England, doth not extend (notwith-standing the Union of the two Kingdoms) to the said People in Scotland: That the kind Intention of Ease to the scrupulous Consciences, with respect to Oaths, which the Legislature of England manifested in the said Act towards the said People, hath not fully answered the good Design thereof, many of the said People, not only in the Northern Counties, but also in divers other Parts of England, remaining scrupulous of using the said Affirmation, even when their own Property is concerned, because they think the Title of the Act seems to intimate, as if it was an Oath, tho' not in usual Forms and that there are Expressions in the Affirmation itself, which are too much like an Oath: That in the Northern Part of Great Britain, called Scotland, the People, called Quakers, . , . all generally of the mind of those, who scruple the taking of the Affirmation in that Part of Great Britain called England: And praying, Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for their Relief both in.

England and Scotland.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for giving Ease to the People, called Quakers, in that Part of the united Kingdom, called Scotland, by establishing the same Affirmation to be taken there, which is en-> joined to be taken in England, instead of an Oath; and that Sir David Dalrymple, Mr. Conyers, and Mr. do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of Thomas Coutts, Gilbert and Fishery

William Gordon, Merchants, on behalf of themselves, and l£neourac«» other North Britains, concerned in the Fishing Trade, ment' was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by the eighth Article of the Act of Union all Fish, exported from Scotland beyond Sea, which shall be cured with.foreign Salt only, shall have the same Eases, Premiums, and Drawbacks, as are allowed to Exporters of the like Fish from England; and the Petitioners have cured, with foreign Salt only, several Quantities of White Herrings, and other Fish, for which there is an Allowance of Ten Shillings and Five Pence for every Barrel of White Herrings, so exported: And praying, they may be allowed the fame, and Relief in the Premises.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, that they did Yesterday attend her Majesty, and present their humble Address, returning to her Majesty the Thanks of this House for her taking Measures to restore the Affairs of Spain, and, for providing foreign Troops for that Service; and that her Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I have always looked upon the War of Spain to be of so great Importance to us, that I can never fail of continuing my utmost Application to support it in the most effectual Manner.

The Satisfaction, you have expressed in your Address, for my Endeavours in this Matter, is extremely acceptable to me.

Mr. Farrer reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for vacating the Settlement, made upon the Marriage of Henry Mayne, and for making a reasonable Provision for the Maintenance of his only Son, (who is an Ideot) during his Life, was committed j that they had . examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that all the Parties concerned) except a Trustee, to preserve the contingent Remainders, who is really not now concerned, a Son being born, and alive) had given their Consents to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that touching the said Trustee, who would not consent to the passing of the said Bill, the Committee had directed him to report the Matter specially to the House; and that the Committee had made several Amendments to the Bill, which they had directed him to report to the House: Which Report, and Amendments, he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the said Amendments were once read throughout, and then a Second time, one by one, and, upon the Question feve-.rally put thereupon, agreed unto by the f)ouse.

And the said Report is as followeth:

That the Committee conceived, there was no need of the Consent of the surviving Trustee, John Nether coat, in this Cafe, because the Trust of Nethercoate is determined by the Birth of the Ideot, and the Death of his Mother; the Custody of the Ideot's Person, and Management of such Estate, as he may have after his Father's Death, being in her Majesty's Disposal, who hath given Leave for this Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments,' be ingrossed.

That it appeared to the Committee, by an Act of Parliament, made in the first Year of her present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for making Provision for the Protestant Children of the Earl of Clanriccard, and Lord Bophin-, which said Act restores the Lord Bophin to his Estate, upon Payment of £.25,000 within the Space of one Year, by Sale, or Mortgage, as the Trustees, thereby appointed, should think fit.

That it also appeared to the Committee, by one other Act, made in the said first Year of her present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for advancing the Sales of the forfeited Estates in Ireland-, in which Ad there is a Clause, impowering the Protestant Trustees, as were appointed pursuant to the said former Act, to raise £.25,000 by Sale of Part of the Lord Bophin's Estate, with Interest at Six per Cent, from the 25th of March, 1703, at three Payments, the last Payment to be on , Vqt, 15,

or before the first of June, 1704, in English Money; and, for default of Payment, all the Premitfes, mentioned in the said former Act, should be veiled in her Majesty, for the Use of the Publick.

That, upon the Credit of the aforesaid Acts, the Petitioners did purchase a considerable Part of the said Lord Bophin's Estate, and by several Payments, made on or before the 10th Day of July, 1704, did pay into the Exchequer \ta Ireland, for the Use of the Publick, the

Sum of£.26,345. is. 6d. as Money valued in Ireland, as appears by an Account, delivered to the Committee by tire Hands of John Stanton, Esquire, and signed by John Pratt, Deputy Receiver General in Ireland-, but £.681,

Part of the said £.25,000 and Interest, not being paid before the said first of June, the said Estate became forfeited in the Crown.

That the Petitioner, Michael Burk, Esquire, attended the Committee, and gave his personal Consent, that a Bill might be brought in, for Relief of the Protestant Purchasers against the Forfeiture, that accrued by the Non-payment of the £.25,000 at the Times appointed by the aforesaid Acts of Parliament.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the Relief of the several Petitioners against the Forfeiture, vested in the Crown by the Non-payment of the £.25,000 at the Times appointed by an Act, made in the first Year of her Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for making Provision for the Protestant Children of the Earl of Clanricard, and Lord Bophin.

And the House being moved accordingly;

Mr. Stanley reported from the Committee, to whom Paterforfs, the Petitions of William Paterjon, and Alexander Grant, &c- Claim*. Esquires, were referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House:

And he read the Reports, and Resolutions, in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Cleric's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

That, upon the Petition of William Paterjon, Esquire,

The Committee having taken into Consideration the Matters contained in the said Petition,

It appeared, that the Petitioner hath been at very great Expence and Pains, and sustained very considerable Losses, on Account, and at the Instance, of the African and Indian Company of Scotland.

That on the 13th of August, 1707, the Petitioner delivered a Representation to the Directors of the African and Indian Company of Scotland, in the Effect following:

That by the Conditions of the Subscriprions of £.300,000 taken at London the 6th of November, 1695, a Part of the then intended Sum of £.600,000 Sterling for the Capital of that Company, it was agreed, that in regard the Petitioner had been at great Pains and Expence in making considerable Discoveries of Trade and Improvements in and to both the Indies, and likewise in procuring needful Powers and Privileges, for a Company of Commerce, from several sovereign Princes and States, that therefore the Petitioner should have 2 per Cent, of the Money, to be subscribed into the said capital Fund, as also 3 per Cent, of the Produce of the said Fund fot Twenty-one Years, but redeemable for 2 per Cent, more of the said Fund at any Time in five Years.

That the said Subscription, by reason of the great Opposition it met with, being broken, and relinquished, the Petitioner was nevertheless, at the earned Solicitations and Request of those principally concerned in Scotland, prevailed upon to take a Journey from London into Scotland, for the Company's Service.

That upon the 6th of October, 1696, the Court of Directors of the said Company, takino the Petitioner's same into Consideration, come to this following Resolution; viz.

" This Court considering the great Expence, that " Mr. William Paterjon, one of the Directors of tlxs " said Company, hath been at for several Years past,

" in making valuable Discoveries of Commerce to both " Indies-, and he having delivered in several curious " Manuscripts, Books, Maps, Journals, and other Papers of Commerce, relating thereto, henceforth to be " appropriated to the Company's Use; and having further evidenced his Affection to his native Country,

and this Company, by relinquishing , and

" any profitable Establishment he had, or may at present have, in that Kingdom, to his evident Damage " and Loss; therefore the said Court of Directors da " hereby allow the said William Paterjon to transfer and " dispose of the Sum of £. 15,000 Sterling of the Subscriptions, now vested in this Court of Directors, that " is to say, of the Eighty-five thousand Pounds of such " Englisho Subscriprions, as are not yet disposed of by " this Court, and to take, and apply to his own proper " Use, the first quarter Part thereof, extending to the " Sum of Three thousand Seven hundred Fifty Pounds Sterling, together also with the like Sum of Three " thousand Seven hundred Fifty Pounds Sterling, being the first quarter Part of the Sum, subscribed by him,

" the said William Paterjon, James Smith, Daniel Lodge,

" James Campbell, and Joseph Cohen d'Azevedo, Merchants in London, amounting in the whole to the Sum of £.7,500 Sterling.

" And further, for his Merit in contriving the principal Designs, and Constancy in promoting the Service,

" of this Company, the said Court of Directors have re- ‘

It appeared to the Committee, that, upon passing the Commission of Equivalent, the Petitioner repaired to Scotland \to receive his Claim; but some few of the Directors had, in the Absence of the Petitioner, and without including his Account, and Claim, made up, and certified the Company's general Account.

lylr. Dayrolle to Mr- Secretary Boyle.

Hogue, March T'T> 170-f.

Right honourable,

I have received by an Express, arrived Today from Brufflels, the inclosed Packet fqr you from Major General Cadogan, with Orders to forward it immediately to the Brill, and desire Monsieur Vanderpool to dispatch a Packet-boat on Purpose with it, as I have done accordingly, by Express. I fee the Major General is almost persuaded, the French defiejn to go on their Project, and d,efired me to press the States to dispatch immediately their Letters to the Province of Zeland, for having the re all possible Assistance in getting the necessary Shipping for an Imbarquation of Troops, and that their Orders may be repeated to the Commodore of their Squadron at Schyrvelt, to fail as soon as the Troops are on Board, with what Men of War he shall have ready what I have performed likewise by word of Mouth to the Pensionary, and by a little Memorial, delivered to the States, when they were fitting Today. After the wasrofe, the Pensionary came out,

and told me, as to the first Point, they have complied with it already, and were going to write again upon that Subject; and, as to the Second, that there are none of their Ships yet at Schonvelt, but would dispatch this very Day, by Express, new Orders to their Admiralties to work Night and Day, and spare no Expences, to fit out the Ships, designed for this present Service; and that the Commodore should have the Instructions, desired by Major General Cadogan. They have received this Morning a Letter from Admiral Bings, of the 28th February, giving Notice of his Arrival at Gravelines with ao Ships, which they believe almost sufficient to prevent the French prosecuting their Design; however, they allure me, they will continue their own Preparations with all possible Diligence. 1 suppose, you will hear from Major General Cadogan, that the pretended Prince of Wales is gone, or ought to go, the 8th Instant from Paris, to imbarque at Dunkirk, and that it was generally believe^ at present in France, that the Design was upon Scotland. The intended Departureof the said Prince has been confirmed an Hour ago, by a Courier, who left the Court of Lorraine Ihurfday last, and was sent to the Lorrain Envoy here, upon some particular Affairs of the Duke, his Master. I am, with all possible Respect,

Right honourable.

Your most humble

and most obedient Servant,

Ja. Dayrolle.

Major Cadogan's Letter to Mr. Secretary Boyle.

Sir, Br, to* , 1704.

I came hither from the Hague on Wednesday last, according to the Orders I had from his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, to be more at hand to find out the real Design of the Enemy's Preparations at Dunkirk. I received this Morning the inclosed Advices from different Places, which I thought too important to defer a Minute dispatching them for England. I go from hence Tomorrow to Oft end, in order to the immediate putting on Board ten of her Majesty's Battalions there at Sluys, and in Zealand, according to the Directions I received from his Grace the Duke of Marlborough. If I find the Accounts contained in the inclosed Advices, true, of which I cannot fail to be exactly informed on my Arrival at Ostend, I shall take care to fend from thence an Advice Boat to the Admiral of her Majesty's Fleet (which I suppose in the Downs') with the bed Intelligence I can get of the Enemies Force, and Design. Two small Ostend Privateers are already sent to lie as close as possibly they can to the Harbour of Dunkirk, to observe the Enemy's Squadron, and to carry Notice of all they can leam to the commanding-Officer of her Majesty's Fleet. I have the Honour to be, with the mofc profound Respect,

Your most obedient and most obliged humble Servant, Wm. Cadogan.

Paris, 7th March, 1708.

THE Prince of Wales is to go this Day from St. Germains to Dunkirk, to imbarque there for Scotland. He will find at Dunkirk 12 French Battalions under the Command of the Count de GaJJe, Lieutenant General, three Irish, commanded by Mr. Dillon (who is likewise Lieutenant General) 14 Men of War, and Frigates, with a great many Transport Ships, and Arms for the Scotch. 'Tis not yet known, whether the Duke of Berwick will go, and command in Chief. He is expected every Moment at Court. This Fleet is to put to Sea the 10th Instant, if the Wind be good. Money will not be wanting for this Expedition. 'TiS said, that the Count de Thoulouft is at the Expence of it. We flatter ourselves here, that the Scotch wait with Impatience for this Prince, and that they have a good Number of Men in Readiness.

YOU have, without doubt, heard of the last News from Scotland. 'Tis true; and Monsieur de Gajfe has Orders to be Tomorrow in the Evening at Dunkirk, to imbarque there with some Troops, and the King of England in Person.

THE King of England is expected this Evening at Dunkirk, and 12 Battalions, commanded by Monsieur de GaJJe, will arrive there at the feme time.

Extract of a Letter from Major General Cadogan to the

Earl of Sunderland, dated at Ostend the 13th of March,

1704, N. S.

THE pretended Prince of Wales arrived on the 10th Instant at Dunkirk, according to the Advice I had the Honour to fend your Lordship in my lad from Brussells. The Design is to land in Scotland, where, the French give out, a Very considerable Party will declare for him.

I have used all imaginable Diligence in providing Shipping for Ten of her Majesty's Battalions, with which I hope to be ready to feil by the 18th or 19th Instant.

ExttaCl of Mr. Cadogaris Letter to the Duke of Marlborough.

Ostend, March, the 13th 1704, N. S.

I have sent out icveral Parties of this Garison, and Bruges, who have brought in a great many Prisoners of the Regiments, that were on their March from Lisle to Dunkirk. They do not agree as to the Number of Battalions designed to be imbarqued, some saying Fifteen, others Twenty. The Count GaJJe is to command them. The last Paris Letters lay, the Pretender's Party in Scotland have sent Assurances, that they will surprize the Cattle of Edinburgh.
