THE House being met;

Mr. Secretary Boyle reported from the Committee, appointed to withdraw, and draw up an Address, to be presented to her Majesty; that they had drawn up the said Address, which they had directed him to report to the House: And which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table i where the same was twice read, and is as follows j viz.

WE, your Majesty's most faithful and obedient Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, do beg Leave to return our most hearty Thanks to yottr Majesty, for being graciously pleased to communicate to your Parliament the Intelligence, you lave received, of an intended Invasion of this Kingdom by the pretended Prince of Wales, supported by a French Power. We are so sensible of the Happiness we enjoy under your Majesty, and are lo affected with the dangerous Consequences of such an Attempt both to your Person, and Government, that, with Hearts full of Concern for your Majesty's Safety, we beseech your Majesty* that as

you will be pleased to take particular Care of your royal Person; and we, on our Parts, are fully and unanimously resolved to Hand by and assist your Majesty with our Lives and Fortunes, in Maintenance of your undoubted Right and Title to the Crown of these Realms, against the pretended Prince of Wales, and all other your Enemies both at home and abroad.

The Care your Majesty has taken for the Defence of your Dominions, and, particularly, in fitting out lo great a Fleet in so lliort a Time, give Satisfaction and Encouragement to all your good Subjects, who are likewise very sensible of the Zeal, the States General have shewn upon this Occasion.

As a further Instance of our Duty, we humbly desire, that you will be pleased to order, that the Laws against Papists, and Non-jurors, be put in Execution; and that Directions be given to seize and secure such Persons, with their Horl'es, and Arms, as your Majesty shall have Cause to suspect are disaffected to your Person and Government.

And as we doubt not, but, by the Blessing of God upon the Continuance of your Majesty's Care, your Enemies will be put to Confusion, so we readily embrace this Opportunity to shew to your Majesty, and the whole World, that no Attempts of this Kind shall deter us from supporting your Majesty in a vigorous Prosecution of the present War against France, till the Monarchy of Spain be restored to the House of Austria, and your Majesty have the glory to compleat the Recovery of the Liberties of Europe.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That this House do agree to the said Address.

Mr. Speaker reported. That both Houses of Parliament did Yesterday present their humble Address to her Majesty; and that thereupon her Majesty was pleased to make the gracious Answer following:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

1 have such intire Dependance on the Providence of God, and so much Trust in the faithful Services of my good Subjects, that I hope, this Attempt will prove dangerous only to those, who undertake it.

Iam extremely sensible ofyour Concern and Affection for me, and my Government, and shall have a very particular Regard to the Advice you give me upon this Occasion.

1 am also very well pleased with the Justice, which you have done the States -General, in taking Notice of their timely Care for our Safety, and their Readiness to give us all possible Assistance.

The firm Resolution, which you express upon all Occasions, of supporting me in bringing this War to a safe and happy Conclusion, as it is most essentially obliging to me, so, I assure myself, it will mightily dishearten our common Enemies, and give the greatest Encouragement and Advantage to all our Allies.

Mr. Manley (according to Order) reported from the Grand Committee for Courts of Justice,

That, at the said Committee, the Right honourable Richard Lord Bulkley, of the Kingdom of Ireland (a Member of this House) made a Complaint against Mr. Serjeant Hooke, one of the Judges of North Wales, that, after the Queen had, at the Request of the Gentlemen of Wales, increased the Salaries of the Judges of Wain, on purpose that they might not receive the Prelents, formerly given, Mr. Serjeant Hooke did, notwithstanding, at the Town of Beaumaris, in the County of insist on a Prc-sent

from that Corporation, and that, the same not being made, the Mayor was fined £.iq.

Whereupon a Day being appointed, for making out the said Complaint, and Mr. Serjeant Hooke having Notice of the same; Counsel was heard, as well to make out the said Complaint, as on the behalf of Mr. Serjeant Hooke.

That, to make out the said Complaint, several Witnesses were examined:

Wm. Peifley, Esquire, who preceded the said Mr. Serjeant Hooke in his said Judge's Place, said, that the said Judges Salaries were increased in the Year 1702, or 1703, at the Request of the Gentlemen of the Country: That he knows nothing of a Present of Coals; but that the last Time he went the Circuit, his Marshal told him, there was no Coals allowed him; but he did not mind it; but paid his Bills, and went away.

That then' they called

Mr. 77/o. Roberts-, who delivered in a Minute of the nomina ministror' taken off the File at the Secondary's

Office; by which it appeared, that Mr. Fra. Edwards, then Mayor, was fined J.zo, but afterwards excused: It did not appear by the said Minute, what was the Occasion of setting the said Fine.

That Mr. Roberts likewise proved a Copy of an Order, made by the Mayor and Corporation 16th August, 1706, against presenting Coals to the Judge.

Mr. Roberts said, that he was present, when Mr. Serjeant Hook sent for the Mayer into Court, about Ten in the Morning, and, upon his coming, stopt Business, to discourse with the Mayor about the Coals; which the Serjeant infilled on, as due of Right, and himself having received them 14 or 15 Years; and the Mayor denied, they were due of Right, and excused the Corporation's giving them, as being very poor; and the Serjeant said, they were never denied, till that pragmatical Man (meaning Mr Edwards)came to be Mayor: That Mr. Ed-

wards laid, He was not pragmatical; and, since Mr. Serjeant Hook insisted on them, as his Right, they would try it with him; and thereupon the Serjeant fined the Mayor £.20. That the Witness stood near, and in hearing of all that was said, but did not hear the Mayor give the Judge any disrespectful Language.

Owen Roberts, Esquire, proved the Copy of the Order, made by the Corporation of Beaumaris, for (lopping the Allowance of Coals to the Judges; which was dated the 16th August, 1706, and subscribed by Mr. Edzvards, as Mayor, and Seven others of the Corporation: And

laid, that he being absent, when the nomina ministror' was called over, was fined £. 5, and, on his Return, waiting on the Serjeant, to pray, his Fine might be excused, the Serjeant laid, he would fine the Mayor for not giving Coals, except the said Order was revoked; and assigned it for the Cause; which the Witness desired him first to consider well of.

Then Mr. Rowland Wynne came to him from the Judge, and asked him to pay for the Coals; and said, then the Judge would take off the Fine: And that afterwards he gave Mr. Kiffin 7 s. 6d. to pay for the Coals, and both the Fines were taken off; but was not himself present in Court, when 'twas done.

That Mr. Serjeant Hooke professed before God, that not one Word of what Mr. Roberts had said, was true; and demanded of him, whether he had not owned, that the Coals had been presented Fourscore Years: To which Mr. Roberts answered, that was many Years before he was born.

Kiffin, Esquire, said, he was present in Court, when Mr. Serjeant Hook sent for the Mayor, and fined him £. 20. That, when the Mayor came into Court, Mr.

Serjeant Hook Hop'd the Proceedings, and entered into a Discourse with the Mayor about the Coals; and said, the Coals was due to him by Right, but that pragmatical Man, the Mayor, had flopped the Coals, to affront the Judges; and bid them fine the Mayor 20, whereupon the Witness moved the Judge to fufjjend fining Mr.

Edwards, the Mayor, he being only one of the Corporation; and that he would give Leave, that the Corporation might he heard by their Counsel: To which he answered, that the Corporation might move to take off the Fine.

That Mr. Serjeant Hooke infilled on the Coals, as his Right; and the Mayor said, if Mr. Serjeant infilled upon it, as a Right, they would try it with him: The Bailiffs said, they did not consent to the Order for flopping of Coals,) and the Recorder gave an Account of their having been allowed to the Judges 50 or 60 Years, but did not say 'twas of Right: That the Mayor used no disrespectful Words.

That Mr. Kiffin said, he carried from Mr. Roberts 7 s. 6 d. to Mr. Serjeant Hook's Landlady, to pay for the Coals; and afterwards the Fine was remitted.

That Francis Edwards, Esquire, the then Mayor, gave an Account, that when he first waited on the Judge to Court, and from thence to his Lodgings, the Judge told him, he had a Quarrel with him for keeping back the Coals; and that he would sue for them: To which the Mayor said, if it was demanded of Right, the Corporation mull defend it: And that on Morning after, when he came into Court, being lent for by the Judge, Proceedings were Hop'd, and the Serjeant falling into Discourse with the said Mr. Edwards about paying for the Coals, the Serjeant called him pragmatical Fellow, and fined him £. 20. Mr. Edwards said, he believes, that the Coals were laid in by the Bailiff before the Assizes, but the Order, made by the Corporation, forbid paying for them: He acknowleged, the Recorder did say, that he had known Coals given for fifty or sixty Years; but he did not say, they were due of Right. Mr. Edwards said, he was then in Commission of the Peace, but did not act; and before the next Session was turned out.

That Mr. Edwards said further, that on Friday Morning the Judge told him in his Chamber, before he went to Court (Lord Bulkley being present) that the Coals were paid for, and he would take off his Fine; To which Mr. Edwards answered, That they were not paid for with his Privity, or Consent: To which the Judge replied, He cared not for that; but would take off the Fine: Which Mr. Edwards heard, was afterwards done.

That on behalf of Mr. Serjeant Hooke several Wit-nefle6 were called:

And Mr.

Then Mr. Serjeant Hook's Counsel's produced a Copy of the Privy Seal, for increasing the Judges Salaries in Wales; which mentions, as an Inducement to the fame, that it was represented to the Queen by the said Justices, that, by reason of the taking away of the Court or Ludlow, the Profits of their respective Places were very much decreased, and were not sufficient, with their aforesaid Salaries and Allowances, to support them with that Dignity, and Respect, as the Queen's Service required.

A Petition of the Royal Af Company of England was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that they have been at great Expence in building and maintaining Fortifications and Factories on the Coastof Africa, for carrying on that Trade, whereby the Western Plantations have been furnished with Negroes, by whole Labour is yearly produced great Riches to this Nation; and that the late Act for settling the Trade to Africa (instead of answering the expected Benefit) hath occasioned the Advance of the Price of Negroes in Guinea, to the Detriment of the Petitioners: And praying the House to take the State of the Trade and Interest on the Coast of Africa into Consideration, and give Support and Relief to the Petitioners, as they shall judge fit.

And Mr. Secretary Boyle acquainted the House, that her Majesty had had the Matter of the said Trade before her, upon a Report from the Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations; and that her Majesty had been, pleased to allow of the Company's laying their Petition before this House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Saturday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the State of the Trade to Africa.

A Petition of the Merchants and Planters, separate Traders to Africa, interested in, and trading to, the Plantations of Virginia and Maryland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that since the passing an Act for settling the Trade to Africa, made in the 9th and 10th Years of King William 3d, whereby the Trade was laid open to all the Subjects of this Kingdom, the same hath greatly improved, both to the Benefit of Merchants and Planters, but under a Burthen of £. 10 per Cent, paid to the Royal African Company, towards maintaining their Forts and Castles, which have been no manner of Benefit to the Petitioners: And praying, they may be relieved from that heavy Burden of Tender Cent, and the Trade so regulated, as may turn to the Advantage of the British Nation in general.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

Sir John Holland reported from the Committee, Yesterday appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to her Majesty, upon the Resolution, and upon the Debate, of the House; that they had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House j and which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table} where the same was twice read, and is as follows; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, humbly wait on your Majesty, to express the great Sense we have of your Grace and Favour, in communicating to us, from the Throne, the Account of the French King's persisting to invade your Dominions, and toim-pose a Pretender upon these Realms, over which your Majesty is rightful and lawful Sovereign.

The small Number of Ships and Troops with which this Project is prosecuted, notwithstanding the great naval Force your Majesty has fitted out with so much Expedition, as it ought to be regarded with Contempt, on the one side, so, on the other, it gives us just Cause to believe, that their chief Dependency is upon some of your Subjects, whole restless Passions and arbitrary Principles, have for some Years engaged them in forming Designs to undermine and destroy the most happy Establishment, that the Government of this Island was ever founded upon.

The Defence of your Majesty's Person and Government, and the Support of the Protestant Succession, are Things fb sacred to us, and your People, that, as a Demonstration of our unfeigned Zeal to aftift and support your Majesty to the utmost of our Power, we do, in the Name of the Commons of Great , give this Assurance, that whatsoever Charge you shall be at in augmenting your Troops at home, and replacing those, you have recalled from abroad, or for such other Services, as your Majesty shall judge necessary upon this extraordinary Occasion, shall be effectually made good j and, as we humbly recommend it to your Majesty, that the severest Punishments may be inflicted upon such, as shall assist in so unnatural a Design, as that of betraying your Majesty, and their Country so we do not doubt, but you will give suitable Encouragement to all those, who shall shew their Fidelity, in opposing the Invader, and his Accomplices, in Scotlan, or wherever the De-feent shall be.

Your Majesty wants no Incitement to a steady Prosecution of the War, in which you are engaged for the common Cause; yet permit us to take this Opportunity to intreat your Majesty, that this Enterprize may no ways divert your constant Vigour; that all the World may fee, that both your Majesty, and your People, are determined to support your Allies in all Parts, whatever Attempts are made at home.

May it please your Majesty:

There can be nothing so dangerous or fatal to the Safety of your royal Person, and the Security of the present happy Establishment, as those Persons, who endeavour to create Divisions and Animositics among your faithful Subjects, or by any artful Methods lessen the justElteem your Majesty has for those, who have eminently, and in so distinguishing a Manner, commanded your Armies, and managed your Treasure, to the Honour and Glory of your Majesty abroad, and the intire Satisfaction of your People at home. We therefore humbly beg Leave to beseech your Majesty to difeoun-tenance all such Persons, and Designs, in the most remarkable Manner.

Resolved, That this House doth agree to the said Address.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of her Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know her Majesty's Pleasure, when fee will be attended by this House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morn- Method of ing, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, returning upon the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Scotc",>e*,*' Act to make further Provision for electing and summoning, Sixteen Peers of Scotland, to fit in the House of Peers in the Parliament of Great , and for trying Peers for Offences committed in Scotland.

Gentlemen,

I give you my hearty thanks for this your repeated Assurance, and certain Proof, of your Zeal for me, and for the Protestant Succession.

I am glad, your Thoughts of the War abroad so per-fedtly agree with my firm Resolution upon that Subject.

You may depend, that no Apprehensions (farther than are reasonable) shall have any Influence on my Measures, while the Cause of Religion and Liberty, with the good Affedtions of my People, are on my Side.

I think all, who endeavour to make Divisions among my faithful Subjects, must be mine and the Kingdom's , Enemies; and I shall never countenance any Persons,

who would go about to lessen the just Esteem, which I have for those, who have done, and continue to do, pie the most eminent Services.

Mr. Trevamon (according to Order) reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Car Jo,

a Genoese Merchant, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, which they had directed him to report to the House; and which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; and it as followeth:

That it appeared to the said Committee, that the Petitioner, Mr. John Curjo, had been a trading Merchant for several Years, and had always a good Reputation, as by the Certificates, annex'd to the Petition; which the Committee examined, and are as follows; viz.

A Certificate of several Merchants of the City of

London, dated the 43d of 1702: Another

from the Envoy of Portugal, dated the 10th of

her, 1705: Another From the Governor of the Bank of England, dated the 10th of , 170^: Another

from several Merchants, and Captains of Ships, dated 8th March, 1705: Besides three several Certificates from the Envoy of Genuoa and Tuscany.

That it also appeared to the said Committee, by the Report of Doctor Bramfion, annex'd to the said Petition, that Simon del Rosario, Merchant, was a Passenger in the George Brigantine, Captain Corfo, Commander, at Carracas, in India, bound for Port Velo, and had on board several Sorts of Merchandizes, viz. Sugars, Mullins, Callicoes, Wine, Brandy, Cocua, Wool, Thread, and Bales of all Sorts of Indian Goods; and that about One hundred Leagues off the Coast of racas, Captain Kidd, the Pirate, came on board of them in an amicable Manner; and understanding, the Brigantine was richly laden, he seized, and carried her away, putting the said Corfo, and his Ship's Company, into a Boat, with some Privisions; but, hefore he turned them out, the said Simon del Rosario saw Kidd open an Iron Chest, and counted 13 Bags of Gold, in Bars, and, in Gold Dull, Eleven or Twelve; and that, whilst he was on board, Corfo lliewed him Diamonds, and other precious Stones; and that the said Corfo was Owner of the said Ship, and all the Goods and Effects, as aforesaid.

That it further appeared by the said Dr. s

Report, that Domingo Serafi Petro Montallo, and Ephraim Naffscta, Mariners, were on board the said

Brigantine; who all laid to the same Effect, as Del Rosario, and swore it before the Court of Admiralty; which Affidavits, signed by Richard , Esquire,

Register, made it more fully appear.

Dr. Bramfion attended, and said, that he had compared the Marks, produced by Corfo, as in the Margent of his Report, and found the same exactly to agree.

And the Statute of Edward 3d read, which lays, '* That if any Merchant, Privy or Stranger, be robbed * of his Goods upon the Sea, and the Goods, so " robbed, come into any Parts within our Realm, and " be will sue for to recover the said Goods, he shall be received to prove the Goods to be his own, by his

Marks, or by Chart, or Coquet, or by good and Jaw-

ful Merchants, Privy or Strangers; and by such Proof the same shall be delivered to the Merchant, without

making other Suit at the common Law." And it Was urged, that the like Proof was fuffreient at common Law, as to Wrecks.

Abraham de Almeda, Merchant, laid, that he knew Mr. Corfo at Cadiz in 1684, and a considerable Merchant, trading in all forts of Merchandizes; afterwards had further Correspondence with him in the Spanish West Indies, at which time he had a very good Ship of his Own, and a Man of Credit and Reputation: And that About six Years ago, or thereabouts* the said coming

tq England, came to him, and fold him, that be had been rohhed by Kidd, the pirate; and desired him to assisi him.

;n what be could, that he might get fqme Recompence for what he had iofi, which was to the Value of £. 26,000, which Mr. Almeda did to the qlmost of his Power.

Mr. Isaac Dias, and Mr. Abraham Nunes said, that they knew Mr. Corfo about 14 or 15 Years ago in the West Indies, and at that Time commanded a Brigantine of his own; and ways always look'd upon to be a very honest Man, and of Substance, before he was robbed, and lofi what he had, by Kidd, as they have been credibly informed.

Mr. Broderick, Merchant, said, he had a Letter in April, 1701, from a Correspondent of his in;

the Purport of which was, that Mr. John Corfo having been robbed by Kidd, the Pirate, to the Value of£.26,000, and desired him to assisi him here in England, he being a very honest Man, and a considerable Trader, 'before those Misfortunes befel him.

Mr. Peter Fancia, and Mr. Richard Burk, Merchants, said, they had Letters in 1701 from Merchant? in Bar-, bqdots, desiring them to assisi Mr. Corfo here in England, he having been robbed by Kidd.

Mr. Ploughmam, Merchant, said, he had a Letter in

1701 from one Mr. Anthill, a Merchant in New , desiring him to assisi Mr. Corfo in what lay in his Power, being a very honest fair dealing Man before robbed by Mr. Kidd.

Sir Charles Hobby said, that he knew Mr. Corfo at New Fork, and Jamaica, and traded with him for Provisions, which he brought from Penfelvania, and always look'd upon him to be a very honest Man; and, since his Arrival in England, has been informed by credible Persons, that he had been robbed by Kidd.

Mr. Viceti, Agent of Genuoa, said, that he knew Mr.

Corfo, about six Years; and had been credibly informed by Merchants in London, and by Letters from Merchants abroad, that he had been robbed by; and knew him to be a very honest Man.

Mr. Geo. Maycock said, that at the Time of Mr.

Corfoe's first coming to England, he lay lick a considerable Time, which was the Occasion of his not prosecuting this Affair sooner.

It appeared further to the Committee, by a Testimo* nial, signed by William Markham, Governor of Penfelvania, that the said Corfo was in the ninth Year of the Reign of King William made free of that Province, and Counties atinext, for his Industry and Sobriety, and for the better securing his Estate to him, and his Heirs, he having taken the Oaths, appointed by Act of Parliament.

Mr. Crawley, Register of tire Court of Admiralty, produced several Papers, relating to the Proceedings against Kidd; whereby no Account appears, where Kidd was, or what Depredations he committed, in the latter End of the Year 1698, or in the Year 1699, nor until he was brought Prisoner for England, in the Year 1700; whereas by all the Affidavits beforementioned, which were made and taken in the Year 1704, it appears, that Corfo was robbed by Kidd about five Years and an half before the making of the said Affidavits, which, by Computation, makes it appear, that the said Corfo was robbed in the Year 1699.

That the Committee having examined the Allegations of the Petition of Lieutenant Francis Lewis, and other Officers, that were upon Half-pay, do find, that the Lord Ranelagh has paid all the Moneys, issued to him

for Half-pay; and yet, nevertheless, by reason of there being Provision made by Parliament for Half-pay Officers for no longer than till Christmas,. 1701, and the Halfpay Officers not being employed till March following, it appears to the Committee, that the seventy-five Days, claimed by the Petitioners, remains due to them, according to their respective Certificates.

That the Committee having examined the Allegations of Captain Fitz Gerald, do find, that notwithstanding the Vote of this House, the 20th of 1699, whereby

he was ordered to be added to the Lift of the Officers, who weie then to have Half-pay, he has received no Benefit thereby', having never been since put upon any Establishment.

We can make no Estimate of the Loss of this Revenue for want of entering Orders in Chancery, the Officers concerned being out of Town; and the Officers, concerned in entering Rules, who are in Town, do own no Loss by the Attorneys omitting to enter Rules to plead, reply, tec. in Causes, wherein they charge their Clients with the Fees and Stamp Duties thereof.

We have been informed of considerable Losses to this Revenue, by the Attorneys Practice of joining several Purchases between several Parties in one Fine; but most of the Officers concerned being out of Town, we have not been able to present any Estimate of that Loss to this honourable House.

What we have before mentioned respects only two of her Majesty's Courts at

As to Plaints, Bails, and Appearances, in inferior Courts, the omitting to enter them, and other Matters, on the requisite Stamps, has been much practised by the Officers and Clerks of those Courts.

If a Man came to enter a Plaint, or Action, they took the Fee of such Entry, and the Stamp Duty, and a Minute of the Action; but many of them seldom or never entered it on stamp Paper or Parchment (having it in their Power to do it, when they found it requisite) unless a Certiorari, Writ of Error, or the like (which happens not in one Cause in 50) made it necessary to enter or record it.

And the like has been practised as to Bails 5 a Minute only, and the Two Shillings Duty, and the Fee thereof, taken, and the Bail not entered on Stamps, unless the Cause proceeded so far, as to have a Jcire facias against the Bail, or forne other suchlike Occasion, as before mentioned (which happens not in one Cause in 50) obliged the Clerk to enter or file the Bail; and so the Clerk, for one Duty answered to the Crown, might get at least 50 to himself.

Upon the Inspections we have caused to be made of the inferior Courts, &c. in several Parts of England, by only two Officers appointed for that Purpose, we have found not entered on the requisite Stamps, or on any Stamps at all.

Besides great Numbers of Declarations, Pleas, Replications, &c. written without Stamps, which ought to have been written on double Peny Stamps; and Citations, and many other Proceedings in ecclesiastical Courts, many of which ought to have been written on double Six-peny and higher Stamps; but, in regard some are doubtful, or disputable, we do not insert the Amount thereof here.

And this Inspection has yet been made only in some Parts of England; and we humbly conceive, that what particular Frauds have been discovered, must bear but a small Proportion to what areundifeovered, the Discoveries of all requiring more Officers to be employed, than this Revenue can well bear.

And we beg Leave to observe, that great Part of the Moneys before mentioned have been paid by several Persons concerned in the inferior Courts,'and Corporations, to intitle themselves to the two several Indemnities, granted in the two last Sessions of Parliament; but how much has been so paid, we cannot set forth, in regard many of the Persons concerned did not pay the same into the Receipt, but have made good the Duties, by taking damp'd Paper, and Parchment, and writing their Omissions thereon: The Truth thereof we cannot discover, until further Inspections can be made.

From the Discovery, already made, we must believe the Practice of defrauding the Stamp Revenue to have been very general all over England.

We therefore thought it our Duty to take such Measures, as we judged necessary, to put a flop to this growing Practice; and believe, if Care had not been taken, this Revenue would have funk to a very great Degree.

We could not bring any Persons to Punishment for such Omjffions, as aforesaid, nor for making one Stamp serve several Times (which, we are satisfied, has been much practised) for want of a Law, until the Ad was made in the first Year of her present Majesty's Reign, for Prevention of Frauds in this Revenue; nor for some time after that Act passed, for want of particular Dise coveries, and sufficient Evidence; and after such Dif-coveries were made, Prosecutions for the Offences discovered were suspended by the two Indemnities, granted in two successive Sessions of Parliament.

All which (together with the Difficulties we have to deal, on behalf of this Revenue, in the Niceties of Law Proceedings) we humbly submit to the Consideration and great Wisdom, of this honourable House.

Edward Lloyd, Henry Cornish,

A Message from her Majesty, by Mr. Aston, Deputy Gentleman Uftier of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her immediately in the'House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend her Majesty.

And, being returned;

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, that her Majesty had been pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several publick and private Bills following:

An Act for assuring to the English Company, trading to the East Indies on account of the united Stock, a longer Time in the Fund and Trade therein mentioned, and for railing thereby the Sum of Twelve hundred thousand Pounds, for carrying on the War, and other her Majesty's Occasions:

An Act for continuing the half Subsidies therein mentioned, with several Impositions, and other Duties, to raise Money by Way of Loan, for the Service of the War, and other her Majesty's necessary and important Occasions; and for charging of Prize Goods, and Seizures; and for taking off the Drawbacks of foreign Cordage; and to obviate the clandestine Importation of wrought Silks:

An Act for the avoiding of Doubts and Questions touching the Statutes of divers Cathedral and Collegiate Churches:

An Act for the better Amendment of that Way which leads from Cherrill, through Caine, to Studley Bridge, in the County of Wilts:

An Act for erecting a Harbour or Key at East -bett, in the Shire of Argyle:

An Act for continuing an Act, made in the Third Year of her Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for punishing Mutiny and Desertion, and false Mullers, and for the better Payment of the Army and Quarters:

An Act for the more effectual Discovery of the Death of Persons pretended to be alive, to the Prejudice of those, who claim Estates after their Deaths:

An Act for repairing the Highways from Old Stratford, in the County of Northampton, to Dunchurch, in the County of Warwick:

An Act for making effectual the Provision, intended by William Bromley, late of Holt Castle, in the County of Worcester, Esquire, for Dorothy Bromley, his youngest Daughter:

An Act for felling the Estate of Thomas Stephens,

Esquire, in the Counties of Chester and Stafford, and for settling of another Estate, of as great or greater Value, in the County of Gloucester, to the same Uses:

An Act for the Reversal of the Attainder of Sir Henry Bond, Bar. in Ireland.

An Act for naturalizing Peter Des Maizeaux, Francis Heilman, John Rifteau, Peter Bouvet, and others:

An Act for vesting in Roger Tuckfield, Esquire, several Lands, purchased for him by Sir William Davye, Bar. deceased:

An Act for making two large Fly-boats, one called the Thomas and Henry, and the other the Richard and Jane, free Ships, t <3trade to Russia.

A PETIT I ON of divers Ship-wrights, Rope-makers, Sail-makers, and other Artificers, and Trades-men, dealing in naval Manufactures, in and about London, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and readj setting forth, that far greater Numbers of Ships have been built, repaired, and fitted out, for Africa, on Account of several Traders thither, since the Act, of the 9th and 10th of K. for laying open that Trade, than were ever employed by the African Company; and that the Petitioners have (with many other'Artificers) received great Benefit thereby: And praying, the said Trade may continue free and open, under such Regulations, as to this honourable House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the Trade to Africa.

To the honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled:

The humble Petition of Captain and Wm. Hammil> Gentleman, in behalf of, and as Agents, and Trustees to and for, the several Colonels, and other commissioned and non-commissioned Officers, and Soldiers, of thfe Irtish Regiments:

THAT your Petitioners, upon the late happy Resolution, assembled, and took up Arms in the Defence of their Religion, Laws, and Liberties, and kept together in a Body until the Month of 16891; about which Time your Petitioners wefe by General Kirke, pursuant to his late Majesty's Orders, formed into Regiments, one Regiment of Horse, two Regiments of Dragoons, and three Regiments of Foot, and bad Commissions the said them accordingly, which bore Date the 20th of delivered Month of July; from which Time the said

Vol. 15.

Regiments irfere tiri&CT the life Comtaand of the rest of the Army.

That In thfe Year 1702 the Accounts of these Regr-taents being fitted, and certified, by the Commissioners of Accounts in Rutland, they had Pay allowed them only from the first of January,. 1689, tho' they had actually served by Commission from the said 20th df July precedent, and had within that Time done great and remarkable Services; particulary on the 30th of July, 1689, they fought and routed, the I*ifh Army, commanded by General Clancarty, at New-town-butler; which Defeat, among other Advantages to the Publick, was thfe happy Cause of theiT railing the Siege of Londonderry the very next Day: The.feid Regiments afterwards lay encamped at Dundalke, from the toth Day of September to the 20th Day of November, 1689, under the Command of Duke Scomberg where they endured much Hard ship by Sickness and otherwise.

That the many Services of your Petitioners, as well before the Time they were formed into Regiments, as well as from the Time they had Commissions, are (o well known, and so fresh in the Memory of several Members of this honourable House, your Petitioners do not think it rfecessary to infill; on them.

That the said Regiments, thro* their great Zeal to the Publick, by their early taking up Arms, having brought down a great Part of the Irish Army into their Country, occasioned their Houses to be burnt, their Goods destroyed, and their Lands to be laid wufte; and the Officers contracted such Debts for Arms, Shoes, and other Necessaries, for their Men, that they ltill labour under the fame.

That his late Majesty King William (of glorious Memory) in or before December, 1689, having sent over Cloaths for the said Regiments, even for every Officer, the said Cloaths, as well as the Provisions delivered them it Dundalke, werfe brought within their Accounts for their Pay, commencing the first D;'y of January, 1689.

That the late King William &nd Queen Mary having been pleased; by their Declaration, of the 22d of February, 1688, among other Things; to declare; that all the Lands and Estates of all such, as should persist in their Rebellion, should be distributed and disposed of to those, that should be aiding and assisting in reducing the said Kingdom to its due Obedience;

The laid Regiments therefore did always hope, tho' their Accounts were dated and certified, and Pay only allowed them from the first of January, 1689, that they would not be only satisfied from the Day they acted by Commission, but that they would be satisfied for their Services, from the Time they first appeared in Arms, to the Day they had Commissions.

May it please your Honours, for as much as a Vote passed the last Sessions of the present Parliament of England, that no Application should be admitted into the House for any former Services, during that Sessions, except such, as should be recommended from the Crown; and for as much as it is humbly hoped, the satisfying and paying of the said Regiments their Pay from the said 20th of July, 1689, to the first of January, 1689, may consist with the Honour and Interest of the Crown, and the Credit and Justice of the Nations;

Your Petitidners therefore most humbly pray your Honours, in tender Consideration of the Premises, to lay the deplorable same of the said Officers and Soldiers before his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant of this Kingdom, earnestly desiring his Excellency to report and recommend the same to her Majesty's royal Care and Companion, that thereby the Account of their Pay for their Services to the first of January, 1689, may be stated, and certified, by the proper Officers, and such Relief given to your Petitioners, as her Majesty shall think fit.

And your Petitioners, as in Duty bound, will ever pray, (dc.

Exr per Tho. Tilfon, Richard Newjlead,

Cler. Park Dom. Com. Will. Hammil.

III. To his Excellency, Thomas Earl of Lord

Lieutenant General and General Governor of Ireland:

The humble Address of the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

May it please your Excellency:

WE, the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assemblfd, having received a Petition from Captain Robert Baird, and William Hammil, Gentleman, in behalf, and as Agents and Trustees to and for, as well the Colonels, and other Field Officers, as the commissioned and non-commissioned Officers, and Soldiers, of eight Regiments of Horse, Foot, and Dragoons, one Independent Company, a Company of Gunners, and a Company of Pioneers, who served their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary (of ever blessed Memory) in the memorable Defence of her Majesty's City of Londonderry, during the Siege thereof setting forth their early and signal Services, and Sufferings, on the late happy Resolution:

That his late Majesty was graciously pleased to account the same of great Consequence to these Nations in general; and that no greater Opportunity could have fallen into the Hands of any Subjects of obliging their Prince, to his great Satisfaction; alluring them, that he would recompence their Services and Sufferings so, as none of them should ever have Cause to repent thereof:

That the honourable the Commons of England voted the said Service to have greatly conduced to the Safety of the three Kingdoms, and addressed his Majesty for a Compensation to the said Garison, and some special Mark of his royal Favour, as a lading Monument of their Services to Posterity: To which his Majesty was pleased to return for Answer, that he would take Care of the said Garison, according to the Desire of the House; and, in pursuance of such his royal Promise, issued several Orders, which hitherto have proved ineffectual to the Petitioners:

That, upon Application made to the honourable the House of Commons of England, a Committee was appointed, to examine the Allegations of the Petition; which said Committee (upon due Proof made of the several Matters therein contained) came to several Resolutions in favour of the Petitioners:

That by reason of some Doubts arising upon the Construction of the Act, forftating and settling the Accounts of the Army, the Commissioners, by the said A ft appointed, did not think fit to state the Petitioners Accounts, as in other Cafes j by means whereof the Petitioners could not be entitled to Debentures, as other the Officers and Soldiers of the Army were:

And praying, that we would lay their Services and Sufferings before your Excellency, with our humble Application, that the same may be transmitted to her Majesty, in order to the Petitioners Relief.

The Services and Sufferings of that Garison are too well known, to be enumerated: Words cannot add to what his late most gracious Majesty has been pleased to say on the Subject, a just Sense whereof the . honourable the House of Commons of England have thought fit to ej^ref*.

Their Accounts have been stated by Charles Fox, Esquire, Paymaster of the Army, pursuant to an Order for chat End, and have likewise been allowed by a Committee of the honourable House of Commons of England

Wherefore with full Assurance we approach your Excellency in behalf of the Petitioners, whose Cafe, by Length of time, and Expence of Solicitation, is become very deplorable, and many of them, and their Families, are in a starving Condition; be-feeching, that your Excellency will please, after the most effectual Manner, to lay the same at her Majesty's royal Feet, to the End her Majesty may, in such Method, as (he shall think fit, recommend the same to her Parliament of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Papers be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House w<ll, upon Mondry Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

A Petition of divers Merchants, and Factors, concerned in the Linen Manufactures of North Britain, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of her Majesty's Subjects employed therein, was presented to the House, and lead; setting forth, that observing, a Clause is allowed to be brought into the Bill for continuing several Duties, that are now expiring, upon various Sorts of Merchandize, by which all European Linens are to be exempted from some Part of the Duties, to which they are now liable; and considering, how destructive such an Exemption will be to the Linen Manufacture of that Part of the united Kingdom, whose Dependence lies chiefly in improving the same: And praying, nothing may be allowed, as Part of the Bill, which does so evidently tend to the Destruction of the Petitioners Trade.

if this shall be her Majesty's Pleasure, we are humbly of opinion, that, for the Security of the Dock at Portsmouth by Sea, the Fortifications of that Garison, together with South Sea Castle, Rlock-house Point,.

Charles and James Fort, and Ports Bridge, should be put into as good a Condition of Defence, as they are capable of; and that Eafiney Point, and the Point at and Stoakes Bay, and also the Point opposite, upon No-mans Land, should be well fortified; and, for the Security of this Dock from the approach of an Enemy by' Land, that there be a regular Fortification erected between the Mill Pond and Fountain Lake.

My Lord,

We are very sensible, that the finishing these Works Will require Time, and a great Sum of Money, tho' we are not yet prepared to lay before your Grace Estimates of the whole Charge thereof; but if it shall be thought necessary, that a Line, with Redoubts and Batteries, and a cover'd Way, palifladoed, be made between the Mill Pond and Fountain Lake, to prevent an Insult upon the Dock by Land, and the Works at Block-house Point, and forne prefen t necessary Works and Repairs to the Fortifications of the Garison, South Sea Castle, and Ports Bridge, shall be begun this Year, the doing thereof, according to the be ft Information we can yet have, will amount to £.77,883. 14 s.

We think it our Duty upon this Occasion to inform your Grace, that in the last Reign the late Sir Martin Beckman, first Engineer to this Office, was, by order of the King, employed at Portsmouth several Months, to survey, design, make Plans, and Estimates, for fortifying the Dock at Portsmouth to the Land, and for doing some Works in the Garison at Block house Point, Ports Bridge, and Gosport; and we find in the Books of the Office an Estimate of the Charge of the fortifying the Dock to the Land only, according to a Draught, approved of, and ligned by the King, in the Year 1699, amounts to £.301,1116. 19J. $d.

But (ince that time about 200 Houses are built upon the Ground, on which that Fortification was proposed to be eroded; and the Purchase of those Houses will be a very great addition to the Charge of such a Fortification, tho' we are of opinion, it is very improper, they should be so near either the Garison, or the Dock.

And the Estimates of the Charge of the said Works, proposed to be done in the Garison at Block-house Point, Ports Bridge, and Gosport, amounts to£.ii2,614. i6r. id. For securing the Dock at Chatham, we are of opinion, that Upnor Castle, Sheerness, and the other Forts and Bat-

teries upon the River Medway, and also the Batteries which were slighted in the late Reign, should be put into a good Condition of Defence, to prevent Attempts of the Enemy by Sea; and that there be a Fortification erected on the rising Ground behind the Dock, to prevent an Insult upon it by Land; the Charge whereof, according to the best Computation we can at present make, will amount to - - - - £.31,500. o. o.

All which is most humbly submitted to your Grace by Your Grace's most obedient and

most humble Servants, Pbo. Erie, C.

Bridges, Ja.

Sir Richard Onslow reported from the Committee, appointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered at the Lords at a Conference, for disagreeing to several Amendments, made by the Lords to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of the Trade to America-, that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

The Commons agree to your Lordships first Amendment in Sk. the 1 ft, L. 13.

The Commons do agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships in the Ryder at the End of the Bill, in 4th Line, with this Amendment, by leaving out, after " otherwise," the Words " except as is herein after " provided;"

Because those Words refer to Clauses A, and B, sent down by your Lordships, to which the Commons have disagreed.

The Commons dilagee to the said Clauses A, and B;

Because they conceive, that by the Amendment, made by your Lordships to the Ryder, as now amended by the Commons, all Rights and Privileges, granted to the East India Company by the Act of Parliament, mentioned in Clause A, are effectually saved, and provided for j and for the same Reason they conceive, there is no Occasion for Clause B.

The Commons agree to your Lordships Amendment, Clause C.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time; were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That a Conference be desired with the Lords upon the Subject-matter of the Amendments, made by their Lordships to the said Bill.

Drawing Sir Robert Davers reported from the Committee, who

Waggons on were appointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Highways. Lort]s at a Conference, for disagreeing to the Amendments, made by the Lords to the Bill, intituled, An Act to repeal a Chuse in an Act, of the seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty (for amending and repairing the Highways) which enjoinsWaggoners to draw with a Poll between the Wheel Horles, or with double Shafts, and to oblige them to draw only with fix Horses, or other Bealls, except up Hills; that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow;

The Commons disagree to your Lordships ill, 3d, and 4th, Amendments;

Because they apprehend, if the Waggoners shall be restrained from drawing with less than fix Horses, it mull necessarily reduce the Loads to so small a Weight (especially in the Northern, as well as Western, Parts or Great Britain, where the Horses are generally small, and the Journeys long) that it'will not answer their travelling Charges, and consequently will bring a new' Tax upon the Subject, by additional Rates for Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, conveyed by Land Carriage to and from the City of London.

The Commons disagree to your Lordships ad and last Amendments;

Because, if fix Horses be as small a Number, as are capable of drawing reasonable Loads only in plain Ways, it must be thought impracticable to draw the same Weight up many of the ftcep and tedious Hills in the Roads of this Kingdom: And the Commons having lodged & dilcretionary Power in the Justices of the Peace, at their General Quarter Sessions, where such Hills do lie, to limit Waggoners to draw up the same with such Number of Horses only, as to them shall be thought reasonable, the Commons cannot apprehend, the Roads will any ways be prejudiced thereby.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put there upon, agreed unto by the House.

Eifliery Encouragement.

Mr. Manley reported from the Committee, appointed to draw up Reasons, 10 be offered to the Lords at a Conference, for disagreeing with their Lordships to the Amendment, by them made to the Bill, intituled, An Act for rendering more effectual the Act, in the first Year of her Majesty "s Reign, for the finishing and adorning the Cathedral Church of St. , London-,

that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Reasons, to be offered to the Lords, for disagreeing to their Lordships Amendment to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making more effectual an Act, made in the first Year of her Majesty's Reign, for finishing and adorning the Cathedral Church of St. Paul's, London.

The Commons cannot agree with your Lordships in leaving out the last Ryder in the said Bill, marked N® z

i ft, Because it did appear to the Commons, upon Examination, that Copper is preferable to any other Covering, both in respect of Duration, and Lightness; and it did likewise appear, that the best British Copper is in all Respects equal, both in Goodness, and Fineness, to that of any other Country; and that there is yearly very considerable Quantities of such Copper made in Great Britain, more than can be used here, and in the Plantations, and of which there is above One hundred Tons in Town; and less than Twenty Tons will answer this Occasion: And therefore the Commons are of opinion, the Manufacture of Copper deserves Encouragement:

ad, Because it did appear, that Lead is subject to Very frequent Repair: And that the necessary Scaffolding for that Purpose, at any one Time, will exceed the Difference of the Charge between Lead and Copper; and that frequent Scaffolding must very much prejudice the Building.

3d, The Commons cannot but take notice, that the Money, for building the said Cathedral, was granted by the Commons; and therefore the Application thereof does belong to them.

For which Reasons, the Commons do disagree with your Lordships said Amendment.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved^hoX a Conference be desired with the Lords upon the Subject-matter of the said Amendment.

Ordered, That Sir Godfrey Copley do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Medlycott and Mr. Fellows:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for regulating the Qualifications of the Elections of the Governor, Deputy Governor, Directors, and Voters, of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, without any Amendment:

The Lords have also agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing several Duties, therein mentioned, upon Coffee, Chocolate, Spices, Pictures, and Mullins, and additional Duties upon several of the said Commodities, and certain Duties upon Callicoes, China Wares, and Drugs, and for continuing the Duties, called the Two-third Subsidies of Tonage and Poundage, for preserving the publick Credit; and for ascertaining the Duties of Coals, exported for foreign Parts; and for securing the Credit of the Bank of England-, and for passing several Accounts of Taxes, raised in the County of Monmouth; and for promoting the Consumption of such Tobacco, as shall have paid her Majesty's Duties; without any Amendment:

The Lords do not insist on their Amendments, made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to repeal a Clause in an Act, of the seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty (for amending and repairing the Highways) which enjoins Waggoners, and others, to draw with a Pole between the Wheel Horses, or with double Shafts, and to oblige them to draw only with fix Horses, <ft other Beasts, except up Hills:

The Lords have also agreed to the Amendments, made by this House to the Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Peter Dubordieu, and others:

The Lords have also agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for limiting a Time for Persons to come in, and make their Claims to any of the forfeited Estates, and other Interests, in Ireland, sold by the Trustees for Sale of those Estates, to the Governor and Company for making hollow Sword-blades in England, and divers other Purchasers, without any Amendment:

The Lords have also agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the further directing the Payment of the Equi* valent Money, without any Amendment:

The Lords have also agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing the Act for ascertaining the Tythes of Hemp and Flax, without any Amendment:

The Lords have agreed to the Amendments, made by this House to the Bill, intituled, An Act for settling and establishing a Court of Exchequer in the North Part of Great Britain called Scotland:

The Lords have also agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enable her Majesty to make Leases and Copies of Offices, Lands, and Hereditaments, Parcel of her Duchy of Cornwall, or annex'd to the fame, without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of the Brewers, Bakers, Grocers, Cheese- Copper mongers, Victualers, and divers other Inhabitants, of Coinage, the Borough of Southwark, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners are informed, some Persons are attempting to obtain a new Licence for a new Coinage of Half-pence and Farthings, tho' the Petitioners are already loaded with great Quantities thereof: And praying the Consideration of the House.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Message from her Majesty, by Mr. Afon, Deputy Royal A font Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her Majesty immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend her Majesty; where her Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to several publick and private Bills:

And to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses.

After which, the Lord Chancellor, by her Majesty's Command, prorogued the Parliament until the ProroS""*k
